commit.message:
[compiler] Allow setState after await in effect functions (#36734)

`react-hooks/set-state-in-effect` flagged setState calls that happen
after an `await` inside an async function invoked from an effect.
Post-await code resumes in a microtask after the effect body has
returned, so the "synchronous setState cascades a render" rationale does
not apply; the lint was a false positive on a common data-loading shape
(15 reactions on the issue).

The fix exempts a setState only when it is *provably* post-await: a
forward must-dataflow over the HIR CFG computes the blocks that begin
after an await has executed on every path from the function entry
(optimistic initialization so loop back-edges do not pessimize the meet,
fixpoint to the greatest solution), plus an intra-block flag for
instructions after an Await in the same block. A setState reachable on
any await-free path still flags, so the conditional-await case remains
an error by design, with a fixture documenting that choice. Suppression
is sound under try/catch because HIRBuilder terminates blocks after each
instruction in a try region, and an awaited rejection also resumes in a
microtask.

Fixtures: post-await setState (event gone), setState before the first
await (still flags), setState after a conditional await (still flags).
First commit documents the false positive via the lint-mode logger
output, second removes it.

Builds on the approach in #36417 by @raashish1601, hardened from a
seen-await flag to the path-sensitive analysis above. Implemented
identically in the TypeScript compiler and the Rust port.

Verification: TS snap 1807/1807, Rust snap 1807/1807, cargo workspace
green, scoped TS-vs-Rust HIR parity harness green.

Closes #34905

---------

Co-authored-by: Raashish Aggarwal <94279692+raashish1601@users.noreply.github.com>

commit.message:
[Flight] Preserve leading `U+FEFF` in text rows (#37625)

The Flight client dropped a leading `U+FEFF` from outlined text rows
when it decoded binary input. `TextDecoder` consumed the character as an
encoding signature, even though it was part of the serialized string.
Both the Node and Web decoders now use `ignoreBOM: true` to preserve it.

Regression tests cover one and two leading U+FEFF characters with normal
chunks and with every UTF-8 byte delivered separately. They also include
an inline-string control. The global `TextDecoder` Flow declaration now
makes `fatal` optional and declares `ignoreBOM`, matching the API.

[XLA:GPU] Clamp per-dimension offsets in dynamic-slice analysis

HLO dynamic-slice and dynamic-update-slice clamp each dimension's start index
i to [0, dim_size[i] - slice_size[i]]. Previously, AnalyzeDynamicSlice and
VerifySliceOffset computed the 1D byte offset directly from unclamped start
indices, relying only on runtime 1D buffer clamping to [0, buffer_size -
slice_size]. When a slice is contiguous because all dimensions major to a
partially-sliced dimension have slice_size == 1, an out-of-bounds offset on a
minor dimension or size-1 dimension could stay within the total buffer bounds
and write or read at the wrong element offset.

Clamp constant offset operands per-dimension in AnalyzeDynamicSlice and
VerifySliceOffset, and for loop-dependent offsets verify that the runtime 1D
buffer clamping matches the per-dimension clamped HLO byte offset on every loop
iteration. Also preserve the sliced operand shape before walking through
bitcasts in DynamicSliceFusion::ResolveParameter so Parameter.shape matches the
slice rank and strides in ComputeSliceOffset.

Fixes #49120

Fix lifetime issues in `ExecutionWatchdogScope` async callbacks.

When `block_host_until_done` is false, `~ExecutionWatchdogScope()` releases the `HangWatchdog::Guard` asynchronously via `stream_->DoHostCallback(...)`, so the guard and its `on_timeout` and `pre_abort` callbacks outlive `ExecutionWatchdogScope` and `GpuExecutable::ExecuteThunks()`.

- Separate `ThunkExecutor::ProgressTracker` from `ThunkExecutor::ScopedProgressTracker` via `std::shared_ptr` so `pre_abort` in `GpuExecutable::ExecuteThunksImpl()` captures `tracker->tracker()` by value while `ScopedProgressTracker` remains a stack-local move-only RAII guard that uninstalls the thread-local pointer when leaving the dispatch scope.

[XLA] Disambiguate `kFusion` instructions in `HloCSE` `CseKey` hash based on the fused computation

Previously, `CseKey::AbslHashValue` in `HloCSE` fell into the `default:` branch for `HloOpcode::kFusion`, only hashing the top-level operands, output dimensions, and the fused computation's root opcode. As a result, distinct `kFusion` instructions sharing operands, output shape, and root opcode collided in `HloCSE`'s `representatives` hash table and triggered expensive `HloFusionInstruction::IdenticalSlowPath` (`HloComputation::Equal`) comparisons.

This change factors out `CseKey::HashInstruction` and applies it to the internal instructions of `instruction->fused_instructions_computation()` (in post-order from `root_instruction()`) when hashing a `kFusion` instruction, skipping operand `unique_id()`s for internal instructions so equivalent `kFusion` instructions continue to hash identically while distinct fused computations are disambiguated.

PR #49007: [XLA:GPU] Rewrite FP8 convolutions in all computations of a module

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49007

### 📝 Summary of Changes

`CudnnFusedConvRewriter::RunImpl` iterates over the non-fusion computations of a module and, for each of them, first runs `F8GraphConv`. If `F8GraphConv` rewrote anything, the function returned immediately, so the loop never reached the remaining computations. Any FP8 convolution in a later computation was left as a plain convolution: it got neither the `__cudnn$convForwardGraph` rewrite nor the bias/activation fusions, and the FP8 fallback later demoted it to a legacy non-FP8 `__cudnn$convForward` call.

This change replaces the early `return` with `any_changed |= changed; continue;`. The `continue` keeps the existing behaviour for the rewritten computation (the remaining fusions only match the legacy conv custom calls and do not apply to graph convolutions), and the loop now processes every computation of the module.

### 🎯 Justification

Hit in practice with JAX 0.10.2 on an RTX 5070 (sm_120, CUDA 12.9, cuDNN 9.24). A `jit` for MCTS self-play evaluates an FP8 convolutional network once in the entry computation and again inside a `lax.while_loop` body. Only one of the two copies was rewritten: the compiled HLO contained 20 `__cudnn$convForwardGraph` calls instead of 40, and the other 20 convolutions ran as legacy f32 convolutions. With this change all 40 are FP8 graph convolutions. Which copy loses depends on the computation order, so the workaround was to keep one copy out of FP8 entirely.

Minimal JAX repro (same FP8 convolution in the entry computation and in a while body):

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import lax

def conv(x, w):
    return lax.conv_general_dilated(x, w, (1, 1), "SAME",
                                    dimension_numbers=("NHWC", "HWIO", "NHWC"),
                                    preferred_element_type=jnp.float32)

@jax.jit
def f(x, w):
    y0 = conv(x, w) # entry computation
    def body(c):
        i, y = c
        return i + 1, y + conv(y.astype(jnp.float8_e4m3fn), w) # while body
    return lax.while_loop(lambda c: c[0] < 4, body, (0, y0))[1]

x = jnp.ones((1, 6, 6, 128), jnp.float8_e4m3fn)
w = jnp.ones((3, 3, 128, 128), jnp.float8_e4m3fn)
hlo = f.lower(x, w).compile().as_text()
print(hlo.count('custom_call_target="__cudnn$convForwardGraph"'),
      hlo.count('custom_call_target="__cudnn$convForward"'))
```

Before this change (jax-cuda12-pjrt 0.10.2): `1 1` (one graph convolution, one legacy convolution). With this change (plugin rebuilt from the same JAX release with the patched XLA): `2 0`.

### 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

### 🧪 Unit Tests

`CudnnFusedConvRewriterTest.TestConvF8InMultipleComputations` in `cudnn_fused_conv_rewriter_test.cc`. The module has two `conditional` branches, each with an FP8 convolution on a different filter. After `ConvRewriter` and `CudnnFusedConvRewriter` (run with a Hopper compute capability, like the existing F8 tests on pre-FP8 hardware) both branch computations must contain a `__cudnn$convForwardGraph` custom call. Without the fix only the first branch visited is rewritten and the test fails on the second one.

### 🧪 Execution Tests

On FP8-capable GPUs the same test additionally compiles the module through the full pipeline, checks with FileCheck that both convolutions are `__cudnn$convForwardGraph` and no legacy `__cudnn$convForward` remains, and compares the result against the interpreter (`RunAndCompare`, `ErrorSpec{0.15, 0.15}`).

Tested locally on an RTX 5070 (sm_120) with the hermetic CUDA toolchain (cuDNN 9.12): `bazel test //xla/backends/gpu/transforms:cudnn_fused_conv_rewriter_test_nvgpu_any --test_filter='*TestConvF8InMultipleComputations*:*.TestConvF8:*TestConvScaledOutputF8'` passes (the new test runs the full-pipeline branch: `fp8_supported: true`). With the test but without the change in `cudnn_fused_conv_rewriter.cc` the new test fails as intended: `branch_b` keeps the legacy `__cudnn$convForward` custom call.

PR #49155: [XLA:GPU] Preserve async ordering across command buffer boundaries

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49155

## 📝 Summary of Changes

Command buffer conversion can split an async region and, in doing so, lose the ordering between operations queued on the same async stream.

An async start/done pair runs its body on an async stream and joins it back to the main stream at the done. When a region cannot be captured (for example a collective that is disabled for command buffers), the pass still captured any convertible region nested inside it. That moves the nested body into a graph launched on the main stream, where nothing waits for the outer operation that is still running on the async stream.

Notation: `CB{...}` is the set of thunks captured into one command buffer; minimum graph size is 1.

**Example 1, nested pair on the same stream.** `A` and `B` both run on async stream `S`, so `A` must finish before `B` starts. `A` cannot be captured; `B` and the ordinary main-stream command `C` can.

```text
Input:   Start(A); Start(B); C; Done(B); Done(A)
Before:  Start(A); CB{Start(B); C; Done(B)}; Done(A)
After:   Start(A); Start(B); CB{C}; Done(B); Done(A)
```

Before, `B`'s body moves into the graph on the main stream, which has no wait for `A` to complete. After, `B` stays on stream `S` and `A → B` is preserved, while `C` still benefits from capture.

**Example 2, nested pair on a different stream (unchanged).** Same shape, but `B` runs on stream `T`. `B`'s body only ever waited on the main stream, never on `S`, so capturing it loses no ordering. The fix is scoped to the stream of the outstanding operation, so this case keeps the behaviour it has today. The same holds after an unmatched start such as a pipelined recv: only its own stream is affected.

```text
Input:   Start(A on S); Start(B on T); C; Done(B); Done(A)
Before:  Start(A); CB{Start(B); C; Done(B)}; Done(A)
After:   Start(A); CB{Start(B); C; Done(B)}; Done(A)
```

**Example 3, loop body joining an outer operation.** `A` cannot be captured; its done sits inside a loop body together with `C`, which reads `A`'s result. With `WHILE` enabled, the body alone looks convertible.

```text
Input:   Start(A); While{ Done(A); C }
Before:  Start(A); CB{ While{ Done(A); C } }
After:   Start(A); While{ Done(A); CB{C} }
```

Inside a graph the done is a no-op, so before this change `C` could run before `A` finishes. After, the done stays a thunk and only `C` is captured.

This affects partially convertible workloads, such as compute overlapped with collectives that are disabled for command buffers.

Part 1 of 3: #49158 moves LHS dependency construction into the emitter; #48900 then preserves async fork/join ordering inside captured command buffers.

c015dcb95f89e46df503008a3de0333867b60dd7 by prasanna8585 <65734642+prasanna8585@users.noreply.github.com>:

Fix unguarded int overflow in ShardingParam and validate on deserialize

ShardingParam::MinorToMajor::ToDeviceList computed a cumulative axis
size product using 32-bit int with no overflow protection
(cum_size *= size), and ShardingParam::verify() computed a dimension-
shard product the same unguarded way, then used it as a modulo
divisor (NumDevices() % total_dim_shards_size) -- if the product
wraps to exactly 0, this is a division by zero.

Confirmed via a faithful standalone extraction of both arithmetic
patterns, compiled with UBSan+ASan: both overflow with individually
plausible input values, and the verify() case produces a real SIGFPE
crash when the product wraps to 0.

Separately, ShardingParam::FromProto never called verify() at all, so
a deserialized ShardingParam (e.g. via
xla/python/ifrt_proxy/server/ifrt_backend.cc's handling of
MakeArraysFromHostBufferShards/Assemble requests) was never validated
before its axis_sizes/dim_shards were used downstream.

This adds an overflow-safe int64_t accumulation with an explicit
range check in verify(), calls verify() from FromProto so deserialized
input is actually validated, and hardens ToDeviceList to fail closed
(CHECK) rather than silently propagate a wrapped value into device-
index computation, on the assumption that verify() should have already
caught it upstream.

[XLA:GPU] Remove side-effecting heroes in DynamicSliceFusionRewriterV2

When `RewriteHero` replaces downstream `dynamic-update-slice` or
`get-tuple-element` instructions rather than the `hero` instruction directly,
`HloComputation::ReplaceInstruction` invokes
`RemoveInstructionAndUnusedOperands` on the downstream instruction. Because
`RemoveInstructionAndUnusedOperands` skips upstream operands that have side
effects (`item->HasSideEffect() && item != instruction`), a side-effecting hero
(such as an FFI custom-call with `custom_call_has_side_effect=true`) and its
sliced operand chain remain alive in the parent computation alongside the newly
created `dynamic_slice_fusion`, causing the side-effecting custom-call to
execute twice.

Transfer control dependencies from `hero` to `fusion` and explicitly invoke
`RemoveInstructionAndUnusedOperands(hero)` when `hero` has side effects and is
not directly replaced. Also check user counts in `ResolveLeafDus` and
`ResolveNonTupleSlicedResult` (and ensure tuple heroes only have unique GTE
users in `HasSupportedShapes`) so DUS chains are only absorbed when the
hero/GTE has a single user, preventing duplicate heroes when external users
exist.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 986687589

[XLA:GPU]: Allow CUFunction in Record API

Record runs after Prepare -> Initialize.

The following events can happen given 2 GPUs within the same process.
TS1. Thread0 (Host) queues a collective kernel on Gpu0. Asynchronously.
     Gpu0 kernel (device) blocks on GPU1 to also execute the corresponding
     collective on Gpu1.
TS2. Thread0 Records a kernal (with FFI). Calls cuModuleLoad and acquires driver
     mutex. However loading cannot finish until Gpu0 (device) is free. So it
     waits.
TS3. Thread1 which lags a bit behind Thread0 calls cuLaunchKernel but blocks
     because the driver lock was taken during TS2. Collective kernel is never
     launched and GPU0 (TS1) keeps waiting.

To prevent this deadlock we must allow FFI users to load kernels during
preparation. Since not all FFI users can use se::Kernel API for loading we can
allow using a function pointer that was loaded and cached by the FFI user
so cuModuleLoad is not called anymore during the record phase.

Note that this problem only exists for users running single process across multiple GPUs.

Reject nouter that doesn't fit in int32 before bounds-check kernel

The bounds-check kernel packs each violation's position into an int32
buffer via GpuAtomicMin. If Index is int64_t and nouter exceeded
INT32_MAX, a position beyond INT32_MAX would truncate to a negative
value when narrowed, which would then be used as a negative pointer
offset when fetching the offending value for the error message.

Guard against this the same way SparseSegmentGradV2Functor already
does for its own nouter/ninner (this file, above): reject the input
with a clear error instead of proceeding with a value that doesn't fit.

Address review: guard nouter==0 and avoid full-array D2H copies

- Wrap the GPU validation logic in `if (nouter > 0)` so it no longer
  reads segment_vec[-1] when indices_vec is empty.
- Replace the synchronous full-array copy of `indices`/`segment_ids` to
  the host with a device-side bounds-check kernel that scans both
  arrays in parallel and records only the position of a violation (if
  any) via GpuAtomicMin into a 2-element int32 buffer. Only that tiny
  buffer is transferred back to the host in the common (valid-input)
  case; the actual offending value is fetched with one additional
  single-element copy only when a violation was actually found, to
  build the error message.

Addresses review feedback from @dmiltr3.

Fix out-of-bounds access in GPU SparseSegment*Grad kernels

SparseSegmentGradFunctor<GPUDevice, ...> (used by SparseSegmentSumGrad,
SparseSegmentMeanGrad, and SparseSegmentSqrtNGrad on GPU) never validated
its `indices` and `segment_ids` inputs before using them to read/write
device memory. The CPU functor bounds-checks every value against the
output-row count and the incoming gradient's row count before using it,
returning InvalidArgumentError on failure; the GPU path had no equivalent
check, so a malformed or out-of-range index caused an out-of-bounds
device read/write, typically surfacing as a fatal
`cudaErrorIllegalAddress` abort that also corrupts the CUDA context for
the rest of the process.

Add the missing validation to the GPU functor by copying the (typically
small) `indices`/`segment_ids` arrays to the host and replicating the
same checks and error messages the CPU functor already uses. Several
existing tests for this were already restricted to `use_gpu=False`
specifically to avoid the crash; this removes that restriction so they
now exercise the fixed GPU path directly.

Fixes #113146.

PR #49146: [XLA:CPU] Replace strict-aliasing-violating type punning with absl::bit_cast

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49146

## [XLA:CPU] Replace strict-aliasing-violating type punning with absl::bit_cast

### Problem
In `onednn_ops_rewriter.cc` and `onednn_op_thunk_test.cc`, converting the IEEE-754 bit representation of `float` epsilon to an `int32_t` config field used pointer-dereference type-punning (`*reinterpret_cast<int32_t*>(&eps)`). Dereferencing an aliased pointer of an incompatible type violates the C++ strict aliasing rule ([basic.lval]), which is undefined behavior and risks miscompilations under aggressive optimization levels.

### Solution
Replace the pointer type-puns with `absl::bit_cast<int32_t>(...)`. This preserves the exact IEEE-754 bit pattern without numeric conversion while adhering strictly to standard aliasing rules.

### Changes
- `xla/service/cpu/onednn_ops_rewriter.cc`: Include `absl/base/casts.h` and use `absl::bit_cast<int32_t>(eps)`.
- `xla/service/cpu/BUILD`: Add `@com_google_absl//absl/base:casts` to `onednn_ops_rewriter` deps.
- `xla/backends/cpu/runtime/onednn/onednn_op_thunk_test.cc`: Include `absl/base/casts.h` and use `absl::bit_cast<int32_t>(epsilon)`.
- `xla/backends/cpu/runtime/onednn/BUILD`: Add `@com_google_absl//absl/base:casts` to `onednn_op_thunk_test` deps.

### Testing
- `git diff --check`: Passed with no whitespace or syntax formatting issues.
- Verified exact 4-file diff matches project include and dependency conventions.

### Risk
Low risk. Behavior-preserving change that preserves identical bit-level values while removing undefined behavior.

PR #47282: [XLA:TSL] Fix silent truncation of ZlibOutputBuffer appends larger than 4 GiB

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/47282

## 📝 Summary of Changes

`ZlibOutputBuffer::Append` passes data that does not fit in the staging buffer directly to zlib by assigning the `size_t` byte count to `z_stream::avail_in`, which is zlib's 32-bit `uInt`. A single `Append` of 4 GiB or more is truncated to `size % 2^32` bytes: the write reports OK, `Close()` produces a well-formed gzip stream, and everything past the truncated count is silently lost.

This change chunks the direct-deflate path so zlib is fed at most `uInt` max bytes per round, and adds a round-trip regression test that appends 4 GiB + 1 MiB in one call. The test lives in its own `size = "large"` target (`zlib_buffers_large_append_test`) because it needs ~4 GiB of memory for the input string; the existing `zlib_buffers_test` stays `small`.

This completes the fix started in 783463ddeb, which addressed the size comparisons but not the `avail_in` assignment (see the reporter's follow-up in the issue).

## 🎯 Justification

Fixes #28159: profiling a large workload makes `jax.profiler.stop_trace()` write the whole Chrome-trace JSON through one `Append` call in `WriteGzippedDataToFile` (`xla/tsl/profiler/rpc/client/save_profile.cc`); above 4 GiB the resulting `<host>.trace.json.gz` decompresses to a truncated JSON document. Fixing `Append` itself (rather than chunking in `save_profile.cc`) also covers the other users of this class (`record_writer`, `xla/service/dump.cc`).

Reproduced at HEAD: appending 2^32 + 2^20 bytes produced a file that decompresses to exactly 2^20 bytes (`size % 2^32`).

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

🐛 Bug Fix

## 🧪 Unit Tests:

- New target `//xla/tsl/lib/io:zlib_buffers_large_append_test` (`size = "large"`, ~4 GiB peak RSS, 8 s at `Z_BEST_SPEED`): single 4 GiB + 1 MiB `Append`, round-tripped through `ZlibInputStream` with full content verification and an end-of-stream check. Fails before this change (first read hits `OUT_OF_RANGE: EOF reached` - the file decompresses to exactly `size % 2^32` = 1 MiB), passes after.
- All 13 test targets in `//xla/tsl/lib/io/...` pass with the change.
- For appends below 4 GiB the loop runs exactly one iteration with the same zlib call sequence as before, so existing behavior is unchanged (covered by the existing round-trip tests, which exercise the direct-deflate branch with data larger than the staging buffer).

## 🧪 Execution Tests:

Not applicable (host-side I/O library; no device execution involved).

📝 Summary of Changes

Fixes #49005.

Fix `IsTopKIndexOutputUsed` so that returning either the complete TopK `(values, indices)` tuple or just its `indices` element as the computation result counts as using the indices.

The check now recognizes a root TopK custom call and uses `!IsDead()` for the `get-tuple-element` instruction that extracts the indices. This preserves the values-only optimization for truly unused indices.

[XLA:GPU] Fix Triton codegen for scans with a tiled scan dimension.

When the scan dimension is tiled, the scan is emitted inside an `scf.for` loop
and the carry of each tile becomes the init of the next one. That carry never
compiled:

*   `LowerScan::ExtractCarries` extracted the last element along the scan
    dimension with a `tensor.extract_slice`, which has no lowering to the
    TritonGPU dialect.
*   For 1D scans, the rank-reduced carry and therefore the `scf.for` `iter_arg`
    was a rank-zero tensor, which is illegal in TritonGPU
    (`BlockedEncodingAttr::get` asserts rank >= 1).

Instead of rank-reducing the scan dimension, the inits and carries of
`xtile.scan` now keep it as a unit dimension and have the same rank as the scan
inputs and outputs. Carries are therefore never rank-zero, and the init is
broadcast over the tile with a `tt.broadcast`, both without any reshapes. A new
`xtile.scan` verifier enforces this.

`tt.scan` does not return the final carry, so it has to be extracted from the
scan output. Gathering it with a `tt.gather` would write the entire tile to
shared memory. Instead, mask all other elements to zero and select the
remaining one with an `or` reduction over the bitcast integer values, which is
exact because zero is the neutral element of `or`. This is the established
pattern for tiled Triton scans, see `triton_helpers.select_one` in PyTorch
inductor and proger/accelerated-scan. It reduces the shared memory of the added
tiled scan tests from 1024 to 16 bytes (1D) and from 4096 to 128 bytes (2D),
and lowers to a single `redux.sync.or.b32` per warp on sm_80 and later.

Also fix `GetDimsToSqueeze`, which keeps one unit dimension by popping the last
entry when all dimensions have size one. For a rank-zero tensor there is no
entry to pop and it read past the end of the `SmallVector`.

None of this was caught because the only scan test reaching the emitter tiled
the whole scan into a single tile, so the carry was dead and got eliminated.
Add tests that check the emitted IR and the numerics of tiled scans.

Suppress @com_google_absl//absl/strings:string_view findings in run_dwyu.py.

`@com_google_absl//absl/strings` exports `string_view.h` in hdrs, so Bazel's layering_check allows including `absl/strings/string_view.h` when `@com_google_absl//absl/strings` is in deps.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 985142787

Share custom kernel binaries between kernel loader specs.

`KernelReuseCache` deduplicates kernel *compilation*, but every consumer deep
copies the compiled binary out of the cache entry, because
`CreateOwnedCubinCustomKernel` takes the CUBIN by value. A module that invokes
the same kernel N times therefore keeps N copies of its CUBIN in memory, and the
Triton fusion emitter copies it twice, because `TritonFusion::EmitResult` holds
the cache entry by value.

Add reference counted `SharedCudaCubinInMemory` and `SharedCudaPtxInMemory`
payloads to `se::KernelLoaderSpec`, keep `KernelReuseCache::Entry::binary` in a
`std::shared_ptr`, and switch the three cached emitter call sites to the new
`CreateSharedCubinCustomKernel` factory. `KernelLoaderSpec` remains a value type
and its accessors keep handing out non-owning views, so every reader - including
`ToProto` - is unaffected. The two emitters that have no cache keep the owning
factory, since they have nothing to share with.

The serialized representation is unchanged; this only removes redundant copies
in memory. Deduplicating the serialized form follows in a later change.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 984990786

Fix tnp.sinc gradient at zero

`tf.experimental.numpy.sinc` evaluates `sin(pi_x) / pi_x` and selects away
from it at `x == 0` with `where`. That discarded branch is 0/0 there, and
`where` still propagates its gradient (0 * nan is nan), so the gradient at
zero came out as `nan` instead of `0`.

Substituting 1 for the denominator in the discarded branch leaves the
forward values bit-for-bit identical (the branch is never selected) while
making it finite, so its contribution is scaled to exactly 0.

Adds a regression test that fails before the change and passes after.

[XLA] Make the LICM size inflation check linear in the loop state width

The size inflation check in WhileLoopInvariantCodeMotion ran before the
invariance test. Every get-tuple-element of an N element loop state therefore
walked the whole tuple shape: Theta(N^2) per loop per run. Test invariance
first, so those get-tuple-elements are rejected before any shape is walked.

unchanged. Also skip the post order for the domain bail out scan and build the
while instruction's debug string only when VLOG reads it. Adds tests for the
ratio decision, tuple operand leaf counting and the linear shape size call
count.

[SPARK-58966][SQL] Resolve SQL variables in UPDATE and MERGE INTO conditions

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

SQL variables declared with `DECLARE` cannot be referenced in the conditions of an
`UPDATE` or `MERGE INTO` statement. This passes `includeLastResort = true` at the nine
condition-resolution sites that make up those clauses, matching what SPARK-57260 did for
`OverwriteByExpression.deleteExpr`.

Variable resolution only runs from `resolveColsLastResort`, which is reached when
`resolveExpressionByPlanOutput` / `resolveExpressionByPlanChildren` are called with
`includeLastResort = true`. Both default the flag to `false`. Plans with no dedicated
resolution rule fall through to the generic operator case in `ResolveReferences`, which
does pass the flag -- which is why `DELETE ... WHERE` already works. `UPDATE` and
`MERGE INTO` each have a dedicated rule that omitted it:

- `UPDATE` condition (`ResolveReferencesInUpdate`)
- `MERGE` `ON` condition
- `MERGE` `WHEN MATCHED` `DELETE` / `UPDATE` conditions
- `MERGE` `UPDATE *` condition
- `MERGE` `WHEN NOT MATCHED` `INSERT` / `INSERT *` conditions
- `MERGE` `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE` `DELETE` / `UPDATE` conditions

This covers every `MergeAction` condition form, so all `MERGE` conditions now resolve
variables consistently.

Assignment values (`SET col = var`, `INSERT VALUES (var)`) are affected by the same root
cause, but they resolve through `resolveExprInAssignment`, which sets
`includeLastResort = false` explicitly rather than by default. That is left unchanged
here pending a decision on whether the explicit `false` was deliberate, so this PR is
scoped to conditions only.

### Why are the changes needed?

Variables resolve in `SELECT`, `INSERT` (including `REPLACE WHERE`) and `DELETE`, but in
no condition of `UPDATE` or `MERGE INTO`, which fails analysis with:

```
[UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION] A column, variable, or function parameter with
name `target_dep` cannot be resolved. SQLSTATE: 42703
```

The message itself offers "A column, variable, or function parameter", so the analyzer
reports that variable resolution was attempted. Nothing in `error-conditions.json`, the
tests, or the docs records a restriction here. Where Spark does intentionally block
variables (SPARK-57360, generated columns) it uses an explicit validation and a dedicated
error class, so the inconsistency looks like an oversight rather than a deliberate
limitation.

This affects both session variables and SQL scripting local variables.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, a bug fix.

Before, against a table using the built-in DSv2 row-level operation framework:

```sql
DECLARE OR REPLACE VARIABLE target_dep STRING DEFAULT 'hr';
UPDATE cat.ns1.test_table SET salary = 0 WHERE dep = target_dep;
-- [UNRESOLVED_COLUMN.WITH_SUGGESTION] ... `target_dep` cannot be resolved. SQLSTATE: 42703
```

After, the statement analyzes and executes, resolving `target_dep` to the declared
variable. Statements that previously succeeded are unaffected: the flag only enables a
last-resort resolution step that runs after normal column resolution fails, so column
references continue to take precedence over same-named variables.

### How was this patch tested?

Six new tests, plus a shared `withSessionVariable` helper in
`RowLevelOperationSuiteBase`:

- `UpdateTableSuiteBase` -- a session variable and a SQL scripting local variable in an
  `UPDATE` condition.
- `MergeIntoTableSuiteBase` -- a variable in the `MERGE` `ON` condition, in the
  `WHEN MATCHED` / `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE` conditions, and in the
  `WHEN NOT MATCHED` `INSERT` and `INSERT *` conditions.

Each test was verified to fail without the fix (raising `UNRESOLVED_COLUMN`) and to pass
with it. The not-matched tests keep a source row that the variable predicate excludes, so
they fail if the variable is resolved but evaluated incorrectly, not just if resolution
fails.

Suites run: `GroupBasedUpdateTableSuite`, `GroupBasedMergeIntoTableSuite`,
`DeltaBasedUpdateTableSuite` and `DeltaBasedMergeIntoTableSuite` -- 289 tests, all
passing. Reverting only the `Analyzer` change makes the two not-matched tests fail with
`UNRESOLVED_COLUMN` on the variable in the `insertaction` condition.

[SPARK-59774][SQL] Warn once, and name the remedy, when a whole-stage codegen method is too long to be JIT compiled

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`CodeCompiler.computeByteCodeStats` logs, at INFO, every generated method whose bytecode is past HotSpot's JIT limit of 8000 bytes (`CodeGenerator.DEFAULT_JVM_HUGE_METHOD_LIMIT`). This PR raises that line to WARN in the one case where it costs the user and they can act on it, and only the first time, on the driver. All of these must hold:

- the method belongs to a whole-stage codegen stage (`GeneratedIteratorForCodegenStage*`);
- it runs per row, not once (not `<init>`, `<clinit>` or `init`);
- the stage keeps whole-stage codegen: the method is at or below `spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit`, so the stage does not fall back;
- the JVM leaves huge methods to the interpreter: `-XX:+DontCompileHugeMethods`, read through `Utils.getVMOptionValue`;
- the method is compiled on the driver, not by a task: the driver compiles each stage before its tasks do.

Every other report, including every one after the first WARN, keeps the existing INFO line unchanged.

Before:
```
INFO CodeGenerator: Generated method too long to be JIT compiled: <class>.<method> is 9513 bytes
```
After, the first time on the driver:
```
WARN CodeGenerator: Generated method too long to be JIT compiled: <class>.processNext is 9513 bytes, so it runs interpreted on every row. Setting spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit to 8000 runs such stages without whole-stage codegen instead. Further methods over the limit are logged at INFO.
```

### Why are the changes needed?

HotSpot does not JIT-compile a method past 8000 bytes (`-XX:+DontCompileHugeMethods`, on by default), so the method runs interpreted, typically several times slower. On stock Spark 4.2.0, widening a projection's consume method from 7945 to 8677 bytes steps it from about 770 to about 4100 ns a row. Spark detects this, but only at INFO. `spark-shell` and `pyspark` run at WARN and never show it, and `spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit`, which could act on it, defaults to 65535, which no compiled method exceeds.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, in the log only: at most one WARN, from the driver, and only in the case above. Everything else is unchanged.

### How was this patch tested?

A new test in `CodeGenerationSuite` covers each case: a stage that falls back, the run-once methods, a class outside whole-stage codegen, a compile under a `TaskContext`, the first WARN (which names the setting and 8000), and INFO afterwards. The SPARK-25113 test asserts that a projection's huge method is still logged at INFO.
```
build/sbt "catalyst/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.expressions.CodeGenerationSuite -- -z SPARK-25113 -z SPARK-59774"
```

[SPARK-59673][SQL] Floor the NAAJ broadcast threshold

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

For a nonnegative `spark.sql.optimizeNullAwareAntiJoin.broadcastThreshold`, this PR allows the
specialized null-aware broadcast hash join when either the dedicated threshold or the applicable
automatic broadcast threshold admits the right side. Regular planning uses
`spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` for runtime statistics when it is set, and
`spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` otherwise. A negative dedicated threshold remains
unlimited.

Threshold eligibility is evaluated before join hints, matching the existing precedence of the
dedicated threshold. Hints affect the fallback only when the specialized NAAJ is not eligible.
The same shared eligibility decision intentionally controls aggregate pushdown: the optimizer
uses estimated statistics before adaptive execution, while join selection may reevaluate the
decision with runtime statistics.

### Why are the changes needed?

If the dedicated NAAJ threshold is lower than the automatic broadcast threshold, it can reject the
specialized null-aware broadcast hash join even though automatic join planning will broadcast the
right side. That fallback uses a nested-loop representation and changes hash lookup from
`O(M + N)` to `O(M * N)` without avoiding the broadcast.

Using the applicable automatic threshold as a floor avoids that regression while preserving the
dedicated threshold as a way to allow the specialized NAAJ above the automatic threshold.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, on unreleased branches and for an internal configuration. A nonnegative dedicated NAAJ
threshold can no longer disable the specialized hash optimization for inputs admitted by the
applicable automatic broadcast threshold.

To disable the specialized optimization without changing automatic broadcast thresholds, set
`spark.sql.optimizeNullAwareAntiJoin=false`. A negative dedicated threshold does not disable the
optimization; it makes the threshold unlimited.

### How was this patch tested?

The patch is covered by the following focused suites:

```
build/sbt \
  "catalyst/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.optimizer.JoinSelectionHelperSuite" \
  "catalyst/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.optimizer.LeftSemiAntiJoinPushDownSuite" \
  "sql/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.JoinSuite -- -z SPARK-36082"
```

The latest local rerun was blocked before compilation because the isolated environment could not
resolve the updated SBT plugins. Whitespace, changed-line length, and non-ASCII checks passed. The
focused suites will run in GitHub Actions.

[SPARK-59685][SQL] Keep clause-free SQL/JSON constructor canonical SQL bound to the built-in

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Since SPARK-59144, a clause-free SQL/JSON function call routes through function resolution, so a same-named routine on the SQL PATH can shadow the built-in. However these built-ins' canonical `sql` omits default clauses, so a call that is a built-in only because of a default clause renders as clause-free SQL; reparsing that under a shadowing PATH binds the routine instead of the built-in.

This PR renders the default clause (`RETURNING STRING`, or `FALSE ON ERROR` for `JSON_EXISTS`) in canonical `sql` so the rendering reparses back to the built-in. A shared `RoutedSqlJsonExpression` trait lets `usePrettyExpression` keep rendering the clean clause-free form for auto-generated column names (which are never reparsed), so display names stay unaffected.

### Why are the changes needed?

Without this, a canonical-SQL round-trip (e.g. persisting and reloading a view) can silently rebind a built-in SQL/JSON function to a user routine that shadows it on the SQL PATH, changing results.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, within unreleased master only. Canonical SQL of a clause-free SQL/JSON constructor now includes its default clause. Auto-generated column names are unchanged -- both top-level and nested (children are rendered in place, so a nested constructor's name gains no synthetic `FORMAT JSON`).

### How was this patch tested?

New unit tests in `JsonValueSuite` / `JsonQuerySuite` / `JsonExistsSuite` / `JsonArraySuite`: each asserts a default-clause constructor's canonical SQL reparses to the built-in under a shadowing PATH (including the zero-arg `JSON_ARRAY()` case), that the emitted SQL round-trips and evaluates correctly, and that top-level and nested auto-generated column names stay clean. No golden-file changes.

[SPARK-59765][SQL][TEST] Generate broadcast joins in full when measuring benchmark query codegen

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`BenchmarkQueryTest.checkGeneratedCode` and `WholeStageCodegenSizeBenchmark` measure the code whole-stage codegen generates for the TPC-DS (and TPC-H, SSB) queries without running them. They plan each query over empty tables with AQE disabled and call `doCodeGen()` on every `WholeStageCodegenExec`. With AQE disabled, `BroadcastHashJoinExec` executes its broadcast while generating code. Over an empty table the relation is `EmptyHashedRelation`, and `HashJoin` then generates a one-line stub instead of the join ("If HashedRelation is empty, hash inner join simply returns nothing"), so the rest of the stage is not generated either. Both instruments therefore measure stubs for every stage with a broadcast join. On master, with the benchmark's setup, 324 of the 2201 stages of the TPC-DS v1.4 and v2.7 queries carry the stub, in 127 of the 129 queries.

This PR generates each stage's code from a copy of the stage in which every broadcast exchange, including one under a `ReusedExchangeExec`, reads one row of non-null default values instead of its child. The joins then generate the code they generate for data. Only the code of the copy is used: the build side is its own stage, found in and measured from the original plan, so the set of stages is unchanged.

- `BenchmarkQueryTest` gets a companion object with `withRowBroadcasts`, which builds the copy, and `generatedCode`, which returns every stage of a plan and its subqueries with its code. `generatedCode` follows an adaptive plan into its current plan and query stages, as `codegenStringSeq` does. The copy is built top down, so a build side is never copied before its exchange is replaced. One replacement per broadcast exchange of a plan is shared by every stage that reads it, so each one-row broadcast runs once. `withRowBroadcasts` fails if any broadcast hash or nested loop join of the copy reads anything but a one-row broadcast, so no join can generate its empty-build-side code unnoticed, whatever the join kind.
- `checkGeneratedCode` iterates `generatedCode(plan)` instead of its own walk.
- `WholeStageCodegenSizeBenchmark` measures through `generatedCode` in place of `codegenStringSeq`. It skips a query only when the query fails to plan. A failure while generating the code, or a query with no whole-stage-codegen subtree, fails the run instead of silently shrinking the totals. Its scaladoc says how broadcast joins are measured.
- The three results files are regenerated. The stage count is unchanged at 2247 and the largest method at 4962 bytes. The source code size grows by about 19% (21.37M to 25.42M characters), the summed per-stage largest method by about 11% (821K to 910K bytes), and the summed constant pool by about 6%.

A single row makes every join key unique, so a hash join generates its unique-key form; a join whose real build side repeats keys also has the loop over matches. That remaining difference is small next to a stub.

### Why are the changes needed?

The benchmark is the instrument for the SPARK-56908 umbrella, and it has understated the generated code of most TPC-DS queries. `checkGeneratedCode` checks stubs in the same way. `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite` already runs it with AQE disabled on master, and the other suites will once SPARK-59764 disables AQE for them.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Test and benchmark only.

### How was this patch tested?

By running the affected suites:
```
build/sbt "sql/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.execution.LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQueryWithStatsSuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQueryANSISuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCHQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.SSBQuerySuite"
```
All six passed, 635 tests, in 48 seconds. No stage generated in full crosses the 8000-byte limit.

As a negative check, with the replacement of broadcast exchanges disabled, 145 of the 150 tests of `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite` fail with `a broadcast hash join reads ..., not a one-row broadcast`. That suite already runs the check with AQE disabled on master, so this is the bug there today.

The results files were generated with `SPARK_GENERATE_BENCHMARK_FILES=1`, running the benchmark's `main` under JDK 17, 21 and 25 in turn. The benchmark measures code sizes, not time, so the machine does not matter. A JDK 25 run through sbt matched the direct run within about 0.01%, the same run-to-run variation the committed files already show between JDKs.

[SPARK-59764][SQL][TEST] Check generated code of benchmark queries with AQE disabled

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`BenchmarkQueryTest.checkGeneratedCode` is meant to check that every whole-stage codegen subtree of a benchmark query compiles, and that its largest generated method is within HotSpot's `HugeMethodLimit` (8000 bytes). It walks `sql(query).queryExecution.executedPlan` without running the query. Since adaptive query execution became the default (SPARK-33679, 3.2.0), that plan is an `AdaptiveSparkPlanExec`, whose `WholeStageCodegenExec` subtrees are created only when the query runs. So the walk finds none, and `TPCDSQuerySuite` (with `TPCDSQueryWithStatsSuite` and `TPCDSQueryANSISuite`), `TPCHQuerySuite` and `SSBQuerySuite` pass without compiling or checking anything. Only `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite`, which disabled AQE itself, kept running the check.

This PR:
1. Mixes `DisableAdaptiveExecutionSuite` into `BenchmarkQueryTest`, so the plans these suites check have their whole-stage codegen subtrees. It also mixes in `QueryTest` explicitly, and drops the now redundant mixin from `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite`.
2. Makes `checkGeneratedCode` fail if it finds no `WholeStageCodegenExec` subtree, or finds an `AdaptiveSparkPlanExec` anywhere in the plan or its subqueries, so the check cannot become vacuous again, entirely or in part, unnoticed.

The `spark.sql.readSideCharPadding=false` override in `TPCDSQuerySuite` and the `modified-q3` exclusion (SPARK-29128) are unchanged.

**Known limitation, not changed here.** The TPC tables these suites create are empty. With AQE off, `BroadcastHashJoinExec` executes its broadcast while generating code, gets `EmptyHashedRelation`, and generates a stub for an inner join and the rest of its stage (`HashJoin.codegenInner`). So stages with an inner broadcast hash join are still checked only in part. Fixing that needs non-empty tables, which changes more than this bug, and is better as a follow-up. The check also covers the non-adaptive plan shape only; covering AQE's runtime shapes would need executed plans over real data.

### Why are the changes needed?

The compile check and the method size check in these suites have not run since 3.2.0 except in `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite`, so a codegen regression in the TPC-DS, TPC-H or SSB queries would mostly not be caught.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Test-only change.

### How was this patch tested?

By running the affected suites:
```
build/sbt "sql/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQueryWithStatsSuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQueryANSISuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCHQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.SSBQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.execution.LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite"
```
All six suites passed, 635 tests, in 1 minute 12 seconds. Generating code with AQE off now runs the broadcasts of broadcast joins, which is part of that time.

As a negative check, with only the new assertion and without `DisableAdaptiveExecutionSuite`, all 22 tests of `TPCHQuerySuite` fail with `no WholeStageCodegenExec subtree found to check in the plan`, which is the bug this PR fixes.

[SPARK-59005][INFRA][FOLLOWUP] Suggest JIRA affects versions for unreleased major and minor releases

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Currently, the merge script's **Affects Version prompt has no default**. When it flags an affected-version mismatch, the committer must type the affected version manually, even when they want to use the same version they just selected for the fix.

For example, a merge into `master` and `branch-4.x`, with the latter targeting the upcoming `4.4.0` release, can produce:

- Affects Version currently in JIRA: `5.0.0`
- Fix Version selected in the merge script: `4.4.0`, unreleased

The selected fix version does not need to be recorded in JIRA yet. The script compares it with the recorded affected version and flags the mismatch.

**Current behavior:** there is no suggestion in the affects-version prompt. The committer must type `4.4.0`; pressing Enter skips the update.

```text
Enter comma-separated affects version(s) (blank to skip):
```

**With this PR:** the prompt offers `4.4.0` as a default, so the committer can press Enter to accept it.

```text
Enter comma-separated affects version(s) [4.4.0] (or 'skip'):
```

This is a follow-up to #58288 under SPARK-59005. The new default is offered only when the **earliest fix version is an unreleased `x.y.0` release**. If the earliest fix version is a patch release or has already been released, the prompt retains its current behavior: no default, and blank input skips the update.

The committer can enter a different version or type `skip` to leave the field unchanged. The existing append/overwrite/keep choices remain, with append as the default, so accepting the suggestion can add `4.4.0` while preserving `5.0.0`.

### Why are the changes needed?

For the example above, the committer currently has to type `4.4.0` manually. Offering it as an editable suggestion makes this correction easier.

[PR #58288](https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/58288) originally proposed deriving affected versions from fix versions. **In [my review](https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/58288#discussion_r3875010858), I suggested avoiding that default for patch backports**, because it could mark the corrective release as affected. In response, [the default was removed entirely](https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/58288#discussion_r3876097956).

**Example 1: A patch backport receives no default.**

Suppose the bug exists in released Spark `4.2.0`, but JIRA currently shows:

- Affects Version: `5.0.0`
- Fix Version: unset

The committer merges the fix into the development line and backports it to `branch-4.2`, targeting releases `4.4.0` and `4.2.1`.

The existing Fix Version prompt suggests:

```text
Enter comma-separated fix version(s) [4.4.0,4.2.1]:
```

After he/she accepts those fix versions, the script flags the affected-version mismatch. Because the earliest fix is a patch release, the Affects Version prompt still has no default. He/she types the version known to contain the bug:

```text
Enter comma-separated affects version(s) (blank to skip): 4.2.0
```

Here, `4.2.0` has the bug and `4.2.1` contains the fix. This preserves the protection requested in [my earlier review](https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/58288#discussion_r3875010858): pressing Enter must not automatically mark the corrective release as affected.

**Example 2: An unreleased major or minor release receives a default.**

Suppose the committer reproduces the bug in a `4.4.0-SNAPSHOT` build, but JIRA currently shows:

- Affects Version: `5.0.0`
- Fix Version: unset

He/she merges the fix into the development line for the upcoming `4.4.0` release.

The existing Fix Version prompt suggests:

```text
Enter comma-separated fix version(s) [4.4.0]:
```

After he/she accepts it, the script flags the affected-version mismatch.

```text
# Before this PR
Enter comma-separated affects version(s) (blank to skip): 4.4.0

# With this PR
Enter comma-separated affects version(s) [4.4.0] (or 'skip'):
```

Using `4.4.0` in both fields is reasonable here: the development build contained the bug, and the upcoming release will contain the fix.

[SPARK-58626][PYTHON][SQL] Optimize evaluating inputs to transpiled UDFs

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`_udf_param_N` in a transpiled option used to be replaced by a copy of the bound argument, so an
argument the body reads N times was evaluated N times. Each one is now a reference to the call's Nth
argument, the argument itself stays on the Python UDF node, and `ConvertToCatalyst` decides per call
what to do with it.

The rule: an argument the body reads more than once is computed once a row, or we don't transpile the
call at all.

However subsequent optimizations may decide to inline some deterministic expressions which will change this.

### Why are the changes needed?

Reading an argument twice evaluated it twice. That's wasted work for anything expensive and a potentiall incorrect for non-deterministic inputs.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes.

- Each argument a body reads is evaluated once a row, so a body reading a `rand()` argument twice sees
  one draw rather than two.
- A body that reads an expensive argument more than once runs as interpreted Python where no column
  fits, instead of lowering with the argument recomputed at each read.
- A call reading both sides of a non-inner join condition, with a parameter read more than once, keeps
  the Python UDF, which `ExtractPythonUDFFromJoinCondition` turns down
  (`UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE.PYTHON_UDF_IN_ON_CLAUSE`) -- the same result as with transpilation off.

### How was this patch tested?

`ConvertToCatalystSuite` for the plan shapes: one column per distinct argument, a column per call, one
column for a call sitting in two slots of one operator, per-argument placement, and the Python UDF kept
for each position that can't hold a column. Plus two for the walkers themselves: `substitute` leaving a
nested call's options alone, and a reference to an argument the call hasn't got being a classed error
rather than an unresolved node. Its helper runs `LogicalPlanIntegrity.validateOptimizedPlan` around
every case, and walks every operator for a dangling reference itself, since
`validateNoDanglingReferences` only ever looks at the root and the root is never the Project this
inserts.

`TranspiledUDFParameterSuite` for real plans: the grouping key's column, the `Aggregate` and lambda
fallbacks, an `Aggregate` whose only call sits in a subquery, the straddling non-inner join, a draw
above a `Join` keeping the join's condition -- at the child and again with a `select` in between -- and
a MERGE instruction condition where an argument that mods by zero only raises if the column is really
there.

`test_udf_transpile_unit.py` for values rather than plans: one evaluation per parameter, a draw per
call, the fallbacks, and `orderBy(u(rand()))`, `repartition(2, u(rand()))` and `groupBy(u(rand()))`,
which used to fail with `INVALID_UDF_PARAMETER_PLACEHOLDER_INDEX`.

[SPARK-59631][SQL] Preserve cached V1 time-travel snapshots after table writes

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This PR adds `FileIndex.isTimeTravel`, defaulting to `false`, so V1 file data sources can
identify immutable time-travel snapshots.

`CacheManager` honors this signal during write-driven cache invalidation by table name and path.
`InsertIntoHadoopFsRelationCommand` marks its path-based recache as write-driven. Existing explicit
refresh operations continue to include time-travel snapshots.

### Why are the changes needed?

[SPARK-53732](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-53732) changed write-driven cache
invalidation from plan matching to table-name matching with `includeTimeTravel = false`. V2
relations honor that flag through `DataSourceV2Relation.timeTravelSpec`, but V1
`LogicalRelationWithTable` was matched only by table name.

For providers that lower a pinned read to `LogicalRelation(HadoopFsRelation(FileIndex))`, the
time-travel state survives only in the `FileIndex`. A write to the live table therefore cleared and
rebuilt the pinned cache. The DataFrame remained registered as cached, but the next action
re-executed its plan, including expensive or non-idempotent UDFs.

The new signal closes this V1 gap without coupling Spark to a specific data source.

JIRA: [SPARK-59631](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-59631)

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. For V1 data sources that identify an immutable snapshot, appending to or overwriting the live
table no longer recomputes an already materialized cache for that snapshot. Live-table caches are
still refreshed after writes, and explicit refresh or uncache operations still include pinned
snapshots.

Before:

```text
is_cached=true
udf_calls=10->20
tokens_same=false
```

After the coordinated Spark and provider changes:

```text
is_cached=true
udf_calls=10->10
tokens_same=true
```

### How was this patch tested?

Added ten tests in `V1TimeTravelCacheSuite` covering name- and path-based invalidation for pinned
and live V1 relations, including a mixed pinned/live union, a real V1 Parquet append through `InsertIntoHadoopFsRelationCommand`, and V2
path invalidation for both time-travel and live `ExtractV2Table` relations. The production-write
test verifies that the pinned cache remains materialized while the live cache is cleared and
refreshed. The V2 tests verify that write-driven invalidation preserves a pinned relation but still
invalidates a live relation, while explicit refresh includes the pinned relation.

`V1TimeTravelCacheSuite`, the focused `CachedTableSuite` time-travel regression, SQL scalastyle,
test scalastyle, and MiMa checks passed.

End-to-end testing reproduced `10->20` UDF executions with unpatched Spark and preserved `10->10`
with the coordinated Spark/provider changes. The provider integration matrix passed all four tests
in both `AUTO` and `NONE` modes.

[SPARK-57897][BUILD][FOLLOWUP] Use AWS SDK bundle in credential-aws

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Use `software.amazon.awssdk:bundle` instead of `sts` in `connector/credential-aws`, sharing the SDK artifact and version already used by `hadoop-cloud`. Update the dependency comment and regenerate the assembly dependency manifest. Removing the modular SDK removes the `netty-nio-client` dependency on `reactive-streams` 1.0.4, leaving 1.0.3 from the existing `aliyun-java-core` dependency.

### Why are the changes needed?

With both `-Pcredential-aws` and `-Phadoop-cloud`, the assembly currently contains the AWS SDK bundle alongside modular SDK jars. The bundle relocates third-party dependencies, so duplicate SDK classes are not binary-compatible even when all artifacts use version 2.35.4. Which jar supplies a duplicated class can determine whether S3A uploads succeed.

For example, the bundle's `TransferListenerInvoker` calls `Logger.logger()` with the relocated SLF4J return type. Loading `Logger` from the modular `utils` jar instead causes:

```text
java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'software.amazon.awssdk.thirdparty.org.slf4j.Logger software.amazon.awssdk.utils.Logger.logger()'
```

This exception appears in the [log artifact](https://github.com/ruanwenjun/spark/actions/runs/35857041511/artifacts/10752217586) from [this CI job](https://github.com/ruanwenjun/spark/actions/runs/35857041511/job/107174192748): `resource-managers/kubernetes/integration-tests/target/integration-tests.log`, line 662 (`KubernetesSuite`, 12:36:15.312) and line 4463 (`VolcanoSuite`, 12:57:13.045) on September 23. Both stacks include `TransferListenerInvoker` and `S3AStoreImpl.putObject`. These exceptions are in the log artifact, not the failure annotations for `DecommissionSuite`. The mixed dependency set was introduced by #58051.

Using the bundle for both modules removes that duplicate class source without changing the AWS SDK version or relying on classpath order.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. It fixes S3A linkage failures in builds that include both optional profiles. Builds using only `credential-aws` now pull in the larger SDK bundle instead of the modular STS dependency.

[SPARK-59689][SQL] Run EXECUTE IMMEDIATE commands at execution time

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` command payloads now run at execution time instead of during analysis.

Previously the `ResolveExecuteImmediate` analyzer rule parsed, analyzed, and *executed* the inner statement during analysis. Now the rule only parses and analyzes:
- a command payload (e.g. `INSERT`, `SET`, `CREATE VIEW`, `REFRESH`) is wrapped in a new logical node `ExecuteImmediateCommand` and planned to a new physical node `ExecuteImmediateExec`, which runs it once at the execution level
- a query is spliced in analyzed and runs lazily as usual
- an `INTO` clause still becomes `SetVariable`

Whether an analyzed payload is a command to defer (vs. a query to splice, and what `INTO` rejects) is decided by `QueryExecution.isEagerlyExecutedCommand`. This is the single source of truth for the shapes that get eagerly executed.

The parameterized-parse logic in `SparkSession.sql` was extracted into a shared `parseParameterizedPlan`.

Execution during analysis is wrong and produces double-execution.

Yes. `EXPLAIN EXECUTE IMMEDIATE '<command>'` no longer executes the command payload, it only shows the plan. Previously the command ran during analysis (e.g. `EXPLAIN EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'DROP TABLE t'` dropped the table). Running `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE '<command>'` directly is unchanged.

[SPARK-59719][SQL] Mark CheckOverflow as null-intolerant to match MakeDecimal

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Declare `CheckOverflow` null-intolerant, matching its sibling `MakeDecimal`:

```scala
override def nullIntolerant: Boolean = true
```

`CheckOverflow` extends `UnaryExpression` and overrides `nullSafeEval`, so `UnaryExpression.eval` returns `null` whenever the child is `null` -- i.e. it already satisfies the null-intolerance contract ("any null input results in null output"). It has simply never been declared null-intolerant. Unlike its siblings `MakeDecimal` and `UnscaledValue`, `CheckOverflow` never mixed in the old `NullIntolerant` trait, so this is a pre-existing gap, not a regression: SPARK-50241 only turned that trait into a `def` for the expressions that already had it, and did not touch `CheckOverflow`.

`Cast` -- which shares the same "throws under ANSI overflow / returns null otherwise" shape -- already declares `nullIntolerant = true`, as do `MakeDecimal`, `UnscaledValue`, and the arithmetic expressions. This aligns `CheckOverflow` with them.

### Why are the changes needed?

`nullIntolerant` is consumed by the optimizer to:
- fold a null-literal input to a null literal (`NullPropagation`), and
- infer `IsNotNull(child)` constraints and push down `IsNotNull` filters (`QueryPlanConstraints.scanNullIntolerantAttribute` / `InferFiltersFromConstraints`).

`CheckOverflow` wraps decimal results throughout the plan (e.g. the decimal serializers in `SerializerBuildHelper`), so declaring the property it already honors lets these optimizations see through it, consistent with `MakeDecimal`. This is a follow-up to the nullability alignment in SPARK-59643 (#58913), addressing a related consistency gap raised in that review.

The direction the optimizer relies on holds even though `CheckOverflow` with `nullOnOverflow = true` can also return `null` from a non-null input on overflow: the contract only requires "null in => null out", not the converse -- the same situation as `Cast`.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. This only declares an optimizer-visible property that `CheckOverflow` already honored at runtime; computed values and error behavior are unchanged. It can enable additional `IsNotNull` filter inference / null folding in query plans, but those are semantics-preserving: an inferred `IsNotNull` only removes rows whose `CheckOverflow` result would already be null, and null folding only fires for null-literal inputs, which never overflow or throw.

### How was this patch tested?

New tests for the newly-enabled optimizer behavior:
- `InferFiltersFromConstraintsSuite`: `IsNotNull('d)` is inferred from a filter `CheckOverflow('d, ...) > 0`.
- `NullPropagationSuite` (new): `CheckOverflow(Literal(null, ...), ...)` folds to a null literal under a NullPropagation-only batch, so the fold is attributable to null-intolerance.

Existing suites pass with no plan or golden-file churn: `DecimalExpressionSuite`, `PlannerSuite`, `AlignUpdateAssignmentsSuite`, `AlignMergeAssignmentsSuite`, plus the TPCDS plan-stability suites, `ExplainSuite`, and the `explain*.sql` golden files (verified the added `IsNotNull` inference does not change those plans).

[SPARK-59529][SQL] Reject ASOF JOIN MATCH_CONDITION operand that references no join input

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

  Make SQL `ASOF JOIN ... MATCH_CONDITION (a op b)` reject an operand that references no join input.

`MATCH_CONDITION` needs each operand to reference exactly one join input: one from the left, one from the right.
`AsOfJoin.operandJoinSide` picks the side from an operand's references:

- only the left input -> left
- only the right input -> right
- the wrong side or both sides -> rejected with `ASOF_JOIN_MATCH_CONDITION_TABLE_REFERENCE`
- no input (a literal, or a call like `current_date()`) -> previously pinned to its syntactic side and accepted (the
bug)

This PR returns `None` for a no-reference operand, so it falls through to the same
`ASOF_JOIN_MATCH_CONDITION_TABLE_REFERENCE` error already used for wrong-side references. The fixed-point
(`ResolveAsOfJoin`) and single-pass (`AsOfJoinResolver`) analyzers share this path, so both behave the same.

### Why are the changes needed?

A query that looks like an as-of join could build a real ASOF join with a constant operand and no nearest-match. Both
of these were accepted before:

```sql
SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1),(6)) l(a) ASOF JOIN (VALUES (10)) r(b)
  MATCH_CONDITION (l.a >= 5);

SELECT * FROM (VALUES (DATE'2024-01-01')) l(a) ASOF JOIN (VALUES (DATE'2024-01-02')) r(b)
  MATCH_CONDITION (l.a >= current_date());
```
The wrong-side case was already rejected:

```sql
SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,2)) l(a,c) ASOF JOIN (VALUES (10)) r(b)
  MATCH_CONDITION (l.a >= l.c);  -- ASOF_JOIN_MATCH_CONDITION_TABLE_REFERENCE
```

This PR makes the no-reference case consistent with it.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, but only in the unreleased line. SQL `ASOF JOIN` is new and off by default (`spark.sql.join.asofJoin.enabled`,
added in 4.3.0). A `MATCH_CONDITION` operand that references no join input now fails analysis with `ASOF_JOIN_MATCH_CONDITION_TABLE_REFERENCE` (SQLSTATE 42K0E) instead of being accepted. No released version is affected.

- `AsOfJoinSQLSuite`: `checkError` tests for a literal operand, `current_timestamp()`, both operands constant, and a
constant operand under the single-pass analyzer. The two tests that asserted acceptance now assert rejection.
- Golden files: added FVT-ASOF-3-024..027 in `join-asof-errors.sql`; removed the old accept case from
`join-asof-expressions.sql` and left a pointer comment; regenerated the `.sql.out` files.

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

- Already accepted, now correct: `STRING` vs a number (`INT`, `DECIMAL`, `DOUBLE`, ...) passed analysis before, but sorted the right buffer as `STRING` while comparing as the numeric type, so it could match the wrong row. Sort and comparison now both use the numeric common type.

[SPARK-59716][SQL] Skip the per-match `UnsafeRow` copy when the AS-OF join right-side buffer is in memory

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`SortMergeAsOfJoinScanner` rescans the buffered right-side group once per left row, and did
`bestMatch = rightRow.copy()` for every right row that improved on the match so far, although only
the final one is ever used.

That copy is only needed when `ExternalAppendOnlyUnsafeRowArray` has switched to its spillable
backing store, whose iterator re-points a single `UnsafeRow` on every `next()`. While the buffer is
in memory the iterator returns the distinct rows it stores, so a retained match stays valid.

This PR exposes that as `ExternalAppendOnlyUnsafeRowArray.isSpillBacked` and copies a match only
when it is true. The flag is read per scan rather than cached, because `clear()` drops the spillable
backing store between equi-key groups.

### Why are the changes needed?

The copies are pure overhead on the common, non-spilled path, and there are `O(matches)` of them per
left row.

`AsOfJoinBenchmark`, `Best Time(ms)` of the "Sort-merge AS-OF join" case, from the regenerated
result files in this PR. `Improvement` is the reduction in best time.

`AS-OF Join (left=10000, right=10000, groups=100)`

| JDK | Before | After | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17 | 53 | 44 | 17.0% |
| 21 | 56 | 49 | 12.5% |
| 25 | 53 | 53 | 0.0% |

`AS-OF Join (left=10000, right=10000, groups=10)`

| JDK | Before | After | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17 | 170 | 110 | 35.3% |
| 21 | 181 | 120 | 33.7% |
| 25 | 180 | 122 | 32.2% |

`AS-OF Join no equi-key (left=10000, right=10000)`

| JDK | Before | After | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17 | 1378 | 804 | 41.7% |
| 21 | 1466 | 870 | 40.7% |
| 25 | 1457 | 942 | 35.3% |

The `groups=100` case buffers only ~100 right rows per group, so the scan is a small part of an
end-to-end time dominated by the shuffle and sort, and the result sits inside its own stdev either
way. The larger-group cases, where the per-left-row scan actually dominates, improve by 32-42%.

Reusing one `UnsafeRow` and copying the winning row's bytes into it was measured too, and did not
help: it removes the allocation but keeps the memory copy, which is what costs here.

[SPARK-59543][SQL] Avoid a per-record SQLConf.get in the JSON charset-decode path

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

When reading JSON with an explicit `encoding` option, `CreateJacksonParser.getStreamDecoder` builds
a `CharsetDecoder` per input record via `CharsetProvider.newDecoder(enc, caller = "Jackson Parser")`,
and `newDecoder`'s two default arguments each call `SQLConf.get`:

```scala
def newDecoder(charset: String,
    legacyCharsets: Boolean = SQLConf.get.legacyJavaCharsets,
    legacyErrorAction: Boolean = SQLConf.get.legacyCodingErrorAction,
    caller: String = "decode"): CharsetDecoder
```

So `SQLConf.get` runs twice per record. This PR resolves the two flags once per reader in
`JSONOptions` and passes them explicitly to `newDecoder`:

- `JSONOptions`: add `legacyJavaCharsets` and `legacyCodingErrorAction` vals resolved from
  `SQLConf.get` at construction (matching the existing SQLConf-derived fields such as
  `writeNullIfWithDefaultValue`).
- `CreateJacksonParser`: thread the two flags through `getStreamDecoder` and the `text`,
  `internalRow`, and `bytes` encoding variants into `CharsetProvider.newDecoder`.
- `TextInputJsonDataSource`: pass the resolved flags from the options at the three closure sites
  (`inferFromDataset`, `readFile`, `readStream`).

Only the single-line/text read path is affected (it calls `getStreamDecoder`). The multi-line path
uses `new InputStreamReader(is, enc)` and never called `newDecoder`, so it is untouched.
`CharsetProvider.newDecoder`'s signature/defaults are unchanged (its other caller, `decode()`,
already passes explicit flags).

### Why are the changes needed?

On an executor task thread `SQLConf.get` constructs a fresh `ReadOnlySQLConf` + `ConfigReader` +
`HashMap` each call. The two flags are constant for the whole task, so reading them per record is
pure allocation churn. This mirrors what CSV already does — `CSVOptions` resolves
`legacyJavaCharsets` once at construction via
`CharsetProvider.forName(_, SQLConf.get.legacyJavaCharsets, ...)`.

Profiling `JsonBenchmark`'s encoding-specified read cases under JFR (`settings=profile`):

- Allocation samples flowing through `getStreamDecoder` together with
  `SQLConf.get`/`ConfigReader`/`ReadOnlySQLConf` drop from ~7,600 to 0.
- `ConfigReader.<init>` drops from ~2% of sampled allocation pressure to absent.
- Wall-clock time is unchanged within run-to-run noise (this is an allocation / GC-pressure
  reduction, not a CPU one).

[SPARK-59699][CONNECT] Make DataFrameReader options case-insensitive

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This PR makes Spark Connect's Python `DataFrameReader.option` handling case-insensitive.
When a new option matches an existing key ignoring case, it removes the existing entry and stores
the newest spelling and value.

It also adds plan serialization coverage for both named-table and data-source reads.

Spark reader option keys are case-insensitive and later calls should override earlier values.
Spark Connect currently stores options in a regular Python dictionary, so differently cased forms
of the same logical key can both reach the protobuf map. The server then resolves those duplicates
from an unordered map, which can select a value that does not match the user's call order.

For example, this should deterministically produce one `versionAsOf` option with value `2`:

```python
spark.read.option("versionAsOf", 0).option("versionasof", 1).option("versionAsOf", 2)
```

The fix preserves the spelling of the most recent key instead of lowercasing keys, so vendor option
names such as `oracle.jdbc.timezoneAsRegion` remain unchanged.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. Spark Connect Python reader options now follow case-insensitive, last-call-wins semantics,
matching the classic DataFrameReader behavior. Workloads that supplied the same logical option
using multiple casing variants now deterministically use the most recently supplied value.

[SPARK-59375][SQL] Check the array size limit in flatten codegen

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`Flatten.genCodeForNumberOfElements` accumulates the result element count into a `long` and hands it to `CodeGenerator.createArrayData` without checking it against `ByteArrayMethods.MAX_ROUNDED_ARRAY_LENGTH`. Interpreted evaluation does check. This PR adds the same check to the generated code so both paths raise the same error.

This is the `flatten` half of the pattern that [SPARK-58631](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-58631) (#57832) fixed for `array_repeat`. `concat` has the identical gap and is fixed in #58703 ([SPARK-59374](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-59374)).

### Why are the changes needed?

The two evaluation paths report different error conditions for the same input:

- Interpreted: `COLLECTION_SIZE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED.FUNCTION`, from `QueryExecutionErrors.arrayFunctionWithElementsExceedLimitError`.
- Codegen: no check, so execution reaches `ArrayData.allocateArrayData`, whose own bound check raises the internal `_LEGACY_ERROR_TEMP_2176` through `QueryExecutionErrors.cannotCreateArrayWithElementsExceedLimitError`.

An internal error condition is not meant to be user facing, and which one a query gets should not depend on whether codegen was used.

Worth noting for reviewers that this is latent rather than something a user hits today. Unlike `array_repeat`, where the element count comes straight from an argument, `flatten` needs its inputs to actually hold that many elements, so an executor will normally run out of memory before the limit is reached. The existing test reaches it only by using a `ConstantColumnVector`, which reports its length without allocating.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, in the sense that the error condition changes for an input that already fails. `flatten` with more than `MAX_ROUNDED_ARRAY_LENGTH` total elements now raises `COLLECTION_SIZE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED.FUNCTION` under codegen, where it previously raised the internal `_LEGACY_ERROR_TEMP_2176`. That matches what interpreted evaluation has always raised. The set of inputs that fail is unchanged.

Added a migration guide entry alongside the one #57832 added for `array_repeat` and `array_insert`, and the one #58703 adds for `concat`, since this is the same kind of change. Happy to drop it if you would rather not document a case that is this hard to reach.

### How was this patch tested?

Extended the existing `Elements exceed limit for flatten()` test in `QueryExecutionErrorsSuite` to run the expression through `GenerateUnsafeProjection` as well as `eval`, asserting the same error from both. That test already builds a large array cheaply with `ConstantColumnVector`, which reports its length without allocating, so nothing large is allocated.

It sits in `QueryExecutionErrorsSuite` rather than in `CollectionExpressionsSuite`, where #57832 put its tests, because `ConstantColumnVector` lives in `sql/core` and is not reachable from a catalyst suite. Extending the existing test also seemed better than adding a second one: the test was already there and simply never exercised codegen, which is how the gap survived.
