issues.title: Bug: `<ViewTransition>` name-prop change does not trigger view transition without child DOM mutation

labels.name: Status: Unconfirmed
labels.description: A potential issue that we haven't yet confirmed as a bug

issues.body:
A `<ViewTransition>` whose `name` prop changes between renders does **not** trigger the view transition update pipeline unless a child DOM mutation also occurs. Hero morphs via name-prop toggling on mounted components silently produce no animation.

> **Update (2026-06-10):** A fix is now proposed in [facebook/react#36728](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/36728). The GitHub Pages live preview below has since been rebuilt against a **patched** React build that includes that fix, so it now demonstrates the *corrected* behaviour, not the bug. To see the original broken behaviour, use the CodeSandbox (unpatched canary) or check out a commit before `cf0fe598` in the reproduction repo.

## React version

- `react`: `19.3.0-canary-46103596-20260305`
- `react-dom`: `19.3.0-canary-46103596-20260305`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Mount two `<ViewTransition>` boundaries wrapping a button and a dialog
2. Toggle the `name` prop between them (one gets `"camera-hero"`, the other `undefined`) via `startTransition` + `addTransitionType`
3. No child DOM mutations occur during the transition

**Reproduction repo:** https://github.com/kjanat/react-canary-19.3.0-view-transition-bug  
**Live preview:** https://kjanat.github.io/react-canary-19.3.0-view-transition-bug/ (now serves a **patched** build that includes the fix, so it no longer reproduces the bug, see the update note above)  
**CodeSandbox:** https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/yx5sdy (broken version)

Toggle between **Broken** and **Workaround** modes to see the difference. Note: on the patched GitHub Pages preview both modes now animate; use the CodeSandbox above (unpatched canary) to observe the original broken vs. workaround contrast.

Minimal repro component:

```tsx
<ViewTransition
  name={heroOwner === 'button' ? 'camera-hero' : undefined}
  share="camera-hero-morph"
  default="none"
>
  <button>Use live camera</button>
</ViewTransition>

<ViewTransition
  name={heroOwner === 'dialog' ? 'camera-hero' : undefined}
  share="camera-hero-morph"
  default="none"
>
  <dialog ref={dialogRef}>{modalContent}</dialog>
</ViewTransition>
```

The `heroOwner` state toggles between `'button'` and `'dialog'` inside `startTransition` with `addTransitionType('camera-modal')`.

## Expected behavior

Opening the modal morphs smoothly from the trigger button to the dialog (shared `camera-hero` element with CSS view-transition animations).

## Actual behavior

Modal appears instantly -- no hero morph animation. See [root cause §1](#1-name-only-changes-do-not-produce-update) for the code path that leads to a zero-opacity cancellation.

### Workaround

Two changes required simultaneously (visible in workaround mode in the reproduction):

1. **`update` prop** -- unblocks VT processing (otherwise `default='none'` gates it out):
   ```tsx
   update={{ default: 'none', 'camera-modal': 'camera-hero-morph' }}
   ```
2. **Forced child DOM mutation** -- sets the internal `Update` flag on the VT fiber:
   ```tsx
   <button data-hero-owner={heroOwner}>Use live camera</button>
   ```

The `data-hero-owner` attribute serves no purpose other than forcing a child DOM mutation that sets a flag which logically should depend on the name change itself.

## Root cause (source references)

All references below are GitHub permalinks to React commit [`4610359651fa10247159e2050f8ec222cb7faa91`][react-commit], matching `react-dom@19.3.0-canary-46103596-20260305`.

### 1. Name-only changes do not produce `Update`

In [`measureViewTransitionHostInstancesRecursive`][measure-recursive], the `Update` flag gates whether `applyViewTransitionName` fires for the new snapshot:

```js
(parentViewTransition.flags & Update) !== NoFlags
  && applyViewTransitionName(instance, newName, className);
```

In this code path, the `Update` flag is set in the mutation phase ([`ReactFiberCommitWork.js#L2634-L2645`][update-flag-set]) when `viewTransitionMutationContext` is `true`:

```js
viewTransitionMutationContext && (finishedWork.flags |= Update);
```

`viewTransitionMutationContext` becomes `true` when a DOM mutation (attribute change, text change, element insertion/removal) occurs within the VT's child subtree during the mutation commit. The `Update` flag can also be set during measurement if `hasInstanceChanged()` detects a bounding-rect change ([L676-681][has-instance-changed]), but in this scenario (name-only prop change, no layout shift), measurements are identical and this path returns false.

When only the VT's `name` prop changes, with no child mutations and no layout change, the flag stays `NoFlags`. Without `Update`, the instance is not passed to `applyViewTransitionName` but is instead pushed to `viewTransitionCancelableChildren`, which leads to a zero-opacity cancellation path in [`ReactFiberConfigDOM.js#L1616-L1640`][cancel-animation]:

```js
current.animate(
  { opacity: [0, 0], pointerEvents: ['none', 'none'] },
  { duration: 0, fill: 'forwards', pseudoElement: '::view-transition-group(' + oldName + ')' },
);
```

> **Note:** this cancellation path is only reachable when the `update` prop unblocks before-mutation snapshot capture and after-mutation measurement. With `default='none'` and no `update` prop, host instances never receive VT names in the first place, so they never reach `viewTransitionCancelableChildren`. The zero-opacity cancellation manifests specifically in the partial-workaround state (setting `update` without also forcing a DOM mutation).

React already detects the name change in `beginWork` at [`ReactFiberBeginWork.js#L3617-L3622`][name-change-detected]:

```js
if (current !== null && current.memoizedProps.name !== pendingProps.name) {
  workInProgress.flags |= Ref | RefStatic;
}
```

This sets `Ref | RefStatic` for ref lifecycle, but it does not propagate into the commit phase as a VT update signal.

### 2. `default='none'` gates out the update path (compounding)

The `share` prop name suggests it controls shared-element/hero morphs, but in the source it is consulted in the **enter/exit pair** path ([`commitEnterViewTransitions`][commit-enter] and [`commitExitViewTransitions`][commit-exit]) and not in the update path. When both VTs stay mounted and only change their `name` prop, React routes through the **update** path, which calls `getViewTransitionClassName(props.default, props.update)` in two phases:

| Phase           | Source permalink                                                       | Gate                                                                |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Before-mutation | [`ReactFiberCommitViewTransitions.js#L489-L513`][before-mutation-gate] | Class name `=== 'none'` → skip old-snapshot VT name application     |
| After-mutation  | [`ReactFiberCommitViewTransitions.js#L768-L803`][after-mutation-gate]  | Class name `=== 'none'` → skip measurement and new-snapshot VT name |

The mutation phase ([`ReactFiberCommitWork.js#L2623-L2633`][update-mutation-gate]) also checks the class name to set `inUpdateViewTransition`, but this variable controls Portal context propagation in the traced code path -- the `Update` flag assignment at [L2634-L2645][update-flag-set] is gated by `viewTransitionMutationContext`, not by the class name.\
So `default='none'` blocks the before/after-mutation phases, while the missing DOM mutation independently blocks the `Update` flag.

### 3. Separate observation: `share` not consulted in update path

The `share` prop is only consulted in the enter/exit pair path and not in the update path. This may be by-design (the update path handles DOM mutations, not shared-element pairing), but the documentation is silent on the expected behavior when only `name` changes on a mounted `<ViewTransition>`.

## Suggested fix

The name-change detection in [`beginWork`][name-change-detected] (`current.memoizedProps.name !== pendingProps.name`) could additionally set the `Update` flag or an equivalent signal, so the commit phase treats the VT as updated even without child DOM mutations.

A cleaner alternative is to keep the fix local to the mutation-phase commit handler for `ViewTransitionComponent`, adding a name-change check alongside `viewTransitionMutationContext`:

```js
} else if (
  viewTransitionMutationContext
  || current.memoizedProps.name !== finishedWork.memoizedProps.name
) {
  finishedWork.flags |= Update;
}
```

This would keep the `Update` flag closer to its apparent current usage (set during mutation phase, consumed in measurement) without changing `beginWork` flag behavior.

Additionally, the `share` className may need to be consulted in the update path when a name change is detected, not only in the enter/exit pair path.

## Docs note

The `<ViewTransition>` documentation distinguishes `share` (enter/exit pairing) from `update` (DOM mutations / layout effects), but does not clarify what should happen when only the `name` prop changes across already-mounted `<ViewTransition>` boundaries. It's unclear whether mounted name toggling is expected to produce a transition or is intentionally unsupported.

}

issues.title: [compiler] Normalize whitespace in JSX string attributes for builtin tags

labels.name: Resolution: Stale
labels.description: Automatically closed due to inactivity

issues.body:
## Summary

Fixes #35481

### Root cause

The Babel JSX transform (`@babel/plugin-transform-react-jsx`) normalizes newlines followed by whitespace in plain JSX string attributes:

```javascript
// @babel/plugin-transform-react-jsx/lib/create-plugin.js:260-263
if (isStringLiteral(value) && !isJSXExpressionContainer(attribute.node.value)) {
  value.value = value.value.replace(/\n\s+/g, " ");
  delete value.extra?.raw;
}
```

This normalization is **skipped** for `JSXExpressionContainer` values. When the React Compiler wraps strings in expression containers (because `\n` matches `STRING_REQUIRES_EXPR_CONTAINER_PATTERN` in the `U+0000-U+001F` range), the JSX transform bypasses normalization. The server code (uncompiled) goes through the standard normalization, creating a hydration mismatch.

### Fix

Apply the **same** `/\n\s+/g` → `" "` normalization that the JSX transform uses, before the expression container check. This ensures compiled output matches the behavior of non-compiled code. After normalization, strings that no longer contain control characters avoid unnecessary expression container wrapping entirely.

### Scope

- **Builtin HTML elements only** (`div`, `span`, etc.) — component props are preserved unchanged
- **fbt operands excluded** — internationalization strings are not modified
- Uses the exact same regex as `@babel/plugin-transform-react-jsx`

### Before (compiled output)

```jsx
// Input: className="\n        flex min-h-screen\n        dark:bg-black\n      "
// Compiled: className={"\n        flex min-h-screen\n        dark:bg-black\n      "}
//           ↑ expression container bypasses JSX transform normalization → hydration mismatch
```

### After (compiled output)

```jsx
// Input: className="\n        flex min-h-screen\n        dark:bg-black\n      "
// Compiled: className=" flex min-h-screen dark:bg-black "
//           ↑ matches JSX transform output, no expression container needed
```

## How did you test this change?

5 fixture tests covering positive and negative scenarios:

| Fixture | Scenario | Expected behavior |
|---------|----------|-------------------|
| `repro-multiline-classname-hydration` | Reporter's exact case: multiline Tailwind className | `\n` + indentation → single space |
| `repro-multiline-classname-newline-indent` | Expression container `{"foo\n  bar\n  baz"}` | `\n\s+` normalized → `"foo bar baz"` |
| `repro-multiline-title-attribute` | `title` with `\n` + indentation | Same normalization as className |
| `repro-multiline-classname-expression` | `{"foo\nbar"}` — `\n` without trailing whitespace | **NOT normalized** (no `\s+` after `\n`, matches JSX transform) |
| `repro-multiline-component-prop-preserved` | `<MyComponent data={"\n"}>` | **NOT normalized** (component, not builtin tag) |

```bash
yarn snap -p repro-multiline-classname-hydration       # 1 Passed
yarn snap -p repro-multiline-classname-newline-indent   # 1 Passed
yarn snap -p repro-multiline-title-attribute            # 1 Passed
yarn snap -p repro-multiline-classname-expression       # 1 Passed
yarn snap -p repro-multiline-component-prop-preserved   # 1 Passed
yarn workspace babel-plugin-react-compiler lint         # Clean
```

issues.title: [RFC] useStore/createStore APIs
issues.body:
**Note: This is a proof of concept for discussion purposes. API is subject to change and may not ship in this form.**

* *Update 2026-01-07: Added description of the `ReactExternalDataSource` interface, clarified behavior of `getState` and explained how we avoid needing to tell the data source about React commits.*

Many libraries in the React ecosystem exist to allow React components to observe non-React state. As of today there is no way for such a library to do this in a way that is acceptably performant while also taking advantage of React transition semantics. This RFC proposes a new API for modeling state that is not conceptually owned by any one React component but which can be observed by multiple React components in a way that avoids unnecessary rerenders while correctly implementing React’s transition semantics.

## Proposed API

At a high level, this proposal consist of an interface which joins two APIs:

### Interface `ReactExternalDataSource`

The `ReactExternalDataSource` interface describes a unit of dynamic non-React state that can be observed in React using `useStore`. In advanced use-cases store/cache libraries could implement this API to allow their state to be safely consumed in React components.

```tsx
export interface ReactExternalDataSource<S, A> {
  // Get the current state of the store. State must be immutable.
  getState(): S,
  // The stable reducer function used by the store to produce new states.
  // Reducer must be pure.
  reducer: (S, A) => S,
  // Subscribe to the store. The callback will be called after the state has
  // updated and includes the action that was dispatched.
  subscribe: (callback: (action: A) => void) => () => void,
};
```

Note that `getState()` here must always returns the “current” version of the data source (the result of applying all the actions in the order in which they were triggered) irrespective of any React transition. Different React roots may be rendering different states at any given time, but the data source itself does not need to be aware of that.

### `useStore`

```tsx
function useStore<S, T>(
  store: ReactExternalDataSource<S, mixed>,
  selector?: (state: S) => T
): T;

```

`useStore` is designed to echo `useContext`. It allows users to observe a store’s value, or a slice/selection of that store value, in a React component. Notably it avoids triggering a render if the observed portion of the store has not changed while still correctly implementing React’s transition semantics including avoiding tearing and correctly implementing [React’s update reordering semantics](https://jordaneldredge.com/react-rebasing/).

### `createStore`

```tsx
function createStore<S, A>(
  initialValue: S,
  reducer?: (S, A) => S
): ReactStore<S, A>;

```

For simple use cases, React provides it’s own simple (~20loc) store implementation which implements `ReactExternalDataSource`. `createStore` is designed to echo `useState` and `useReducer`. If a reducer is not provided, the `dispatch` method of the store mirrors `setState` in that it accepts either a new value, or an updater function. If a reducer *is* provided, the `dispatch` method accepts a concrete action value which is passed to the reducer.

The returned `ReactStore` object implements `ReactExternalDataSource` and also exposes a `.dispatch(action)` method.

## Example Usage

```tsx
const store = createStore(1);

function App() {
  const value = useStore(store);
  return <button onClick={() => store.dispatch(prev => prev + 1)}>
    {value}
   </button>;
}

```

## Implementation Details

The core problems that any implementation of a concurrent compatible store API must solve are:

1. When a store reader mounts sync during a transition, it must observe the pre-transition state, and then update to the new state with all other components.
2. If a store update is dispatched sync while one or more other updates to the store are still pending as part of a transition, it must correctly model React’s [update reordering semantics](https://jordaneldredge.com/react-rebasing/).

To address these problems, the current implementation maintains a reference counted registry of currently observed stores at each React root. As stores update, each root is able to track which state updates are pending and which have flushed to the UI. When a new component mounts sync, it’s able to find the “current” state value for that store in its React root even if other updates are pending. When a sync update is triggered while a previous update is still pending within that root, the update (action + reducer) can be applied on top of the “current” state for that React root.

Note that the underlying data source does not need to be told when an update commits, and is never aware of any non-canonical states that React produces when sync updates interrupt transition updates. Those temporary states are created by React itself using: `source.reducer(comittedState, syncAction)`.

(See “Unsolved Problems” below for some limitations associated with the ref counting portion of this approach).

For maintaining per-component state, this implementation currently leverages the internal `updateReducerImpl` function, but eagerly pre-computes each update’s value, and explicitly triggers transition fixups, instead of allowing the update queue to be computed during render. This is likely not the cleanest approach, but was minimally invasive while still allowing us to take advantage of the many battle tested detailed of the `updateReducerImpl` implementation, which felt like a good balance for a proof of concept. I expect we will eventually want to either create a custom fork of `updateReducerImpl` for this API, or at least refactor `updateReducerImpl` so that it can be sensibly reused by this API.

## Existing Alternative Solutions

Today existing libraries are choosing between one of a few imperfect existing solutions:

1. `useReducer` + `useContext` this works and is correct, but quickly becomes impractical in the real world due to the performance implications of `useContext` triggering rerenders on every state update.
2. `useSyncExternalStore` this API allows the efficient observation of non-React state, but it prevents updates to stores from participating in React transitions.
3. Rolling their own per-component subscription using `useEffect`. This is fraught with challenges and I believe it’s impossible to fully match React’s transition semantics. I believe [this](https://github.com/thejustinwalsh/react-concurrent-store/tree/main/packages/use-store/src/experimental) is the closest anyone has been able to get, but it makes unsafe assumptions about React and still has known edge cases which are incorrect or have sub-optional performance.

## Unsolved Problems

The current implementation is not perfect. It has some known limitations, but I wanted to share it in its current state to get feedback before continuing with the work/discussion needed to address these issues. But, for the sake of completeness I’ve captured them here:

### Lifetimes

In the edge case where a React root starts observing a store while that store is already updating as part of a transition, the current implementation will incorrectly observe the post-transition value of that store even though the transition is still pending. I believe resolving this issue would require all React roots to know about all stores that are updating as part of transitions, even if they are not observing that store. This is somewhat tricky to implement without interfering with the GC of either stores or React roots. I suspect there is a solution here using WeakRefs, but its possible there is a simpler approach that I am overlooking.

### Custom equality

A key feature of this API is avoiding rerenders when the value observed by a component has not changed. To determine if the result of evaluating a selector has changed, we currently use [`Object.is`](http://object.is/) which is the standard in React. However, in many cases this is not sufficient, and libraries like Redux provide mechanisms for providing custom equality functions for determining if a selector’s value has changed. I believe our API should enable this behavior by either allowing the user provide a third `isEqual` argument to `useStore` when providing a selector, *or* by calling the selector with both the current state value *and* the previous state value.

Neither of these are currently implemented since our current approach of leveraging `updateReducerImpl` does not allow us to easily “see” the currently rendered/rendering value for a given lane.

### Categorically avoiding unnecessary rerenders

The current implementation reuses the logic from `useReducer` to model per-component state updates. This allows us to reuse a bunch of known-correct logic to get something working correctly quickly. However, `useReducer` has known/accepted issues where it will trigger a rerender despite the value not actually changing. This may be less acceptable for `useStore` than it is for `useReducer` since `useStore` with a selector is specifically designed to avoid unnecessary renders.

Updating the `useReduce` logic to avoid useless renders would be nice, though it seems the task is tricky enough that previous attempts have been reverted and not reattempted.

  10. If you haven't already, complete the CLA.

  Learn more about contributing: https://reactjs.org/docs/how-to-contribute.html
-->

## Summary

This PR fixes a race condition bug in React DOM's Server-Side Rendering where the `$RS` (completeSegment) function doesn't check if `parentNode` is null before accessing it.

**Problem:**
During Suspense boundary resolution in production builds, the `completeSegment` function can encounter a race condition where DOM nodes are removed by other rendering or hydration work, causing `parentNode` to become `null`. This results in the error: `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'parentNode')`.

**Solution:**
Added null safety checks in the `completeSegment` source implementation before DOM manipulation. This ensures the generated `$RS` runtime safely exits if either required node or its parent has already been removed.

The inline runtime string is generated from this source via `yarn generate-inline-fizz-runtime`.

**Affected code:**
`packages/react-dom-bindings/src/server/fizz-instruction-set/ReactDOMFizzInstructionSetShared.js`

The generated inline runtime in `ReactDOMFizzInstructionSetInlineCodeStrings.js` is derived from this source.

Fixes #35056 


<!--
 Explain the **motivation** for making this change. What existing problem does the pull request solve?
-->

## How did you test this change?

**1. Minimal Reproduction:**
Created a minimal Next.js application that consistently reproduces the bug:
- Repository: https://github.com/ponharu/react-issue
- Setup: Next.js 16.0.1 + React 19.2.0 + Chakra UI v3 with Suspense boundaries
- Steps: Production build with async page component (1s delay) + Suspense fallback

**2. Verification:**
- **Before fix**: Error occurred consistently when reloading the page multiple times
- **After applying the fix**: Error no longer occurs, page renders correctly
- Applied the fix to all affected compiled files in Next.js project and verified in production environment

**3. Commands run:**
```bash
yarn generate-inline-fizz-runtime

# Applied fix to production build
npm run build
npm run start

# Tested multiple page reloads to trigger race condition
# Monitored browser console for errors
```

**4. Environment tested:**
- Next.js 16.0.1 (production build)
- React/React DOM 19.2.0
- Chakra UI v3
- Node.js 24.11.0
- Browser: Google Chrome 142.0.7444.60

Note: This is a minimal defensive fix that adds null checks without changing the core logic. The race condition is timing-sensitive and more likely to occur with CSS-in-JS libraries like Chakra UI.

issues.title: Feature Request: [eslint-plugin-react-hooks] Provide a way for custom hooks with a dependency array to accept seemingly redundant dependencies
issues.body:
- #33041

Since React doesn't provide a native way to define a dependency array for resetting state, I have to resort to a user-land implementation of this functionality. Here is the signature of the hook I use:

```ts
function useDerivedState<S>(
  initialState: S | ((previousState?: S) => S),
  deps: DependencyList,
): [S, Dispatch<SetStateAction<S>>]
```

Please check https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/33041#issuecomment-2923900312 for details and full code.

In order to get warnings about missing dependencies, I add this rule to my ESLint config:

```ts
'react-hooks/exhaustive-deps': [
  'warn',
  { additionalHooks: 'useDerivedState' },
]
```

Unfortunately, that leads to warnings in cases where there shouldn't be any. Here is an example:

```ts
const [collapsed, setCollapsed] = useDerivedState(() => true, [collapsible]);
```

The reason is that `collapsible` is listed as a dependency, but not present in the initializer function's body, so the linter plugin thinks it's unnecessary. However, this is intended: it is desired that `collapsed` is reset to `true` whenever `collapsible` changes.

Such seemingly redundant dependencies are currently only accepted for the effects family of hooks. They got this special treatment shortly after the `exhaustive-deps` rule was introduced, see https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/14920#issuecomment-471070149.

The test for whether a hook belongs to the effects family is very simple: it's enough that the hook's name includes the substring `"Effect"` at the end of it, or followed by a symbol other than a lowercase letter.

https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/ee76351917106c6146745432a52e9a54a41ee181/packages/eslint-plugin-react-hooks/src/rules/ExhaustiveDeps.ts#L1334

Now, I could of course rename my `useDerivedState` hook to something like `useDerivedStateEffect`, but this would be a despicable misnomer since not only is the hook's functionality nothing like that of `useEffect`, but also its whole idea is to fight how effects are used all over the place for deriving state despite it being a terrible anti-pattern (#33041 has a detailed explanation).

A couple more workarounds I can think of:

1.
    ```ts
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
    const [collapsed, setCollapsed] = useDerivedState(true, [collapsible]);
    ```

    Simply suppressing the warning. Dirty.
2.
    ```ts
    const [collapsed, setCollapsed] = useDerivedState(() => {
      collapsible; // eslint-disable-line @typescript-eslint/no-unused-expressions
      return true;
    }, [collapsible]);
    ```

    Forcing `collapsible` to be referenced in the initializer function's body, but now a different warning has to be suppressed.

    This is more verbose and a little confusing, but especially in more complex cases where we don't only have one single dependency, I would go for this option because I wouldn't want to disable the `exhaustive-deps` rule completely.

    (By the way, Biome's `useExhaustiveDependencies` rule [allows ignoring only a specific dependency](https://biomejs.dev/linter/rules/use-exhaustive-dependencies/#ignoring-a-specific-dependency). This alone make me kind of want to give Biome a try. Very inspiring!)
3.  
    ```ts
    const [collapsed, setCollapsed] = useDerivedState(() => {
      return collapsible || true;
    }, [collapsible]);
    ```

    There shouldn't be any problem with this, right? Well, turns out there is, and it's that with this code, TypeScript for whatever reason decides that the type of `collapsed` is `true` rather than `boolean`, so it has to be specified manually:

    ```ts
    const [collapsed, setCollapsed] = useDerivedState<boolean>(() => {
      return collapsible || true;
    }, [collapsible]);
    ```

    I'm really clueless about why TypeScript thinks `collapsible || true` is of type `true` while a simple `true` expression is of type `boolean`. Probably I should open an issue about this in TypeScript's repo, but if anyone here has any idea, please let me know 🙏

    Anyway, I shouldn't be writing stupid code like this just to get around the linter plugin's limitations.

I suggest introducing support for the following kind of configuration:

```ts
'react-hooks/exhaustive-deps': ['warn', {
  additionalHooks: [
    { name: 'useDerivedState', allowExtraDeps: true },
    { name: 'useDefinitelyNotAnEffect', allowExtraDeps: false },
    /^(useMyCustomHook|useMyOtherCustomHook)$/,
  ]
}]
```

Probably quite self-explanatory, but here are some details:

- `additionalHooks` can now accept objects of this shape:
  
    ```ts
    { name: string | RegExp, allowExtraDeps?: boolean }
    ```

    If `allowExtraDeps` is undefined, the decision on whether to report seemingly redundant dependencies should be made just the same way it is made now. Otherwise, it should be based on that property's value.
- I think it's better not to convert the `name` properties from string to regexes, but treat strings as values that should be matched exactly. Before, regexes couldn't be used directly because the config file had to be in JSON format, and that is why strings were converted to regexes. With the new flat config format, that is no longer necessary to have regex support.
- In addition to strings, regexes and object of the proposed shape, `additionalHooks` should also accept arrays of those values so that each one of them can be configured individually.

The proposed object shape could also be extended to allow even more flexibility, like for example what the aforementioned Biome rule offers with its [`closureIndex` and `dependenciesIndex` options](https://biomejs.dev/linter/rules/use-exhaustive-dependencies/#validating-dependencies) (this would solve #25443), or with its [`stableResult` option](https://biomejs.dev/linter/rules/use-exhaustive-dependencies/#stable-results) (this would solve #16873)

issues.title: Add `<ViewTransition>` Component

labels.name: React Core Team
labels.description: Opened by a member of the React Core Team

issues.body:
This will provide the opt-in for using [View Transitions](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) in React. View Transitions only trigger for async updates like `startTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, Actions or `` revealing from fallback to content. Synchronous updates provide an opt-out but also guarantee that they commit immediately which View Transitions can't. There's no need to opt-in to View Transitions at the "cause" side like event handlers or actions. They don't know what UI will change and whether that has an animated transition described. Conceptually the `` component is like a DOM fragment that transitions its children in its own isolate/snapshot. The API works by wrapping a DOM node or inner component: ```js import {ViewTransition} from 'react'; ``` The default is `name="auto"` which will automatically assign a `view-transition-name` to the inner DOM node. That way you can add a View Transition to a Component without controlling its DOM nodes styling otherwise. A difference between this and the browser's built-in `view-transition-name: auto` is that switching the DOM nodes within the `` component preserves the same name so this example cross-fades between the DOM nodes instead of causing an exit and enter: ```js {condition ? : } ``` This becomes especially useful with `` as this example cross-fades between Skeleton and Content: ```js }> ``` Where as this example triggers an exit of the Skeleton and an enter of the Content: ```js }> ``` Managing instances and keys becomes extra important. You can also specify an explicit `name` property for example for animating the same conceptual item from one page onto another. However, best practices is to property namespace these since they can easily collide. It's also useful to add an `id` to it if available. ```js ``` The model in general is the same as plain `view-transition-name` except React manages a set of heuristics for when to apply it. A problem with the naive View Transitions model is that it overly opts in every boundary that *might* transition into transitioning. This is leads to unfortunate effects like things floating around when unrelated updates happen. This leads the whole document to animate which means that nothing is clickable in the meantime. It makes it not useful for smaller and more local transitions. Best practice is to add `view-transition-name` only right before you're about to need to animate the thing. This is tricky to manage globally on complex apps and is not compositional. Instead we let React manage when a `` "activates" and add/remove the `view-transition-name`. This is also when React calls `startViewTransition` behind the scenes while it mutates the DOM. I've come up with a number of heuristics that I think will make a lot easier to coordinate this. The principle is that only if something that updates that particular boundary do we activate it. I hope that one day maybe browsers will have something like these built-in and we can remove our implementation. A `` only activates if: - If a mounted Component renders a `` within it outside the first DOM node, and it is within the viewport, then that ViewTransition activates as an "enter" animation. This avoids inner "enter" animations trigger when the parent mounts. - If an unmounted Component had a `` within it outside the first DOM node, and it was within the viewport, then that ViewTransition activates as an "exit" animation. This avoids inner "exit" animations triggering when the parent unmounts. - If an explicitly named `` is deep within an unmounted tree and one with the same name appears in a mounted tree at the same time, then both are activated as a pair, but only if they're both in the viewport. This avoids these triggering "enter" or "exit" animations when going between parents that don't have a pair. - If an already mounted `` is visible and a DOM mutation, that might affect how it's painted, happens within its children but outside any nested ``. This allows it to "cross-fade" between its updates. - If an already mounted `` resizes or moves as the result of direct DOM nodes siblings changing or moving around. This allows insertion, deletion and reorders into a list to animate all children. It is only within one DOM node though, to avoid unrelated changes in the parent to trigger this. If an item is outside the viewport before and after, then it's skipped to avoid things flying across the screen. - If a `` boundary changes size, due to a DOM mutation within it, then the parent activates (or the root document if there are no more parents). This ensures that the container can cross-fade to avoid abrupt relayout. This can be avoided by using absolutely positioned children. When this can avoid bubbling to the root document, whatever is not animating is still responsive to clicks during the transition. Conceptually each DOM node has its own default that activates the parent `` or no transition if the parent is the root. That means that if you add a DOM node like `
` this won't trigger an "enter" animation since it was the div that was added, not the ViewTransition. Instead, it might cause a cross-fade of the parent ViewTransition or no transition if it had no parent. This ensures that only explicit boundaries perform coarse animations instead of every single node which is really the benefit of the View Transitions model. This ends up working out well for simple cases like switching between two pages immediately while transitioning one floating item that appears on both pages. Because only the floating item transitions by default. Note that it's possible to add manual `view-transition-name` with CSS or `style={{ viewTransitionName: 'auto' }}` that always transitions as long as something else has a `` that activates. For example a `` can wrap a whole page for a cross-fade but inside of it an explicit name can be added to something to ensure it animates as a move when something relates else changes its layout. Instead of just cross-fading it along with the Page which would be the default. There's more PRs coming with some optimizations, fixes and expanded APIs. This first PR explores the above core heuristic.

issues.title: Bug: eslint-plugin-react-hooks@5.0.0 only detects english component names

labels.name: Status: Unconfirmed
labels.description: A potential issue that we haven't yet confirmed as a bug

labels.name: Resolution: Stale
labels.description: Automatically closed due to inactivity

issues.body:
React version: eslint-plugin-react-hooks@5.0.0

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Create a functional component with a name such as `ÄndraVärde` that starts with a non english upper case letter
2. Run the linter

## The current behavior
Sample error:
>   23:20  error  React Hook "useSelectedState" is called in function "ÄndraVärde" that is neither a React function component nor a custom React Hook function. React component names must start with an uppercase letter. React Hook names must start with the word "use"  react-hooks/rules-of-hooks

## The expected behavior
The linting should allow non english component names, React does.

## The problem
Version 5.0.0 included the changes made in #25162 which modified the following method:
https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/e1378902bbb322aa1fe1953780f4b2b5f80d26b1/packages/eslint-plugin-react-hooks/src/RulesOfHooks.js#L43-L50

This code only allows english upper case letters `A-Z` which is not enough.

## Proposed solution
Use `.toUpperCase()` and compare the result:
```js
function isComponentName(node) { 
  return node.type === 'Identifier' && node.name[0] == node.name[0].toUpperCase(); 
} 
```

This should work with a lot more languages at least.

issues.title: Bug: Infinite rendering resulting in freezing of tab/browser

labels.name: Resolution: Stale
labels.description: Automatically closed due to inactivity

issues.body:
<!--
  Please provide a clear and concise description of what the bug is. Include
  screenshots if needed. Please test using the latest version of the relevant
  React packages to make sure your issue has not already been fixed.
-->
React is not preventing infinite rendering/looping and results in freezing of browser. 

The root cause of this issue is because the dependency array of `useEffect` compares object/array by reference. But, this is a serious issue because 
- This is a common trap people might get into because of dynamic nature of Javascript, and people might not know the thing they are passing to dependency array is a primitive value or an array/object.
- React should catch this infinite rendering and throw a helpful error. This error is already thrown by React for some of the cases. But, clearly React does not catch this for all the cases.
- The documentation of  `useEffect` does not have a single reference to this gotcha - guarding against passing object/array to the dependency array, since reference of the object/array is being checked, not a deep comparison value. Some solutions already exist like https://github.com/kentcdodds/use-deep-compare-effect, https://stackoverflow.com/questions/54095994/react-useeffect-comparing-objects/63965274#63965274. But, only people who are aware of this behaviour of `useEffect` will reach out to these solutions (or they might manually deep compare with their own custom hook as some people do in the linked stackoverflow link)

It would also be helpful if `useEffect` includes a helpful option like 
```javascript
useEffect(() => {
 // myArray, myObject gets new reference on evey render
}, [myArray, myObject], {
   deepCompare: true/false // it would be helpful to have this instead of reaching for custom hooks/npm packages
})
```

React version:
`16.12.x` (any latest version)

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Click the `codesandbox` link - https://codesandbox.io/s/apollo-client-uselazyquery-example-forked-kmc1u?file=/src/App.js. 
2. Click `Topics` link and then select `Countries` link. 

`Warning`: Please be aware that tab/browser will freeze. It is better to open the console before hand, so that you can see the looping from console logs.

<!--
  Your bug will get fixed much faster if we can run your code and it doesn't
  have dependencies other than React. Issues without reproduction steps or
  code examples may be immediately closed as not actionable.
-->

Link to code example:

[CodeSandbox reproduction](https://codesandbox.io/s/apollo-client-uselazyquery-example-forked-kmc1u?file=/src/App.js)

<!--
  Please provide a CodeSandbox (https://codesandbox.io/s/new), a link to a

  problem. You may provide a screenshot of the application if you think it is
  relevant to your bug report. Here are some tips for providing a minimal
  example: https://stackoverflow.com/help/mcve.
-->

Current behavior:
- React does not prevent infinite loop/rendering. Browser tab freezes, and the end user has no idea that the tab has freezed. They have to force quit the tab.


Expected behavior:
- React should give a helpful warning that an infinite render/loop is going on.

issues.title: Fix fatal crash on invalid input rank in GPU linear algebra ops

labels.name: size:M
labels.description: CL Change Size: Medium

issues.body:
### Description
Fixes a fatal crash (`SIGABRT` / `Aborted (core dumped)`) in GPU linear algebra operations (`tf.linalg.det`, `tf.linalg.slogdet`, `tf.linalg.logdet`, `tf.linalg.cholesky`, `tf.linalg.inv`, `tf.linalg.solve`, `tf.linalg.qr`) when given inputs with rank < 2 (such as a 0-D scalar). Reported in #76730.

### Reproducer
```python
import tensorflow as tf

with tf.device('/GPU:0'):
  # 0-D scalar input
  x = tf.zeros([])
  tf.linalg.det(x)
```
**Before this change:**
The process is killed immediately by `SIGABRT`:
```
tensorflow/core/framework/tensor_shape.cc:361: Check failed: d >= 0 (0 vs. -1)
Aborted (core dumped)
```
No Python exception is raised; the entire Python runtime / interpreter crashes.

**After this change:**
Cleanly raises `tf.errors.InvalidArgumentError: Input must have rank >= 2, got 0` matching CPU behavior.

### Root Cause
In GPU linear algebra kernels (`DeterminantOpGpu`, `LogDeterminantOpGpu`, `CholeskyOpGpu`, `MatrixInverseOpGpu`, `MatrixSolveOpGpu`, `QrOpGpu`), input dimension queries were executed *before* input rank validation:
```cpp
// E.g. in DeterminantOpGpu / MatrixInverseOpGpu:
const Tensor& input = context->input(0);
const int ndims = input.dims();
const int64_t n = input.dim_size(ndims - 1);  // <-- ndims - 1 evaluates to -1 when ndims == 0

OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(context, ndims >= 2, ...);
```
When `input` has rank 0 (scalar `tf.zeros([])`), `ndims = 0`, so `ndims - 1` evaluates to `-1`. In `tensor_shape.cc:361`, `TensorShapeBase::dim_size(int d)` calls `CHECK_GE(d, 0)`. When `d = -1`, the `CHECK` fails and calls `abort()`, killing the process.

Likewise:
- In `QrOpGpu`, `input.dim_size(ndims - 2)`, `input.dim_size(ndims - 1)`, and `input.template flat_inner_dims<Scalar, 3>()` were called before `OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(context, ndims >= 2, ...)`.
- In `MatrixSolveOpGpu`, `input.dim_size(ndims - 1)` and `rhs.dim_size(ndims - 1)` were called before `OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(context, ndims >= 2, ...)` and `OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(context, rhs.dims() == ndims, ...)`.

In contrast, other GPU kernels (e.g. `svd_op_gpu.cu.cc:356`, `lu_op_gpu.cu.cc:94`, and `self_adjoint_eig_v2_op_gpu.cc:51`) and CPU kernels (via `LinearAlgebraOp::AnalyzeInputs`) validate `ndims >= 2` before indexing into inner dimensions.

### Solution
Hoist `OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(context, ndims >= 2, ...)` (and `OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(context, rhs.dims() == ndims, ...)` in `MatrixSolveOpGpu`) before accessing `dim_size(ndims - 1)` or `dim_size(ndims - 2)` across:
- `tensorflow/core/kernels/linalg/determinant_op.cc` (`DeterminantOpGpu` and `LogDeterminantOpGpu`)
- `tensorflow/core/kernels/linalg/cholesky_op_gpu.cu.cc` (`CholeskyOpGpu`)
- `tensorflow/core/kernels/linalg/matrix_inverse_op.cc` (`MatrixInverseOpGpu`)
- `tensorflow/core/kernels/linalg/matrix_solve_op.cc` (`MatrixSolveOpGpu`)
- `tensorflow/core/kernels/linalg/qr_op_impl.h` (`QrOpGpu`)

This ensures rank validation runs first, returning a standard `InvalidArgumentError` instead of terminating the process with `SIGABRT`.

### Testing
Added `testInvalidRank` tests across graph and eager modes with `use_gpu=True` covering rank 0 (scalar) and rank 1 (vector) inputs across:
- `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/linalg/determinant_op_test.py`
- `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/linalg/cholesky_op_test.py`
- `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/linalg/matrix_inverse_op_test.py`
- `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/linalg/matrix_solve_op_test.py`
- `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/linalg/qr_op_test.py`

All lines adhere to Google C++ and Python style guidelines (<= 80 characters per line).

Fixes #76730.

issues.title: Add TensorFlow PR Review Agent workflow and implementation

labels.name: size:XL
labels.description: CL Change Size:Extra Large

issues.body:
## Description

This PR introduces an automated TensorFlow PR Review Agent for reviewing pull request changes using static analysis and semantic review.

The agent combines:

Pylint analysis for modified Python files
Gemini-based semantic review using Google ADK
TensorFlow-specific review guidelines
Structured GitHub pull request reviews
Commit-level idempotency
Re-review support for new commits
Gemini model fallback handling

## Workflow

The review is triggered when the N**eeds Review** label is applied to a pull request.

The workflow:

1. Retrieves the pull request metadata and diff.
2. Categorizes the pull request.
3. Runs Pylint on modified Python files.
4. Performs semantic review using Gemini.
5. Validates the generated findings.
6. Posts a structured review to the pull request.

The agent also tracks the reviewed commit SHA to avoid duplicate reviews of the same commit and supports re-review when a new commit is pushed.

## Security

The workflow uses **pull_request_target** with the trusted repository workflow.

PR changes are inspected without checking out or executing PR-controlled code. Modified Python files are materialized into an isolated temporary directory for Pylint analysis with path validation and the trusted TensorFlow Pylint configuration.

The Gemini API key is provided through the GitHub Actions secret **API_NEEDS_REVIEW** and is not stored in the repository.

## Validation

The implementation was validated in a private sandbox with:

Commit-level idempotency testing
Pylint integration and diff filtering
Gemini model fallback testing
End-to-end review flow testing
New-commit re-review testing

The validation suite completed successfully with 18/18 tests passing in a clean Python 3.11.11 environment using the exact pinned dependency versions.
Validation was performed with:
- python 3.11.11
- google-adk==2.9.1
- google-genai==2.24.0
- requests==2.34.2
- python-dotenv==1.2.3
- pylint==3.3.9

The complete test suite passed with 18/18 tests passing.

## Review Event

The current implementation maps the generated overall assessment to GitHub review events:

No actionable review comments → APPROVE
Changes required → REQUEST_CHANGES
Otherwise → COMMENT

Thanks!

issues.title: Enable libnvjitlink unconditionally in XLA.
issues.body:
Enable libnvjitlink unconditionally in XLA.

Previously, libnvjitlink support was gated behind the `enable_libnvjitlink_support` build flag (which defaulted to `false` in OSS) and split across `nvjitlink_impl` and `nvjitlink_stub` targets. Because all supported CUDA versions now include libnvjitlink, the conditional build graph is no longer needed.

Compile xla/stream_executor/cuda/nvjitlink.cc unconditionally in //xla/stream_executor/cuda:nvjitlink and remove the `enable_libnvjitlink_support` build flag, `libnvjitlink_support_enabled` config setting, and xla/stream_executor/cuda/nvjitlink_stub.cc. Keep //xla/stream_executor/cuda:nvjitlink_support only to disable libnvjitlink under MemorySanitizer.

To support OSS wheel builds that dynamically load CUDA libraries via stubs, add //xla/tsl/cuda:nvjitlink (backed by xla/tsl/cuda/nvjitlink_stub.cc and `GetNvJitLinkDsoHandle()` in xla/tsl/platform/default/dso_loader.cc). In `kAuto` compilation mode, check `GetNvJitLinkVersion()` before `LoadedNvJitLinkHasKnownIssues()` so stub builds without `libnvJitLink.so` at runtime fall back cleanly to `ptxas` and `nvlink`.

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49271

📝 Summary of Changes
Upgrade the vendored curl pin from **8.21.0** to **8.22.0** so `@curl` still builds against the current tarball.

- Bump the archive pin in `workspace2.bzl` (`https://curl.se/download/curl-8.22.0.tar.gz`, `strip_prefix = curl-8.22.0`, SHA256 `d54dd598bf05927a726deb38df31c6a255ba83ff1de57c5d1464dac3ed8f44a1`).

issues.title: Expand kShuffle permute instructions into a gather in the shuffle expander.
issues.body:
Expand kShuffle permute instructions into a gather in the shuffle expander.

Extend `ShuffleExpander` to expand `ShuffleMode::Permute` shuffles, allowing
compiler pipelines to lower them into known ops when target backends do not
provide a native permute lowering.

Specifically, this commit introduces:
* **ShuffleExpander (`shuffle_expander.h/cc`)**: Expand `kShuffle::kPermute`
  instructions into a single `kGather` of unit slices, which takes one element
  of the operand per element of the result. The gather needs a coordinate for
  every dimension, so the start indices are built from the permute `indices`:
  they are converted to a type that holds every dimension size, reshaped and
  broadcast to hold one coordinate per shuffled dimension for every element of
  the result, and concatenated with a `kIota` for each dimension that the
  shuffle leaves in place. Shuffling every dimension in order skips that and
  gathers on the indices directly.
* **Testing**: Add unit tests in `ShuffleExpanderTest` covering one shuffled
  dimension, every dimension in and out of order, rank 1 operands,
  non-adjacent shuffled dimensions, and narrow index types.

Reverts 2484ff68384d85b2e879a437133caa2658de226f

issues.body:
Expand kShuffle multi_rotate instructions into a gather in the shuffle expander.

Extend `ShuffleExpander` to expand `ShuffleMode::MultiRotate` shuffles, allowing
compiler pipelines to lower them into known ops when target backends do not
provide a native multi-rotate lowering.

Specifically, this commit introduces:
* **ShuffleExpander (`shuffle_expander.h/cc`)**: Expand
  `kShuffle::kMultiRotate` instructions through the same `kGather` that
  `kShuffle::kPermute` expands into. Every multi-rotate can be rewritten as a
  permute, so the `multi_shifts` are materialized at compile time into the
  indices of the permute that moves the elements the same way
  (`shuffle::GetMultiRotatePermuteIndices`), giving a
  multi-rotate -> permute -> gather pipeline.
* **Testing**: Add unit tests in `ShuffleExpanderTest` covering an outer
  rotated dimension, the innermost rotated dimension, and rank 1 operands.

issues.body:
[XLA] Keep loop-carried copies for recurrent accumulators under disjoint regions.

xla_disjoint_read_write_regions on a while loop lets copy insertion elide the
defensive loop-carried copy. That is unsafe for a recurrent accumulator, whose
dynamic-update-slice update value is computed from a dynamic-slice of the same
buffer. Detect that read-modify-write cycle via reachability and keep the copy
for such slots; every other slot still honours the attribute.

issues.title: PR #49376: [GPU] Rewrite copies of large constant fills before copy fusion
issues.body:
PR #49376: [GPU] Rewrite copies of large constant fills before copy fusion

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49376

## Summary of changes

Replace entry-computation copies of large constant-fill fusions with independent fills, in a small GPU pass immediately after `CopyInsertion` and before `CopyFusion`.

For `early = consumer(copy(fill()))` and `late = consumer(fill())`, the early consumer receives its own fill. The scheduler can delay the original initializer until the later consumer, while retaining separate writable buffers. An unused original fill is removed during replacement.


Before:
```
  init  = fusion()         // body: constant -> broadcast
  copy  = copy(init)
  early = consumer(copy)
  late  = consumer(init)
```
After:
```
  clone = fusion()         // cloned constant -> broadcast
  early = consumer(clone)
  init  = fusion()         // original fill
  late  = consumer(init)
```

In the before pattern, copy(init) forces the shared initializer to be materialized for early, and its buffer must remain live until late. If the consumers are far apart, that long lifetime can overlap other large allocations and increase peak memory.

The rewrite only accepts direct, identical-shape/layout copies of zero-operand loop fusions containing a scalar literal and its broadcast. It preserves the 1 MiB threshold and rejects relevant control dependencies and sharding.

## Justification and contribution

Memory optimization for shared initialization buffers used by separated consumers, including activation and accumulation buffers in pipelined workloads. 

| GA | Initial GiB/GPU, disabled → enabled | Post-PGLE GiB/GPU, disabled → enabled | Median step seconds, disabled → enabled |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 70.90 → 70.90 | 68.84 → 71.03 | 1.013 → 1.009 |
| 3 | 83.00 → 80.15 | 82.40 → 72.47 | 1.498 → 1.512 |
| 16 | 82.45 → 79.59 | 81.09 → 71.71 | 8.060 → 8.048 |

Memory is compiled buffer assignment per GPU. Timings are medians of steps 8–14 from single paired runs; PGLE profiles and schedules vary, so these do not establish a precise performance difference. GA2 maximum logged loss difference: 0.001. GA3 maximum logged loss difference: 0.000. GA16 maximum logged loss difference: 0.000. 

HLO confirms that the paired 3 GiB attention initializers become independent single-output fills. After PGLE, the late fill moves after the middle loop in both GA3 and GA16. The initial schedule delays it but still retains it across that loop.

## Validation


```text
bazel test -c opt --repo_env=HERMETIC_PYTHON_VERSION=3.12 \
  //xla/backends/gpu/transforms:constant_fill_copy_rewriter_test \
  //xla/backends/gpu/transforms:copy_fusion_test \
  //xla/service/gpu:pre_scheduling_copy_insertion_pipeline
```



Copybara import of the project:

--
5d57c1bd8dc8a9d8370685a86d36b79afac99fd8 by Shaogang Wang <shawnw@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Rewrite copies of large constant fills before copy fusion

Add a local entry-computation rewrite after copy insertion so copies of large scalar-constant fill fusions can be initialized independently. Preserve separate writable values and let scheduling shorten initializer live ranges.

Keep the 1 MiB threshold and legality guards, without consumer traversal or changes to CopyFusion. Test the rewrite, rejection cases, pipeline compatibility, and reduced scheduled peak memory.

--
71d315502e2543c30c15093e3a463162013c43fc by Shaogang Wang <shawnw@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Remove the orphaned fill computation in ConstantFillCopyRewriter

Replacing copy(fill) with a fresh fill removes the original fusion
instruction when the copy was its last user, but removing an instruction
only clears its pointer to the fused computation and never deletes the
computation itself. Nothing between this pass and the end of the
pre-scheduling copy-insertion pipeline prunes computations, so the dead
fill body reached module dumps, FusionWrapper, and the scheduler until a
later HloDCE dropped it.

Call RemoveUnusedComputations when the pass changed anything, and assert
in the removal test that the fill body is gone and the module holds only
the entry computation and the cloned fill body.

--
1577e42d8454da8e69c4e3e1c6c855b715255f83 by Shaogang Wang <shawnw@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Carry copy annotations onto the rematerialized fill

The rewriter replaces any copy of a fill, not only the ones CopyInsertion
adds. A pre-existing copy can carry a scheduling group id, a stream
assignment in its backend config, or provenance metadata, and the cloned
fill silently dropped all of it because ReplaceInstruction only copies
these when the new instruction has none of its own.

Merge the copy's frontend attributes, metadata, and GpuBackendConfig into
the clone before the replacement, letting the copy's populated fields win
on conflict while the fill keeps its own fusion config and unrelated
attributes. Add a test covering conflicting and disjoint annotations.

Also replace the hand-written scalar-constant-broadcast check with
hlo_query::IsBroadcastOfScalarConstant, and drop the control-dependency
guards on instructions inside the fused body: HloComputation::Clone
preserves internal control edges, so they never affected the rewrite.
The parameterized test case that existed only to exercise them is
removed with them.

--
6e0107bf84d71de879cb4877bfbcd4ebeb3cddd8 by Shaogang Wang <shawnw@nvidia.com>:

[GPU] Address review comments in ConstantFillCopyRewriter

Reuse the fill directly when the copy is its only use and clone only when
other users keep the original alive, so no fusion body is ever orphaned
and RemoveUnusedComputations is no longer needed.

Leave a copy alone when every use of its fill reaches the copy's sole
consumer: all of those buffers are live there regardless, so a separate
fill would only add a launch and let the scheduler pull it away from the
consumer. CopyFusion then folds the copy into the fill as before.

Look through a single-user, bitwidth-preserving bitcast between the copy
and the fill, as CopyFusion does, so such copies are not fused back into
the fill. The copy becomes a bitcast of the cloned fill, or is replaced by
the existing bitcast when nothing else uses it.

Drop TransferCopyAnnotations: copies from CopyInsertion carry no
annotations, Clone keeps the fill's own, and ReplaceInstruction copies the
rest when the replacement has none.


Merging this change closes #49376

issues.title: Fix uninitialized memory output in SparseSegmentGrad ops for empty inputs

labels.name: size:S
labels.description: CL Change Size: Small

labels.name: prtype:bugfix
labels.description: PR to fix a bug

issues.body:
When inputs to `sparse_segment_sum`, `sparse_segment_mean`, or `sparse_segment_sqrt_n` are empty (`indices = []` and `segment_ids = []`), their corresponding gradient ops (`SparseSegmentSumGrad`, `SparseSegmentMeanGrad`, `SparseSegmentSqrtNGrad`) return uninitialized dirty memory from the allocator pool instead of zeros. Reported in #72785.

### Reproducer
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.python.ops import gen_math_ops

# Dirty allocator memory pool
for _ in range(5):
    a = tf.fill([500, 400], 42.0)
    del a

grad = tf.ones([0, 400], dtype=tf.float32)
out = gen_math_ops.sparse_segment_sum_grad(
    grad=grad,
    indices=tf.constant([], dtype=tf.int32),
    segment_ids=tf.constant([], dtype=tf.int32),
    output_dim0=500,
)

# Returns tensor of shape [500, 400] filled with 42.0! (200,000 uninitialized floats)
print("Dirty value count:", (out.numpy() == 42.0).sum(), "out of", out.numpy().size)
# Output: Dirty value count: 200000 out of 200000
```

### Root Cause
In `tensorflow/core/kernels/segment_reduction_ops_impl.h`, `SparseSegmentGradOpBase::Compute` allocates the output tensor buffer:
```cpp
TensorShape output_shape = input.shape();
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, output_shape.SetDimWithStatus(0, M));
Tensor* output = nullptr;
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, context->allocate_output(0, output_shape, &output));
if (M == 0 || N == 0) return;
```
`context->allocate_output` obtains an uninitialized buffer from the memory allocator. When `N == 0` (empty `indices` and `segment_ids`) and `M = output_dim0 > 0`, the kernel returned immediately at line 1345 without zeroing the allocated buffer.
Since no indices were gathered during the forward pass, the true mathematical gradient with respect to `data` is zero. In training loops (such as embedding lookup layers with sparse/empty features), returning uninitialized memory causes silent weight corruption where embedding tables are updated with garbage values from prior operations.

### Solution
In `tensorflow/core/kernels/segment_reduction_ops_impl.h`:
1. Included `#include "tensorflow/core/kernels/fill_functor.h"`.
2. Updated the return condition in `SparseSegmentGradOpBase::Compute`:
```cpp
if (M == 0) return;
if (N == 0) {
  functor::SetZeroFunctor<Device, T> set_zero;
  set_zero(context->eigen_device<Device>(), output->flat<T>());
  return;
}
```
- If $M == 0$, the output tensor has 0 elements, so returning is a no-op.
- If $N == 0$ and $M > 0$, `functor::SetZeroFunctor<Device, T>` sets the output tensor to zero across both CPU and GPU devices.

### Testing
- Added regression test `testGradientEmptyIndicesAndSegmentIds` to `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/math_ops/segment_reduction_ops_test.py` verifying that `SparseSegmentSumGrad`, `SparseSegmentMeanGrad`, and `SparseSegmentSqrtNGrad` produce exact zero-filled tensors across `float16`, `float32`, and `float64` for both $M > 0$ and $M == 0$.
- All tests pass cleanly.

Fixes #72785.

issues.title: Compile only the taken branch of an If with a constant predicate

labels.name: awaiting review
labels.description: Pull request awaiting review

labels.name: size:M
labels.description: CL Change Size: Medium

labels.name: prtype:bugfix
labels.description: PR to fix a bug

issues.body:
Fixes #128039. Root cause of openxla/xla#49328 and openxla/xla#49130.

`XlaIfOp` compiles both branches of a conditional even when its predicate is a compile-time constant, and joins them with `xla::DynamicConditional`. When the branches have different static output shapes, that pads them to a common bounded-dynamic shape, so an `If` that can only ever take one branch still produces a dynamically shaped result. Downstream ops that cannot handle dynamic dimensions then fail. `tf.image.rot90` builds exactly this, a case over `k` whose branches return `[H,W,C]` or `[W,H,C]`, which is why `rot90` followed by `fftshift` or `idct` fails under `jit_compile=True` for every `k`.

`XlaCaseOp` already avoids this: `GetPrunedBranchesAndIndex` compiles only the selected branch when the branch index is a compile-time constant. This does the same for `If`, `StatelessIf` and `XlaIf`.

## Change

When `ctx->ConstantInput(0, ...)` resolves the predicate, compile the taken branch and use it for both sides of the conditional. Everything after that is unchanged and sees two identical results: tensor-array gradient collection, `ValidateShapes`, token handling and resource updates. The second compilation is a hit in `XlaCompiler`'s function cache, and the conditional now has matching static branch shapes, so `DynamicConditional` has nothing to pad. When the predicate is not a compile-time constant, nothing changes.

Nested conditionals are covered without extra work. `PropagateConstIntoIfNode` already bakes constant inputs into each branch body as it rewrites it into a `*_const_*` function, so the inner `If` ops that `rot90` builds for `k=2` and `k=3` also see a literal constant predicate and are pruned in turn.

## Tests

Two tests in `tensorflow/compiler/tests/cond_test.py`, compiled as whole functions with `jit_compile=True` in eager mode. That is what makes the predicate a compile-time constant; compiling the `If` alone under `test_scope()` passes the predicate as a parameter, so a graph-mode test would pass with or without this change.

- `testIfBranchIsPruned`: a constant-true `tf.cond` whose else branch returns the result of an op with no XLA kernel. Mirrors `case_test.py::testBranchIsPruned`. The unsupported op's result is returned so it cannot be pruned as dead code before reaching XLA.
- `testConstantPredicateKeepsTakenBranchShape`: `fftshift(rot90(x, k))` for `x` of shape `[2,16,3]` and `k` in 0..3, compared against eager.

Both fail on tf-nightly 2.22.0-dev20260921:

```
testIfBranchIsPruned: InvalidArgumentError: Detected unsupported operations when trying to compile graph cond_false_4[] on XLA_CPU_JIT: ReadFile
testConstantPredicateKeepsTakenBranchShape: UnimplementedError: Dynamic dimension propagation on DynamicSlice where a partial dimension is selected %fftshift.39 = f64[16,<=16,3]
```

Both pass with this change, in the default and the MLIR bridge variants.

## Verification

Built from master at `9edd58f` with this change, as the Linux aarch64 wheel, in the `ml-build-arm64` CI image with `--config=release_arm64_linux`, and compared against tf-nightly 2.22.0-dev20260921 in the same container. This branch is on current master; `if_op.cc` and `cond_test.py` are unchanged between the two, and the `BUILD` change applied without conflict. Results:

- The repro now returns `(16, 2, 3)` under XLA, matching eager.
- `rot90` followed by `fftshift` or `idct`, for `k` in `{-1, 0, 1, 2, 3}` on rank 3 and rank 4 inputs, matches eager in 20 of 20 cases, up from 0 of 20. That covers the nested predicates for `k=2` and `k=3`.
- The pre-optimization HLO of the repro:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| entry result | `f64[16,16,3]` | `f64[16,2,3]` |
| rot90 conditional | `(f64[<=16,<=16,3])`, `dynamic_builder` branches | `(f64[16,2,3])`, the taken branch on both sides |
| Roll's `dynamic-slice` | `f64[16,<=16,3]`, sizes `{16,16,3}` | `f64[16,2,3]`, sizes `{16,2,3}` |
| bounded-dynamic dimensions in the module | 35 | 0 |

- With `TF_CPP_VMODULE=xla_compiler=1`, the taken branch is compiled once and the second `CompileFunction` for it returns from the cache; the untaken branch is never compiled.
- `cond_test`, `case_test`, `eager_test` and `jit_test`, run before and after: the only status changes are the two new tests going from failing to passing. `tensor_array_ops_test` is `run_v1_only`, so it is skipped in both.
- Cases that exercise the rest of `XlaIfOp` all match eager after the change: a predicate only known at run time, which still compiles both branches; a constant `False`; a predicate that is constant only through value inference; a resource variable updated differently in each branch, where only the taken branch's update is applied; a TensorArray written in both branches; and nested constant predicates with differing branch shapes, which failed before.

## Not in this change

- `RollOp` still cannot handle a genuinely dynamic input, such as a runtime `k` or a `tf.where`-shaped tensor. With a runtime `k` it fails the same way; with a `tf.where` input it silently returns a wrong result. That needs `RollOp` to handle bounded-dynamic dimensions and is a separate change.
- XLA's rejection of partial dynamic slices is correct and is not touched. Relaxing it would make this case compile to a wrong result.

issues.title: XLA compiles both branches of a `tf.cond` with a constant predicate, turning static shapes dynamic (breaks `tf.image.rot90` under `jit_compile=True`)

labels.name: type:bug
labels.description: Bug

labels.name: comp:xla
labels.description: XLA

labels.name: awaiting PR merge
labels.description: awaiting PR merge
tensorflow 2.21.0

issues.body:
### Issue type

Bug

### TensorFlow version

tf-nightly 2.22.0-dev20260921 (`v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f`), CPU. Reproduced on both macOS arm64 and Linux aarch64.

### Current behavior?

`tf.image.rot90` followed by an op that cannot take a dynamically shaped input fails to compile under `jit_compile=True`, even though every shape involved is static and `k` is a constant. This is the tf2xla root cause behind openxla/xla#49328 (`rot90` → `tf.signal.fftshift`) and openxla/xla#49130 (`rot90` → `tf.signal.idct`), which surface as different XLA errors from the same cause.

It is not limited to the default `k=1`. For `k` in `{-1, 0, 1, 2, 3}`, on rank 3 and rank 4 inputs, and with either `fftshift` or `idct` downstream, all 20 combinations fail under XLA while eager succeeds.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```python
import tensorflow as tf
x = tf.random.uniform([2, 16, 3], dtype=tf.float64)
def f(x):
  return tf.signal.fftshift(tf.image.rot90(x))
print(f(x).shape)                    # eager: (16, 2, 3)
tf.function(f, jit_compile=True)(x)  # XLA: UnimplementedError
```

```
UnimplementedError: Dynamic dimension propagation on DynamicSlice where a partial dimension is selected %fftshift.39 = f64[16,<=16,3]{2,1,0} dynamic-slice(%fftshift.36, %fftshift.38, %fftshift.37, %fftshift.37), dynamic_slice_sizes={16,16,3}, metadata={op_type="Roll" op_name="fftshift" ...}
```

### Root cause

Confirmed from the pre-optimization HLO (`--xla_dump_to`) and the tf2xla source:

1. `rot90` builds a `control_flow_case.case` over `k`, which becomes nested `If` ops. Their branches have different static shapes: `[16,2,3]` for odd `k`, `[2,16,3]` for even `k`.
2. The outer predicate reaches `XlaIfOp` as a literal constant, `%cond.23 = pred[] constant(true)`. The nested predicates are literal constants too inside their branch bodies (`%cond.13 = pred[] constant(false)`), because `PropagateConstIntoIfNode` rewrites each branch into a `*_const_*` function with its constant inputs baked in.
3. `XlaIfOp::Compile` (`tensorflow/compiler/tf2xla/kernels/if_op.cc`) nonetheless always compiles both branches and joins them with `xla::DynamicConditional`, which pads the mismatched shapes to a common bound. So a conditional with a constant-true predicate yields a dynamic `f64[<=16,<=16,3]`:

   ```
   %cond.23 = pred[] constant(true)
   %cond.24 = (f64[<=16,<=16,3]) conditional(%cond.23, %cond.22, %cond.22), true_computation=%dynamic_builder.4, false_computation=%dynamic_builder.14
   ```

   `XlaCaseOp` does not have this problem: `GetPrunedBranchesAndIndex` compiles only the selected branch when the index is a compile-time constant.
4. `fftshift` lowers to `Roll` with shifts from `tf.shape`, which become `get-dimension-size`. `RollOp` (`roll_op.cc`) takes the axis length and slice size from `InputShape`, which is the bound (16), and emits `concatenate` then `dynamic-slice(sizes = bounds)`. XLA's dynamic-dimension inference rejects a partial slice of a dynamic dimension, which is the error above.

The check in XLA is correct and should not be relaxed. For this input the runtime length of dimension 1 is 2, but the slice starts at `16 - (1 mod 16) = 15`, reading padding. The compiled module's result type is a static `f64[16,16,3]` instead of `[16,2,3]`.

The same happens with an untaken branch that XLA cannot compile at all: a constant-true `tf.cond` whose else branch uses an op without an XLA kernel fails with `Detected unsupported operations when trying to compile graph cond_false_…`, although that branch can never run.

### Related, separate

`RollOp` also returns a wrong result without any error when its input really is dynamically shaped, for example from `tf.where`:

```python
v = tf.range(10, dtype=tf.float32)
f = lambda t: tf.roll(tf.gather(t, tf.where(t > 3.)[:, 0]), 1, 0)
f(v)                                  # [9. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8.]
tf.function(f, jit_compile=True)(v)   # [7. 8. 9. 0. 0. 0. 0. 0. 0. 0.]
```

This is independent of the conditional problem above and needs `RollOp` to handle bounded-dynamic dimensions; happy to file it on its own.

issues.title: Return 0 from the zero branch of the xlogy/xlog1py/xdivy GPU kernels

labels.description: Pull request awaiting review

labels.name: size:M
labels.description: CL Change Size: Medium

issues.body:
Fixes #127913. Follow-up to #127946, which fixed the CPU kernels for the same ops.

On GPU, `xdivy`, `xlogy` and `xlog1py` do not run the Eigen functors in `cwise_ops.h`. They run the MLIR-generated kernels built from `tensorflow/core/kernels/mlir_generated/op_definitions/*.mlir.tmpl`, and those select `x` itself in the zero branch:

```
%21 = chlo.broadcast_compare %19, %5 {comparison_direction = EQ}   // x == 0
%22 = chlo.broadcast_divide %19, %20                               // x / y
%23 = chlo.broadcast_select %21, %19, %22                          // x == 0 ? x : x / y
```

So `-0` comes back as `-0`. The GPU kernels also flush denormals, so a subnormal `x` compares equal to zero and is returned unchanged, which is the `1e-40` reported in #127913. The CUDA CI jobs on #127946 showed both, before its tests were scoped to CPU: on GPU they returned `-0`, and `2.938736e-39` for a subnormal input.

## Changes

- **The six kernel templates** (`xdivy`, `xlogy`, `xlog1py` and their `_cmplx` variants): all 48 selects now take the zero constant that the comparison already uses, rather than `x`. Every rewrite was made by a script that first checked the select's condition is `chlo.broadcast_compare %x, %5 {EQ}` and that its `on_true` operand is that same `%x`.
- **`xlog1py_cmplx` compared `x` against `1+0j` instead of `0`.** Its `%5` was `dense<(1.0, 0.0)>` and is used only as that comparison operand, so the complex kernel selects `x` and returns `1` for `xlog1py(1, y)` whatever `y` is, and for `xlog1py(0, -1)` computes `0 * log1p(-1)`, which is `nan`. That is from reading the template; the new test checks both on GPU. It is now zero, like the other five templates.
- **`BinaryXopyPat` in `lower_tf.td`**, the TF-dialect lowering the templates follow, selects `$zero` instead of `$x`. This mirrors `BinaryNoNanPat` directly above it, which lowers `div_no_nan` and `mul_no_nan` the same way. The `lower_tf.mlir` checks, which asserted the old operand, are updated.

This matches TensorFlow's other implementations of these ops: the tf2xla kernels in `binary_ops.cc` already select `ZerosLike(x)`, and the Eigen scalar path returns `0`.

## Tests

A new `XopsGpuKernelTest` in `math_ops_test.py`, run only on GPU (`run_gpu_only` with `force_gpu`), so that it tests the generated kernels and does not depend on #127946:

- `-0` gives `+0` for all three ops, in float16, float32 and float64.
- `xdivy` of a subnormal by itself is `0` or `1`, never the subnormal.
- Complex `xlog1py(1, 1)` is `log 2` and `xlog1py(0, -1)` is `0`.

It is placed apart from the classes #127946 extends, and #127946's test changes still apply cleanly on top of this branch.

## Verification

I do not have a GPU, so the numerics are left to the CUDA CI jobs. What I could check, building in the `ml-build-arm64` CI image:

- `//tensorflow/compiler/mlir/tensorflow/tests:lower_tf.mlir.test` passes.
- Every GPU instantiation of the six templates, 15 combinations of template and dtype, instantiated with the same substitutions as `build_defs.bzl`, parses and verifies with `kernel-gen-opt` and lowers with `--chlo-legalize-to-hlo`, both before and after this change. After lowering, the rewritten selects become `mhlo.select` with the scalar zero broadcast in through `mhlo.dynamic_broadcast_in_dim`.
- The new tests skip cleanly on a machine without a GPU.

That verification was run on master at `9edd58f` with this exact diff applied, because the nine files touched here are identical there and at this branch's base, and the build cache matched that commit.

issues.title: [XLA] Fix while-loop buffer double counting in NoFragmentationStatsHeap.
issues.body:
[XLA] Fix while-loop buffer double counting in NoFragmentationStatsHeap.

Previously, NoFragmentationStatsHeap::ShareWith only delegated to Alloc, which caused shared buffers (such as while-loop init/parameter/result/root tuples) and reused operand buffers to be double counted in current_heap_size_.

Track shared buffers via a disjoint-set union with path compression (FindRoot) and reference counting in NoFragmentationStatsHeap so that memory is counted once per shared buffer group and deallocated only when the last reference is freed.

issues.body:
## Summary

Fixes #127753.

Include the aliasing pattern of primal inputs and packed tangents in the
`ConcreteFunction` forward/backward function cache key.

JVP wrappers capture external tensors by identity. When several inputs refer to
the same tensor, the generated graph's capture mapping reflects that sharing.
Previously, the cache key included tangent indices but not tensor sharing, so a
later call with distinct tangents could reuse a graph built for shared tangents.
This produces incorrect derivatives, including the reported `2.4` instead of
`4.2` for the nested forward derivative of `(m * m) * m` at `x = 0.7`.

The new key records normalized alias indices, not actual tensor IDs, so fresh
tensors with the same sharing pattern still reuse the generated functions. The
alias key is only computed when input tangents are present.

Regression coverage includes:
- Switching between shared and distinct tangents in both orders, with and without
  an active reverse-mode tape, and checking cache reuse with fresh tensors.
- Nested forward derivatives of reused identity, sine, and square intermediates
  in float32/float64, with eager and `tf.function` execution.
- The reused matrix intermediate from the issue.

## Validation

Local validation used Python 3.13 on macOS arm64 with
`tf-nightly==2.22.0.dev20260923`. The source test modules were loaded against the
installed runtime, with the exact edited
`ConcreteFunction._select_forward_and_backward_functions` method compiled from
the checkout and installed on the runtime class. This is not a full source build.

- New regressions: **18 passed**; **10 fail** without the patch.
- Source `forwardprop_test.py`: **93 passed, 4 skipped, 2 baseline failures** out
  of 99. Both remaining failures occur with and without this patch:
  `testNonTensorInputs` and `testShapeMismatchRaisesError`. The Nightly wheel
  lacks the newer input-validation behavior expected by those source tests.
- Source `polymorphic_function/gradients_test.py`: **42 passed, 2 skipped**.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

Bazel and GPU validation were not run locally. The relevant source-build targets
for CI are:

```sh
bazel test //tensorflow/python/eager:forwardprop_test \
  //tensorflow/python/eager/polymorphic_function:gradients_test
```

issues.title: Preserve metadata payloads when normalizing GPU executable backend configs.
issues.body:
Preserve metadata payloads when normalizing GPU executable backend configs.

`HloModuleProto.payloads` is shared by `backend_config_payload` and `OpMetadata.metadata_payload`. `NormalizeBackendConfig` in the split GPU executable writer rebuilt the payload table from normalized backend configs only and then replaced the module's table, dropping every interned metadata string. The serialized executable was left with dangling metadata payload IDs, so loading an AOT-compiled executable failed in `InlineMetadataPayloadsFromProtoPayloadTable` with "Invalid metadata payload id N with payloads size M".

Re-intern metadata payload strings into the new deduplicated table and remap their IDs alongside the backend configs, returning an error for out-of-range IDs instead of indexing out of bounds.
