issues.body:
PR #49271: Upgrade curl to 8.22.0.

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49271

📝 Summary of Changes
Upgrade the vendored curl pin from **8.21.0** to **8.22.0** so `@curl` still builds against the current tarball.

- Bump the archive pin in `workspace2.bzl` (`https://curl.se/download/curl-8.22.0.tar.gz`, `strip_prefix = curl-8.22.0`, SHA256 `d54dd598bf05927a726deb38df31c6a255ba83ff1de57c5d1464dac3ed8f44a1`).
- Refresh `third_party/curl.BUILD` for the 8.22.0 layout:
  - DNS sources moved to `lib/vdns/` (`asyn-*`, `cf-dns`, `dnscache`, `doh`, `hostip*`, `httpsrr`)
  - add `lib/api`, `lib/http_httpsig` (RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures), `lib/curl_ed25519`, `lib/uint-hashset`
  - drop removed `lib/config-riscos.h`
  - add `src/toolx/tool_time` for the curl binary
- No `CurlHttpRequest` / `LibCurl` API changes. The 8.21.0 integration still applies (`CURLOPT_UPLOAD`, `uint64_t` wrapper with `long` casts in `LibCurlProxy`).

🎯 Justification
XLA/TSL uses libcurl for cloud HTTP (`CurlHttpRequest`: GCS and related object-store traffic). Staying on 8.21.0 leaves that path on a release with published libcurl CVEs that 8.22.0 fixes, including HTTP/2 server-push UAF ([CVE-2026-18924](https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2026-18924.html)), connection-reuse / auth issues, cookie-policy bypasses, and TLS pinning / CA-store flaws. The explicit `curl.BUILD` source list must move with the tarball or `@curl` fails to compile.

Follow-up to #47219 (8.21.0). Changelog: https://curl.se/ch/8.22.0.html

♻️ Cleanup

N/A — third-party pin / BUILD refresh only; no compiler change.

None added. Existing `//xla/tsl/platform/cloud:curl_http_request_test` still covers the wrapper; no CurlHttpRequest behavior change.

issues.title: [XLA] Reuse a reachability map while its computation is unchanged
issues.body:
[XLA] Reuse a reachability map while its computation is unchanged

HloReachabilityMap::Build computes the transitive closure of a
computation as an n by n bit matrix. For a 237k instruction computation
that is 7 GB and 1.7 s. One compile of a large decode module builds 25
maps of that computation, 42 s. Seven of them repeat a build made
earlier in the same pass run and produce the same bits, 10 s.

Build now records the computation, its unique id, its graph epoch and
its local id bound. Every method that edits bits or indices marks the
map edited. IsCurrentFor is true while none of that changed.
BuildOrReuse keeps such a map and otherwise releases it before building
the new one. MultiOutputFusion::RecomputeReachability uses it. The
generic fusion loop asks the subclass for a current map through a
protected hook before building its own. Every write to an input of
Build bumps the epoch or shrinks the bound. A reused map therefore has
the bits and indices a fresh build would have.

Tests: hlo_reachability_test pins reuse on no change, rebuild after each
kind of change including Cleanup, and no reuse after any edit.
instruction_fusion_test pins that the fusion loop uses the map of the
subclass.

issues.title: Fix GPU bucketize op truncation when boundaries contain fractional values

labels.name: awaiting review
labels.description: Pull request awaiting review

labels.name: kokoro:force-run
labels.description: Tests on submitted change

labels.name: ready to pull
labels.description: PR ready for merge process

labels.name: size:M
labels.description: CL Change Size: Medium

labels.name: prtype:bugfix
labels.description: PR to fix a bug

issues.body:
`tf.raw_ops.Bucketize` / `math_ops._bucketize` returns incorrect results on GPU when boundaries contain fractional values and the input tensor has integer dtype (`int32` or `int64`). Reported in #70343.

### Reproducer
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.python.ops.gen_math_ops import bucketize

# input=[0, 1, 2, 3], boundaries=[0.1, 1.1]
with tf.device('/CPU:0'):
  print(bucketize(input=[0, 1, 2, 3], boundaries=[0.1, 1.1]))
  # Returns: [0, 1, 2, 2] (Correct)

with tf.device('/GPU:0'):
  print(bucketize(input=[0, 1, 2, 3], boundaries=[0.1, 1.1]))
  # Returned: [1, 2, 2, 2] (Bug: 0 was placed into bucket 1 instead of 0)
```

### Root Cause
In `tensorflow/core/kernels/bucketize_op_gpu.cu.cc`, `BucketizeCustomKernel` performed boundary comparison at line 66 as follows:
```cpp
if (!(value < static_cast<T>(boundaries[l]))) {
```
The boundaries attribute in `Bucketize` is typed `list(float)`, and `boundaries[l]` is a `float`. When the input type `T` is an integer type (`int32_t` or `int64_t`), `static_cast<T>(boundaries[l])` truncated the floating-point boundary towards zero:
- `static_cast<int32_t>(0.1f)` truncated to `0`
- `static_cast<int32_t>(1.1f)` truncated to `1`

This converted the boundaries `[0.1, 1.1]` into `[0, 1]`. For `value = 0`, the kernel evaluated `!(0 < 0)` $\to$ `true`, falsely concluding that $0 \ge 0.1$ and assigning `0` to bucket 1 instead of bucket 0.

In contrast:
- On CPU (`tensorflow/core/kernels/bucketize_op.cc`), `std::upper_bound` compares `input(i)` (type `T`) against `boundaries_vector` (type `float`), which under C++ arithmetic promotions converts integer inputs to `float` (and `float` boundaries to `double` if input is `double`), preserving fractional boundary precision.
- In XLA (`tensorflow/compiler/tf2xla/kernels/bucketize_op.cc`), inputs are explicitly converted to `F32` (or `F64` if `DT_DOUBLE`).

### Solution
This PR determines the appropriate comparison type `CompType` based on input type `T`:
```cpp
using CompType = typename std::conditional<std::is_same<T, double>::value,
                                           double, float>::type;
```
and evaluates the boundary comparison in `CompType`:
```cpp
if (!(static_cast<CompType>(value) <
      static_cast<CompType>(boundaries[l]))) {
```
- For `double` inputs, `boundaries[l]` is promoted to `double`.
- For `float`, `int32_t`, and `int64_t` inputs, values are promoted to `float`.

This eliminates boundary truncation on GPU and aligns GPU behavior with CPU and XLA implementations.

### Testing
- In `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/math_ops/bucketize_op_test.py`:
  - Added `testIntWithFloatBoundaries` verifying `int32` and `int64` inputs with fractional boundaries `[0.1, 1.1]` (issue #70343 reproducer), negative and positive fractional boundaries `[-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5]`, and near-integer fractional boundaries `[0.999, 1.001]`.
  - Added `testInt64` and `testDouble` to cover all supported dtypes.
  - Enabled `use_gpu=True` in test sessions.
- In `tensorflow/compiler/tests/bucketize_op_test.py`:
  - Added `testIntWithFloatBoundaries` testing `int32` and `int64` under XLA.
- All 10 tests in `bucketize_op_test.py` pass cleanly.

Fixes #70343.

issues.title: [XLA:GPU]: Fix caching issue with kernels when unrolling while loops
issues.body:
[XLA:GPU]: Fix caching issue with kernels when unrolling while loops

When while loops are unrolled the same thunk is called with `Record` multiple times for different loop iterations. Currently `CustomCallRecordState` stored a single sequence of `XLA_FFI_Command*`, so during update only the last recorded sequence of commands was passed to the FFI record API, overwriting the last iteration and leaving earlier iterations of the while loop with stale buffer pointers.

Keying the state by the sink command pointer returned on `RecordCreate` (and passed back via `RecordUpdate::command`) so each unrolled iteration updates its own recorded command sequence.

issues.title: Parse split-proto merge records from a riegeli::Chain without flattening.
issues.body:
Parse split-proto merge records from a riegeli::Chain without flattening.

`HandleProtoMergeRecord` read each record into a flat `absl::string_view` and
then called `MergeFromString`. For records larger than a riegeli buffer (e.g.
an HLO module carrying hundreds of MB of constants) the decoded record spans
several blocks, and producing a flat view forces riegeli to copy it into a
contiguous scratch buffer first.

Read the record as a `riegeli::Chain` instead, which shares the decoded
blocks, and parse it with `riegeli::ParseMessage(..., set_merge(true))`,
which consumes the chain directly.

issues.title: [Build][CUDA/Clang] Scope gpu_prim pass-failed suppression to GPU targets

labels.name: awaiting review
labels.description: Pull request awaiting review

labels.name: size:S
labels.description: CL Change Size: Small

labels.name: comp:core
labels.description: issues related to core part of tensorflow

issues.body:
Under `GOOGLE_CUDA`, `gpu_prim.h` currently contains an unbalanced:

```cpp
#pragma clang diagnostic ignored "-Wpass-failed"
```

Because `gpu_prim.h` is a public header, this changes Clang's diagnostic state for the remainder of every translation unit that includes it. Code appearing after the include can therefore have its own `-Werror=pass-failed` policy silently overridden.

This change removes the pragma from the header and applies `-Wno-pass-failed` through `gpu_copts` on the GPU Bazel targets whose compile actions transitively include `gpu_prim.h`.

The warning suppression is still retained where it is needed for CUDA/CUB compilation, but it no longer leaks from a header into unrelated code in the including translation unit. Target-level compiler options also cover diagnostics emitted during later template instantiation and optimization phases.

All current direct and transitive owners were enumerated: 25 production targets and one GPU test target. `depthwise_conv_op` already used the same target-scoped suppression.

For `gpu_prim_helpers_test`, this also adds an optional trailing `extra_copts` parameter to `tf_gpu_only_cc_test` and forwards it to the generated GPU library. The default preserves all existing call sites.

Fixes #127641

## Testing

- `buildifier -mode=check` passes for all modified BUILD/Starlark files.
- `git diff --check` passes.
- Bazel action queries confirmed that all 128 affected `CppCompile` actions receive `-Wno-pass-failed`.
- An unrelated GPU target (`cast_op_gpu`) receives no such flag.
- All 26 affected targets were successfully built with TensorFlow's hermetic Clang/CUDA configuration (`--config=cuda_clang`), completing 23,217 actions.

issues.title: Reuse the deserialized HLO module when loading an AOT executable.
issues.body:
Reuse the deserialized HLO module when loading an AOT executable.

`GpuAotCompilationResult` already deserializes the `HloModule`, but
`LoadExecutable` deserialized it again via `GpuExecutable::FromProto`. With
large constants (e.g. frozen weights), each deserialization copies every
literal, so loading paid that cost twice.

`GpuExecutable::FromProto` now takes an optional `debug_module`, and the
result passes in the module it already owns. To allow sharing,
`GpuExecutable::Params::debug_module` and the constructor now take a
`std::shared_ptr<HloModule>`, which matches what the base `Executable` stores.
Existing `unique_ptr` callers convert implicitly.

issues.title: Write `ExecutableAndOptionsProto` records uncompressed.
issues.body:
Write `ExecutableAndOptionsProto` records uncompressed.

`serialized_executable` is already a snappy-compressed split
`GpuExecutableProto` (see `WriteSplitGpuExecutable`). Compressing the outer
container again saves no space (dropping it adds 0.06% on a 330 MB
executable), but it costs an extra compression pass on write and a full
decompression pass on load.

Riegeli stores the compression type per chunk, so readers don't change and
existing artifacts still load.

Alternative considered: leave the inner proto uncompressed and compress the
outer one instead. That would mean deciding per use case when to skip
compression, which adds logic for little gain, since the outer proto is
small apart from `serialized_executable`.

Return a ready empty vector from typed JoinFutures on empty input

`Future<std::vector<T>>({})` cannot select the templated converting
constructors of `Future`, because a braced-init-list cannot deduce `U`.

`Map`, `OnReady` or `Await` on it dereferences a null `AsyncValue`.

issues.title: PR #49333: Bump Eigen to pick up the Householder underflow and overflow fixes
issues.body:
PR #49333: Bump Eigen to pick up the Householder underflow and overflow fixes

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49333

Bumps Eigen from `ea13a98` (2026-03-15) to `74ce7e6d` (2026-08-19) to pick up two upstream fixes to `makeHouseholder`, motivated by tensorflow/tensorflow#127912.

## Why

At the current pin, `makeHouseholder` forms each reflector from `tail.unwind().squaredNorm()`. In float32 that loses a vector whose entries square into the subnormal range, and overflows to `inf` for one whose entries square past `FLT_MAX`. Eigen fixed both in August:

- `e8010934` (2026-08-18) Householder: Preserve significant small vector tails
- `74ce7e6d` (2026-08-19) Householder: Preserve reflectors for large components

TensorFlow's CPU `tf.linalg.qr` kernel calls `Eigen::HouseholderQR` directly (`qr_op_impl.h`) and picks up Eigen through this pin, so both symptoms are visible there today on a well-conditioned 2x2 matrix, `scale * [[1, 2], [3, 4]]`:

| scale | `Q @ R` residual at `ea13a98` | at `74ce7e6d` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `1e-22` | `5.469e-01` | `0.000e+00` |
| `1e-20` | `5.477e-01` | `0.000e+00` |
| `1e+00` | `4.867e-08` | `4.867e-08` |
| `1e+19` | `nan` | `0.000e+00` |
| `1e+20` | `nan` | `0.000e+00` |

These come from compiling the same `HouseholderQR<Matrix>` call the TensorFlow kernel makes against each commit, with the three defines from `eigen_archive.BUILD`. The `1e-20` row matches what `tf.linalg.qr` returns in TensorFlow 2.21.0 and the nightly exactly, and TensorFlow 2.21.0 returns an all-NaN `Q @ R` for the `1e19` case.

I bumped to the fix commit rather than to Eigen master to keep the delta as small as possible. It is still 530 upstream commits across 1,923 files. Happy to move it to a later commit if that is preferred.

## Checks

- **Checksum.** `EIGEN_SHA256` is computed from the exact URL the `.bzl` builds, with the commit parsed back out of the edited file. Downloading the current pin the same way reproduces its `35c6126e...` byte for byte, so GitLab's archives are deterministic.
- **`strip_prefix`.** The tarball's top directory is `eigen-74ce7e6d59a83b8fd6a3d7eea7fe1fba72403eb3`.
- **`eigen_archive.BUILD`.** The `src/**` globs still cover every source file: in both versions only `.md` and `.txt` files fall outside them. All three defines the target sets are still referenced by the new sources.
- **Broader smoke test.** Tensor contraction on a `ThreadPoolDevice`, reductions, `half` and `bfloat16` casts, and QR, BDCSVD, self-adjoint eigensolver, LLT and partial-pivot LU all compile with the BUILD defines and give identical results, to the printed digit, at both commits.
- **Mirror.** The `mirror.tensorflow.org` URL will not have this tarball until someone mirrors it; `tf_http_archive` falls back to the GitLab URL in the meantime, as `repo.bzl` describes.

## Needs attention on import

The `LINT.ThenChange` pairs this pin with `tensorflow/lite/tools/cmake/modules/eigen.cmake`, which lives in TensorFlow rather than here. It is on `ea13a98` too, so its `GIT_TAG` should move to `74ce7e6d59a83b8fd6a3d7eea7fe1fba72403eb3` alongside this.

## Not verified

A full XLA or TensorFlow build and test run; I am relying on CI for that, and a 530-commit Eigen range is the main risk here. I also have not checked whether XLA's own CPU QR lowering goes through this Eigen code. In TensorFlow, `jit_compile=True` on CPU shows the same `1e-20` failure, so if that path does not use `makeHouseholder` it needs a separate fix.

issues.body:
[XLA] Allow overriding live range analysis for Buffer Assignment

HloLiveRange for async ops is correct, but pessimistic when it comes to
context shapes. An implementation may define the async computation of
call-start.1 to execute sequentially after the async computation of
call-start.0, in which case there will be no live range overlap between the
two context shapes, hence no interference.

This change introduces `LiveRangeInterferenceOptions` to specify custom
interference rules for buffer assignment and optimizes active allocation
reuse in `FastMerge`.

issues.title: [XLA:GPU][NFC] Make the PriorityFusion decision chain non-blocking
issues.body:
[XLA:GPU][NFC] Make the PriorityFusion decision chain non-blocking

`GetTiledRunTimeDataCached` blocks a thread pool worker in `Await()` while it
waits for the tiling search. That is safe only as long as the cost model
evaluates its candidates inline.

This change converts the whole decision chain to continuation-passing style so
that no thread pool worker ever blocks:

```
GetTiledRunTimeDataCached           -> GetTiledRunTimeDataCachedAsync
CanFuseTriton                       -> CanFuseTritonAsync
CanFuse                             -> CanFuseAsync
CanFuseCached                       -> CanFuseCachedAsync
CanFuseWithAllNonBitcastUsers       -> CanFuseWithAllNonBitcastUsersAsync
FindPossibleConsumersForTriton...   -> ...Async
CalculateProducerPriority           -> CalculateProducerPriorityAsync
```

After this change `PriorityFusion` blocks in exactly two places,
`ComputePriorities` and `DequeueNextProducer`, and both run on the thread
driving `PriorityFusion::Run`, which holds no pool slot. `AwaitFusionDecision`
documents that contract for its two callers.

This change is a no-op since the cost model is still passed a null executor. Enablement will come in a following change.

issues.title: Fix always-true is_gpu check in GraphMemory::InferFromTrace

labels.name: ready to pull
labels.description: PR ready for merge process

labels.name: size:S
labels.description: CL Change Size: Small

labels.name: prtype:bugfix
labels.description: PR to fix a bug

labels.name: comp:core
labels.description: issues related to core part of tensorflow

issues.body:
## Problem

`GraphMemory::InferFromTrace` (`tensorflow/core/grappler/costs/graph_memory.cc:176`) decides whether a device is a GPU with:

```cpp
const bool is_gpu = (device_name.find("GPU:") || device_name.find("gpu:"));
```

`std::string::find` returns `std::string::npos` when there is no match, and `npos` converts to `true`. The first `find` is `false` only when the name starts with `GPU:`. In that case the second `find` returns `npos`, which is `true`. So `is_gpu` is always `true`, as the Sonar report in #56481 says.

`is_gpu` gates the `_swap_to_host` handling below it. Because the check always passes, `_swap_to_host` inputs are also dropped from the liveness computation on CPU devices, which can change the CPU peak-memory estimate. The memory optimizer never sets `_swap_to_host` itself. Its swapping pass reads the attr as a manual annotation, and its own heuristic picks swap candidates only on devices of type `GPU`. So the wrong estimate needs a CPU node that carries the attr by hand.

## Fix

Compare each `find` against `std::string::npos`:

```cpp
const bool is_gpu = device_name.find("GPU:") != std::string::npos ||
                    device_name.find("gpu:") != std::string::npos;
```

I kept both spellings because `memory_optimizer_test.cc` places its swap-test nodes on lowercase `/gpu:0`.

## Test

`CpuIgnoresSwapToHost` in `graph_memory_test.cc` mirrors the existing `GpuSwapping` test on `/CPU:0`. It runs `InferStatically` on the trivial test graph, sets `_swap_to_host` on `AddN_1`, runs it again, and expects the CPU peak memory and its live-tensor set to be unchanged.

## Verification

I built and ran the tests locally in the `tensorflow/build:latest-python3.10` image (CPU-only build).

Without the fix, the new test fails. The CPU live-tensor set shifts the same way `GpuSwapping` expects on GPU:

```
[ RUN      ] GraphMemoryTest.CpuIgnoresSwapToHost
tensorflow/core/grappler/costs/graph_memory_test.cc:225: Failure
Expected equality of these values:
  cpu_tensors
    Which is: { "AddN:0", "AddN_1:0", "AddN_2:0", "Sign:0", "Sign_1:0" }
  swapped_cpu_tensors
    Which is: { "AddN:0", "AddN_1:0", "AddN_2:0", "AddN_3:0", "AddN_4:0" }
[  FAILED  ] GraphMemoryTest.CpuIgnoresSwapToHost (1 ms)
[  PASSED  ] 5 tests.
```

With the fix, `graph_memory_test` passes, including the existing `GpuSwapping` test:

```
[       OK ] GraphMemoryTest.Basic (56 ms)
[       OK ] GraphMemoryTest.UnknownBatchSize (0 ms)
[       OK ] GraphMemoryTest.MultiDevice (1 ms)
[       OK ] GraphMemoryTest.GpuSwapping (2 ms)
[       OK ] GraphMemoryTest.CpuIgnoresSwapToHost (0 ms)
[       OK ] GraphMemoryTest.CtrlDependencies (1 ms)
[  PASSED  ] 6 tests.
```

`memory_optimizer_test`, whose swap tests use `/gpu:0` devices on a virtual cluster, also passes with the fix:

```
//tensorflow/core/grappler/costs:graph_memory_test                       PASSED in 4.8s
//tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers:memory_optimizer_test_cpu          PASSED in 4.4s
//tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers:memory_optimizer_test_gpu          PASSED in 4.0s
Executed 3 out of 3 tests: 3 tests pass.
```

Fixes #56481

issues.title: `tf.linalg.svd` under `jit_compile=True` (XLA) returns **wrong singular values and a wrong reconstruction** for a small-scale but **well-conditioned** float32 matrix; standard eager SVD is correct

labels.name: type:bug
labels.description: Bug

labels.name: comp:xla
labels.description: XLA
tensorflow 2.21.0

issues.body:
### Issue type

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

binary

### TensorFlow version

2.22.0-dev20260921(GIT_VERSION v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f)

### Custom code

Yes

### OS platform and distribution

Linux Ubuntu 22.04(kernel 6.8, glibc 2.35)

### Mobile device

N/A

### Python version

3.12.13

### Bazel version

N/A(binary install)

### GCC/compiler version

N/A(binary install)

### CUDA/cuDNN version

CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.26(pip nvidia-*-cu12)

### GPU model and memory

NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB)

### Current behavior?

`tf.linalg.svd` under `jit_compile=True` (XLA) computes **wrong singular values** and a **wrong
reconstruction** for a well-conditioned float32 matrix that has merely been scaled down. XLA returns the
diagonal entries as the "singular values" and reconstructs a diagonal matrix, dropping the off-diagonal
entries; standard eager SVD, and float64, are correct. Although the individual `U` and `V` factors are
not unique, the reconstructed product `U·diag(S)·Vᵀ` must reproduce the input matrix; therefore factor
sign/basis ambiguity cannot explain the observed reconstruction error — it is a genuine correctness error.

**Root cause (hypothesis).** A scale sweep with a **fixed** `A0` (fixed condition number) shows the
**failure transition occurs between scales `1e-6` and `1e-7`**, which is strongly consistent with the
fixed absolute `epsilon = 1e-6` used by the XLA SVD implementation. This strongly suggests that an
**absolute** stopping/zeroing threshold is making the algorithm **scale-sensitive**: for this fixed matrix
family, scaling the input below roughly this regime causes meaningful intermediate quantities to fall
below the absolute threshold and be treated as negligible, breaking scale invariance. Subnormal
intermediates may further aggravate the problem, but they are **not** necessary to explain the failure:
at scale `1e-7` the input quantities (`~1e-7`) are already many orders of magnitude above the smallest
normal float32 (`~1.17e-38`), yet XLA already fails.

## Scale sweep (fixed `A0` ⇒ fixed conditioning; residual computed in float64)

`A0 = [[1,2],[3,4]]` fixed (cond ≈ 14.9 at every scale). Relative reconstruction residual `‖U·diag(S)·Vᵀ − A‖/‖A‖`,
computed after casting to float64 so the residual itself is scale-immune:

| scale | eager resid | XLA resid |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 9.7e-8 | 9.7e-8 |
| 1e-2 | 3.0e-7 | 1.7e-7 |
| 1e-4 | 1.3e-7 | 2.4e-7 |
| **1e-6** | 4.0e-7 | 2.0e-7 |
| **1e-7** | 3.4e-7 | **0.658** ← XLA breaks |
| 1e-10 | 1.6e-7 | **0.658** |
| 1e-15 | 1.3e-7 | **0.658** |
| 1e-20 | 9.7e-8 | **0.658** |

**Conclusion: the result depends on absolute scale, not on the matrix conditioning** (cond is fixed
throughout). The failure transition occurs between scales `1e-6` and `1e-7`; eager stays correct at every
scale. This is strongly consistent with the fixed absolute `epsilon = 1e-6` in the XLA SVD implementation
and strongly suggests an absolute stopping/zeroing threshold is making the algorithm scale-sensitive.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import tensorflow as tf, numpy as np

A0 = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])          # cond ~ 15 (well-conditioned)
A  = tf.constant(1e-20 * A0, tf.float32)     # 1e-20 is a NORMAL float32

def svd_recon(a):
    s, u, v = tf.linalg.svd(a, full_matrices=False, compute_uv=True)
    return s, u @ tf.linalg.diag(s) @ tf.linalg.matrix_transpose(v)

def rel_resid(recon, a):                      # compute in float64 so the residual itself is scale-immune
    recon = np.asarray(recon, np.float64); a = np.asarray(a, np.float64)
    return np.linalg.norm(recon - a) / np.linalg.norm(a)

with tf.device("/GPU:0"):
    s_e, r_e = svd_recon(A)                                        # standard eager
    s_x, r_x = tf.function(svd_recon, jit_compile=True)(A)         # XLA

print("eager S:", s_e.numpy(), " recon resid:", rel_resid(r_e.numpy(), A.numpy()))
print("XLA   S:", s_x.numpy(), " recon resid:", rel_resid(r_x.numpy(), A.numpy()))
print("numpy S:", np.linalg.svd(1e-20*A0, compute_uv=False))
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
eager S: [5.465e-20 3.660e-21]  recon resid: 0.0
XLA   S: [4.000e-20 1.000e-20]  recon resid: 0.658      # wrong S, diagonal reconstruction
numpy S: [5.465e-20 3.660e-21]
```

issues.title: Fix lifetime issues in `ExecutionWatchdogScope` async callbacks.
issues.body:
Fix lifetime issues in `ExecutionWatchdogScope` async callbacks.

When `block_host_until_done` is false, `~ExecutionWatchdogScope()` releases the `HangWatchdog::Guard` asynchronously via `stream_->DoHostCallback(...)`, so the guard and its `on_timeout` and `pre_abort` callbacks outlive `ExecutionWatchdogScope` and `GpuExecutable::ExecuteThunks()`.

- Copy `ExecutionTimeoutHandler` by value in `ExecutionWatchdogScope::Arm()` instead of capturing a raw `const GpuExecutableRunOptions*` pointer that can dangle when callers allocate `GpuExecutableRunOptions` on the stack.

issues.body:
### Description of changes

This PR fixes fatal process crashes (`CHECK_GE(work_element_count, 0)`) and out-of-bounds illegal memory writes in GPU convolution filter transformation kernels when the filter tensor element count exceeds the 32-bit limit.

#### Problem & Root Cause
In CUDA/GPU convolution execution paths (`LaunchConvOpImpl`, `LaunchFusedConv2DOp`, `LaunchConv2DBackpropInputOpGpuImpl`, and `LaunchConvBackpropInputOpImpl`), filter tensors are transformed using `functor::TransformFilter<GPUDevice, T, int, NDIMS>()` via `To32Bit(...)`:
- When `filter.NumElements() > INT32_MAX` (e.g. `3 * 100 * 8044155 = 2,413,246,500`), the element count overflows signed 32-bit `int` to `-1,881,720,796`.
- In `GetGpuLaunchConfig`, this negative count triggered a fatal abort in `gpu_launch_config.h`:
  ```
  Check failed: work_element_count >= 0 (-1881720796 vs. 0)
  ```
- If the overflow wraps around to a positive integer $< 2^{31}-1$, the kernel `ShuffleInTensor3Simple` was launched with truncated threads and 32-bit index computations, causing `compute-sanitizer` to detect out-of-bounds illegal memory writes.

#### Solution
1. In `tensorflow/core/kernels/conv_ops_impl.h`, `conv_ops_fused_impl.h`, `conv_grad_input_ops.cc`, and `conv_grad_input_ops_3d.cc`, add upfront `FastBoundsCheck(filter.NumElements(), std::numeric_limits<int32>::max())` validation before launching the 32-bit GPU filter transformations, returning clean `errors::InvalidArgument` errors.
2. In `tensorflow/core/kernels/conv_2d_gpu.h`, guard `TransformFilter` and `ReverseTransformFilter` against non-positive `out.size()` (`if (TF_PREDICT_FALSE(out.size() <= 0)) return;`) to ensure defense-in-depth across direct callers.
3. In `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/nn_ops/conv_ops_test.py`, add a regression unit test `testConv2DFilterExceeds32BitLimit`.

Fixes #87457
Fixes #87438

issues.title: Fix complex abs GPU NaN output for infinite inputs per IEEE-754

labels.name: awaiting review
labels.description: Pull request awaiting review

labels.name: size:S
labels.description: CL Change Size: Small

labels.description: PR to fix a bug

issues.body:
### Description of changes

This PR fixes a numerical discrepancy and IEEE-754 / ISO C99 compliance bug in `tf.math.abs` (`ComplexAbs`) when executed on GPU (CUDA / ROCm) for complex floating-point numbers (`complex64`, `complex128`).

#### Problem & Root Cause
Under IEEE-754 Section 9.2.1 and ISO C99 Annex F.9.4.3:
$$\text{hypot}(\pm\infty, \text{NaN}) = +\infty \quad \text{and} \quad \text{hypot}(\text{NaN}, \pm\infty) = +\infty$$
On CPU, `std::abs(std::complex<T>)` internally delegates to `std::hypot`, correctly adhering to this standard and returning `+inf`.

However, on CUDA / ROCm devices, Eigen's generic `scalar_abs_op<std::complex<T>>` evaluated the modulus as $\sqrt{\text{real}^2 + \text{imag}^2}$. When either component is infinite and the other is `NaN`, this evaluates to $\sqrt{\infty + \text{NaN}} = \text{NaN}$. Furthermore, computing $\text{real}^2$ directly suffers premature intermediate overflow for values where $|\text{component}| > \sqrt{\text{FLT\_MAX}} \approx 1.84 \times 10^{19}$.

#### Solution
1. In `tensorflow/core/kernels/cwise_ops.h`, specialize `Eigen::internal::scalar_abs_op` for `std::complex<float>` and `std::complex<double>` under `GOOGLE_CUDA || TENSORFLOW_USE_ROCM`, invoking `::hypotf` and `::hypot` on device (and `std::hypot` on host). This matches the existing convention used for `scalar_arg_op`.
2. In `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/math_ops/cwise_ops_unary_test.py`, add `testComplexAbsSpecialValues` validating IEEE-754 behavior across `complex64` and `complex128` on both CPU and GPU (`_compareBoth`).

Fixes #115734.

issues.body:
[XLA] Disambiguate `kFusion` instructions in `HloCSE` `CseKey` hash based on the fused computation

Previously, `CseKey::AbslHashValue` in `HloCSE` fell into the `default:` branch for `HloOpcode::kFusion`, only hashing the top-level operands, output dimensions, and the fused computation's root opcode. As a result, distinct `kFusion` instructions sharing operands, output shape, and root opcode collided in `HloCSE`'s `representatives` hash table and triggered expensive `HloFusionInstruction::IdenticalSlowPath` (`HloComputation::Equal`) comparisons.

This change factors out `CseKey::HashInstruction` and applies it to the internal instructions of `instruction->fused_instructions_computation()` (in post-order from `root_instruction()`) when hashing a `kFusion` instruction, skipping operand `unique_id()`s for internal instructions so equivalent `kFusion` instructions continue to hash identically while distinct fused computations are disambiguated.

labels.name: ready to pull
labels.description: PR ready for merge process

labels.description: CL Change Size: Small

labels.description: PR to fix a bug

labels.name: comp:core
labels.description: issues related to core part of tensorflow

issues.body:
### Summary of Changes

This PR resolves #109519 by fixing an integer overflow in `detail::GpuGridRange` and `RangeInitKernel` that caused illegal global memory writes in CUDA/ROCm kernels processing large tensors (such as `UniqueOpGPU` with inputs approaching `INT32_MAX`).

#### Root Cause
In `detail::GpuGridRange<T>::Iterator::operator++()` (`tensorflow/core/util/gpu_device_functions.h`), index increments were computed as `index_ += delta_`. When `index_` is near `INT32_MAX`, adding grid stride `delta_` causes signed 32-bit integer overflow, wrapping `index_` to negative values. Because the termination condition in `operator!=` checks `index_ < other.index_` (where `other.index_ == end_`), the loop did not terminate on overflow, resulting in out-of-bounds global writes (such as `detail::RangeInitKernel<int>` reported by Compute-Sanitizer). Additionally, `RangeInitKernel` used the deprecated macro `GPU_1D_KERNEL_LOOP` which forced 32-bit integer indexing even when parameterized with 64-bit types.

#### Fix Details
1. **Prevent Overflow in `GpuGridRange` Iterator**:
   - `Iterator` now records the range boundary `end_`.
   - In `operator++()`, checked `if (delta_ != 0 && end_ - index_ <= delta_) index_ = end_; else index_ += delta_;`. This safely clamps `index_` to `end_` prior to overflow, ensuring clean termination upon comparing against `end()` without any negative wrap-around.
2. **RangeInitKernel Grid-Stride modernization**:
   - In `tensorflow/core/kernels/gpu_prim_helpers.h` and `tensorflow/core/kernels/dynamic_partition_op_gpu.cu.cc`, replaced `GPU_1D_KERNEL_LOOP(i, size)` with `for (T i : GpuGridRangeX<T>(size))` to properly respect type parameter `T` and eliminate truncation/overflow.

Fixes #109519.

issues.title: Validate boxes tensor is finite in CropAndResize gradients

labels.name: ready to pull
labels.description: PR ready for merge process

labels.description: CL Change Size: Medium

issues.body:
## Problem

When `tf.raw_ops.CropAndResizeGradBoxes` or `tf.raw_ops.CropAndResizeGradImage` is invoked with a `boxes` tensor containing `NaN` or non-finite values (such as `+inf` or `-inf`), the gradient computation causes invalid memory access or a segmentation fault (`SIGSEGV`).
Specifically, in #124955, passing `NaN` coordinates in `boxes` led to undefined floating point cast to integer indexing in the backprop kernels, terminating the Python runtime with a crash.

## Root Cause

In `CropAndResizeGradImageOp::ComputeAsync` and `CropAndResizeGradBoxesOp::ComputeAsync` (`tensorflow/core/kernels/image/crop_and_resize_op.cc`), the operators check:
- `boxes.dims() == 2`
- `boxes.dim_size(0) == num_boxes`
- `boxes.dim_size(1) == 4`

However, unlike forward validation or safe numerical preconditions, they did not check whether the float elements in `boxes` are finite before feeding them into coordinate transformation and bilinear interpolation backprop loops. When coordinates are `NaN` or infinite, index computation produces invalid array offsets, crashing the process with SIGSEGV.

## Solution

1. In `CropAndResizeGradImageOp::ComputeAsync`, validate upfront:
   ```cpp
   OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(
       context, boxes.tensor<float, 2>().isfinite().all(),
       absl::InvalidArgumentError("boxes must contain only finite values."),
       done);
   ```
2. In `CropAndResizeGradBoxesOp::ComputeAsync`, validate upfront:
   ```cpp
   OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(
       context, boxes.tensor<float, 2>().isfinite().all(),
       absl::InvalidArgumentError("boxes must contain only finite values."),
       done);
   ```
   This matches the upfront validation requirement requested by maintainer review on related gradient operations.
3. Added unit tests in `tensorflow/python/ops/image_grad_test.py` (`CropAndResizeGradNonFiniteTest`) verifying that passing `NaN` and `Inf` to both `CropAndResizeGradBoxes` and `CropAndResizeGradImage` cleanly raises `InvalidArgumentError` instead of crashing with SIGSEGV.

## Testing

- Unit tests added to `image_grad_test.py`:
  - `test_crop_and_resize_grad_boxes_nan_raises_invalid_argument`
  - `test_crop_and_resize_grad_image_nan_raises_invalid_argument`
  - `test_crop_and_resize_grad_boxes_inf_raises_invalid_argument`
  - `test_crop_and_resize_grad_image_inf_raises_invalid_argument`
- Verified syntax, Eigen/Tensor types (`boxes.tensor<float, 2>().isfinite().all()`), and `absl::InvalidArgumentError` error format.

## Risk

Very low. Only non-finite input tensors (`NaN`, `Inf`) that previously caused undefined memory access / SIGSEGV are rejected with an explicit `InvalidArgumentError`. Valid float inputs are unaffected.

## Issue

Fixes #124955

issues.title: Fix unsorted_segment_mean count saturation for reduced-precision dtypes

labels.name: awaiting review
labels.description: Pull request awaiting review

labels.name: python

issues.body:
Fixes #127818

### Problem
When computing `tf.math.unsorted_segment_mean` (or `tf.math.unsorted_segment_sqrt_n`) on reduced-precision floating-point types such as `bfloat16` or `float16`, the computed segment mean returns incorrect results (e.g. returning `1.0` instead of `0.5` for segments of size 512 with alternating zeros and ones).

### Root Cause
In `_unsorted_segment_N` (`tensorflow/python/ops/math_ops.py`), segment counts were computed by generating an `array_ops.ones` tensor with `dtype=data.dtype` and summing it using `gen_math_ops.unsorted_segment_sum`.
For `bfloat16`, which has only 7 bits of mantissa, adding `1.0` to numbers >= 256.0 rounds down to 256.0 because `1.0` is smaller than the unit in the last place (ULP) for 2^8. As a result, the running count `N` froze at 256.0 regardless of how many elements were in the segment, causing `summed / N` to divide by 256.0 instead of 512.0 (256.0 / 256.0 = 1.0). For `float16` (10 bits of mantissa), a similar saturation occurs at 2048.0.

### Solution
In `_unsorted_segment_N`:
1. Generate `ones_tensor` with `dtype=segment_ids.dtype` (integer: `int32` or `int64`) rather than `data.dtype`.
2. Compute the exact element count integer sum via `gen_math_ops.unsorted_segment_sum`.
3. Clamp the count to at least 1 via `gen_math_ops.maximum(n, 1)`.
4. Cast the exact integer count to `data.dtype` using `cast(n, dtype=data.dtype)` prior to returning.

### Testing
- Added regression unit test `testUnsortedSegmentMeanLargeSegmentReducedPrecision` to `tensorflow/python/kernel_tests/math_ops/segment_reduction_ops_test.py` covering `bfloat16` and `float16` across segment sizes n in {512, 1024}.
- Verified syntax with `py_compile`.

### Risk
Very low. Preserves existing mathematical semantics while eliminating floating-point count saturation and precision loss for reduced-precision dtypes.

issues.title: Avoid re-logging non-variable input tensors post-evaluation in calibrator

labels.name: comp:lite
labels.description: TF Lite related issues

labels.name: ready to pull
labels.description: PR ready for merge process

labels.name: size:M

issues.body:
Fixes #127842

### Problem
When evaluating operators during model calibration in `tensorflow/lite/tools/optimize/calibration/calibrator.cc`, input tensors were being logged twice: once prior to kernel invocation, and again after kernel invocation. When the `MemoryPlanner` / `ArenaPlanner` reuses an input tensor's memory buffer for an output tensor to save memory (as documented in `tensorflow/lite/core/subgraph.cc`), the second logging pass records the output tensor's values into the input tensor's calibration statistics, corrupting the input min/max ranges and subsequent quantization.

### Root Cause
In `LoggingEval` (`calibrator.cc`), all `loggable_inputs` were re-logged after `kernel_invoke` with the original intent of capturing in-place state changes for variable tensors (such as LSTM cells). However, non-variable input tensors do not undergo in-place state changes during invocation; their values are already captured accurately prior to invocation. If their underlying buffer is reused by the memory planner for an output tensor, re-logging them post-invocation reads the overwritten output data instead of the input data.

### Solution
In `calibrator.cc`, check `if (tensor.is_variable)` before re-logging input tensors post-invocation. Non-variable input tensors are already logged prior to kernel invocation and are skipped post-invocation, preventing overwritten shared buffers from corrupting input calibration statistics while preserving state logging for variable tensors (e.g. LSTM cells).

### Testing
- Added regression test `NonVariableInputsNotReLoggedPostInvocation` in `tensorflow/lite/tools/optimize/calibration/calibrator_test.cc` to verify that non-variable inputs maintain their pre-invocation calibration statistics.
- Verified C++ style and syntax conformance.

### Risk
None. Non-variable inputs do not change values during evaluation, so their pre-invocation logging captures their true values. Variable tensors retain their post-invocation logging.

issues.body:
Introduce ShuffleMode::MultiRotate to kShuffle instruction.

A `multi_rotate` rotates each element within a dimension independently of each
other. It has `multi_shifts` as its attribute that specifies the amount
each element of the rotated dimension is shifted by.

Specifically:

- HLO IR & Parser: `ShuffleMode.MultiRotate` carries the indices as an
`xla.LiteralProto`. The text form is `shuffle(x), dimensions={0}, mode=multi_rotate, multi_shifts=s32[3,1] {{2},{0},{1}}`.

- Shape Inference & Verifier: reject indices that are not integers, that have
the wrong rank or dimension sizes for the operand and dimensions.

- XlaBuilder API: `shuffle::MakeMultiRotateMode` builds the mode with the given
`multi_shifts`; `GetMultiShifts` and `GetMultiShiftsShape` read it back.

- HLO-to-MHLO / StableHLO Translation: lower to a single `stablehlo.gather`
over unit slices using the same mechanism that `ShuffleMode.Permute` uses.
All multi-rotates can be rewritten as permute so it goes through a
multi-rotate -> permute -> gather pipeline

issues.title: Return +0 from the zero branch of the xlogy/xlog1py/xdivy packet ops

labels.name: ready to pull
labels.description: PR ready for merge process

labels.name: size:M
labels.description: CL Change Size: Medium

labels.name: prtype:bugfix
labels.description: PR to fix a bug

issues.body:
Refs #127913. This fixes the CPU half of the problem; the GPU case in that report comes from separate kernels, described below, and needs its own change.

`xlogy_op`, `xlog1py_op` and `xdivy_op` in `tensorflow/core/kernels/cwise_ops.h` return `Scalar(0.)` from their scalar path when `x == 0`, but their packet paths select `x` itself for those lanes:

```cpp
Packet mask = pcmp_eq(x, zeros);
...
return pselect(mask, x, x_div_y);
```

The two only agree when `x` is exactly `+0`. This changes the three selects to return `zeros`, matching the scalar path, the documented "0 if x == 0", and TensorFlow's own XLA kernels for these ops, which already select `ZerosLike(x)` in `tensorflow/compiler/tf2xla/kernels/binary_ops.cc`. `div_no_nan` and `mul_no_nan` in the same file already get this right, masking with `pandnot` so the lane is a true zero.

These functors are TensorFlow's own. They live in `namespace Eigen::internal` inside TensorFlow's `cwise_ops.h` so that they can specialize Eigen's `functor_traits`, but Eigen itself has no `xlogy`, `xlog1py` or `xdivy`: none of those names appear anywhere in Eigen at TensorFlow's pinned commit or at Eigen master.

## The symptom this fixes

An `x` of `-0` compares equal to zero without being `+0`, so the sign of the result depends on the size of the tensor: tensors shorter than one SIMD packet go through the scalar path and the rest through the packet path. On TensorFlow 2.21.0 on aarch64 (x86_64 shows the same `-0` at `n=16`):

```
xdivy(-0., 3.)   n=1: +0   n=3: +0   n=4: -0   n=16: -0   n=1024: -0
```

`xlogy` and `xlog1py` behave identically.

## What this does not fix

TensorFlow has more than one implementation of these three ops, and they disagree:

| implementation | zero branch returns |
| --- | --- |
| Eigen functors, scalar path (`cwise_ops.h`) | `0` |
| Eigen functors, packet path (`cwise_ops.h`) | `x`, fixed here |
| MLIR-generated GPU kernels (`core/kernels/mlir_generated/op_definitions/{xdivy,xlogy,xlog1py}*.mlir.tmpl`) | `x` |
| TF-dialect lowering, `BinaryXopyPat` in `compiler/mlir/tensorflow/transforms/lower_tf.td` | `x` |
| tf2xla, `binary_ops.cc` | `0` |

On GPU these ops run the MLIR-generated kernels, which compute `chlo.broadcast_select(x == 0, x, ...)`. That is what #127913 reports: under the CUDA build's flush-to-zero, a subnormal `x` compares equal to zero and is returned unchanged. The generated templates follow the same pattern as `lower_tf.td`, so the fix is the same change in both places, and I will send it separately so that it can be checked by the GPU CI on its own.

## Tests

The existing tests compare with `assertAllClose`, which cannot tell `-0` from `+0`, so they never saw this. New tests in `math_ops_test.py` check the sign bit for `-0` inputs at sizes 1, 3, 4, 16 and 1024, covering both sides of the packet width, in float16, float32 and float64, for all three ops. They are pinned to CPU with `test_util.force_cpu()`, since the GPU kernels are not the code this changes.

Against the unfixed 2.21.0 wheel, all three fail in both graph and eager mode. With this change, `math_ops_test_cpu` passes in CI.

## Verification

I could not build TensorFlow, so beyond CI I checked the functors directly, with their code verbatim, compiled against the pinned Eigen `ea13a98`:

- In isolation, the scalar and packet paths now agree for `-0` and for subnormals, with flush-to-zero on or off, and unflushed nonzero results are bit-identical.
- Run through Eigen Tensor evaluation the way `BinaryFunctor` runs it, `out.device(d) = in0.binaryExpr(in1, functor)` on a `ThreadPoolDevice` for sizes 1 through 100003, the old code reproduces the size dependence above exactly, `-0` in float from `n=4`, and in double already at `n=3` since a double packet is two lanes, and the new code returns `+0` at every size.

labels.description: Pull requests that update Python code

Description

testExecutionModeIsStoredThreadLocal's per-thread self.assertEqual(ctx.execution_mode, mode) runs inside threading.Thread target functions. Python's threading module doesn't propagate exceptions from a thread back to the caller via .join() — an AssertionError raised there is only printed to stderr and the thread dies, but the test method itself completes normally and reports PASS. So if execution_mode ever stopped being properly thread-local, this test would never actually catch it.

Fix: each thread now catches any exception into a per-thread slot in a shared list; after all threads join, the main thread re-raises the first captured exception, if any.

issues.title: Refactor MonitoredTimer to use thread-local storage

labels.name: awaiting review
labels.description: Pull request awaiting review

labels.name: size:S
labels.description: CL Change Size: Small

labels.name: python
labels.description: Pull requests that update Python code

issues.body:
Description

MonitoredTimerSections, used by MonitoredTimer's avoid_repetitive_counting feature, was a single module-level list shared across all threads. The feature's docstring describes it as guarding against recursive re-entry within one call stack ("if already in a monitored timer section with the same name, skip counting"), but the shared list meant two unrelated threads legitimately calling the same monitored function concurrently would corrupt each other's state — one thread's active section would cause an independent thread's identically-named section to be spuriously treated as recursive and skipped, silently undercounting the metric.

Fix: moved the section-tracking list into threading.local(), so each thread's recursion state is isolated from every other thread's. Added the missing import threading.

Confirmed the bug and the fix with two concurrency reproductions (not against the real pywrap_tfe-backed Counter/cell — using a stand-in FakeCell and the exact MonitoredTimer logic, since no C-extension build is available here):

Two threads, same section name, deliberate overlap (one sleeps mid-section) — before the fix, the second thread's call was silently skipped (count came out to 1 instead of 2); after the fix, both are correctly counted.
Same-thread recursive nesting still correctly skips the inner, re-entrant call — confirming the fix doesn't remove the actual intended behavior, only the cross-thread leakage.

issues.body:
[XLA] Answer MakeFreeChunksList from a merged occupied range index

GlobalDecreasingSizeBestFitHeap::MakeFreeChunksList visited every chunk overlapping a buffer's live window and sorted them by offset. That is O(N K log K) per heap of N buffers with K overlapping chunks. BufferIntervalTree now keeps a segment tree over the T schedule times whose nodes hold the merged occupied memory ranges. A query reads O(log T) of those lists in place of the tree walk over the K chunks; their pieces are sorted as before. The free lists, chunks and offsets are unchanged; trees that saw a Remove after their first query keep visiting their nodes.

issues.title: Optimize Concat CPU performance with contiguous Axis-0 fast-path

labels.name: ready to pull
labels.description: PR ready for merge process

labels.name: size:M
labels.description: CL Change Size: Medium

labels.name: comp:core
labels.description: issues related to core part of tensorflow

issues.body:
This PR optimizes the CPU implementation of Concat (`ConcatCPUImpl`) by introducing a contiguous fast-path for outermost dimension concatenation and eliminating heap allocation churn in worker threads.

### Problem
1. When concatenating along the outermost dimension (`dim0 == 1`, such as `axis=0` batch or sequence concatenation), all input tensors are already completely contiguous in memory. Upstream code treats this as a 2D matrix, evaluating row-sharding math, row skips, and column limits.
2. Worker threads spawned by `Shard` allocate dynamic heap memory (`std::vector<const T*> inp; inp.reserve(num_inputs);`) on every invocation, causing memory allocator contention on multi-core CPU servers.
3. The single-thread fallback threshold was set to 16KB, paying thread pool dispatch and synchronization latency on small operations where a single-core linear memory copy completes much faster.

### Solution
1. **Contiguous Axis-0 Fast-Path:** Added direct contiguous block copying when `dim0 == 1`. For payloads `< 1 MB` or single-core execution, it performs sequential copies via `copier.Copy` (direct `memcpy` for trivially copyable types) with zero threading overhead. For payloads `≥ 1 MB`, it performs prefix-sum slice partitioning across the thread pool.
2. **Zero Heap Allocations in Thread Workers:** Replaced dynamic `std::vector` inside the worker lambda with stack-allocated `absl::InlinedVector<const T*, 16>`, and replaced Eigen coordinate lookups with direct raw pointer offsets (`inputs[j]->data() + skipped_rows * sizes[j]`).
3. **Threshold Tuning:** Raised multi-row single-threaded threshold from 16KB to 64KB.

Closes #127919.

issues.body:
### System information
- **OS Platform and Distribution:** macOS, Linux (Ubuntu/Debian)
- **TensorFlow installed from:** source / master
- **TensorFlow version:** master

### Describe the problem
In the current CPU implementation (`tensorflow/core/kernels/concat_lib_cpu.h`), all concatenations are processed by flattening tensors into 2D matrices and running them through a row-sharding algorithm.

This introduces three main bottlenecks:
1. **Inefficient Outermost Dimension Concatenation:** When concatenating along `axis=0` (or outermost dimension `dim0 == 1`), every input tensor is already completely contiguous in memory. Upstream code treats this as a 2D matrix, evaluating row skips, seeking partial row offsets, and invoking thread workers even for small payloads.
2. **Dynamic Heap Allocations on Worker Threads:** Every worker thread spawned by `Shard` allocates `std::vector<const T*> inp; inp.reserve(num_inputs);` on the heap inside the worker lambda on every invocation, causing heap churn and allocator lock contention on multi-core CPU servers.
3. **Low Threading Threshold:** The single-thread fallback threshold was set to 16KB. Launching thread pool workers on small payloads incurs 10–50 µs of synchronization latency, whereas a single core can execute the contiguous memory copy directly.

### Proposed Fix
1. Introduce a contiguous block fast-path for `dim0 == 1` with sequential execution for payloads `< 1 MB` and prefix-sum slice partitioning across the thread pool for larger payloads.
2. Replace dynamic worker heap allocations with stack-allocated `absl::InlinedVector<const T*, 16>` and direct raw pointer offsets (`inputs[j]->data() + skipped_rows * sizes[j]`).
3. Raise multi-row single-threaded threshold to 64KB.

### Related PR
PR #127922 has been opened with the implementation.

issues.title: PR #48907: [XLA:GPU] Allocate collective memory buffers before other transient buffers
issues.body:
PR #48907: [XLA:GPU] Allocate collective memory buffers before other transient buffers

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/48907

Stacked on #48834 (step 1). Step 2 of the plan discussed with the allocator author to let default memory grow past the preallocated fraction.

## 📝 Summary of Changes

- `GenerateBufferAllocations` now resolves an execution's buffers in two passes: parameters, constants, thread-local buffers and every collective memory (S(1)) transient buffer first, then the remaining transient buffers.
- Both passes keep allocation index order, so S(1) placement stays deterministic across ranks and the result is still indexed by allocation index.
- Error propagation and alignment checking are unchanged; copy-protected output buffers are allocated after this loop as before.

## 🎯 Justification

S(1) buffers back NCCL symmetric windows and can only live in the fixed, preallocated part of the shared BFC arena, while a follow-up will let S(0) grow the arena from the top on OOM. If S(0) and S(1) allocations interleave, S(0) can fill the preallocated region and trigger growth before an S(1) temp asks for space it can no longer get. Allocating S(1) first within each execution removes that ordering hazard; it is behavior-neutral today because the arena is fixed.

## 🚀 Kind of Contribution

♻️ Cleanup, 🧪 Tests

## 🧪 Unit Tests

`//xla/service/gpu:gpu_executable_buffer_allocator_test` (new, CPU only)

- `AllocatesCollectiveMemoryBeforeOtherTransientBuffers`
- `KeepsAllocationIndexOrderWithoutCollectiveMemory`
- `ReturnsDefaultMemoryFailureAfterCollectiveMemoryIsAllocated`

All 3 tests pass locally; the existing `//xla/service/gpu:gpu_executable_va_remap_allocator_test` (14 tests) still passes with the reordered loop.

## 🧪 Execution Tests

None added; the change only reorders allocation requests within an execution.

Copybara import of the project:

--
b69a4f6f029bc4eb1f753c66d32efaa41a398f4b by Shawn Wang <shawnw@nvidia.com>:

[XLA:GPU] Anchor collective memory at the lower end of the shared BFC arena

With spatial partitioning, one preallocated BFC allocator serves both the
default memory space S(0) and the collective memory space S(1) from
opposite ends of a fixed address range. S(1) buffers back NCCL symmetric
windows, so their offsets must be identical across ranks, which only holds
while the end they are anchored to never moves.

Swap the ends in the PjRt GPU client: serve S(1) from the lower end, the
range base that is fixed for the lifetime of the arena, and S(0) from the
upper end. Default memory keeps kLower when the shared pool is not active,
because a non-partitioned allocator only serves the lower end.

This is the first step toward letting the default memory space grow past
the preallocated fraction: with S(1) pinned at the base, the top of the
range is the only boundary a future extension would move, so growth can
never disturb symmetric offsets.

Validating that the two ends are interchangeable exposed one asymmetry in
BFCAllocator: the lower end applied the classic "do not split a small
remainder" heuristic even when carving from the shared central gap, so a
lower allocation near exhaustion could absorb gap bytes and make later
lower offsets depend on upper activity, while the upper end always split
exactly but never kept slack when reusing its own holes. Make the policy
the same at both ends: carving from the central gap always splits exactly,
and reusing an own-tagged hole follows the classic heuristic. Without
spatial partitioning nothing changes.

Tests:
- bfc_allocator_test: mirror the upper-end symmetric-memory tests for the
  lower end (SpatialKeepsLowerOffset, SpatialSkipsUpperHole,
  SpatialLowerReclaimsAfterUpperFill, SpatialLowerOffsetsStable with the
  coarse collective alignment under randomized upper churn) and pin the
  split policy (SpatialGapCarveSplitsExactlyAtBothEnds,
  SpatialHoleReuseKeepsSlackAtBothEnds).
- se_gpu_pjrt_client_test: SharedPoolAnchorsCollectiveMemoryAtLowerEnd
  checks that collective buffers grow upward below every default buffer
  and default buffers grow downward from the top of the arena;
  GrowableBfcServesBothMemorySpaces covers the non-partitioned fallback.

--
3e2285f56815c6769fc403a23148866fc90fe5f6 by Shawn Wang <shawnw@nvidia.com>:

Use ASSERT_OK_AND_ASSIGN in the new GPU client tests

Switch the two new tests in se_gpu_pjrt_client_test.cc from
TF_ASSERT_OK_AND_ASSIGN to the preferred ASSERT_OK_AND_ASSIGN macro, as
requested in review.

--
87fa5cbed3bcff1a656a2723662a53df9f344c31 by Shawn Wang <shawnw@nvidia.com>:

[XLA:GPU] Clarify BFC split terminology and invariants

Introduce the default non-partitioned mode and replace references to
classic BFC behavior. Explain that central-gap allocations use the rounded
request size, keeping the unused space available and handling alignment
padding as same-tag free holes.

Pass the source chunk to ShouldSplitChunk and DCHECK that it is not the
central gap. The heuristic also handles same-tag holes in partitioned
mode, so checking that spatial partitioning is disabled would reject
valid calls.

Update the existing test comments to use the same terminology.

--
7ea53dabb8f6371d6f4cada47d23de1a8ab395f0 by Shawn Wang <shawnw@nvidia.com>:

[XLA:GPU] Allocate collective memory buffers before other transient buffers

With the shared spatially partitioned BFC arena, collective memory S(1)
backs NCCL symmetric windows and can only live in the fixed, preallocated
part of the arena, while default memory S(0) is meant to be allowed to
grow past it in a follow-up. Today GenerateBufferAllocations hands out an
execution's transient buffers in allocation index order, so S(0) and S(1)
allocations interleave and S(0) pressure can take the space S(1) needs
before S(1) asks for it.

Resolve allocations in two passes: first parameters, constants,
thread-local buffers and every S(1) transient buffer, then the remaining
transient buffers. Both passes keep allocation index order, so S(1)
placement stays a deterministic function of the program, and the result
is still indexed by allocation index. Error propagation and alignment
checking are unchanged. Copy-protected output buffers, which are
allocated after this loop, are not affected.

This is step 2 of the plan to grow default memory past the preallocated
fraction; step 1 anchored S(1) at the lower end of the arena.

Tests: new gpu_executable_buffer_allocator_test with a recording device
allocator checks that collective requests precede all other requests
while the returned BufferAllocations remain indexed by allocation index,
that index order is kept when no collective buffers exist, and that a
default memory allocation failure is still propagated.


Merging this change closes #48907

issues.body:
### Issue type

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

binary

### TensorFlow version

2.22.0-dev20260921(GIT_VERSION v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f)

### Custom code

Yes

### OS platform and distribution

Linux Ubuntu 22.04(kernel 6.8, glibc 2.35)

### Mobile device

N/A

### Python version

3.12.13

### Bazel version

N/A(binary install)

### GCC/compiler version

N/A(binary install)

### CUDA/cuDNN version

CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.26(pip nvidia-*-cu12)

### GPU model and memory

NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB)

### Current behavior?

`tf.raw_ops.QuantizeAndDequantizeV3` takes a **dynamic** `num_bits` input. Eager execution and plain
`tf.function` (graph) both validate it and raise `InvalidArgumentError` when `num_bits ≤ 0`. Under
`jit_compile=True` (XLA), the same call **silently returns a result** instead of raising.

This is not merely "backends disagree on invalid input": the eager V3 kernel reads the dynamic
`num_bits` and explicitly requires `num_bits_val > 0` (else `InvalidArgumentError`), whereas the XLA V3
lowering reads `ctx->Input(3)` and directly computes `2^num_bits` with **no range check** — so the XLA
path is missing the input constraint the eager path enforces. TF already treats validation gaps for this
op as bugs (e.g. #99456 / #87421: hard crash / `Check failed: d >= 0` instead of `InvalidArgumentError`).

**Expected:** compiled matches eager/graph — `num_bits ≤ 0` raises `InvalidArgumentError`.
**Actual:** `jit_compile=True` silently produces a result (`num_bits=0 → [-0,…]`; `num_bits=-1 → [-4,…]`).

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import os
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = "-1"
import tensorflow as tf

inp = tf.constant([-1., 0., 1., 2.], tf.float32)
lo, hi = tf.constant(-1., tf.float32), tf.constant(2., tf.float32)

def g(x):
    return tf.raw_ops.QuantizeAndDequantizeV3(
        input=x, input_min=lo, input_max=hi,
        num_bits=tf.constant(0, tf.int32), range_given=True)   # num_bits=0 is out of range

print("eager:", end=" ")
try: print(g(inp).numpy())
except Exception as e: print("RAISED", type(e).__name__)                 # InvalidArgumentError

print("graph:", end=" ")
try: print(tf.function(g)(inp).numpy())
except Exception as e: print("RAISED", type(e).__name__)                 # InvalidArgumentError

print("xla  :", tf.function(g, jit_compile=True)(inp).numpy())           # [-0. -0. -0. -0.]  <-- silent, WRONG
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
eager: RAISED InvalidArgumentError
graph: RAISED InvalidArgumentError
xla  : [-0. -0. -0. -0.]          # jit_compile silently accepts an out-of-range num_bits
```

### Issue type

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

binary

### TensorFlow version

2.22.0-dev20260921(GIT_VERSION v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f)

### Custom code

Yes

### OS platform and distribution

Linux Ubuntu 22.04(kernel 6.8, glibc 2.35)

### Mobile device

N/A

### Python version

3.12.13

### Bazel version

N/A(binary install)

### GCC/compiler version

N/A(binary install)

### CUDA/cuDNN version

CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.26(pip nvidia-*-cu12)

### GPU model and memory

NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB)

### Current behavior?

On GPU, `tf.math.xdivy` returns a wrong result for **subnormal** float32 inputs. `xdivy(x, y)` is defined
as `x / y` (and `0` when `x == 0`). For a genuinely nonzero subnormal such as `x = y = 1e-40` (bit
pattern `int32 = 71362`, a well-formed IEEE-754 subnormal), the correct result is `1.0`. The standard op
— eager execution **and** plain `tf.function` (graph, no XLA) — instead returns ≈ the numerator `x`
(`~1e-40`). `jit_compile=True` (XLA) returns the correct `1.0`. float64 is correct everywhere.

So the standard (non-XLA) `xdivy` is the wrong side; XLA-GPU is correct. TF already treats `xdivy`
numerical wrong-results as bugs (e.g. #51643: `xdivy` under `@tf.function` returns `0` for large inputs).

**Expected:** `xdivy(1e-40, 1e-40) == 1.0` (and matches XLA / float64).
**Actual:** eager and graph return `~1e-40` (≈ the numerator).

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import tensorflow as tf

x = tf.constant(1e-40, tf.float32)   # nonzero subnormal (bitcast int32 = 71362)
y = tf.constant(1e-40, tf.float32)

with tf.device("/GPU:0"):
    print("eager:", tf.math.xdivy(x, y).numpy())                                  # ~1e-40  <-- WRONG (should be 1.0)
    print("graph:", tf.function(lambda a, b: tf.math.xdivy(a, b))(x, y).numpy())  # ~1e-40  <-- WRONG
    print("xla  :", tf.function(lambda a, b: tf.math.xdivy(a, b),
                                jit_compile=True)(x, y).numpy())                   # 1.0     <-- correct
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
eager: 1e-40
graph: 1e-40
xla  : 1.0
```

issues.title: the standard **Eigen-based** `tf.linalg.qr` loses numerical accuracy for a small-scale but **well-conditioned** float32 matrix (`A = 1e-20·[[1,2],[3,4]]`, `‖Q@R − A‖/‖A‖ ≈ 0.55`); XLA-GPU handles the same input correctly (residual 0)

issues.body:
### Issue type

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

binary

### TensorFlow version

2.22.0-dev20260921(GIT_VERSION v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f)

### Custom code

Yes

### OS platform and distribution

Linux Ubuntu 22.04(kernel 6.8, glibc 2.35)

### Mobile device

N/A

### Python version

3.12.13

### Bazel version

N/A(binary install)

### GCC/compiler version

N/A(binary install)

### CUDA/cuDNN version

CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.26(pip nvidia-*-cu12)

### GPU model and memory

NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB)

### Current behavior?

TensorFlow's standard **Eigen-based** `tf.linalg.qr` loses numerical accuracy for a small-scale but
**well-conditioned** `float32` matrix, while **XLA-GPU** handles the same input correctly. TF documents
the QR contract as `A = Q @ R`. For `A = 1e-20 * [[1,2],[3,4]]` (condition number ≈ 15 — well-conditioned;
`1e-20` is a normal float32, far above the smallest normal `~1.17e-38`):

- standard `tf.linalg.qr` (Eigen, float32): `Q@R` drops the `A[1,0]=3e-20` entry to `0.0` → relative
  residual `‖Q@R−A‖/‖A‖ ≈ 0.55`.
- XLA-GPU (`jit_compile=True`, float32): `Q@R` reproduces `A` exactly → relative residual `0`.
- float64 is correct (~1e-16) everywhere.

The likely mechanism is intermediate underflow: a column-norm square `(1e-20)^2 ≈ 1e-40` falls into the
subnormal range and is lost in the Eigen HouseholderQR path, whereas XLA-GPU's QR lowering avoids it. The
input is well-conditioned and the scale is a normal float32, so this is a numerical-accuracy problem in
the standard (Eigen-based) `tf.linalg.qr`, not ill-conditioning and not a device-specific driver bug.

**Expected:** the standard `tf.linalg.qr` matches XLA-GPU / float64 — `Q@R` reconstructs `A` (small
relative residual).
**Actual:** the standard (Eigen-based) `tf.linalg.qr` in float32 gives residual ≈ 0.55.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import tensorflow as tf, numpy as np

A0 = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])          # cond ~ 15 (well-conditioned)
A  = tf.constant(1e-20 * A0, tf.float32)     # 1e-20 is a NORMAL float32

def recon(a):
    q, r = tf.linalg.qr(a)
    return q @ r

with tf.device("/GPU:0"):
    e = recon(A).numpy()
    x = tf.function(recon, jit_compile=True)(A).numpy()

res = lambda M: np.linalg.norm(M - A.numpy()) / np.linalg.norm(A.numpy())
print("eager f32 residual:", res(e))   # ~0.55  (A[1,0]=3e-20 dropped to 0)
print("XLA   f32 residual:", res(x))   # 0.0    (exact)
print("eager Q@R[1,0]:", e[1,0], "| XLA Q@R[1,0]:", x[1,0], "| true 3e-20")
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
eager f32 residual: 5.477e-01
XLA   f32 residual: 0.000e+00
eager Q@R[1,0]: 0.0 | XLA Q@R[1,0]: 3e-20 | true 3e-20
```

### Issue type

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

binary

### TensorFlow version

2.22.0-dev20260921(GIT_VERSION v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f)

### Custom code

Yes

### OS platform and distribution

Linux Ubuntu 22.04(kernel 6.8, glibc 2.35)

### Mobile device

N/A

### Python version

3.12.13

### Bazel version

N/A(binary install)

### GCC/compiler version

N/A(binary install)

### CUDA/cuDNN version

CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.26(pip nvidia-*-cu12)

### GPU model and memory

NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB)

### Current behavior?

A bare Python-int operand to `tf.subtract` is coerced to the tensor's dtype under **eager** execution,
but under `tf.function` (graph) and `jit_compile=True` (XLA) the Python int is first converted to
`int32`, so `Sub(int32, float32)` raises a dtype-mismatch `TypeError`. This is exactly the mismatch
reported for `tf.math.multiply`/`tf.pow` in **#125373** and fixed by **#125387** — but the fix added the
Python-scalar coercion to `multiply`/`pow` (and `divide`) only; `tf.subtract` was missed and still
diverges.

Source (current master / nightly, `tensorflow/python/ops/math_ops.py`):

```python
def multiply(x, y, name=None):          # FIXED by #125387
    ...
    if not tensor_util.is_tf_type(x) and tensor_util.is_tf_type(y):
        x = ops.convert_to_tensor(x, dtype=y.dtype.base_dtype, name="x")   # <- coercion
    ...

def subtract(x, y, name=None):          # STILL MISSING the same coercion
    return gen_math_ops.sub(x, y, name)
```

**Expected:** `tf.subtract(5, float32_tensor)` behaves like `multiply`/`pow` after #125387 — eager,
graph and XLA all coerce the Python scalar and agree.
**Actual:** eager returns the coerced float32 result; graph and XLA raise `TypeError: Input 'y' of 'Sub'
Op has type float32 that does not match type int32 of argument 'x'`.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import os
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = "-1"
import tensorflow as tf

a = tf.constant([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]], tf.float32)

f = lambda t: tf.subtract(5, t)          # bare Python int 5 + float32 tensor
print("eager:", f(a).numpy().tolist())                                  # [[4,3],[2,1]]  (coerced)
print("graph:", tf.function(f)(a).numpy().tolist())                     # TypeError (int32 vs float32)
print("xla  :", tf.function(f, jit_compile=True)(a).numpy().tolist())   # TypeError (int32 vs float32)

# contrast: multiply/pow were fixed by #125387 and now agree across all three
g = lambda t: tf.multiply(5, t)
print("multiply eager/graph/xla all:", g(a).numpy().tolist(),
      tf.function(g)(a).numpy().tolist(),
      tf.function(g, jit_compile=True)(a).numpy().tolist())
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
eager: [[4.0, 3.0], [2.0, 1.0]]
graph: TypeError: Input 'y' of 'Sub' Op has type float32 that does not match type int32 of argument 'x'.
xla  : TypeError: Input 'y' of 'Sub' Op has type float32 that does not match type int32 of argument 'x'.
multiply eager/graph/xla all: [[5,10],[15,20]] [[5,10],[15,20]] [[5,10],[15,20]]
```

issues.title: In OpenXLA builds, `googletest.patch` adds `hdrs` to `cc_library(name = "gtest_main")` for Bazel `layering_check` compatibility, which disables BANT DWYU's empty-`hdrs` keep heuristic. Without `includes` or `keep_dep` on `gtest_main`, BANT DWYU fails to index `gtest_main`'s headers under `gtest/*.h` and `gmock/*.h` and suggests removing `@com_google_googletest//:gtest_main` from test targets.
issues.body:
In OpenXLA builds, `googletest.patch` adds `hdrs` to `cc_library(name = "gtest_main")` for Bazel `layering_check` compatibility, which disables BANT DWYU's empty-`hdrs` keep heuristic. Without `includes` or `keep_dep` on `gtest_main`, BANT DWYU fails to index `gtest_main`'s headers under `gtest/*.h` and `gmock/*.h` and suggests removing `@com_google_googletest//:gtest_main` from test targets.

Add `includes` and `tags = ["avoid_dep", "keep_dep"]` to `gtest_main` in `googletest.patch` so `gtest_main` satisfies `gtest`/`gmock` header includes and is never removed by DWYU, while `avoid_dep` ensures `:gtest` is still preferred when suggesting missing dependencies (and omitting `alwayslink = True` avoids duplicate `main()` ODR violations in targets that also transitively depend on `//tensorflow/core:test_main`).

### Issue type

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

### Source

binary

### TensorFlow version

2.22.0-dev20260921(GIT_VERSION v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f)

### Custom code

### OS platform and distribution

Linux Ubuntu 22.04(kernel 6.8, glibc 2.35)

### Mobile device

N/A

### Python version

3.12.13

### Bazel version

N/A(binary install)

### GCC/compiler version

N/A(binary install)

### CUDA/cuDNN version

CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.26(pip nvidia-*-cu12)

### GPU model and memory

NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB)

### Current behavior?

`tf.math.in_top_k(predictions, targets, k)` returns a **wrong result under `jit_compile=True` (XLA)**
when `targets` contains an **out-of-range class index** (i.e. `target ∉ [0, num_classes)`). Eager
execution and plain `tf.function` (graph, no XLA) both correctly return `False` for an out-of-range
target; XLA silently returns `True`.

The CPU/GPU `InTopK` kernel explicitly range-checks the target (out-of-range → `cannot_say` →
`False`), so this is documented, well-defined behavior — not gather-style "anything goes on OOB".

**Mechanism (why XLA returns `True`).** The XLA lowering builds a one-hot style mask `target == class_i`
to pick the target's prediction, then reduces. For an out-of-range target **no class matches**, so the
masked reduction yields a *fabricated* target value of `0` (the reduction identity). `in_top_k` then
computes `num_greater = count(predictions > fabricated_target_value)` and returns `num_greater < k`.
With `predictions = [0, 0]` and the fabricated value `0`, `num_greater = 0 < k = 1 → True` (wrong;
should be `False`). This also explains why the bug only shows when the fabricated `0` makes
`num_greater < k`: with `predictions = [1,2,3]` and an OOB target, `num_greater = 3 ≥ 1 → False`, so no
visible divergence.

**Expected:** compiled matches eager/graph — an out-of-range target yields `False`.
**Actual:** `jit_compile=True` returns `True`.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import os
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = "-1"   # reproduces CPU-only (and on GPU)
import tensorflow as tf

def fn(p, t, k):
    return tf.math.in_top_k(predictions=p, targets=t, k=k)

p = tf.constant([[0., 0.]])   # 2 classes -> valid targets are 0, 1
t = tf.constant([2])          # 2 is OUT OF RANGE
k = tf.constant(1)

print("eager:", fn(p, t, k).numpy())                                  # [False]  (correct)
print("graph:", tf.function(fn)(p, t, k).numpy())                     # [False]  (correct)
print("XLA  :", tf.function(fn, jit_compile=True)(p, t, k).numpy())   # [ True]  <-- WRONG (silent)
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
eager: [False]
graph: [False]
XLA  : [ True]        # jit_compile=True silently returns the wrong result
```

labels.name: type:bug
labels.description: Bug

labels.name: comp:ops

issues.body:
### Issue type

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

binary

### TensorFlow version

2.22.0-dev20260921(GIT_VERSION v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f)

### Custom code

Yes

### OS platform and distribution

Linux Ubuntu 22.04(kernel 6.8, glibc 2.35)

### Mobile device

N/A

### Python version

3.12.13

### Bazel version

N/A(binary install)

### GCC/compiler version

N/A(binary install)

### CUDA/cuDNN version

CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.26(pip nvidia-*-cu12)

### GPU model and memory

NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB)

### Current behavior?

`tf.nn.avg_pool` with a `VALID` window larger than the input along one spatial dim produces a
**0-sized** output dimension, per TF's own documented VALID formula
`out = ceil((in - filter + 1) / stride)` (e.g. `in=1, filter=2, stride=1 → ceil(0/1) = 0`). In **eager**
this is handled correctly: it returns a well-formed empty tensor (a 0 in the output shape). Under
`tf.function` (graph) and `jit_compile=True` (XLA), the static shape inference instead raises
`ValueError: Negative dimension size caused by subtracting 2 from 1`.

The output size is **0, not negative** — eager computes it fine. The static path appears to compute the
intermediate `in - filter = -1` and reject it before applying the `+1`/`/stride`/`ceil` that the VALID
formula specifies (which would give `0`). So a legal zero-output pooling is rejected at trace time.

**Expected:** graph/XLA match eager — a VALID window giving a 0-sized output yields an empty tensor
(shape with a 0), consistent with the documented formula.
**Actual:** graph/XLA raise `Negative dimension size`.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import os
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = "-1"
import tensorflow as tf

x = tf.constant([[[[1., 2., 3.], [7., 8., 9.]]]])   # shape [N=1, H=1, W=2, C=3]
f = lambda t: tf.nn.avg_pool(t, ksize=[1, 2, 2, 1], strides=[1, 1, 1, 1], padding='VALID')
# VALID: H_out = ceil((1-2+1)/1) = 0, W_out = ceil((2-2+1)/1) = 1

print("eager:", f(x).shape)                                   # (1, 0, 1, 3)  -- empty tensor, OK
print("graph:", tf.function(f)(x).shape)                      # ValueError: Negative dimension size
print("xla  :", tf.function(f, jit_compile=True)(x).shape)    # ValueError: Negative dimension size
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
eager: (1, 0, 1, 3)
graph: ValueError: Negative dimension size caused by subtracting 2 from 1 for '{{node AvgPool}}'
xla  : ValueError: Negative dimension size caused by subtracting 2 from 1 ...
```

issues.title: PR #49301: [XLA:GPU][oneAPI] Allow null pointer kernel arguments for sycl kernels
issues.body:
PR #49301: [XLA:GPU][oneAPI] Allow null pointer kernel arguments for sycl kernels

Imported from GitHub PR https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/49301

LLVM might retain unused 0-sized kernel arguments and mark them as `readnone` instead of removing them. The runtime will not allocate any memory and return nullptr. Hence, a valid kernel can carry a null pointer argument. 
This PR relaxes the sycl kernel launch null argument check so that valid kernels with nullptr arguments are not rejected.

This helps fix `xla/backends/gpu/codegen/emitters/tests/scatter/sorted_empty_indices.hlo` test with the oneAPI backend.
This issue came to light after https://github.com/openxla/xla/commit/f12e3c4264471c510649e30533185878688861fa added a test with empty indices for a scatter operation.

labels.description: Bug

labels.name: comp:ops
labels.description: OPs related issues
