issues.body:
### Issue type

Bug

### Have you reproduced the bug with TensorFlow Nightly?

Yes

### Source

binary

### TensorFlow version

2.22.0-dev20260921(GIT_VERSION `v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f`)

### Custom code

Yes

### OS platform and distribution

Linux Ubuntu 22.04(kernel 6.8, glibc 2.35)

### Mobile device

N/A

### Python version

3.12.13

### Bazel version

N/A(binary install)

### GCC/compiler version

N/A(binary install)

### CUDA/cuDNN version

CUDA 12.9 / cuDNN 9.26(pip `nvidia-*-cu12`)

### GPU model and memory

NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB)

### Current behavior?

`tf.math.sign` in **eager** mode flushes subnormal (denormal) `float32` inputs to zero, so a
genuinely nonzero subnormal such as `1e-40` — which is a well-formed IEEE-754 positive number
(`bitcast` to int32 = `71362`, i.e. a nonzero bit pattern) — yields `sign = 0` instead of the
documented `1`. The public contract of
[`tf.math.sign`](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/math/sign) is exactly
`y = -1 if x < 0; 0 if x == 0; 1 if x > 0` for real `x`, with **no** "subnormal counts as zero"
clause, and `1e-40 > 0` is true. The flush happens in eager on **both CPU and GPU**. In contrast,
`tf.function(jit_compile=True)` (XLA) on GPU returns the correct `[1, -1]`, and NumPy and JAX also
return `[1, -1]`.

**Expected:** `tf.math.sign([1e-40, -1e-40]) == [1., -1.]` (matching the documented contract and
NumPy/JAX/XLA).
**Actual:** eager returns `[0., -0.]`.

This is closely related to the accepted subnormal-handling bug #118644 (`tf.math.rsqrt` on
subnormal float32) and is a distinct operator instance of the same class.

### Standalone code to reproduce the issue

```shell
import tensorflow as tf

x = tf.constant([1e-40, -1e-40], dtype=tf.float32)   # genuine nonzero subnormals

print("bitcast :", tf.bitcast(x, tf.int32).numpy())  # [71362, -2147412286] -> truly nonzero
print("greater :", tf.math.greater(x, 0.0).numpy())  # eager: [False False]  (also flushed)
print("sign eager:", tf.math.sign(x).numpy())        # [0. -0.]   <-- WRONG (should be [1, -1])

sign_xla = tf.function(lambda t: tf.math.sign(t), jit_compile=True)
print("sign XLA  :", sign_xla(x).numpy())            # GPU: [1. -1.]  <-- correct

import numpy as np
print("numpy sign:", np.sign(x.numpy()))             # [1. -1.]   <-- reference
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
bitcast : [     71362 -2147412286]
greater : [False False]
sign eager: [ 0. -0.]        # eager flushes subnormal -> 0   (both CPU and GPU)
sign XLA  : [ 1. -1.]        # XLA (GPU) does not flush -> correct
numpy sign: [ 1. -1.]        # NumPy reference -> correct
```

issues.title: [XLA] Let backends skip LHS memory pressure tracking without a memory limit
issues.body:
[XLA] Let backends skip LHS memory pressure tracking without a memory limit

Without a memory limit the memory pressure state of the latency hiding
scheduler cannot influence any scheduling decision. It only feeds
GetMemoryPeak(), the schedule dump and logging. Building it walks every
instruction, operand and subshape of the module and replays every
sequence. On large modules that is a measurable part of the pass. A new
SchedulerConfig field, track_memory_pressure_without_limit (default true),
lets a backend skip that work; SchedulerCore::IsTrackingMemoryPressure()
tells whether GetMemoryPeak() is meaningful. A memory limit or the schedule
dump still forces tracking. Schedules are unchanged.

issues.title: [XLA] Index the multi output fusion cycle search by local id
issues.body:
[XLA] Index the multi output fusion cycle search by local id

InstructionFusion builds one reachability map per computation and never
updates it. MultiOutputFusionCreatesCycle trusts the map for a positive
answer and otherwise runs a depth first search of the current graph from
the producer. The search kept its visited set and the consumer's
predecessor set in two hash sets keyed by the instruction unique id.

A target is an operand or control predecessor of the consumer, other than
the producer, with an incoming edge. A consumer without one returns before
the search. The search now marks targets and visited nodes in one vector
indexed by the local instruction id, allocated only when a search is
needed. The consumer starts out visited, since none of its transitive
successors can be one of its predecessors. As before, the map is never
updated after it is built. The answers are unchanged. The helper becomes a
protected static member of InstructionFusion so that the unit test can
call it.

On a decode module with a 180k instruction computation, one run of the
pass made 599 such searches. They visited 48 million nodes and took 7.3 s.
Of those checks, 318 now return without a search; the other 281 searches
take 1.7 s.

Tests: instruction_fusion_test pins cycles the map misses, revisits, local
id holes, leaf and control predecessors, and a trusted stale positive.

Reverts 26c5bf8fa501a54abc70923851556f4361b26f84

issues.title: Propagate NaN in tf.experimental.numpy.heaviside

labels.name: ready to pull
labels.description: PR ready for merge process

labels.name: comp:ops
labels.description: OPs related issues

labels.name: size:M
labels.description: CL Change Size: Medium

issues.body:
## Description

`tf.experimental.numpy.heaviside` did not propagate NaN from its first argument, diverging from NumPy.

### Root cause

The implementation selects the result with

```python
array_ops.where_v2(x1 < 0, 0, array_ops.where_v2(x1 > 0, 1, x2))
```

TensorFlow's relational operators (`x1 < 0`, `x1 > 0`) return `False` for NaN inputs, so for `x1 = nan` neither branch is taken and the expression falls through to `x2` — returning e.g. `1.0` instead of `nan`.

### Fix

Mask out NaN elements of the first argument and return NaN for them, matching NumPy:

```python
if np.issubdtype(x1.dtype.as_numpy_dtype, np.inexact):
  if not np.issubdtype(dtype.as_numpy_dtype, np.inexact):
    result = math_ops.cast(result, np_utils.result_type(float))
  nan = constant_op.constant(np.nan, dtype=result.dtype)
  result = array_ops.where_v2(math_ops.is_nan(x1), nan, result)
```

Integer dtypes cannot represent NaN, so the mask is only applied to floating-point inputs. The integer-input result is still promoted to floating point (as before), so behavior there is unchanged.

### Scope note

This fixes `tf.experimental.numpy.heaviside` in this repository. `tf.keras.ops.heaviside` is implemented in the separate `keras-team/keras` package and is intentionally not covered by this PR.

## Test plan

- Added `testHeaviside` (standard `x1 < 0` / `x1 == 0` / `x1 > 0` cases), `testHeavisideNaNPropagation` (NaN from `x1` is propagated) and `testHeavisideIntegerInputs` (integer inputs still promoted to float).
- Verified with `verify/tf_env.sh` on TF 2.21.0 and nightly 2.22.0.dev: `heaviside([nan, 0, -1, 1], [1, 1, 1, 1])` now returns `[nan, 1, 0, 1]`, matching `np.heaviside`.
- Reverse check: reverting the change makes `testHeavisideNaNPropagation` fail (returns `1.0` instead of `nan`), confirming the test locks the bug.

Related: #127819

issues.title: [MINOR][TESTS] Make column resolution error differences explicit
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This follow-up to #58777 removes the API-dependent `assert_column_resolution_error` helper from the shared column tests. Classic error conditions are asserted inline, while the Connect tests with intentionally different public errors are explicitly overridden and documented in `ColumnParityTests`.

This addresses the concern raised in https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/58777#issuecomment-5699678816.

### Why are the changes needed?

An inherited Connect parity test normally communicates identical Classic and Connect behavior. Selecting different expected errors through an overridden helper hid observable error-condition differences inside otherwise inherited tests. Explicit Connect overrides make those differences visible and prevent future parity analysis from treating them as identical behavior.

This follows the existing `master` convention for tests that produce different exceptions in Classic and Connect. The shared [`test_udtf_with_invalid_return_type`](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/e985bd4b9cbfa02f937d7be2c585586a3375dda9/python/pyspark/sql/tests/test_udtf.py#L706-L719) expects `PySparkTypeError` with `UDTF_RETURN_TYPE_MISMATCH`, while [`UDTFParityTests` explicitly overrides the same test](https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/e985bd4b9cbfa02f937d7be2c585586a3375dda9/python/pyspark/sql/tests/connect/test_parity_udtf.py#L36-L59) to expect Connect `InvalidPlanInput`.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. This is a test-only refactoring.

### How was this patch tested?

The following commands passed:

```
build/sbt -Phive package
.venv/bin/python python/run-tests.py --testnames "pyspark.sql.tests.test_column ColumnTests"
.venv/bin/python python/run-tests.py --testnames "pyspark.sql.tests.connect.test_parity_column ColumnParityTests"
.venv/bin/python python/run-tests.py --testnames "pyspark.sql.tests.connect.test_parity_column ColumnParityTestsWithNonStrictDFColResolution"
```

Both Connect suites had one expected skip: `test_validate_column_types`, which requires JVM access. The changed files also pass `git diff --check` and an in-memory Python syntax compilation check.

`BenchmarkQueryTest.checkGeneratedCode` and `WholeStageCodegenSizeBenchmark` generate the code of the TPC-DS, TPC-H and SSB queries over empty tables. issues.title: [SPARK-59781][PYTHON] Raise FIELD_STRUCT_LENGTH_MISMATCH instead of truncating rows longer than the schema in createDataFrame
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Two places in `python/pyspark/sql/types.py` turn a tuple or list row into the internal tuple with `zip`: `_create_converter.convert_struct` (`zip(obj, converters)`, used when a field needs a Python-side converter, i.e. string, struct or null type) and `StructType.toInternal` (`zip(self.fields, obj, self._needConversion)`, used when a field needs conversion, e.g. date or timestamp). `zip` stops at the shorter side, so a row with more values than the schema loses its trailing values without any error. This PR checks `len(obj)` against the number of fields at both sites and raises `PySparkValueError` with the existing error class `FIELD_STRUCT_LENGTH_MISMATCH`, which is what the type verifier already raises for the same row when `verifySchema=True`. The dict and object branches (matched by field name) and the pass-through branches (already checked by the JVM) are unchanged.

### Why are the changes needed?

In PySpark Classic, `createDataFrame` from an RDD (the schema is inferred from the first row by default) or from a local list with `verifySchema=False` silently drops data:

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, Row

spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[1]").getOrCreate()
sc = spark.sparkContext
print(spark.createDataFrame(sc.parallelize([("a", 1), ("b", 2, 3)])).collect())
print(spark.createDataFrame(sc.parallelize([Row(a="x", b=1), Row(c=3, a="y", b=2)])).collect())
print(spark.createDataFrame([("a", 1), ("b", 2, 3)], "x string, y long", verifySchema=False).collect())
```

Before, on master:

```
[Row(_1='a', _2=1), Row(_1='b', _2=2)]
[Row(a='x', b=1), Row(a='3', b=None)]
[Row(x='a', y=1), Row(x='b', y=2)]
```

The value 3 is gone in the first and third case, and the second case has wrong values in both columns rather than just a dropped tail. Whether a user gets an error or a wrong result depends on the column types: the same rows with only long columns fail in the JVM with `STRUCT_ARRAY_LENGTH_MISMATCH`, `verifySchema=True` fails with `FIELD_STRUCT_LENGTH_MISMATCH`, and Spark Connect fails with `AXIS_LENGTH_MISMATCH` for every variant. The RDD path with an explicit schema and `verifySchema=False` (for example `"x string, y long, d date"` with a four-value row) only reaches `StructType.toInternal`, which is why both sites need the check.

After:

```
pyspark.errors.exceptions.captured.PythonException: ... pyspark.errors.exceptions.base.PySparkValueError: [FIELD_STRUCT_LENGTH_MISMATCH] Length of object (3) does not match with length of fields (2).
```

(raised in the Python worker at the first action for the RDD cases, and directly from `createDataFrame` for the local list.)

SPARK-11868 quoted this zip in 2015, but its example is a Row with a missing key, i.e. a row shorter than the schema; the 2016 comment on that ticket already shows the JVM rejecting it with the length error, which is why it was resolved as Cannot Reproduce. The longer-row case still truncated.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, for PySpark Classic, and only for malformed input. A tuple, list or Row with more values than the schema has fields, which was silently truncated when a field needed a converter or conversion, now fails with `FIELD_STRUCT_LENGTH_MISMATCH`. The three sibling paths already fail for this input: the no-converter path (`STRUCT_ARRAY_LENGTH_MISMATCH` from the JVM), `verifySchema=True` (`FIELD_STRUCT_LENGTH_MISMATCH`) and Spark Connect (`AXIS_LENGTH_MISMATCH`). A row with fewer values than fields, which failed in the JVM with `STRUCT_ARRAY_LENGTH_MISMATCH` at the first action, now fails with `FIELD_STRUCT_LENGTH_MISMATCH` instead, up front for a local list and in the Python worker for an RDD. Rows with the right number of values, dict rows and objects are not affected. Because `StructType.toInternal` is shared, two other paths get the same check when a field of the struct needs conversion: struct results of non-Arrow Python UDFs (`useArrow=False`, or `spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled=false`; the conf defaults to true since 4.2), where a longer result was truncated and a shorter one failed in the JVM; and the state tuples of `applyInPandasWithState` and `transformWithState`, where a state tuple longer than the user-declared state schema was truncated silently and now fails the query with `FIELD_STRUCT_LENGTH_MISMATCH`.

### How was this patch tested?

Added two tests to `python/pyspark/sql/tests/test_types.py`: `test_infer_schema_row_length_mismatch` (RDD input with the schema inferred from the first row: a longer tuple, a Row with an extra key, a shorter tuple; the error surfaces at the first action) and `test_create_dataframe_row_length_mismatch_without_verification` (local list with `verifySchema=False`: one longer row per site, `"x string, y long"` for the converter and `"y long, d date"` for `StructType.toInternal`, plus a shorter row; exact error class and parameters). `test_parity_types.py` skips the RDD test like the other RDD tests and overrides the local-list test to assert `AXIS_LENGTH_MISMATCH` for the same inputs. Without the fix both Classic tests fail (the rows come back truncated, or the shorter rows raise the JVM error instead); with the fix they pass, and reverting either guard alone makes the sub-cases for that site fail again. Ran the full `test_types`, `test_parity_types`, `test_dataframe_creation`, `test_parity_dataframe_creation`, `test_udf` and `test_pandas_grouped_map_with_state` modules locally, and the snippet above on unmodified and patched trees in Classic and Connect sessions, with the Python worker importing the patched code.

### Was this patch authored or co-authored using generative AI tooling?

Authored by Li Guo, assisted by Claude Code (Fable 5.1).

issues.title: [SPARK][CORE][SQL][SHUFFLE] Restore interrupt status after catching InterruptedException
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This PR restores the thread interrupt status in several `catch (InterruptedException)` blocks that currently swallow the exception without calling `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`.

When a method catches `InterruptedException` and does not re-throw it, the Java concurrency contract requires restoring the interrupt flag so that callers higher up the call stack can detect the interruption. Failing to do so can cause threads to miss cancellation signals, leading to tasks that fail to terminate, resource leaks, or silent misbehavior in concurrent code.

### Why are the changes needed?

Swallowing `InterruptedException` without restoring the interrupt status is a well-known Java concurrency anti-pattern (see Java Concurrency in Practice, Section 7.1.3, and [IBM DeveloperWorks](https://www.ibm.com/developerworks/library/j-jtp05236/)). Spark already follows the correct pattern in many places (e.g., `HiveServer2.java:152`, `RemoteBlockPushResolver.java:992`), and this PR aligns the remaining instances.

Apache Spark has previously fixed similar issues (e.g., SPARK-51083 in `JavaUtils.java`), which shows awareness of this pattern.

### Fixed locations

| File | Method | Issue |
|------|--------|-------|
| `LauncherServer.java` | `close()` | Swallows interrupt during `serverThread.join()` |
| `LauncherServer.java` | `waitForClose()` | Swallows interrupt during `connThread.join()` |
| `CLIService.java` | `getOperationStatus()` | Swallows interrupt during `Future.get()` |
| `SessionManager.java` | `sleepFor()` | Swallows interrupt during `wait()` in timeout checker |
| `SessionManager.java` | `stop()` | Swallows interrupt during `awaitTermination()` |
| `SSLFactory.java` | `destroy()` | Swallows interrupt during trust manager cleanup |
| `BlockStoreClient.java` | `getHostLocalDirs()` | Swallows interrupt during `createClient()` |

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. This is a correctness fix for thread interrupt handling that does not change any public API or user-visible behavior.

### How was this patch tested?

Manual code inspection. Each fix adds a single `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` call after the existing catch logic, which is a safe, additive change that preserves the original behavior while correctly propagating the interrupt status.

issues.title: [SPARK-59778][SQL] Add display-only properties to the Table API
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Add a backward-compatible `Table.displayProperties()` API whose default implementation returns `properties()`. Use it for metadata display commands:

- `DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED`
- `SHOW TBLPROPERTIES`
- `SHOW TABLE EXTENDED`

Semantic and persistence paths, including `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, continue to use `Table.properties()`.

### Why are the changes needed?

Catalog implementations may need to expose transient, catalog-owned metadata such as labels alongside table properties. Returning that metadata from `Table.properties()` also serializes it into `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, which incorrectly makes display-only metadata look like persisted, reproducible DDL.

The default implementation preserves existing connector behavior and binary compatibility, while allowing connectors to opt in to a separate display view.

issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Make more side-effect causing behavior in the Spark Web UI POST v.s. GET/HEAD when not deployed on YARN. Also validate that the requests have a CSRF token.

Even in YARN deployments GETs which have pre-fetch headers (`x-moz`: `prefecth`) will be rejected with 403.

`app/kill`, `driver/kill`, `app/hold`, `app/resume` all require CSRF tokens now, however `worker/kill` does not as it is an exposed API for operators.

Missing CSRF tokens will 403 & a HEAD/GET request will 405 unless deployed on YARN or fallback behavior is explicitly enabled.

Browser pre-fetch and agents making assumptions on POST v.s. GET "verbs." In general GETs should be side-effect free which is why things like crawlers browsers and agents may choose to prefect them which when the GET is not side-effect free causes undesired behavior.

Yes new config flag, also pressing back on POST pages often behaves differently in browsers.

New UI test, both "regular" in MasterWebUISuite and UISuite but also added additional selenium tests.

issues.title: [SPARK-8682][SQL] Support range join for range-predicate joins
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Add a broadcast range join for range-predicate joins that today fall back to `BroadcastNestedLoopJoinExec`. It is off by default (`spark.sql.join.broadcastRangeJoin.enabled`).

`ExtractRangeJoinKeys` recognizes three shapes. When more than one matches, point-in-range wins, then interval overlap, then a partial range.

- **Point-in-range.** One side is a point and the other is `(low, high)`, for example `p >= lo AND p <= hi` or `p BETWEEN lo AND hi`. The keys are `(point, point)` and `(low, high)`. The build side is an interval index, probed with `overlapping(point, point)`.

- **Interval overlap.** Both sides are `(low, high)`, for example `a.lo < b.hi AND b.lo < a.hi`. The keys are `(low, high)` on each side. The build side is an interval index, probed with `overlapping(low, high)`.

- **Partial range.** One cross-side inequality, one column per side, for example `a < b` or `a > b`. The keys are those two columns. The build side is a sorted point index. `<` and `>` share that index. The join scans `upTo` or `from` according to which side holds the lower bound.

The index returns a superset. Inclusivity, extra conjuncts, and collation stay on the original condition and are evaluated for each candidate. Null keys are not matches. An equi-join key still wins, so an equality plus a range predicate stays a hash join.

Supported join types are inner, left outer, right outer, left semi, and left anti. The preserved side is streamed. Full outer stays a broadcast nested loop join. A `BROADCAST` hint is honored only when that build side is supported. `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL` stays a cartesian product. Types the index can order (including a UDT ordered as its SQL type, and collated strings) are recognized. Arrays, intervals, and other orderable types stay a nested loop join.

`BroadcastExchangeExec` builds the index through `RangeBroadcastMode`. Under AQE, `LogicalQueryStageStrategy` rebuilds the operator when that mode matches. Bound-key nullability is normalized so a stage rewrite still satisfies `BroadcastDistribution`.

This is a broadcast index for a side that already fits the broadcast threshold. It is not a sort-merge range join for two large sides, and there is no `RANGE_JOIN` hint.

### Why are the changes needed?

A range predicate such as an IP lookup or an interval overlap has no equality key, so Spark plans `BroadcastNestedLoopJoinExec` and compares every streamed row with every build row. A broadcast index probes that same small side in logarithmic time and then rechecks the original predicate.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, behind a new configuration that defaults to false, so plans are unchanged unless it is turned on. Compared with released Spark, the configuration does not exist. On master, with it enabled, a supported range predicate is planned as `BroadcastRangeJoinExec` instead of `BroadcastNestedLoopJoinExec`.

```sql
SET spark.sql.join.broadcastRangeJoin.enabled = true;

SELECT s.id, l.zip_id
FROM signin_ip s
JOIN ip_lookup l
  ON s.ip_add_int BETWEEN l.begin_ip AND l.end_ip;
```

Answers match the nested loop join. Full outer, an equality key, an unsupported type, and a non-deterministic key keep the previous plan. Overlapping build intervals make the index larger than the build table, and the existing `spark.sql.maxBroadcastTableSize` check still applies to the index.

### How was this patch tested?

Unit and SQL tests:

- `ExtractRangeJoinKeysSuite`: point-in-range, overlap, partial range, and rejected types.
- `RangeIndexSuite`: interval sweep, keys that compare equal but are not identical, and point-index bounds.
- `RangeJoinSuite`: boundary inclusivity, both build sides, outer, semi, anti, partial `upTo`/`from`, and interval overlap.
- `RangeJoinSQLSuite`: the conf off and on, `BETWEEN`, hints, join types, a residual predicate, collation, AQE, and whole-stage codegen.
- `AdaptiveQueryExecSuite`: broadcast reuse, nullability after AQE, build-side validation, and partition coalescing.

Local benchmark against broadcast nested loop join ([`RangeJoinBenchmark`](https://issues.apache.org/jira/secure/attachment/13084756/RangeJoinBenchmark.scala), Apple M2 Max, OpenJDK 17). Selective cases probe 400,000 rows against 4,000 build rows. Best-time ratio:

| Case | Nested loop | Range join | Ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Point-in-range inner, build ranges | 3793 ms | 57 ms | 66.6X |
| Point-in-range left / right outer | 4492 / 4467 ms | 56 / 55 ms | 80.6X / 81.2X |
| Point-in-range left semi / left anti | 2076 / 3917 ms | 50 / 41 ms | 41.9X / 94.5X |
| Interval overlap inner, build right | 3809 ms | 37 ms | 103.1X |
| Interval overlap left / right outer | 4022 / 4307 ms | 51 / 54 ms | 79.1X / 80.0X |
| Interval overlap left semi / left anti | 3911 / 4198 ms | 34 / 37 ms | 115.3X / 113.8X |
| Partial `<` / `>`, selective build side | 2749 / 2689 ms | 71 / 67 ms | 38.8X / 40.4X |
| Point-in-range, date / timestamp | 3877 / 3754 ms | 50 / 51 ms | 76.9X / 73.3X |
| Point-in-range, decimal | 9898 ms | 75 ms | 131.9X |
| Point-in-range, `UNICODE_CI` string | 212142 ms | 1464 ms | 144.9X |

issues.title: [WIP][SS] Saturate state-watermark microsecond re-expansion to avoid overflow
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

The join state watermark, which is tracked in milliseconds, is converted back to microseconds at two sites:

1. The state eviction predicate built in `WatermarkSupport.watermarkExpression` (`ms * 1000`).
2. The time-interval range scan in `StreamingSymmetricHashJoinExec`, which computes each scan bound as `eventTime + offset`.

For a join range condition with an astronomical interval, the resulting state watermark can exceed the representable timestamp range. In that case `ms * 1000` and `eventTime + offset` overflow `Long`:

- In the eviction predicate the overflow is silent and flips the comparison, so the operator can evict all state.
- In the range scan the overflow produces a wrong, too-narrow scan window, so the join can miss matches.

This PR routes both conversions through saturating helpers added to `WatermarkSupport`:

- `millisToMicrosSaturating(millis: Long): Long` clamps `millis * 1000` to `Long.MaxValue` / `Long.MinValue` instead of wrapping.
- `addMicrosSaturating(a: Long, b: Long): Long` performs saturating addition for the `eventTime + offset` bound.

An out-of-range bound now saturates to the timestamp boundary (evict all / evict none / full scan) instead of wrapping. Values within the representable range are unchanged.

### Why are the changes needed?

Silent `Long` overflow when re-expanding a millisecond state watermark to microseconds is a correctness bug for stream-stream joins with large range conditions: it can either evict all state or narrow the range-scan window and drop otherwise-matching rows. Saturating to the timestamp boundary preserves the intended semantics at the extremes.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Behavior only changes for state watermarks that fall outside the representable timestamp range, where the previous behavior was an overflow/wrap-around bug. Values within range are converted exactly as before.

### How was this patch tested?

Added unit tests in `StreamingSymmetricHashJoinHelperSuite` covering both helpers, including exactly-scalable boundary values and one-past-the-boundary inputs that previously overflowed:

- `millisToMicrosSaturating saturates instead of overflowing`
- `addMicrosSaturating saturates instead of overflowing`

issues.title: [WIP][SQL] Make changelog loading state-option-aware
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This PR makes changelog loading follow the same state-option model as table loading.

It:

* adds `TableCatalog.changelogStateOptionKeys()`, defaulting to
  `tableStateOptionKeys()`;
* passes only connector-declared changelog-state options to `loadChangelog`, while
  preserving the complete option map on batch and streaming relations for scan planning;
* pins changelogs during analysis by catalog, identifier, `ChangelogContext`, and
  changelog-state options, so matching references share one `Changelog` instance without
  conflating scan-only options;
* forwards the new changelog APIs through `DelegatingCatalogExtension`; and
* prevents changelog relations from colliding with ordinary table-cache entries or being
  rebuilt through generic table refresh paths that cannot reconstruct CDC post-processing.

### Why are the changes needed?

Table loading already separates options that select table state from options used later for
scan planning. Changelog loading currently receives every option and independently loads the
same changelog for each reference. This conflates scan-only options with changelog identity and
prevents precise reuse.

Changelog relations also share a catalog identifier with their base tables. Treating them as
ordinary tables during cache lookup or refresh can select or rebuild the wrong relation.
Connector-declared changelog-state keys provide a precise identity for safe per-analysis reuse
while retaining all scan options where they are needed.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. This changes the evolving V2 catalog changelog API contract. Catalogs can override
`changelogStateOptionKeys()` when changelog state is selected by keys different from table state;
by default, it inherits `tableStateOptionKeys()`.

Spark now passes only those declared options to `loadChangelog`. Spark-parsed CDC state remains
in `ChangelogContext`, and the complete user option map remains available during scan planning.
Repeated references with the same context and state options reuse one changelog instance. There
is no SQL syntax change.

### How was this patch tested?

Added unit coverage for changelog-state option projection and defaults, delegation, batch and
streaming resolution through SQL and DataFrame APIs, changelog reuse and separation by state or
context, nested analysis-context propagation, generic refresh safety, table-cache isolation, and
changelog cache eviction during recache.

The focused suites have not yet been run because this is an initial draft. Static validation
completed successfully with `git diff --check`, changed-source line-length checks, and ASCII
checks.

issues.title: [SPARK-59774][SQL] Warn once, and name the remedy, when a whole-stage codegen method is too long to be JIT compiled
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`CodeCompiler.computeByteCodeStats` logs, at INFO, every generated method whose bytecode is past HotSpot's JIT limit of 8000 bytes (`CodeGenerator.DEFAULT_JVM_HUGE_METHOD_LIMIT`). This PR raises that line to WARN in the one case where it costs the user and they can act on it, and only the first time, on the driver. All of these must hold:

- the method belongs to a whole-stage codegen stage (`GeneratedIteratorForCodegenStage*`);
- it runs per row, not once (not `<init>`, `<clinit>` or `init`);
- the stage keeps whole-stage codegen: the method is at or below `spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit`, so the stage does not fall back;
- the JVM leaves huge methods to the interpreter: `-XX:+DontCompileHugeMethods`, read through `Utils.getVMOptionValue`;
- the method is compiled on the driver, not by a task: the driver compiles each stage before its tasks do.

Every other report, including every one after the first WARN, keeps the existing INFO line unchanged.

Before:
```
INFO CodeGenerator: Generated method too long to be JIT compiled: <class>.<method> is 9513 bytes
```
After, the first time on the driver:
```
WARN CodeGenerator: Generated method too long to be JIT compiled: <class>.processNext is 9513 bytes, so it runs interpreted on every row. Setting spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit to 8000 runs such stages without whole-stage codegen instead. Further methods over the limit are logged at INFO.
```

### Why are the changes needed?

HotSpot does not JIT-compile a method past 8000 bytes (`-XX:+DontCompileHugeMethods`, on by default), so the method runs interpreted, typically several times slower. On stock Spark 4.2.0, widening a projection's consume method from 7945 to 8677 bytes steps it from about 770 to about 4100 ns a row. Spark detects this, but only at INFO. `spark-shell` and `pyspark` run at WARN and never show it, and `spark.sql.codegen.hugeMethodLimit`, which could act on it, defaults to 65535, which no compiled method exceeds.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, in the log only: at most one WARN, from the driver, and only in the case above. Everything else is unchanged.

### How was this patch tested?

A new test in `CodeGenerationSuite` covers each case: a stage that falls back, the run-once methods, a class outside whole-stage codegen, a compile under a `TaskContext`, the first WARN (which names the setting and 8000), and INFO afterwards. The SPARK-25113 test asserts that a projection's huge method is still logged at INFO.
```
build/sbt "catalyst/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.expressions.CodeGenerationSuite -- -z SPARK-25113 -z SPARK-59774"
```

issues.title: [SPARK-59765][SQL][TESTS] Generate broadcast joins in full when measuring benchmark query codegen
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`BenchmarkQueryTest.checkGeneratedCode` and `WholeStageCodegenSizeBenchmark` measure the code whole-stage codegen generates for the TPC-DS (and TPC-H, SSB) queries without running them. They plan each query over empty tables with AQE disabled and call `doCodeGen()` on every `WholeStageCodegenExec`. With AQE disabled, `BroadcastHashJoinExec` executes its broadcast while generating code. Over an empty table the relation is `EmptyHashedRelation`, and `HashJoin` then generates a one-line stub instead of the join ("If HashedRelation is empty, hash inner join simply returns nothing"), so the rest of the stage is not generated either. Both instruments therefore measure stubs for every stage with a broadcast join. On master, with the benchmark's setup, 324 of the 2201 stages of the TPC-DS v1.4 and v2.7 queries carry the stub, in 127 of the 129 queries.

This PR generates each stage's code from a copy of the stage in which every broadcast exchange, including one under a `ReusedExchangeExec`, reads one row of non-null default values instead of its child. The joins then generate the code they generate for data. Only the code of the copy is used: the build side is its own stage, found in and measured from the original plan, so the set of stages is unchanged.

- `BenchmarkQueryTest` gets a companion object with `withRowBroadcasts`, which builds the copy, and `generatedCode`, which returns every stage of a plan and its subqueries with its code. `generatedCode` follows an adaptive plan into its current plan and query stages, as `codegenStringSeq` does. The copy is built top down, so a build side is never copied before its exchange is replaced. One replacement per broadcast exchange of a plan is shared by every stage that reads it, so each one-row broadcast runs once. `withRowBroadcasts` fails if any broadcast hash or nested loop join of the copy reads anything but a one-row broadcast, so no join can generate its empty-build-side code unnoticed, whatever the join kind.
- `checkGeneratedCode` iterates `generatedCode(plan)` instead of its own walk.
- `WholeStageCodegenSizeBenchmark` measures through `generatedCode` in place of `codegenStringSeq`. It skips a query only when the query fails to plan. A failure while generating the code, or a query with no whole-stage-codegen subtree, fails the run instead of silently shrinking the totals. Its scaladoc says how broadcast joins are measured.
- The three results files are regenerated. The stage count is unchanged at 2247 and the largest method at 4962 bytes. The source code size grows by about 19% (21.37M to 25.42M characters), the summed per-stage largest method by about 11% (821K to 910K bytes), and the summed constant pool by about 6%.

A single row makes every join key unique, so a hash join generates its unique-key form; a join whose real build side repeats keys also has the loop over matches. That remaining difference is small next to a stub.

### Why are the changes needed?

The benchmark is the instrument for the SPARK-56908 umbrella, and it has understated the generated code of most TPC-DS queries. `checkGeneratedCode` checks stubs in the same way. `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite` already runs it with AQE disabled on master, and the other suites will once SPARK-59764 disables AQE for them.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Test and benchmark only.

### How was this patch tested?

By running the affected suites:
```
build/sbt "sql/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.execution.LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQueryWithStatsSuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQueryANSISuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCHQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.SSBQuerySuite"
```
All six passed, 635 tests, in 48 seconds. No stage generated in full crosses the 8000-byte limit.

As a negative check, with the replacement of broadcast exchanges disabled, 145 of the 150 tests of `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite` fail with `a broadcast hash join reads ..., not a one-row broadcast`. That suite already runs the check with AQE disabled on master, so this is the bug there today.

The results files were generated with `SPARK_GENERATE_BENCHMARK_FILES=1`, running the benchmark's `main` under JDK 17, 21 and 25 in turn. The benchmark measures code sizes, not time, so the machine does not matter. A JDK 25 run through sbt matched the direct run within about 0.01%, the same run-to-run variation the committed files already show between JDKs.

issues.title: [SPARK-59764][SQL][TESTS] Check generated code of benchmark queries with AQE disabled
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`BenchmarkQueryTest.checkGeneratedCode` is meant to check that every whole-stage codegen subtree of a benchmark query compiles, and that its largest generated method is within HotSpot's `HugeMethodLimit` (8000 bytes). It walks `sql(query).queryExecution.executedPlan` without running the query. Since adaptive query execution became the default (SPARK-33679, 3.2.0), that plan is an `AdaptiveSparkPlanExec`, whose `WholeStageCodegenExec` subtrees are created only when the query runs. So the walk finds none, and `TPCDSQuerySuite` (with `TPCDSQueryWithStatsSuite` and `TPCDSQueryANSISuite`), `TPCHQuerySuite` and `SSBQuerySuite` pass without compiling or checking anything. Only `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite`, which disabled AQE itself, kept running the check.

This PR:
1. Mixes `DisableAdaptiveExecutionSuite` into `BenchmarkQueryTest`, so the plans these suites check have their whole-stage codegen subtrees. It also mixes in `QueryTest` explicitly, and drops the now redundant mixin from `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite`.
2. Makes `checkGeneratedCode` fail if it finds no `WholeStageCodegenExec` subtree, or finds an `AdaptiveSparkPlanExec` anywhere in the plan or its subqueries, so the check cannot become vacuous again, entirely or in part, unnoticed.

The `spark.sql.readSideCharPadding=false` override in `TPCDSQuerySuite` and the `modified-q3` exclusion (SPARK-29128) are unchanged.

**Known limitation, not changed here.** The TPC tables these suites create are empty. With AQE off, `BroadcastHashJoinExec` executes its broadcast while generating code, gets `EmptyHashedRelation`, and generates a stub for an inner join and the rest of its stage (`HashJoin.codegenInner`). So stages with an inner broadcast hash join are still checked only in part. Fixing that needs non-empty tables, which changes more than this bug, and is better as a follow-up. The check also covers the non-adaptive plan shape only; covering AQE's runtime shapes would need executed plans over real data.

### Why are the changes needed?

The compile check and the method size check in these suites have not run since 3.2.0 except in `LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite`, so a codegen regression in the TPC-DS, TPC-H or SSB queries would mostly not be caught.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Test-only change.

### How was this patch tested?

By running the affected suites:
```
build/sbt "sql/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQueryWithStatsSuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCDSQueryANSISuite org.apache.spark.sql.TPCHQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.SSBQuerySuite org.apache.spark.sql.execution.LogicalPlanTagInSparkPlanSuite"
```

As a negative check, with only the new assertion and without `DisableAdaptiveExecutionSuite`, all 22 tests of `TPCHQuerySuite` fail with `no WholeStageCodegenExec subtree found to check in the plan`, which is the bug this PR fixes.

issues.title: [SPARK-59749][SQL] Accept empty STRUCT operands in ASOF JOIN MATCH_CONDITION
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?
  ASOF JOIN `MATCH_CONDITION` now accepts operands that are, or contain, an empty struct (`STRUCT<>`). The operand check 
  was "orderable and contains no empty struct". It is now only "orderable", the same rule `min_by` and `max_by` use for 
  their ordering column. An array of empty structs compares each element as one value.
  
  Now accepted (same type on both sides): `STRUCT<>`, `STRUCT<x: STRUCT<>>`, `ARRAY<STRUCT<>>`. An empty struct against a
  non-empty struct stays rejected.
  
While testing these operands, I found and fixed two bugs in composite `MATCH_CONDITION` operands. They also affect  types with no empty struct:
- A forward match (`<` or `<=`) could pick the wrong right row when an operand holds a NULL array element or a NULL struct field. The join picked the row with the smallest distance, and a NULL inside the operand breaks that distance. A forward match now takes the first right row that passes the condition. The right side is sorted ascending, so that row is the smallest. Nearest joins (DataFrame API) still use the distance.
- An `ARRAY<STRUCT>` operand whose fields have different types (for example `INT` and `TIMESTAMP`) passed the type  check, then failed with `DATATYPE_MISMATCH.DATA_DIFF_TYPES`. The per-element distance now keeps the field distances in a struct instead of an array.

### Why are the changes needed?

The comparison operator already accepts these pairs: `named_struct() >= named_struct()` is `true`, because two empty 
structs are equal. ASOF rejected them with an error that says the operands must be orderable, but `STRUCT<>` is 
orderable. 

The two bugs gave a wrong row or a confusing error for valid queries. A forward match must return the smallest right 
value that satisfies the condition.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. This query failed and now runs:

```sql
SELECT * FROM VALUES (named_struct()) AS l(s)
ASOF JOIN VALUES (named_struct()) AS r(s)
MATCH_CONDITION (l.s >= r.s);
-- before: [ASOF_JOIN_MATCH_CONDITION_INVALID_TYPE] ... Got: "STRUCT<>" and "STRUCT<>".
```

Two empty structs are equal, so `>=` and `<=` match, and `>` and `<` find no match. A NULL empty struct never matches. 

Forward matches with NULL parts now return the smallest matching row:

```sql
SELECT r.tag FROM VALUES (ARRAY(CAST(NULL AS INT))) AS t(a)
ASOF JOIN VALUES (ARRAY(CAST(NULL AS INT), CAST(NULL AS INT)), 'nn'), (ARRAY(5), 'five') AS r(a, tag)
MATCH_CONDITION (t.a <= r.a);
-- before: five; after: nn (NULL sorts first: [null] < [null, null] < [5])
```

`ARRAY<STRUCT>` operands with fields of different types now run instead of failing with `DATATYPE_MISMATCH.DATA_DIFF_TYPES`.

### How was this patch tested?

Unit tests in `AsOfJoinMatchConditionTypesSuite`, `ResolveAsOfJoinSuite`, and `AsOfJoinSQLSuite` for the accepted and rejected type pairs and the array element distance. Execution tests in `AsOfJoinSortMergeSQLSuite` assert the matched row for all four operators, for: an empty struct, a struct with only an empty field, a NULL empty struct, a struct with an empty field and an int field (column and tuple form), and arrays of empty structs. Golden cases in `join-asof-datatypes.sql`.

New execution tests in `AsOfJoinSortMergeSQLSuite` cover the two bug fixes: forward matches with NULL array elements and NULL struct fields (column and tuple form, `<` and `<=`), and `ARRAY<STRUCT>` operands with fields of different types for all four operators. The existing `SortMergeAsOfJoinSuite` and `DataFrameAsOfJoinSuite` cover DataFrame forward and nearest joins, tolerance, and spill.

issues.title: Shuffle tracking prevents dynamic allocation from removing executors after `collect()` / `toPandas()`
issues.body:
When using dynamic allocation with shuffle tracking enabled, executors that participated in a shuffle remain alive indefinitely after a `collect()` or `toPandas()` action has completed.

Configuration:

```text
spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=true
spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout=60s
spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout=1m
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled=true
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.timeout=infinity
```

For example:

```python
pandas_df = spark.sql("...").toPandas()
```

After the action completes, the executors that produced shuffle data are not removed after `spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout`.

The same behavior can be reproduced with:

```python
df.collect()
```

I also observed that shuffle files are present in `$SPARK_LOCAL_DIRS` on the executor pods (`shuffle_*.data`, `shuffle_*.index`, etc.).

Interestingly, setting a finite value for:

```text
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.timeout
```

allows the executors to be removed, which suggests that shuffle tracking is what prevents their removal.

My question is whether this behavior is expected.

`collect()` and `toPandas()` are terminal actions that materialize their result on the driver. Once the action has completed successfully, there should presumably be no further consumer of the shuffle output produced by the query.

Therefore, I would expect the executors to become eligible for removal after `spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout`, even if shuffle files produced during the query still physically exist on the executors.

Is there a reason why the shuffle is still considered active after the `collect()` / `toPandas()` action has completed? Or is this an expected limitation/behavior of shuffle tracking?

For comparison, setting:

```text
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.timeout=1m
```

allows the executors to be removed, whereas:

```text
spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.timeout=infinity
```

keeps them alive.

issues.title: [SPARK-59757][CORE] Harden BytesToBytesMap after failed reset allocation
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Harden `BytesToBytesMap` after `reset()` fails to allocate a replacement pointer array. Reset clears the map page and growth state before allocation. A later lookup, `getArray()`, or `maxNumKeysIndex()` retries the allocation when memory is available.

Concurrent `safeLookup()` callers share one safely published replacement array. `free()` and destructive iteration remain terminal, with explicit failure instead of accidentally restoring the array. The lock-order requirement around recovery allocation is documented.

Add on-heap and off-heap regression coverage for reuse, repeated allocation failures, semantic keys, growth state, concurrent recovery, array accessors, and terminal states.

### Why are the changes needed?

This hardens the low-level `BytesToBytesMap` contract after a transient allocation failure. Previously, a failed reset could leave a null pointer array and stale page state. A caller that catches the `SparkOutOfMemoryError` and later reuses the map could encounter `NullPointerException` or append into a freed page.

No in-tree production caller currently catches the `SparkOutOfMemoryError` thrown by `reset()`, so this change does not claim that a Spark query can resume from that failure. For callers that do recover, a later array-dependent operation either restores an empty usable map or reports `SparkOutOfMemoryError` again if memory remains unavailable.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No.

issues.title: [SPARK-59605][SQL] Handle NULL literal in ORC IN filter pushdown
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`OrcFilters` builds an ORC `SearchArgument` by mapping every `IN` list value through
`castLiteralValue`, which casts the value to `Number` and dereferences it — throwing
`NullPointerException` on a `NULL` literal. This PR filters `NULL` literals out of the
`IN` list before casting: the remaining non-null values are pushed as before, and if no
non-null value remains (e.g. `id IN (NULL)`) no filter is pushed.

### Why are the changes needed?

`SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN (1, 3, NULL)` on an ORC table fails when
`spark.sql.orc.filterPushdown=true`, while returning the correct rows when pushdown is off:

```
java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Number.longValue()" because "value" is null
  at org.apache.spark.sql.execution.datasources.orc.OrcFilters$.castLiteralValue(OrcFilters.scala:167)
  at org.apache.spark.sql.execution.datasources.orc.OrcFilters$.buildLeafSearchArgument(OrcFilters.scala:284)
```

A `NULL` in an `IN` list is inert under three-valued logic — `x IN (.., NULL)` is TRUE only
for non-null matches and NULL otherwise — so `IN (1, 3, NULL)` selects the same rows as
`IN (1, 3)`. Dropping the NULL yields a `SearchArgument` that prunes exactly the right
stripes, and Spark re-applies the full predicate after the scan. `ParquetFilters` already
handles `NULL` in its `IN` branch, so this brings ORC in line.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. `IN` predicates containing a `NULL` literal on ORC tables with filter pushdown enabled
no longer throw a `NullPointerException`; they return the same rows as with pushdown disabled.
No change for `IN` lists without a `NULL`.

### How was this patch tested?

New unit test in `OrcFilterSuite` asserting `IN (1, 3, NULL)` produces the same
`SearchArgument` as `IN (1, 3)`, `IN (NULL)` produces none, and the `Not(IN(...))` cases
behave consistently. New end-to-end test in `OrcQuerySuite` reading an ORC table with
`id IN (1, 3, NULL)` and asserting identical results with `spark.sql.orc.filterPushdown`
on and off.

issues.title: [SPARK-59752][INFRA] dev/scalastyle: annotate style violations that report a column
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?
`dev/scalastyle` emits inline GitHub `::error` annotations for scalastyle violations reported through sbt's logger, matching lines of shape `[error] <path>:<line>: <message>`. The regex required whitespace immediately after `:<line>:`, on the assumption that the absence of a `:<col>:` distinguishes it from a genuine Scala compiler error of shape `[error] <path>:<line>:<col>: <msg>`. That assumption doesn't hold for every scalastyle checker -- the `nonascii` checker's sbt-logger output includes a column, e.g. `[error] .../StringExpressionsSuite.scala:1065:17: nonascii.message`, which matched neither regex branch and so silently got no annotation.

This PR makes the column optional in both regex branches (the native-console-writer branch already captured an optional column but discarded it) and threads it through to GitHub's `::error ...,col=<n>` annotation parameter when present.

A genuine Scala compiler error can't reach this code path: `project/SparkBuild.scala`'s `enableScalaStyle`/`cachedScalaStyle` deliberately does not attach style checking to `(Compile / compile)`, precisely so a broken compile elsewhere can't cascade into the style job (and vice versa) -- see the comment above `enableScalaStyle`.

### Why are the changes needed?
Without this, a scalastyle violation from a checker that reports a column (e.g. `nonascii`) still correctly fails the build, but gets no inline "Files changed" annotation -- exactly the problem this script's annotation logic exists to prevent (per its own comment: "Without this, a violation cascades into ~7 red CI checks... forcing the user to download a full job log to find the actual violation"). A contributor hitting this checker has to download the full job log to find the violation.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?
No. This only affects GitHub Actions CI annotations for `dev/scalastyle`, a contributor-facing tooling script; it doesn't change Spark's behavior, build output, or the pass/fail result of any check.

### How was this patch tested?
- Verified the regex against four synthetic cases (both formats, with and without a column), confirming the fix and no behavior change for the two cases that already worked.
- End-to-end: temporarily introduced a real non-ASCII character outside an existing `scalastyle:off` block in `StringExpressionsSuite.scala`, ran `dev/scalastyle` with `GITHUB_ACTIONS=true`, confirmed the violation is now annotated with file/line/column (`::error file=...,line=60,col=3,title=Scalastyle::nonascii.message`) instead of being silently dropped, then reverted the temporary change.

issues.title: [SPARK-59212][K8S][INFRA][3.5] Pin the Minikube container runtime to docker in K8s CI
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Backport the applicable part of #58502 (`680855bea73`) to `branch-3.5` by passing `--container-runtime=docker` to the `minikube start` invocation used by the Kubernetes integration test job.

`branch-3.5` starts Minikube directly (downloading the `latest` binary) rather than via `medyagh/setup-minikube`, so this backport passes the CLI flag instead of the action's `container-runtime` input. The OIDC E2E job updated by the master change does not exist on `branch-3.5`, so this backport changes only the Kubernetes integration test job.

### Why are the changes needed?

Minikube 1.39.0 changed its default container runtime from Docker to containerd. The Kubernetes integration test builds Spark images through `minikube docker-env`, but the containerd Docker shim does not implement enough of the Docker API for Buildx. Image construction therefore fails while booting BuildKit with:

```
failed to inspect pulled image moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1: Error response from daemon: 404 page not found
```

This currently breaks the `branch-3.5` Kubernetes integration check on forks: the job runs on non-`apache/spark` repos when the `kubernetes` module is touched, and `.github` changes map to the `root` module in `dev/is-changed.py`, so they trigger it too. Pinning the runtime to Docker restores the real Docker daemon expected by the image build.

This is the `branch-3.5` counterpart of the already-merged #58533 (4.3), #58502 (master); SPARK-59212 was merged to master, 4.x, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 but not 3.5.

issues.title: [SPARK-57897][BUILD][FOLLOWUP] Use AWS SDK bundle in credential-aws
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Use `software.amazon.awssdk:bundle` instead of `sts` in `connector/credential-aws`, sharing the SDK artifact and version already used by `hadoop-cloud`. Update the dependency comment and regenerate the assembly dependency manifest. Removing the modular SDK removes the `netty-nio-client` dependency on `reactive-streams` 1.0.4, leaving 1.0.3 from the existing `aliyun-java-core` dependency.

This follows up on #58051 under [SPARK-57897](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-57897).

### Why are the changes needed?

With both `-Pcredential-aws` and `-Phadoop-cloud`, the assembly currently contains the AWS SDK bundle alongside modular SDK jars. The bundle relocates third-party dependencies, so duplicate SDK classes are not binary-compatible even when all artifacts use version 2.35.4. Which jar supplies a duplicated class can determine whether S3A uploads succeed.

For example, the bundle's `TransferListenerInvoker` calls `Logger.logger()` with the relocated SLF4J return type. Loading `Logger` from the modular `utils` jar instead causes:

```text
java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'software.amazon.awssdk.thirdparty.org.slf4j.Logger software.amazon.awssdk.utils.Logger.logger()'
```

This exception appears in the [log artifact](https://github.com/ruanwenjun/spark/actions/runs/35857041511/artifacts/10752217586) from [this CI job](https://github.com/ruanwenjun/spark/actions/runs/35857041511/job/107174192748): `resource-managers/kubernetes/integration-tests/target/integration-tests.log`, line 662 (`KubernetesSuite`, 12:36:15.312) and line 4463 (`VolcanoSuite`, 12:57:13.045) on September 23. Both stacks include `TransferListenerInvoker` and `S3AStoreImpl.putObject`. These exceptions are in the log artifact, not the failure annotations for `DecommissionSuite`. The mixed dependency set was introduced by #58051.

Using the bundle for both modules removes that duplicate class source without changing the AWS SDK version or relying on classpath order.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. It fixes S3A linkage failures in builds that include both optional profiles. Builds using only `credential-aws` now pull in the larger SDK bundle instead of the modular STS dependency.

### How was this patch tested?

- `build/sbt -Pcredential-aws -Phadoop-cloud 'credential-aws/test'` and `build/sbt -Pcredential-aws 'credential-aws/test'`: all 69 existing tests passed in each configuration.
- Reproduced the exact `NoSuchMethodError` with AWS SDK 2.35.4 modular `utils` before `bundle` on the classpath. The same transfer-listener call passes with only `bundle`:

  ```java
  new software.amazon.awssdk.transfer.s3.internal.progress.TransferListenerInvoker(
      java.util.List.of(new software.amazon.awssdk.transfer.s3.progress.TransferListener() {}))
      .transferInitiated(null);
  ```

issues.title: [SPARK-58209][SQL] Mark CallMethodViaReflection and XPathExtract stateful to prevent data races
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Mark `CallMethodViaReflection` as `stateful` so that `freshCopyIfContainsStatefulExpression()` gives each evaluation its own instance, and add a comment naming the protected state: the reusable `buffer` array that `evalInternal` fills with the argument values before handing it to the reflective call.

Two tests are added to `CallMethodViaReflectionSuite`:

- the expression reports `stateful` and a fresh copy is a distinct instance that still evaluates;
- a two-thread test in which the first evaluation blocks in its second argument, after writing its first argument into the buffer, while a second evaluation runs to completion. On a shared instance the second evaluation overwrites the first one's argument and the first call returns `m20` instead of `m10`; with fresh copies both results are correct.

This supersedes #57371 by @huanghanyu-vungle, narrowed per @peter-toth's review there: the `XPathExtract` and `UserDefinedGenerator` overrides were judged inert (`XPathExtract` is `RuntimeReplaceable` and its state lives in a `Literal`-captured evaluator; generators never reach a fresh-copy site), so only the `CallMethodViaReflection` change is kept. The JIRA title still names all three expressions; it can be narrowed to match when this is merged.

### Why are the changes needed?

Sub-task of SPARK-58154. `CallMethodViaReflection` keeps a per-instance `buffer` for the reflection arguments but was not marked stateful, so the fresh-copy mechanism skipped it. When one instance is evaluated from two threads at once, for example sibling DataFrames derived from a common parent whose projections over a `LocalRelation` are evaluated on the driver by `ConvertToLocalRelation`, one thread's arguments can be overwritten by the other's between filling the buffer and making the call, producing silently wrong results.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Concurrent evaluation of the same `reflect` / `java_method` call now returns the correct result instead of racing; single-threaded behavior is unchanged.

### How was this patch tested?

New tests in `CallMethodViaReflectionSuite`:

```
build/sbt "catalyst/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.expressions.CallMethodViaReflectionSuite"
```

All 13 tests pass (11 existing, 2 new). Removing the `stateful` override makes the two-thread test fail deterministically with `m20 did not equal m10`.

issues.title: [SPARK-59748][CORE] Loser tree + small-k linear merge for UnsafeSorterSpillMerger
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

`UnsafeExternalSorter` merges its sorted spill runs (plus the in-memory run) in `UnsafeSorterSpillMerger` using a `java.util.PriorityQueue<UnsafeSorterIterator>`. Emitting each record does `poll()` + `add()` -- two O(log k) sift passes -- and every comparison calls `getKeyPrefix()` on both runs, falling to the record comparator on a prefix tie.

This replaces the heap with two run-count-dependent strategies and caches the prefix:

- a **linear min-scan** for a small number of runs (`<= 8`), and
- a **loser (tournament) tree** above that -- one replace-top adjustment (~`log2(k)` comparisons) per record, with no re-insertion;
- each live run's current key prefix is cached in a parallel `long[]`, refreshed when the run advances, so comparisons read a cached `long` instead of calling `getKeyPrefix()`, falling to the record comparator only on a prefix tie.

The `UnsafeSorterSpillMerger` constructor and its `addSpillIfNotEmpty` / `getSortedIterator` methods are unchanged, so both the single-round merge and the bounded multi-round merge (`UnsafeSorterBoundedSpillMerger`) benefit. Ordering is preserved: key prefix first, then the record comparator on a tie.

A `UnsafeSorterSpillMergerBenchmark` is added under `core` to measure the merge in isolation.

### Why are the changes needed?

The `PriorityQueue` does two sift passes per record (poll + add) and its comparison indirection is comparatively expensive. A loser tree does a single replace-top per record at the same O(log k), and for a handful of runs a flat linear scan is cheaper still. Low-cardinality / duplicate-heavy keys -- frequent prefix ties -- are exactly the workloads that spill and merge most.

`UnsafeSorterSpillMergerBenchmark` (merge CPU only: in-memory runs, 4.19M records) reports time-per-record vs. the `PriorityQueue` baseline, by run count `k`:

```
distinct prefixes:   k=2 1.46x   k=4 2.00x   k=8 2.14x   k=16 1.88x   k=64 1.79x
duplicate prefixes:  k=2 1.32x   k=4 1.50x   k=8 1.48x   k=16 1.60x   k=64 1.42x
```

This isolates merge CPU and excludes spill read/decode I/O, so it is an upper bound on the end-to-end effect; a forced-spill end-to-end measurement is a reasonable follow-up. This PR is a draft pending that measurement.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. This is an internal change to the external-sort spill merge. The merged output ordering is unchanged (key prefix, then the record comparator on a tie), and there are no API or configuration changes.

### How was this patch tested?

Existing `UnsafeExternalSorterSuite` and its radix subclass `UnsafeExternalSorterRadixSortSuite` pass (58 tests); their multi-spill and bounded-merge cases exercise both the linear and loser-tree paths, and ordering semantics are unchanged. Added `UnsafeSorterSpillMergerBenchmark` for the numbers above (the results file is not committed).

issues.title: [SPARK-59747][CORE] Don't retry compaction of rolled event log files with malformed input
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

In `FsHistoryProvider.compact()`, catch `CharacterCodingException` thrown while compacting rolled event log files, log it at WARN, and still record `lastEvaluatedForCompaction` for the current index.

### Why are the changes needed?

When the rolled event log files that are eligible for compaction contain bytes that are not valid UTF-8, `EventLogFileCompactor` fails with a `MalformedInputException` while replaying them to initialize the event filter builders. `compact()` only records `lastEvaluatedForCompaction` after compaction succeeds, and the exception reaches the generic handler, which logs it at ERROR.

The listing replay stops early, so it never reaches the malformed bytes and the application keeps being listed. Each time the last (non-compacted) event log file grows, the log is reprocessed and compaction of the same unchanged rolled files is tried again. For a long-running application this logs a full stack trace at ERROR on every scan until a new event log file is rolled. Rolled files are no longer modified, so the retry can never succeed.

With this change, compaction for that index is skipped, and it is only tried again once a new event log file is rolled. Other failures are handled as before.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes, but only in History Server logs. When compaction fails because the event log files contain malformed input, the History Server logs a WARN once per rolled event log index instead of an ERROR on every scan. The application listing and replay are unchanged, and the event log files are left uncompacted as before.

### How was this patch tested?

Added a new test to `FsHistoryProviderSuite`. It writes a rolled event log file with a malformed UTF-8 sequence after the events used for listing, then checks that the application is still listed, no compact file is created, and `lastEvaluatedForCompaction` is recorded. The test fails without this change (`None did not equal Some(2)`, with `MalformedInputException` logged at ERROR) and passes with it.

```
build/mvn -pl core -am test -Dtest=none -DwildcardSuites=org.apache.spark.deploy.history
```

issues.body:

### What changes were proposed in this pull request?
<!--
Please clarify what changes you are proposing. The purpose of this section is to outline the changes and how this PR fixes the issue. 
If possible, please consider writing useful notes for better and faster reviews in your PR. See the examples below.
  1. If you refactor some codes with changing classes, showing the class hierarchy will help reviewers.
  2. If you fix some SQL features, you can provide some references of other DBMSes.
  3. If there is design documentation, please add the link.
  4. If there is a discussion in the mailing list, please add the link.
-->

This PR makes the `CALL` statement invoke its stored procedure at command-execution time rather than during analysis.

Background: a V2 stored procedure's result schema is known only after the procedure has been invoked -`BoundProcedure.call` returns the result sets as `Scan`s whose schema is read afterwards. Previously the analyzer rule `InvokeProcedures` ran the whole optimizer on the resolved-and-bound `Call` (`session.sessionState.optimizer.execute(c)`) to fold the arguments, invoked the procedure, and replaced the `Call` with a `CommandResult` - all during analysis. As a result, merely analyzing a `CALL` (for example asking for its schema) executed the procedure.

Key changes:
- Remove the `InvokeProcedures` analysis rule and its registration, so procedures are no longer invoked during analysis. Procedure resolution and binding (`ResolveProcedures`, `BindProcedures`) are unchanged and still run in the analyzer.
- Add a physical operator `CallExec` that invokes `BoundProcedure.call` when the node is executed. The procedure is invoked lazily and exactly once; both `output` and the result rows are derived from the resulting scans.
- Plan an executable `Call` to `CallExec` in `DataSourceV2Strategy`; a non-executing `Call` (as produced for EXPLAIN) still maps to `ExplainOnlySparkPlan`.
- Update callers that need a `CALL`'s real schema/output to use the new accessors.
- Remove the now-unused `ExecutableDuringAnalysis` trait; `Call` no longer mixes it in.
- Document the behavior change in the SQL migration guide.

### Why are the changes needed?
<!--
Please clarify why the changes are needed. For instance,
  1. If you propose a new API, clarify the use case for a new API.
  2. If you fix a bug, you can clarify why it is a bug.
-->

Invoking a procedure during analysis is a side effect in the wrong phase: analyzing a query should not run it. Any path that only needs a `CALL`'s schema - most notably the Spark Connect schema-only analyze request - would execute the procedure as a side effect of analysis. Running the procedure at execution time makes `CALL` behave like every other command (its work happens when the statement is executed) and confines the side effect to actual execution.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?
<!--
Note that it means *any* user-facing change including all aspects such as new features, bug fixes, or other behavior changes. Documentation-only updates are not considered user-facing changes.

If yes, please clarify the previous behavior and the change this PR proposes - provide the console output, description and/or an example to show the behavior difference if possible.
If possible, please also clarify if this is a user-facing change compared to the released Spark versions or within the unreleased branches such as master.
If no, write 'No'.
-->

Yes.

- Spark Connect: a client that inspects only the schema of a `CALL` DataFrame (for example `df.schema` or `df.columns` without collecting) previously triggered a schema-only analyze request that executed the procedure and reported its result columns. It now does not execute the procedure and reports an empty schema; the procedure runs, and its real result schema is reported, once the `CALL` is executed (for example when results are collected).
- Classic (non-Connect) `spark.sql("CALL ...")` is unaffected: it goes through the command path and executes the procedure when the DataFrame is created, reporting the real result schema.

This is documented in `docs/sql-migration-guide.md`.

issues.title: [MINOR][YARN] Dump thread stacks when SparkContext initialization times out in ApplicationMaster
issues.body:
## What changes were proposed in this pull request?

When SparkContext initialization times out in YARN cluster mode, the ApplicationMaster fails the application with exit code 13 and only advises to "check earlier log output for errors". However, in real production incidents the driver thread is often blocked *silently* (slow/contended node, a blocking call with no logging, etc.) and there is **no** earlier log output at all, leaving operators with no way to tell where the driver thread was stuck.

This PR logs thread stack traces when the timeout fires, before failing the application:
1. The stack trace of the user application thread (driver) — usually the most relevant one;
2. A full thread dump of all threads for extra context.

The dump is best-effort: any failure while capturing it is swallowed so it never masks the original timeout error.

## Why are the changes needed?

Production example: a long-running SQL engine (Kyuubi) failed with `java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException: Futures timed out after [100000 milliseconds]` and exit code 13. The driver stdout showed ~80 seconds of complete silence right after `SparkEnv` initialization finished. Cross-checking the HDFS NameNode and Hive Metastore logs proved the driver issued zero external I/O during the hang, so the usual suspects (slow NN/HMS calls) were all ruled out — but without a thread dump there was still no way to pinpoint the blocking frame. With this change, the AM log would directly show what the driver thread was blocked on.

## Does this PR introduce any user-facing change?

No. It only adds error-level log output on an application-failure path.

## How was this patch tested?

- Built the module and its dependency chain: `./build/mvn -Pyarn -pl resource-managers/yarn -am package -DskipTests`
- `scalastyle:check` on `resource-managers/yarn` and `checkstyle:check` on `common/utils-java` both pass
- `ApplicationMasterSuite` passes

The `runDriver` timeout path has no existing test harness (it requires a live YARN RM), and this is a logging-only change on a failure path, so no new test is added.

issues.title: [SPARK-59146][SQL] Retain qualified access to source columns after pipe SET
issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

This PR preserves the qualified input row of each SQL pipe `SET` assignment. It adds a transparent `PipeSetInput` logical-plan marker whose original qualified output is exposed as qualified-access-only metadata and materialized only when a parent expression needs it.

The fixed-point and single-pass analyzers both understand the marker. Occurrence-aware output merging preserves source order and repeated attributes, while metadata pruning keeps retained columns out of the visible `SET` schema and unqualified stars. The marker is removed after analysis.

The change also handles Spark Connect plan-ID resolution, qualified-star expansion, metadata-column overlap, and struct-field/table-alias name collisions without changing ordinary metadata or USING-join behavior.

### Why are the changes needed?

Pipe `SET` replaces an assigned column in its projection. The original attribute is consequently dropped, even though Spark documents that table aliases continue to refer to original row values after an assignment. For example, `t.a` currently fails to resolve here:

```sql
VALUES (1, 10) AS t(a, b)
|> SET a = a + 1
|> SELECT a, t.a;
```

The assigned value must remain available as `a`, while `t.a` must resolve to the original value.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. Qualified references to columns affected by pipe `SET` now resolve to the original input value instead of failing analysis. In the example above, the result is `(2, 1)`. The visible `SET` schema and unqualified `SELECT *` output are unchanged.

### How was this patch tested?

Added Catalyst and SQL regression coverage for scalar qualified access, qualified and unqualified stars, sequential assignments, repeated source attributes, intervening operators, USING joins, struct/table-alias collisions, metadata columns, plan IDs, and fixed-point/single-pass analyzer parity.

The following checks passed:

```text
build/sbt catalyst/Test/compile
build/sbt 'catalyst/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.catalyst.analysis.AnalysisSuite -- -z "SPARK-59146"'
build/sbt 'sql/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.analysis.resolver.ResolverGuardSuite -- -z "SPARK-59146"'
build/sbt 'sql/testOnly org.apache.spark.sql.SQLQueryTestSuite -- -z pipe-operators.sql'
build/sbt catalyst/scalastyle catalyst/Test/scalastyle sql/Test/scalastyle
```

issues.body:
### What changes were proposed in this pull request?

Adds an `IGNORE NULL UPDATES` clause to the Declarative Pipelines Auto CDC SQL syntax
(`CREATE FLOW ... AS AUTO CDC INTO ...` and `CREATE STREAMING TABLE ... FLOW AUTO CDC ...`),
matching the partial-update support already exposed over Spark Connect (SPARK-59446) and the
Python API (SPARK-59447). When set, null values in an incoming update are ignored and the
existing target value is preserved.

The clause has three forms, mirroring the existing `COLUMNS` and `TRACK HISTORY ON` clauses:

- `IGNORE NULL UPDATES` -- ignore nulls on all columns.
- `IGNORE NULL UPDATES ON (col, ...)` -- ignore nulls only on the listed columns.
- `IGNORE NULL UPDATES ON * EXCEPT (col, ...)` -- ignore nulls on all columns except those listed.

Details:

- Grammar (`SqlBaseParser.g4` / `SqlBaseLexer.g4`): adds a new non-reserved keyword `UPDATES`
  and an `autoCdcIgnoreNullClause` rule wired into `autoCdcParameters`.
- Catalyst: `AutoCdcParams`, `AutoCdcInto`, and `CreateStreamingTableAutoCdc` carry
  `ignoreNullUpdates: Boolean` plus the include/except column lists; `AstBuilder` parses the
  clause (rejecting a duplicate clause), and both build sites forward the fields.
- Dataflow graph: `SqlGraphRegistrationContext.buildChangeArgs` maps the parsed clause onto
  `ChangeArgs.ignoreNullSelection`. Unlike the column and track-history selections, "all columns"
  is distinct from "absent": the bare clause becomes an empty `ExcludeColumns` selection, while an
  absent clause leaves ignore-null updates off (`None`).

Execution of ignore-null updates is handled separately (SPARK-59183) and is out of scope here.

### Why are the changes needed?

Auto CDC ignore-null updates were reachable over Spark Connect and the Python API but not from
the SQL syntax. This change closes that gap so the feature is available across all Declarative
Pipelines authoring surfaces.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. The Auto CDC SQL syntax gains an `IGNORE NULL UPDATES [ON ...]` clause, and `UPDATES` becomes
a non-reserved keyword.

### How was this patch tested?

- `AutoCdcParserSuite`: new positive parse tests for all three forms under both
  `CREATE FLOW ... AS AUTO CDC INTO` and `CREATE STREAMING TABLE ... FLOW AUTO CDC`, plus
  clause-ordering, duplicate-clause rejection, missing-parentheses rejection, and a test that the
  new `UPDATES` keyword remains usable as an identifier. The previous negative test asserting the
  clause was unsupported is replaced.
- `SqlPipelineSuite`: new tests asserting the resulting `ChangeArgs.ignoreNullSelection` for the
  all-columns, include-list, and except-list forms, and that an absent clause leaves it unset.
- `UnsupportedOperationsSuite`: updated for the new plan fields.
- Regenerated the `keywords.sql.out` golden files and updated the JDBC and Thrift server keyword
  expectations for the new `UPDATES` keyword; refreshed the ANSI compliance keyword table.
