- [ ] I have added or updated relevant docs, including release notes if applicable.
- [ ] I have attached screenshots in both light and dark modes for any UI changes.

---

`_SEP_UNSAFE` in `django/core/signing.py` uses the character class `[A-z0-9-_=]`. The `A-z` range is the classic ASCII-range regex typo: it spans `A` (0x41) through `z` (0x7A) inclusive, which sweeps in six punctuation characters that sit between `Z` and `a` in ASCII (`[ \ ] ^ _` `` ` ``) in addition to the intended `A-Z` and `a-z`.

```pycon
>>> import re
>>> p = re.compile(r'^[A-z0-9-_=]*$')
>>> p.match('^')   # True -- should be False, '^' is not in A-Za-z0-9-_=
>>> p.match('{')   # False -- correctly rejected
```

This regex is used to reject "unsafe" `sep` values passed to `Signer`/`TimestampSigner`. The typo only makes the *rejected* set larger than the documented rule, not smaller — it fails safe. It's not a security issue, just an incorrect validation: a handful of legitimate separator choices (e.g. `sep="^"`) are wrongly rejected with a `ValueError`.

Fix:

```python
_SEP_UNSAFE = _lazy_re_compile(r"^[A-Za-z0-9-_=]*$")
```

Also updates the corresponding `ValueError` message text (which repeated the same `A-z0-9-_=` typo) and adds a regression test covering the previously-misrejected characters.

Tested via `tests/signing/tests.py` (21/21 passing, including the new `test_sep_excluded_ascii_range`).

issues.title: Fixed #37356 -- Raised NotImplementedError on window filtering when a composite pk is selected.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37356

#### Branch description

`get_qualify_sql()` masks the outer query by column aliases, but a composite primary key selected with `values()` / `values_list()` is compiled to N columns with a single alias, so the outer query could not address all of them: `values("pk", ...)` raised `IndexError` and `values_list("pk", ...)` returned corrupted rows. Supporting this needs a selection to carry one alias per column, so per the ticket discussion this raises `NotImplementedError` instead, consistent with how other single-expression contexts reject composite keys.

Model-instance queries select individual columns and are unaffected. The primary key that aggregation selects internally is also left alone, so `count()` over a filtered window keeps working. Adds a sentence to the composite primary key docs.

issues.title: Fixed #37354 -- Fixed ordering and grouping by position past a composite pk.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37354

#### Branch description

`_order_by_pairs()` and `get_group_by()` refer to selections by select-list position, counted one per selection. A composite primary key is one selection compiled to N columns, so every position after it was too low: `values_list("pk", "email").order_by("email")` emitted `ORDER BY 2` (the second pk column) instead of `ORDER BY 3`, returning rows in the wrong order without raising. `GROUP BY` had the same drift, masked on PostgreSQL by functional dependency when the composite key is the primary key. Positions are now advanced by the number of columns each selection is compiled to.

Rebased over the #37222 fix in the same loop. Two PostgreSQL tests cover `distinct()` after a composite pk, one of them with a duplicated selection as well, so both the first-position and the width behaviors are exercised together; both crashed with the DISTINCT ON / ORDER BY mismatch before this change.

issues.title: Fixed #37353 -- Fixed row truncation of composite pks selected with distinct().
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37353

#### Branch description

`SQLCompiler.col_count` is the number of selections, but it is used to slice physical row columns when extra ordering columns are appended to the select clause (`distinct()` combined with `order_by()` on an unselected field). A composite primary key is one selection compiled to N columns, so the slice cut into the key itself and `values("pk").distinct().order_by("email")` returned `{'pk': (1,)}`. The compiler now tracks the number of columns rows are composed of separately and truncates against that.

This is a data-loss bug on a supported path, so it may qualify for backports beyond the usual regression window; happy to add release notes for whichever branches the mergers want.

issues.title: Fixed #37357 -- Handled out-of-range year in admin date_hierarchy.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37357

#### Branch description

`ChangeList.get_filters()` catches only `ValueError` around the `datetime(...)`
construction in the admin `date_hierarchy` handling, while the `to_date`
computation sits outside the `try`. An out-of-range year query parameter
therefore escapes as an unhandled exception (HTTP 500) instead of the intended
`IncorrectLookupParameters` (which the changelist view turns into a redirect to
`?e=1`):

- `?<datefield>__year=9999` — `datetime(9999, 1, 1)` succeeds, then
  `to_date = from_date.replace(year=from_date.year + 1)` raises
  `ValueError: year 10000 is out of range` (outside the `try`).
- `?<datefield>__year=99999999999999999999` — `datetime(...)` raises
  `OverflowError`, which `except ValueError` does not catch.

Any authenticated staff user with view permission on a model whose admin sets
`date_hierarchy` (a common configuration) can trigger it. This change catches
`(ValueError, OverflowError)` and moves the `to_date` computation inside the
`try`, matching the handling Django already uses for this int-to-datetime
parsing pattern in `views/generic/dates.py`, `views/static.py`,
`template/defaultfilters.py`, and `contrib/auth/views.py`. A regression test is
added in `tests/admin_changelist`.

issues.title: Fixed #37344 -- Enabled FETCH_PEERS batching for instances loaded by select_related.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37344

#### Branch description

When using `select_related()` with `fetch_mode(FETCH_PEERS)`, `RelatedPopulator.populate()` did not initialize or attach `peers` to populated related model instances. issues.title: Fixed #21777 -- Made request exception handling robust to signal receiver failures.

labels.name: coverage
labels.description: Generate a comment with a coverage diff

issues.body:
`response_for_exception()` and `get_exception_response()` used `Signal.send()`, which propagates any exception raised by a connected `got_request_exception` receiver. A failing receiver could therefore prevent the original exception from ever reaching `handle_uncaught_exception()`, crashing the request instead of producing a 500 response. Switched to `send_robust()`, which already logs receiver failures instead of propagating them, and captured exception info from the bound exception object instead of `sys.exc_info()` to avoid a related timing issue.

#### Trac ticket number

ticket-21777

#### Branch description

Fixes a crash in Django's exception-handling pipeline: if a `got_request_exception` signal receiver itself raises (e.g. a failing rollback-on-error handler), the original exception is dropped and the request crashes out of the WSGI handler stack instead of returning a 500 response.

issues.title: Fixed #37089 -- Made ignore_warnings() match substrings by default.
issues.body:
Supersedes #21767, which was closed by mistake — its fork had been deleted, so
GitHub would not reopen it — and #21927, which the quality bot closed because I
filled in this description incorrectly (malformed ticket reference and a missing
checklist); GitHub would not reopen that one either. Opening a fresh PR as
suggested by @jonbiemond. Apologies for the noise.

#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37089

#### Branch description

`ignore_warnings()` passes its `message` argument straight to
`warnings.filterwarnings()`, which compiles it as a regular expression and
matches it with `re.match()`. That is inconsistent with the other test
helpers: `assertWarnsMessage()` does a substring check and `assertWarnsRegex()`
uses `re.search()`.

Two consequences bite callers:

* Regex metacharacters in a message are not matched literally, so
  `ignore_warnings(message="get_connection() is deprecated.")` silently fails
  to ignore the warning it names — `()` is parsed as an empty group.
* The pattern is anchored at the start, so a fragment such as
  `message="is deprecated"` never matches.

The workaround is to write `r".*" + re.escape(...)` by hand, and Django's own
test suite already carried a number of those, e.g.:

```python
ignore_warnings(
    category=RemovedInDjango2028Warning,
    message=re.escape("Directly creating EmailBackend instances is deprecated."),
)
```

This PR matches `message` as a literal substring of the warning's message, for
consistency with `assertWarnsMessage()`, and adds `message_re` for the cases
that genuinely want a regular expression. Passing both raises `TypeError`.

Following review, the arguments are now explicit rather than `**kwargs`
forwarded to `filterwarnings()`: `category` and `message` are
positional-or-keyword, `module`, `lineno` and `message_re` are keyword-only,
and `append` is no longer accepted. `category`, `module` and `lineno` are
passed straight through, so `module` keeps the regular-expression behavior it
has today.

The substring match is built as `rf"(?s:.*)(?-i:{re.escape(message)})"`, where
`(?s:.*)` allows any prefix including newlines and `(?-i:...)` undoes the
`re.IGNORECASE` that `filterwarnings()` compiles with, so matching is
case-sensitive like `assertWarnsMessage()`.

Callers in the test suite that pre-escaped their patterns were updated to pass
the literal message. One call site keeps regex matching via the new argument:
`tests/mail/test_backends.py`, which matches an alternation over setting names.

`ignore_warnings()` is undocumented, but it is importable from `django.test`,
so a release note is included. As discussed on the ticket, no deprecation path
is proposed since this is internal API.

issues.title: Fixed #37330 -- Fixed crash on transforms over unbound annotation fields.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37330



*Reopening: this went up as #21903 before the ticket was claimed and the bot closed it automatically, as it should have. The ticket is claimed now. The branch and commit are unchanged.*

#### Branch description

Applying a transform to an annotation alias crashes with `AttributeError` when the annotation's `output_field` is not attached to a model:

```python
Book.objects.annotate(
    published=ExpressionWrapper(F("pubdate"), output_field=DateField())
).values("published__year")
```
```
AttributeError: 'DateField' object has no attribute 'model'
```

`Value(..., output_field=DateField())` fails the same way. The crash comes from `django/db/models/sql/query.py`:

- `names_to_path()` resolves an annotation name to `self.annotations[name].output_field`
- `annotate()` does not require that field to be attached to a model
- `setup_joins()`'s `final_transformer()` calls `field.get_col(alias)`
- `Field.get_col()` dereferences `self.model`, which is not there

What makes this a bug rather than an unsupported operation is that the *same query* works when the annotation's `output_field` happens to be a model field:

| annotation | `.values("a__year")` |
|---|---|
| `annotate(a=F("pubdate"))` | works — `django_datetime_extract(year, "…"."pubdate")` |
| `annotate(a=ExpressionWrapper(F("pubdate"), output_field=DateField()))` | `AttributeError` |
| `annotate(a=Value(date(2026, 1, 1), output_field=DateField()))` | `AttributeError` |

The first and second mean the same thing to a user. The outcome depends on how the annotation was spelled, not on what it asks for. And an `AttributeError` escaping the ORM is not a usable error either way — `add_fields()` catches `FieldError` to build a helpful message, and this bypasses it.

`names_to_path()` already anticipates exactly this case a few lines earlier:

```python
try:
    model = field.model._meta.concrete_model
except AttributeError:
    # QuerySet.annotate() may introduce fields that aren't attached to a model.
    model = None
```

This makes `final_transformer()` consistent with that: when there is no model to build a `Col` from, apply the transforms to the annotation expression instead. The generated SQL for the `F()` case is unchanged; the two crashing cases now produce the transform over the annotation expression.

#### On the ticket

Opened as ticket-37330 at @jacobtylerwalls' request. I searched Trac first, as he asked: the closest precedent is #34921, the same class of failure — an unsuccessful `self.model` access on an unbound field, there in `DateTimeField.to_python()`. I also searched "unbound annotation", "output_field model attribute" and "has no attribute model"; #36787 and #37248 are the nearest hits and neither covers this path, both being closed with different symptoms.

This is separate from #37308, which also covers whether lookups on aliases should resolve at all — a design question this does not touch.

#### Testing

Two regression tests in `tests/annotations/tests.py`. Reverting only `query.py` and keeping the tests fails exactly those two with the `AttributeError` above, and nothing else.

Full suite on SQLite: **19817 tests, OK** (1939 skipped, 4 expected failures) — 2 more than the 19815 on the unpatched tree, which are the two added here. `black`, `flake8` and `isort` clean.

- [x] **If AI tools were used**, I have disclosed which ones, and fully reviewed and verified their output.

Claude Code was used to investigate the ticket, reduce the failure to the three cases above, and draft the change. I have reviewed the diff, and every result quoted here was produced by running the code — the SQL in the table, the causal revert check, and the suite counts.

issues.title: Fixed #22088 -- Preserved significant whitespace in XML serialization.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number
<!-- Replace XXXXX with the corresponding Trac ticket number. -->
<!-- Or delete the line and write "N/A - typo" for typo fixes. -->

ticket-22088

#### Branch description
<!-- Provide a concise overview of the issue or rationale behind the proposed changes. Minimum five words. -->

The XML deserializer stripped the text of every `<field>` element, so a value
with leading or trailing whitespace did not survive a `dumpdata`/`loaddata`
round trip, even though the serializer wrote it out correctly:

    >>> ct = ContentType(pk=1, app_label="\tBaz", model="  lead_and_trail  ")
    >>> xml = serializers.serialize("xml", [ct])
    >>> back = list(serializers.deserialize("xml", xml))[0].object
    >>> back.app_label, back.model
    ('Baz', 'lead_and_trail')

The `.strip()` cannot simply be removed: it is what allows a hand-indented
fixture to load as intended, and without it such a value would load as
`"\n    Reference\n"`.

So the two cases have to be told apart, and XML already has the mechanism for
saying "the whitespace here is mine": `xml:space="preserve"`. The serializer now
sets it on fields whose value would otherwise not round trip, and the
deserializer strips only when the marker is absent. Fixtures without the
attribute behave exactly as before, and the attribute is only emitted when
needed, so ordinary dumps are unchanged.

`getFieldText()` is applied to the regular field path, which is what the ticket
reports. The natural-key and m2m paths still strip unconditionally; I left them
alone to keep the change scoped, and can extend it if reviewers prefer.

A release note is included under *Backwards incompatible changes → Miscellaneous*,
alongside the `DjangoJSONEncoder` entry, since this changes serializer output.

issues.title: Refs #6148 -- Added schema-qualified table references.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

[ticket-6148
](https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/6148)
#### Branch description

Added `SchemaQualifiedTable` for referencing existing schema-qualified database tables from unmanaged Django models.

`SchemaQualifiedTable` stores the table and schema names separately so that database backends can quote each identifier correctly. PostgreSQL enables this feature through `supports_schema_qualified_table_references`.

The ORM supports schema-qualified references in `SELECT`, `JOIN`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` queries. The change also supports migration serialization and prevents these existing tables from being managed by Django.

Tests run locally:

```
python tests/runtests.py schema_qualified_tables --verbosity 2 --parallel 1
python tests/runtests.py schema_qualified_tables queries migrations check_framework.test_model_checks --verbosity 1 --parallel 1
python docs/lint.py
make -C docs html SPHINXOPTS=-W
```

The PostgreSQL integration test is skipped when running with SQLite and will be exercised by the PostgreSQL test environment.

issues.title: Fixed #37177 -- Reduced per-middleware context switching under ASGI.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number
ticket-37177

#### Branch description
Relying on `MiddlewareMixin.__acall__()` to handle async requests imposed per-middleware context switching, defeating `BaseHandler`'s intent to transition only once per middleware chain.

To minimize breaking changes, `MiddlewareMixin`'s default value did not change: only the values on Django's own subclasses. Use cases where the prior behavior is preferable (in order to avoid pinning a thread per request) are fleshed out in docs.

See alternatives considered, below

#### AI Assistance Disclosure (REQUIRED)
<!-- Please select exactly ONE of the following: -->
- [ ] **No AI tools were used** in preparing this PR.
- [x] **If AI tools were used**, I have disclosed which ones, and fully reviewed and verified their output.

I double-checked my understanding of the cases where the prior behavior would be preferable with Claude, and workshopped the release note & commit message.

#### Checklist
- [x] This PR follows the [contribution guidelines](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/internals/contributing/writing-code/submitting-patches/).
- [x] This PR **does not** disclose a security vulnerability (see [vulnerability reporting](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/internals/security/)).
- [x] This PR targets the `main` branch. <!-- Backports will be evaluated and done by mergers, when necessary. -->
- [x] The commit message is written in past tense, mentions the ticket number, and ends with a period (see [guidelines](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/dev/internals/contributing/committing-code/#committing-guidelines)).
- [x] I have not requested, and will not request, an automated AI review for this PR. <!-- You are welcome to do so in your own fork. -->
- [x] I have checked the "Has patch" ticket flag in the Trac system.
- [x] I have added or updated relevant tests.
- [x] I have added or updated relevant docs, including release notes if applicable.
- [x] I have attached screenshots in both light and dark modes for any UI changes.

#### Alternatives considered
* Flipping the value on `MiddlewareMixin` itself
  - This only gives DRY benefits, at the expense of possible silent breaking changes (user subclassed `MiddlewareMixin`, overrode `__acall__()`)
  - We could DRY this out later, with a deprecation path, see below, but I'm leaving that out of this first push to keep backporting into 6.1 on the table.
* Deprecating `MiddlewareMixin.__acall__()`
  - This does seem useful for some cases (see docs where I fleshed this out: some users may legitimately prefer the extra transitions!)
  - The future instead for Django's built-in middlewares is probably closer to https://github.com/django/new-features/issues/102#issuecomment-4587612916, where there's a sketch of writing out explicit `__acall__()` methods.
  - Separate discussion IMO
* Making `async_capable` a property that introspects whether the hooks are coroutines (mentioned on ticket):
  - There cannot be coroutines on those hooks in the wild; they're unconditionally run through `sync_to_async()`.

/cc @Arfey @carltongibson @nessita

issues.title: Fixed #37140 -- Advised against filtering on iterables containing NULL.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number
<!-- Replace XXXXX with the corresponding Trac ticket number. -->
<!-- Or delete the line and write "N/A - typo" for typo fixes. -->

ticket-37140

#### Branch description
This PR documents a pitfall when using subqueries on the right-hand side of `__in` lookups. Due to SQL's three-valued logic, if the subquery returns any `NULL` values, executing `exclude(field__in=subquery)` translates to `NOT IN` in SQL and will evaluate to `UNKNOWN` for all rows, silently returning an empty queryset.

Following feedback from core ORM developers on the ticket, this PR:
* Adds a warning under the `in` lookup reference in `docs/ref/models/querysets.txt` describing the `NULL` logic pitfall.
* Documents the recommended workaround: explicitly excluding `NULL` values from the subquery using `filter(inner_field__isnull=False)`.
* Adds a cross-reference note under the `exclude()` method documentation pointing to the new warning.
* Followes Django's 80-character documentation line-wrapping guidelines.

issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

#### Branch description
This PR implements the accepted feature from [new-features#115](https://github.com/django/new-features/issues/115) to allow dynamic formatting in the `{% now %}` tag.

Previously, the `now` tag relied on a hardcoded string slice (`[1:-1]`) to strip quotes, which prevented passing context variables and caused silent, malformed output when quotes were missing.

- Updated `def now()` to use `parser.compile_filter()`.

issues.title: Fixed #37066 -- Wrapped async iteration sites in (maybe_)aclosing.
issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37066

#### Branch description

Several places in Django consume a (possibly user-supplied) async iterable with a bare `async for` (or `[... async for ... in ...]` comprehension) without wrapping it in `contextlib.aclosing()`. When the consumer exits the loop early — via `break`, `return`, an exception in the body, or cancellation that lands while the generator is suspended at a `yield` (between `__anext__` calls, on a user-body `await`) — the underlying async generator is not closed at that point. Its `aclose()` is deferred until asyncio's asyncgen finalizer hook fires it (next loop tick if the generator is collected promptly, or `loop.shutdown_asyncgens()` at teardown), so any `try`/`finally` inside the generator (database transactions, connection releases, file handles, locks) runs at a non-deterministic later time, and may not run at all if the generator outlives the loop.

`django/core/handlers/asgi.py` already uses `aclosing(aiter(response))` for exactly this reason. This PR applies the same pattern at every other site and adds a small `maybe_aclosing` helper for cases where the iterable may be caller-supplied (and so may not have `aclose()`).

Sites wrapped (one per `async for` / async comprehension over a not-locally-defined iterable):

- `contrib/auth/backends.py`: `_aget_permissions` (`aclosing`)
- `core/paginator.py`: `AsyncPage.__aiter__` (`maybe_aclosing`)
- `core/paginator.py`: `AsyncPage.aget_object_list` (`maybe_aclosing`)
- `db/models/query.py`: `QuerySet.aiterator` (`aclosing`, single hoisted wrap across both prefetch and no-prefetch branches)
- `http/response.py`: `StreamingHttpResponse.streaming_content` (`awrapper`) (`maybe_aclosing`)
- `http/response.py`: `StreamingHttpResponse.__iter__` (`to_list`) (`maybe_aclosing`)
- `http/response.py`: `StreamingHttpResponse.__aiter__` (`aclosing`)
- `shortcuts.py`: `aget_list_or_404` (`aclosing`)
- `test/client.py`: `aclosing_iterator_wrapper` (`maybe_aclosing`)
- `utils/text.py`: `acompress_sequence` (`maybe_aclosing`)

Regression tests cover the four sites where an early-exit consumer can observe the leak (`StreamingHttpResponse.__aiter__`, `acompress_sequence`, `AsyncPage.__aiter__`, `aclosing_iterator_wrapper`) plus unit tests for the `maybe_aclosing` helper. Each regression test fails on `main` and passes with the fix applied.

`maybe_aclosing` is added as public API in `django.utils.asyncio` (alongside `async_unsafe`), with a docstring and a section in `docs/topics/async.txt`.

issues.body:
#### Trac ticket number

[ticket-31908](https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/31908)

#### Branch description

This PR adds parallel testing support to the Oracle database backend in Django. In Oracle, this is implemented by creating separate tablespaces and users/schemas for each parallel worker, following the "empty clone + migrations" strategy used by other backends like PostgreSQL.

Key changes include:
- Implementing [_clone_test_db](cci:1://file:///e:/GitHub/django/django/db/backends/base/creation.py:292:4-299:9) to handle the creation of cloned tablespaces and users.
- Overriding [destroy_test_db](cci:1://file:///e:/GitHub/django/django/db/backends/oracle/creation.py:255:4-311:69) to properly clean up these suffixed resources, as Oracle's `NAME` (SID/Service Name) remains constant across clones.
- Updating internal helper methods in [DatabaseCreation](cci:2://file:///e:/GitHub/django/django/db/backends/sqlite3/creation.py:11:0-156:29) to support a [suffix](cci:1://file:///e:/GitHub/django/django/db/backends/oracle/features.py:224:4-226:78) parameter for generating unique resource names (e.g., `test_user_1`, `test_tblspace_1`).
- Enabling the `can_clone_databases` feature flag for the Oracle backend.

This approach avoids external dependencies on Oracle utilities like `expdp` and `impdp`, making it compatible with standard development environments.

issues.title: BUG: .str and .dt accessors raise on dictionary-encoded ArrowDtype
issues.body:
On current main, the `.str` and `.dt` accessors reject Series backed by dictionary-encoded `ArrowDtype`, even though the equivalent plain `ArrowDtype` (and `Categorical`, for `.str`) work fine.

Repro:

```python
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa
import datetime

# .str on dictionary-encoded strings
s = pd.Series(
    pd.array(['a', 'b', 'a'],
             dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.dictionary(pa.int32(), pa.string())))
)
s.str.upper()
# AttributeError: Can only use .str accessor with string values, not unknown-array

# .dt on dictionary-encoded timestamps
arr = pa.DictionaryArray.from_arrays(
    pa.array([0, 1, 0], type=pa.int32()),
    pa.array([datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1), datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 2)],
             type=pa.timestamp('us')),
)
s2 = pd.Series(pd.arrays.ArrowExtensionArray(arr))
s2.dt.year
# AttributeError: Can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values
```

Expected: both accessors work, decoding through the dictionary the way `Categorical` does (`pd.Series(pd.Categorical(['a', 'b', 'a'])).str.upper()` works fine).

What I found reading the code:

- `.str`: `StringMethods._validate` does `values = getattr(data, "categories", data)` to blow up categoricals before inferring. `ArrowExtensionArray` has no `.categories`, so `lib.infer_dtype` sees the raw arrow array and returns `"unknown-array"`, which is not in the allowed list.
- `.dt`: `CombinedDatetimelikeProperties.__init__` gates the arrow path on `data.dtype.kind in "Mm"`. `ArrowDtype.kind` only returns `"M"` when `pa.types.is_timestamp(self.pyarrow_dtype)` is true, which is false for dictionary types, so it falls back to the numpy object kind `"O"`.

So both accessors need to look through dictionary encoding to the value type, similar to how categoricals are handled.

Environment: pandas main (3.2.0.dev1), pyarrow 25.0.1, Python 3.12, Linux.

issues.title: BUG: to_json(date_format="iso") segfaults on a failed allocation — NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback returns NULL without setting errorMsg
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

`int64ToIso` returns `NULL` only when its allocation fails, so the example injects a single
failed `malloc` of the exact size it requests (42 bytes for `date_unit="ms"`) with an
`LD_PRELOAD` shim. Nothing else about the frame is unusual.

```c
// failmalloc.c — gcc -shared -fPIC -o failmalloc.so failmalloc.c -ldl
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <dlfcn.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdio.h>

static size_t target_size = 0;
static int armed = 0, fired = 0;

void failmalloc_arm(size_t size) { target_size = size; armed = 1; fired = 0; }

void *malloc(size_t size) {
  static void *(*real)(size_t) = NULL;
  if (!real)
    real = dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "malloc");
  if (armed && !fired && size == target_size) {
    fired = 1;
    fprintf(stderr, "[failmalloc] returning NULL for size=%zu\n", size);
    return NULL;
  }
  return real(size);
}
```

```python
# repro.py
import ctypes, faulthandler
import pandas as pd

faulthandler.enable()

frame = pd.DataFrame({"t": pd.to_datetime([1616409000123] * 50, unit="ms").as_unit("ms")})

ctypes.CDLL("./failmalloc.so").failmalloc_arm(ctypes.c_size_t(42))

print(frame.to_json(orient="records", date_format="iso"))
```

```
$ PYTHONMALLOC=malloc LD_PRELOAD=./failmalloc.so python repro.py
[failmalloc] returning NULL for size=42
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x0000004002102f00 [python] (most recent call first):
  File ".../pandas/io/json/_json.py", line 292 in write
  File ".../pandas/io/json/_json.py", line 241 in to_json
  File ".../pandas/core/generic.py", line 2623 in to_json
  File "repro.py", line 12 in <module>

Current thread's C stack trace (most recent call first):
  ...
  Binary file ".../pandas/_libs/json.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so", at +0x8ae0
```

### Issue Description

A failed allocation inside the ISO datetime conversion is dereferenced as a `NULL` string
instead of raising, because the encoder's `NULL` signal is `enc->errorMsg` and this path never
sets it:

1. `int64ToIso` (`pandas/_libs/src/datetime/date_conversions.c`) allocates the output buffer and
   returns `NULL` after `PyErr_NoMemory()` if that fails. It also returns `NULL` when
   `make_iso_8601_datetime` fails.
2. `NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback` (`pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c`) forwards
   that result unchanged, without setting `((JSONObjectEncoder *)tc->encoder)->errorMsg`.
3. `ultrajsonenc.c`, `case JT_UTF8`, tests only `enc->errorMsg` before using the value:

```c
    value = enc->getStringValue(obj, &tc, &szlen);
    if (enc->errorMsg) {
      enc->endTypeContext(obj, &tc);
      return;
    }
    Buffer_Reserve(enc, RESERVE_STRING(szlen));
    ...
      if (!Buffer_EscapeStringUnvalidated(enc, value, value + szlen)) {
```

So `Buffer_EscapeStringUnvalidated` runs on `value == NULL`, which segfaults.

Sibling callbacks in the same file follow the opposite convention and do set `errorMsg` before
returning `NULL` — `PyTimeToJSON` and the type-check branch of `PyDateTimeToIsoCallback` both
do `((JSONObjectEncoder *)tc->encoder)->errorMsg = "";`. Two more callbacks look to have the
same gap as the one above:

- `NpyTimeDeltaToIsoCallback` forwards `int64ToIsoDuration`, which has the same two `NULL`
  returns.
- `PyDateTimeToIsoCallback` sets `errorMsg` for the type check, but forwards the result of
  `PyDateTimeToIso` (which has several `NULL` returns) unchecked.

This looks like a remaining instance of the class of bug reported in #66356 and fixed by #66357
and #66797 — neither of those passes touched the ISO datetime/timedelta callbacks.

Reproduced on 3.0.5 and on `main` at `3.1.0.dev0+2036.gbe9eebf87e`, both Python 3.14 /
linux-x86_64. 3.0.6 contains no changes to these files.

For context on why this isn't only theoretical: we hit a SIGSEGV in `pandas/_libs/json...so`
beneath `DataFrame.to_json(orient="records", date_format="iso")` in CI, serialising a ~45k-row
frame with a tz-aware `datetime64[ms, UTC]` column under memory pressure from several parallel
test workers. I can't attribute that crash with certainty — the shipped extension module is
stripped, so the C stack has no symbols — but this is the only unchecked-`NULL` path I could
find on it, and the per-value allocation count makes a transient failure plausible.

### Expected Behavior

`MemoryError` (or the relevant exception) propagates to the caller, consistent with how other
allocation failures in the encoder are handled — e.g. `Buffer_Realloc` calls
`SetError(NULL, enc, "Could not reserve memory block")`.

Setting `errorMsg` in the three callbacks before returning `NULL` would be enough; adding a
`value == NULL` check alongside the `enc->errorMsg` check in `JT_UTF8` would make the encoder
robust to any future callback with the same omission.

### Installed Versions

<details>

```
INSTALLED VERSIONS
------------------
commit                : e68db09ecf6427d1b62e565bacf17f2e525a3032
python                : 3.14.7
python-bits           : 64
OS                    : Linux
machine               : x86_64
byteorder             : little
LOCALE                : C.UTF-8

pandas                : 3.0.5
numpy                 : 2.5.3
```

Also reproduced on `3.1.0.dev0+2036.gbe9eebf87e` (nightly wheel).

</details>

issues.title: BUG: groupby.rank with Arrow string dtype (#59088)
issues.body:
Closes #59088

### What does this PR do?
ArrowExtensionArray._groupby_op fell through to _to_masked() for string and large_string Arrow dtypes. _to_masked has no conversion for strings and raises NotImplementedError, which the groupby machinery surfaces as:
```text
TypeError: rank is not supported for string[pyarrow] dtype
TypeError: rank is not supported for large_string[pyarrow] dtype
```
This PR routes how == "rank" through a python-backed StringArray before that fallback, so rank runs through the existing cython/numpy implementation. Reductions (sum, first, last, any, all, idxmin, idxmax, ...) are unaffected — their code path is unchanged.

### Example
Previously:
```python
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "key": [1, 1, 2, 2],
        "value": pd.arrays.ArrowExtensionArray(
            pa.array(["b", "a", "d", "c"], type=pa.string())
        ),
    }
)
df.groupby("key")["value"].rank()
```
raised:
```text
TypeError: rank is not supported for string[pyarrow] dtype
```
### After this change:
returns:

```text
0    2.0
1    1.0
2    2.0
3    1.0
Name: value, dtype: float64
```
The same works for pa.large_string() and honors method, ascending, and na_option, matching the result for pandas' "string" dtype using lexicographic ordering.

### Changes
- Added a how == "rank" branch to ArrowExtensionArray._groupby_op that builds a python-storage StringArray and delegates to its _groupby_op for string and large_string Arrow dtypes.
- Added a StringArray import in pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py.
- Added regression tests test_rank_arrow_string_dtype and test_rank_arrow_string_dtype_with_na.
- Added a What's New entry under Groupby/resample/rolling.

### Testing

issues.title: BUG preserve row alignment in grouped resampling on columns

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

issues.body:
Fixes #59350, an existing report from 2024. This is a fix contribution, not a newly discovered upstream issue.

With the pandas 3.0.6 release, grouped resampling on a datetime column can silently assign values to the wrong time bins when row labels are a permutation of row positions:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "group": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
        "date": pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=4, freq="min"),
        "value": [100, 200, 1000, 2000],
    },
    index=[1, 0, 3, 2],
)
df.groupby("group").resample("1min", on="date").agg({"value": "sum"})
```

The observed values for group a are 200 then 100 instead of 100 then 200; group b is similarly reversed (2000 then 1000 instead of 1000 then 2000). The fix constructs each group's time grouper from that group's datetime values and avoids interpreting arbitrary row labels as positional offsets. Regression coverage exercises both dict aggregation and Series selection with permuted and arbitrary labels.

Validation: reproduced against the unmodified pandas 3.0.6 wheel. The equivalent fix applied to that wheel passes eight targeted regression/control cases (including ordinary resampling and index-/level-based group resampling); Ruff checks/format and Python compilation pass on this checkout. The source checkout lacks built C extensions, so its in-tree pytest module could not be loaded locally; CI is needed for full-tree validation. Prevalence and affected downstream analyses are unknown. The earlier #59408 PR was closed unmerged and does not cover this multi-group/custom-index reproduction.

Fixes #69443

## What was happening

Assigning a length-1 NumPy array into a PyArrow-backed column of a 1-row frame blew up with `TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]'`:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")})
df.loc[:, "A"] = df["A"].astype(float).round(6)  # TypeError
```

The trail: `SingleBlockManager.setitem_inplace` unwraps a length-1 1-d array down to 0-d before handing it to the EA, and `ArrowExtensionArray._box_pa_scalar` then passed that 0-d array straight into `pa.scalar`, which cannot consume an ndarray. PyArrow raised `ArrowInvalid`, which surfaced as the `TypeError` above.

## The fix

In `_box_pa_scalar`, a 0-d ndarray is now unboxed to its NumPy scalar with `value[()]` before reaching `pa.scalar`. I used `[()]` rather than `.item()` deliberately: it preserves the dtype, so a `datetime64` stays a `datetime64` scalar instead of collapsing to an int. The same 0-d value also tripped `ArrowStringArray._validate_setitem_value` on its `len(value)` check, so it gets the same unboxing there and flows into the existing scalar branch. Genuinely invalid values still raise `TypeError` exactly as before.

## Tests

- New regression test `test_setitem_0d_ndarray` in `pandas/tests/extension/test_arrow.py`, covering the exact issue repro, the multi-row broadcast case (a length-1 array assigned into a 2-row frame), and the `string[pyarrow]` path.
- `pandas/tests/extension/test_arrow.py -k setitem`: 3282 passed, 42 xfailed.
- `pandas/tests/extension/test_string.py -k setitem`: all passing.
- The repro script additionally verified `int64[pyarrow]` and `timestamp[ns][pyarrow]` columns, plus that invalid values (e.g. strings into a float column) still raise `TypeError`.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass on all changed files; whatsnew entry added under ExtensionArray in `v3.1.0.rst`.

Developed through Sanjay's Muse agent (model: Muse Spark). It reproduced the issue, traced the root cause through the setitem path, drafted the fix, the regression test, and the whatsnew entry, and ran the test suites above. The diff is the complete change set: two small unboxing guards, one regression test, one whatsnew line.

`BaseBuffer` required a `mode` property, so objects like `io.IOBase` and botocore's `StreamingBody` failed to type-check as `ReadBuffer`/`ReadCsvBuffer`. No pandas code reads `mode` through the protocol; the only read is guarded by `hasattr` in `_is_binary_mode` (runtime support for `StreamingBody` was added in GH-52252).
```python
df.sort_index(axis=1, level="B", key=lambda x: np.argsort(index_natsorted(x)))
# KeyError: 'Level B not found'
```

`level=1` works, as does a key that returns a named `Index`. `_ensure_key_mapped_multiindex` applies the key to each level and rebuilds the `MultiIndex` with `from_arrays(mapped)`, which takes the names from the mapped arrays. A key that returns an ndarray gives an unnamed level, so `sortlevel("B")` can't find it.

As @rhshadrach suggested in the issue, the name is now set internally rather than requiring the key to return a named `Index`: the rebuilt `MultiIndex` gets `names=index.names`. `ensure_key_mapped` already wraps the key's result in an `Index`, so no other change is needed. This only affects `MultiIndex`, since `level` is a no-op on a flat index.

The test sorts by level name with a key returning an ndarray, on both axes, and fails on main. The sort tests in `tests/frame/methods`, `tests/series/methods`, `tests/indexes/multi/test_sorting.py`, `tests/test_sorting.py` and `tests/indexes/test_base.py` pass (2078 passed).

issues.title: BUG: retain DatetimeIndex freq in concat regardless of input order (GH#64253)

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

issues.body:
- [x] closes #64253
- [x] [Tests added and passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#writing-tests) if fixing a bug or adding a new feature
- [x] All [code checks passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#pre-commit).
- [x] Added [type annotations](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#type-hints) to new arguments/methods/functions.
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.

### Problem

`union_indexes` combines `DatetimeIndex` inputs pairwise. When an intermediate union is not contiguous (e.g. `s1 ∪ s3` before `s2` is added), `DatetimeIndex._union` falls back to the generic set path and `_with_freq("infer")`. Inference cannot recover an offset such as `CustomBusinessDay(holidays=...)` from the values, so `freq` becomes `None` and stays `None`, making the result depend on the order of the inputs. The same path is hit by `pd.DataFrame({dict of Series})`.

The bug still reproduces on current `main`; the earlier "not replicable" comment on the issue mistook the `Pandas4Warning` about the default `sort` for the assertion failing.

### Fix

Following the review on the previous attempt (#66295): do not try to preserve `freq` at every pairwise step; validate once at the end. A private helper `_maybe_restore_freq` is called at the two points where the combined index is final (`union_indexes` "special" branch, and after `safe_sort_index` in `_get_combined_index`). It is a no-op unless the result is a monotonic `DatetimeIndex` with `freq is None` and *all* inputs are `DatetimeIndex` sharing the same non-None `freq`; in that case it runs `_validate_frequency` against the final values and re-attaches the `freq` only if they conform. Nothing is inferred, and non-conforming results (e.g. the tz-aware `America/Santiago` DST case from the issue, which has a real gap) keep `freq=None`.

### Test

`test_concat_datetimeindex_freq_order_independent` is parametrized over `sort=True/False/None` (the `None` case also asserts the existing `Pandas4Warning`). Without the fix the `True` and `None` cases fail; with it all three pass. `pandas/tests/indexes`, `frame`, `series`, `reshape`, `resample`, `tseries`, `window`, `groupby` pass locally.

issues.title: ENH: Add optional checkpointing and recovery for long-running apply operations

labels.name: IO Data
labels.description: IO issues that don't fit into a more specific label

labels.name: Apply
labels.description: Apply, Aggregate, Transform, Map

issues.body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Long-running Series.apply() and DataFrame.apply() operations can be vulnerable to unexpected process or kernel termination.

Currently, intermediate results are kept in memory until the operation completes. If the Python process terminates unexpectedly, all successfully computed intermediate results may be lost, even if most or all rows have already been processed.

It would be useful to provide an optional checkpointing mechanism that periodically persists completed results during apply() execution.

For example, users could specify a checkpoint file and checkpoint interval. If execution is interrupted, a subsequent run could restore the checkpoint and continue processing only the remaining rows.

This could be particularly useful for expensive per-row operations such as API requests, machine learning inference, LLM calls, network operations, or computationally expensive transformations.

The goal would not be to handle the process crash itself, since pandas cannot execute recovery code after the process has already terminated. Instead, intermediate results would be persisted proactively during normal execution so that they can be recovered afterwards.

### Feature Description

result = df[“column”].apply(
expensive_function,
checkpoint=“apply_checkpoint.pkl”,
checkpoint_every=10,
)

### Alternative Solutions

for i, value in df["column"].items():
    df.at[i, "result"] = expensive_function(value)

    if i % 10 == 0:
        df.to_pickle("checkpoint.pkl")

### Additional Context

_No response_

issues.title: BUG: loc assignment of a length-1 NumPy array into a PyArrow column raises TypeError

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue that has not been reviewed by a pandas team member

issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")})
df.loc[:, "A"] = df["A"].astype(float).round(6)
# TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]'

df2 = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0, 5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")})
df2.loc[:, "A"] = df2["A"].astype(float).round(6)  # OK
```

### Issue Description

On a 1-row DataFrame, df.loc[:, col] = <NumPy ndarray/Series> into an existing PyArrow-backed column raises TypeError, even when every value is a valid float (e.g. 5000.0). The same assignment succeeds when the frame has 2 or more rows.

5000.0 is not invalid. The error text is misleading.

What happens:

The RHS is a length-1 float64 array, array([5000.]).
SingleBlockManager.setitem_inplace unwraps any 1-d length-1 ndarray to a 0-d array to avoid the NumPy 1.25 deprecation (value[0, ...], added in [#52906](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/52906)):
if isinstance(value, np.ndarray) and value.ndim == 1 and len(value) == 1:
    value = value[0, ...]  # array([5000.]) -> array(5000.)
is_list_like(array(5000.)) is False, so ArrowExtensionArray._box_pa takes the scalar path.
pa.scalar(np.ndarray(...), type=pa.float64()) fails:
ArrowInvalid: Could not convert array(5000.) with type numpy.ndarray: tried to convert to double
pandas 3 rewraps that as TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]' and, unlike 2.x, does not fall back to recasting the column.
This is the same unwrap that #59249 / #57923 / #65452 discuss for object-dtype cells. Here the symptom is different and is a hard error on valid numeric data, not an API question about whether a cell should store array([1.]) vs 1.0.

Related, but not the same report:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/59249
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/57923
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/65452

### Expected Behavior

A valid float should be written into the double[pyarrow] column. 1-row and N-row frames should behave the same.

A narrow fix would be enough and does not require settling the whole single-element listlike-RHS matrix in #65452, for example:

in _box_pa_scalar, if value is a 0-d ndarray, use value.item() before pa.scalar, or
in setitem_inplace, skip the length-1 unwrap when the target is an ExtensionArray.

### Installed Versions

<details>

python   : 3.13.5
pandas   : 3.0.5   (also reproduced the failure mode on 3.0.6 source; main still has the unwrap)
pyarrow  : 25.0.0
numpy    : 2.5.2
OS       : Windows

On pandas 2.2.3 / 2.3.3 the same assignment does not raise. It emits

FutureWarning: Setting an item of incompatible dtype is deprecated...

and recasts the column to NumPy float64. pandas 3 turned that warning into this TypeError, so the 1-row unwrap now surfaces as a hard failure on Arrow columns.

Confirmed on all released pandas 3.0.x; 3.0.6 fixed a different loc[:, col] Arrow issue (GH 67990, CoW aliasing), not this one.

</details>

issues.title: ENH: ArrowExtensionArray should be supported by HDFStore

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue that has not been reviewed by a pandas team member

issues.body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Currently, writing data containing ArrowExtensionArrays to HDF5 fails. Since Numpy objects are pickled anyways, I don't see why Pandas should not also automatically pickle ArrowExtensionArrays.

For NumPy pickling, see these lines: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/4fde542d9691acc218c6293165619dcb397e6a8b/pandas/io/pytables.py#L3998-L4001

For a minimal working example (not working) - to test with both pa.array examples:

```
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

# Nested Arrow array
#arr = pa.array([[1, 2], [3], [4, 5, 6]])
arr = pa.array([["123"]])

# DataFrame with Arrow-backed column
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "jets": pd.Series(arr, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(arr.type))
    }
)

# Triggers PyTables serialization
df.to_hdf("test.h5", key="df")
```

### Feature Description

The cheapest solution is to add

```python3
            elif isinstance(value.dtype, ArrowDtype):
                vlarr = self._handle.create_vlarray(
                    self.group, key, _tables().ObjectAtom(), filters=self._filters
                )
                vlarr.append(value)
```

below the branch https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/4fde542d9691acc218c6293165619dcb397e6a8b/pandas/io/pytables.py#L4024 .

### Alternative Solutions

One could also check array types and e.g. string arrays could be saved correctly. However then after loading, they are no longer PyArrow data and this does not solve saving arbitrary data.

### Additional Context

Since Uproot uses ExtensionArrays in https://github.com/scikit-hep/uproot5/pull/734 , Uproot loaded data can no longer always be stored as HDF5. This is described in https://github.com/scikit-hep/uproot5/issues/1706 .
It is realistic that Uproot moves to ArrowExtensionArrays - at least I suggested that in Pull Request https://github.com/scikit-hep/uproot5/pull/1718 . Currently it uses `AwkwardExtensionArray` from `awkward-pandas`, but that is deprecated.
Meaning the effort of not fearing failures when saving data read from a ROOT file as HDF5 now transferred to making Pandas support `ArrowExtensionArray`s for HDF5 export.

issues.title: BUG: GroupBy.agg with as_index=False and MultiIndex column grouping key raises ValueError

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

issues.body:
---
Closes GH-39103

---

### Reproduction

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({("col0", "l0"): [0, 0, 1], ("col1", "l1"): [10, 20, 30]})
df.groupby(("col0", "l0"), as_index=False).agg({("col1", "l1"): ["min", "max"]})
```

```text
ValueError: Item must have length equal to number of levels.
```

### Root cause

`_insert_inaxis_grouper` in `pandas/core/groupby/groupby.py` decides whether the `as_index=False` group key has already been inserted by the aggregation itself. For a `MultiIndex` columns frame, the str-name path pads the key to the columns' `nlevels` (`("key", "", ...)`, per GH-17024 / GH-28549), but a tuple name of fewer levels than `result.columns.nlevels` was returned unchanged, and `result.insert(0, name, lev)` then failed with the "Item must have length equal to number of levels" `ValueError`.

### Fix

`full_key()` now also pads tuple names when `len(name) < result.columns.nlevels`, and the membership check uses `full_key(name)` so it looks up the exact key that will be inserted (previously a partial-tuple lookup which additionally raised `PerformanceWarning` on un-lex-sorted `MultiIndex` columns, surfaced as an error under CI's `filterwarnings`).

The inserted grouper column now exactly matches the canonical `groupby(..., as_index=True).agg(...).reset_index()` output.

### Verification

- Issue repro now returns the expected padded columns `[("col0", "l0", ""), ("col1", "l1", "min"), ("col1", "l1", "max")]`, byte-identical to the `as_index=True` + `reset_index()` form for `agg`, `describe`, and multi-tuple-grouper cases
- New tests: `test_groupby_agg_as_index_false_multiindex_column` (padded columns, existing column order, empty input) and `test_groupby_as_index_false_multiindex_column_matches_reset_index` (agg/describe/multi-tuple equivalence)
- `pandas/tests/groupby/`: 24447 passed, 866 skipped, 43 xfailed
- Sweep of `pandas/tests/resample/`, `pandas/tests/apply/`, `pandas/tests/reshape/`: green (2 unrelated pre-existing tzdata DST failures, confirmed identical on `main`)
- `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` clean (repo-pinned ruff 0.16.6); `aggregate/` suite green under `-W error`

issues.title: BUG: numexpr results use a nonstandard int64 type, breaking select_dtypes (GH#17945)

labels.name: expressions
labels.description: pd.eval, query, pd.col

issues.body:
closes #17945

numexpr returns int64 results as `longlong` (`'q'`), whereas numpy's int64 is `long` (`'l'`) on Linux/macOS. The dtypes compare equal but `dtype.type is not np.int64`, so e.g. `select_dtypes("int64")` silently dropped the column. This hit `DataFrame.eval`/`pd.eval`, and also plain arithmetic/`where` on data large enough to be routed through numexpr.

Results from the three numexpr call sites are now viewed (no copy) as numpy's standard dtype when they differ.

### Background
Fixes #20442. Pure Python specifies that `None == None` evaluates to `True`. However, in pandas, comparing a Series of objects with scalar `None` previously short-circuited into NumPy's NA logic (treating `None` like `np.nan`), returning `False` universally for `None == None`.

issues.title: BUG: keep left/right index dtype in Index.join on mismatched dtypes (GH#63371)

labels.name: Reshaping
labels.description: Concat, Merge/Join, Stack/Unstack, Explode

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

issues.body:
closes #63371

When the two indexes have different dtypes, `Index.join` casts both to a common dtype and returned the result in that dtype even for `how="left"`/`"right"`, where every value comes from one side. The join still runs in the common dtype; the result is now rebuilt from the kept side via its indexer, so it keeps that side's dtype (including 1-to-many joins). `inner`/`outer` are unchanged.

This follows the thread's consensus to fix left joins generally rather than special-casing `str.cat`, and carries through `align`, `DataFrame.join`, `merge` and `str.cat`. It also removes an asymmetry where `ser1.align(ser2, join="left")` gave a `str` index on one result and `object` on the other. The empty-index path already kept the left dtype.

Behavior change: 14 existing tests asserted the old cast and are updated.

- [ ] I did **not** use AI to develop this pull request.
- [x] I used AI to develop this pull request. I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`, I have reviewed and understood every change, and I have described above how I used it and exactly which tool, model version, and effort setting — e.g. `claude opus 4.8 (xhigh)`, not just `claude`.

## What happened

As reported in #66593: for an arrow-backed string `Index`, `_get_engine_target()` returns `vals.astype(object)` — a distinct object-dtype copy that the cached lookup engine retains for its lifetime — and `memory_usage(deep=True)` accounted for neither that array nor its `PyUnicode` payloads. On the reporter's 500k-row repro only the hashtable growth (~16.9 MB) was reported where ~61 MB was actually allocated (3.6x under-report).

## What I did

`Index.memory_usage` now adds, when `deep=True` and the engine's mapping is populated:

- `engine.values.nbytes` — the retained pointer array, and
- `lib.memory_usage_of_objects(engine.values)` — its boxed strings,

**only** when the engine's array is an object-dtype copy that was not already counted, i.e. the Index's own array is an `ArrowExtensionArray` and the engine's array is neither `self._values` nor `self._values._ndarray`. This keeps the shared-array cases exactly as before:

- `object` dtype: engine array *is* `self._values` → unchanged
- `string[python]`: engine array *is* `StringArray._ndarray` → unchanged
- arrow-backed `str`/`string`: engine owns an exclusive copy → now counted

This is the shape the issue itself suggested (count the engine's retained values plus `lib.memory_usage_of_objects` when deep and not shared). Accounting was placed in `Index.memory_usage` rather than in `IndexEngine.sizeof`/`HashTable.sizeof` because the engine cannot tell whether its array is shared with the Index — only the Index knows that — so doing it in the engine risks double-counting the `object`/`string[python]` cases.

Note on exactness: as in the existing deep accounting for object dtype, this uses `sys.getsizeof` sums (`memory_usage_of_objects`), so the number is an accounting estimate, not RSS. On the repro it now lands at 61,408 kB growth vs the ~61.4 MB the reporter measured.

### Repro numbers (Linux x86_64, built from this branch)

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| reported growth (500k × 40-byte str, `str` dtype / arrow storage) | 16,908 kB | **61,408 kB** |
| engine object array | 4,000 kB (unaccounted) | counted |
| its PyUnicodes | 40,500 kB (unaccounted) | counted |
| object-dtype growth (must not change) | 16,908 kB | 16,908 kB |
| `string[python]` growth (shares `_ndarray`; must not change) | 16,908 kB | 16,908 kB |

The propagation to `DataFrame.memory_usage(deep=True)` (one `.loc` on a string-indexed frame) is fixed transitively since it sums `Index.memory_usage(deep=True)`.

## Tests

- `tests/indexes/test_old_base.py`: two new regression tests — the arrow-backed case asserts the engine-build growth covers `held.nbytes + Σ sys.getsizeof`; the object-dtype case pins the no-double-count invariant (`after - before == engine.sizeof(deep=True)`). The first fails on main, passes here.
- `tests/base/test_misc.py::test_memory_usage`: the shared module-level fixture objects can carry a *populated* nested engine (categorical categories / MultiIndex levels) left over from earlier tests; since deep now correctly counts those engines' retained copies, the fixture setup clears nested engines recursively so each parametrization starts pristine. (Without this, `res == res_deep` fails for `categorical`/`tuples`/`multi` purely due to test-order cross-contamination, not the fix.)
- Ran: `pandas/tests/indexes` (17,906 passed; the single `tzlocal` failure reproduces on unmodified main in this environment), `pandas/tests/base` (all pass), plus `frame/methods/test_info.py`, `series/methods/test_info.py`, `arrays/categorical/test_analytics.py`, `arrays/string_/test_string.py`, `extension/base`, `apply/test_frame_apply.py`, `frame/test_subclass.py`, `arrays/sparse/test_array.py` — all pass. `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` clean on the touched files.

issues.title: BUG: isinstance(obj, DateOffset) deadlocked when called from a C extension under a tracer
issues.body:
`OffsetMeta.__instancecheck__` and `__subclasscheck__` passed
`stacklevel=find_stack_level()` to their deprecation warnings. `find_stack_level`
walks the Python stack, and these two hooks are reachable from a C extension's
callback — `pa.array()`'s type inference calls `isinstance(obj, pandas.DateOffset)`
on each element of an object array. Running Python there re-enters the active
tracer, and `coverage`'s `data_lock` is not reentrant, so the process hangs:

```python
import warnings, numpy as np, pandas as pd

arr = pd.array([pd.Timedelta("1h"), None], dtype="duration[ns][pyarrow]")
other = np.empty(2, dtype=object)
other[:] = [pd.offsets.Hour(1)] * 2

warnings.simplefilter("error")
arr != other
```

`python repro.py` completes. `python -m coverage run repro.py` never returns.

| | warnings normal | warnings as errors |
|---|---|---|
| no coverage | ok | ok |
| `coverage run` | ok | **hangs** |

The hung stack, with pyarrow's C++ frames invisible to `faulthandler` between
`pa.array` and `find_stack_level`:

```
coverage/collector.py:242 in lock_data
pandas/util/_exceptions.py:41 in find_stack_level
pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py:876 in _box_pa_array   # pa.array(value, mask=mask)
pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py:723 in _box_pa
pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py:1176 in _cmp_method
```

`find_stack_level` exists to skip pandas-internal frames when a warning is raised
deep inside pandas. `isinstance`/`issubclass` are builtins that add no Python
frame, so in a metaclass hook there is never anything to skip and the walk can
only ever return the immediate caller. `stacklevel=1` is therefore equivalent and
free. Note it is `1` rather than `2`: the Cython-compiled hook does not
materialise a frame that `warnings` counts, so `2` would point one frame too far
out. The new test pins the attribution rather than the literal.

Only the two `OffsetMeta` hooks change. The other `find_stack_level()` calls in
`offsets.pyx` are in ordinary functions, where the walk is still needed.

This is what has been timing out every py312/py313 job on GH-68456 since
2026-09-11; those jobs run under `--cov` with warnings as errors.

issues.title: API: should the _supports_2d contract require repeat(axis=...)?

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: ExtensionArray - New Method Request
labels.description: Suggestion to add a new method to the EA base class/interface.

issues.body:
`ExtensionDtype._supports_2d` documents what a third-party array must provide to
declare itself 2-D capable (`pandas/core/dtypes/base.py`):

> Arrays that support 2D values should:
>
> - implement Array.reshape
> - subclass the Dim2CompatTests in tests.extension.base
> - `_concat_same_type` should support `axis` keyword
> - `_reduce` and reductions should support `axis` keyword

`repeat` is not on that list, and the base implementation actively rejects an axis:

```python
# pandas/core/arrays/base.py
def repeat(self, repeats, axis: AxisInt | None = None) -> Self:
    nv.validate_repeat((), {"axis": axis})
```

while the backing-array implementation both defaults to and honours one:

```python
# pandas/_libs/arrays.pyx
def repeat(self, repeats, axis: int | np.integer = 0):
```

In-tree this never shows, because the only dtypes with `_supports_2d = True` are
`DatetimeTZDtype` and `PeriodDtype`, whose arrays are `NDArrayBacked`. A third-party
array that implements the four documented requirements and inherits
`ExtensionArray.repeat` would raise
`ValueError: the 'axis' parameter is not supported in the pandas implementation of repeat()`.

This matters because the gate internals use to decide "may I treat this as 2-D" is

```python
def is_1d_only_ea_dtype(dtype) -> bool:
    return isinstance(dtype, ExtensionDtype) and not dtype._supports_2d
```

so anything reaching a 2-D code path is exactly the `_supports_2d` audience. Broadcasting
a 1-D value across several columns wants `value.reshape(1, -1).repeat(ncols, axis=0)`, which
works for both in-tree types and for any `NDArrayBacked` array, but is not something the
documented contract entitles pandas to call.

Two ways to resolve it:

1. Add `repeat` with `axis` support to the `_supports_2d` requirements, and relax the base
   signature/validation for 2-D-capable arrays. This documents what pandas already needs and
   costs existing third-party authors nothing until they opt into `_supports_2d`.
2. Treat `repeat(axis=)` as out of contract and require internals to spell 2-D broadcasting
   with only the four documented operations, e.g. `value.repeat(ncols).reshape(-1, ncols)`.
   That is contract-clean but produces a C-contiguous result where the current spelling gives
   an F-contiguous one, which changes the stored block's layout on the NumPy path.

No in-tree caller passes `axis=` to an ExtensionArray's `repeat` today, so nothing is broken
right now; this is about whether such a call is legitimate going forward.

issues.title: BUG: loc/iloc setitem raised for a 2D value in a single object cell

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

issues.body:
Follow-up to a post-merge review comment on GH-66702, where @jorisvandenbossche asked why a 2D value set into a single `object` cell is a shape mismatch rather than simply stored.

It shouldn't be. The answer depended on block layout:

```python
value = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

# more than one dtype -> split path
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": np.zeros(2, dtype=object), "b": [0, 0]})
df.iloc[0, 0] = value
# ValueError: Must have equal len keys and value when setting with an ndarray

# single block -> stored
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": np.zeros(2, dtype=object), "b": np.zeros(2, dtype=object)})
df.iloc[0, 0] = value  # df.iloc[0, 0] is value
```

Same divergence for a list of `ndarray`/`Series`/`Index`/`ExtensionArray` rows and for a 2-D `ndarray`. Verified identical in 2.3.3, 3.0.6 and `main`, so this is long-standing rather than a regression; GH-64230 and GH-66702 only moved which value kinds reach the raise.

Cause is branch order in `_setitem_with_indexer_split_path`: the `_is_2d_value_for_columns` check runs ahead of the branch that stores nested data in a single cell, so the shape rules for a multi-column selection get applied to a one-cell selection. Single-block frames never take that path, which is why they store.

This moves the single-cell branch above the 2-D check, canonizing the single-block answer. It also hops the "multiple rows in a single column" branch, which is inert here: that branch requires `not is_scalar(pi)`, and `_is_scalar_access` implies `is_scalar(pi)`.

`raise` -> `store` is strictly widening, so nothing that works today changes.

The test that pinned the old behavior is inverted and re-aimed at the property: it now parametrizes the second column's dtype, which is what decides single- vs multi-block, so the block-layout equivalence is what is under test. With the code change reverted, exactly the 12 multi-block parametrizations fail and the 12 single-block ones pass.

Still divergent after this, left alone deliberately: `df.iloc[0, 0] = some_dataframe` stores the single column as a `Series` on the split path and the whole frame on the single-block path, because the `ABCDataFrame` branch sits above the one moved here.

issues.title: Fix: prefer column over index level in groupby

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

issues.body:
closes #33657

### What does this PR do?

When a label passed to `DataFrame.groupby()` matches both a column label and an index level name, pandas currently raises a `ValueError` because the label is considered ambiguous.

This PR makes `DataFrame.groupby()` prefer the column label in this case.

The `level=` argument remains available when grouping by the index level explicitly.

### Example
Previously:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(
    2,
    index=pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
        [range(4), list("abcd")],
        names=["I", "II"],
    ),
    columns=["I"],
)

df.groupby("I")
```
raised: ValueError: 'I' is both an index level and a column label, which is ambiguous.

After this change:
```python
df.groupby("I")
```
groups by the column "I".

Grouping by the index level can still be done explicitly:
```python
df.groupby(level="I")
```
### Changes
- Changed `DataFrame.groupby()` to prefer a column label when the grouping key matches both a column label and an index level name.
- Removed the ambiguity check that previously raised a `ValueError` for this case.
- Added a regression test for the ambiguous column/index-level case.
- Verified that explicit level= grouping continues to use the index level.
- Added a What's New entry for the bug fix.
 
### Testing

Added the regression test : `test_groupby_column_preferred_over_index_level`.

The targeted test passes :

```text
1 passed, 101 deselected
```
The full test suite passes:

```text
24723 passed, 861 skipped, 44 xfailed
```

labels.name: Indexing

issues.body:
closes #48867

Redo of GH-68943 (reverted by GH-68971) as a deprecation rather than an immediate raise.

`BaseMaskedArray.__setitem__` now emits a `Pandas4Warning` when numpy stored a scalar altered to fit instead of rejecting it; the 3.x result is unchanged. numpy range-checks a python scalar whatever the key, but a numpy scalar only for a signed dtype under an integer or slice key — so an unsigned dtype with any key, or a signed one with a fancy or boolean key, silently stored the wrong value. That second case covers `where`/`mask`/`replace`/`putmask`, which all arrive with a mask key: `pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="Int8").where(mask, np.int64(1000))` gives `-24` today. Warning after the store rather than before keeps the paths where numpy raises untouched, without having to encode which key/dtype combinations it checks.

Two notes on the GH-68943 thread. The premise there — that the fillna et al cases "currently actually gave a correct but upcasted result" — holds for the *numpy-backed* dtypes, not the masked ones: every masked path either raises `OverflowError` or stores the value altered, and none upcast. And `Series.fillna` is not covered by this PR, on main or on the branch — it raises `OverflowError` from `scalar_fillna_inplace` before reaching `__setitem__`. Since numpy-backed `where` does upcast, the consistent 4.0 endpoint for masked may be to upcast rather than to raise; worth settling before enforcement.

`shift(fill_value=)` and the float-overflow arm are left alone, as in GH-68943.

issues.title: BUG: MultiIndex setops split a string operand entry into its elements (GH#39699)

labels.name: setops
labels.description: union, intersection, difference, symmetric_difference

issues.body:
Note: this does **not** close GH-39699, which asks for the opposite change — see the last section.

`MultiIndex._convert_can_do_setop` passes a raw list-like operand straight to `MultiIndex.from_tuples`, which accepts any indexable row and so decomposes a string or bytes entry into its elements. When the entry's length matches `nlevels`, the setop treats it as a tuple of level values:

```python
mi = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]])
mi.intersection(["ac"])              # MultiIndex([('a', 'c')])  -- "ac" is not in mi
mi.union([b"ac"])                    # adds (97, 99)
mi.intersection([("a", "c"), "bd"])  # "bd" matches ('b', 'd')
```

The four setops now raise the existing `TypeError("other must be a MultiIndex or a list of tuples")` for such an operand. Everything else keeps its existing path through `from_tuples`, including `np.void` rows and null entries, which `lib.to_object_array_tuples` deliberately expands to an all-null row.

Two deliberate behavior changes worth a reviewer's attention:

- Splitting a length-`nlevels` label has two outcomes today — it matches spuriously when the characters line up, and returns the right answer by accident when they don't. Both now raise, so e.g. on 2-level columns `cols.difference(["id"])` returned both columns before and now raises. A deprecation cycle isn't really available, since it would mean continuing to return `('a', 'c')` from `mi.intersection(["ac"])` for another release; the `MultiIndex.isin` change in GH-20252 is the local precedent for going straight to raising.
- On a one-level `MultiIndex` a single-character label used to match. Any longer label already raised.

On GH-39699 itself: it asks for `mi.intersection(["some_col"])` to return an empty index, as it did on 1.1.5. That result was the same split — `"some_col"` became an 8-level MultiIndex, which then intersected to empty. Ten existing assertions pin `TypeError` for a raw list of non-tuples, so raising seemed the consistent reading, and I've left the issue open for that separate question.

issues.title: BUG: Timestamp rejected fold with positional date components (GH#52117)

labels.name: Timezones
labels.description: Timezone data dtype

labels.name: Timestamp
labels.description: pd.Timestamp and associated methods

issues.body:
closes #52117

`Timestamp.__new__` validates `fold` before the `if/elif` chain that decides which of the three calling forms is in play. The guard accepted only the keyword-component form or a naive datetime, so the *positional* by-component form — where `ts_input` holds the integer year — fell through to the "possibly unambiguous input" error, whose own advice is to build from components:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp(2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc, fold=0)
ValueError: Cannot pass fold with possibly unambiguous input: ...
>>> pd.Timestamp(year=2020, month=1, day=1, hour=0, minute=0, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc, fold=0)
Timestamp('2020-01-01 00:00:00+0000', tz='UTC')
```

The fix exempts that form too, keyed on both leading arguments being integers rather than on `year` alone, so the guard cannot admit an input the dispatch chain routes to an earlier arm (null-like, `float` and `bool` first arguments all reach `elif` arms above the positional one).

This also removes a limitation GH-31930 documented in the 3.1.0 whatsnew: `datetime.__replace__` reconstructs subclasses through the 8-positional-argument form and passes `fold` when it is nonzero, so `copy.replace()` raised on any `fold=1` timestamp. That clause is deleted and the test pinning it now pins the fixed behavior.

issues.title: PERF: out-of-band pickling of a sliced DataFrame (GH#55781)

labels.name: Performance
labels.description: Memory or execution speed performance

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

labels.name: IO Pickle
labels.description: read_pickle, to_pickle

issues.body:
closes #55781

numpy serializes an ndarray out of band (PEP 574) only when it is C- or F-contiguous, so a sliced `DataFrame` — whose block values are a strided view of the parent — had its data copied into the pickle stream rather than shared with the consumer. `Block.__reduce_ex__` now makes such a block contiguous when the protocol can actually use a buffer.

The gate is `protocol >= 5` on a non-contiguous, non-object ndarray. Below protocol 5 the copy is waste: numpy copies again via `tobytes` and peak memory doubles. Object dtype numpy refuses out of band whatever the layout, as it does `datetime64`/`timedelta64` — which is why extending this to the EA-backed blocks would buy nothing. At protocol 5 peak memory is unchanged, since main already paid a `tobytes` copy on the same block, while an out-of-band consumer goes from 0 buffers to 1.

Two things worth flagging for review. The issue's own reproducer no longer shows the bug — block layout has changed since it was filed, so a column slice is already contiguous; the surviving case is the row slice, which is also the one that matters to the frameworks in the report, since they partition by rows. And the win is confined to out-of-band consumers: `pickle.dumps` defaults to protocol 4, and `to_pickle` passes no `buffer_callback`, so neither changes.

Only block values are covered. A step-sliced frame's `Index` and a `Series`' values reach the pickler by other routes and still go in band.

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Sparse
labels.description: Sparse Data Type

issues.body:
closes #45284

`SparseArray.__getitem__` read a boolean `SparseArray` mask off its `sp_index` alone, which assumes no stored value ever equals the mask's own `fill_value`. An op result violates that — `_sparse_array_op` gives the result the union of both operands' indices — so `arr[arr > other]` returned the wrong elements. Comparisons against an array-like and logical ops between two boolean `SparseArray`s both produce such a mask; a scalar comparison does not, since that result is re-sparsified. The fix selects on `sp_values` instead.

That same fast path returned before reaching `check_array_indexer`, so a mask of the wrong length was never rejected — every other spelling of the same mask raises `IndexError`. Added the check there, with the message `check_array_indexer` uses.

`Series`/`DataFrame`-level indexing was unaffected throughout: those routes densify the mask before it reaches `SparseArray.__getitem__`.

The issue also asks for `s > [3, 3, 4, 1, 0, 0]` to report `Indices: array([3])` rather than storing every position. That is the density of the op result rather than its values, and it is left to GH-45126 — re-sparsifying comparison results conflicts with `test_cmp_object_subtype_scalar_keeps_sparse_index` (GH-68586).

issues.title: BUG: sparse binary ops left stored values equal to the result's fill_value (GH#45126)

labels.name: Numeric Operations
labels.description: Arithmetic, Comparison, and Logical operations

labels.name: Sparse
labels.description: Sparse Data Type

issues.body:
closes #45126
closes #45284

`SparseArray` binary operations left stored values equal to the result's `fill_value` in `sp_index`: the splib kernels return the union of the operands' indexes, and the other arms reuse an operand's own. Indexing a `SparseArray` with such a comparison result then selected every element, and `density`/`npoints`/`memory_usage` overstated how much the result stores. The same operation also gave a different `sp_index` depending on subtype, because the object route already re-sparsified while the numeric one did not.

`_wrap_result` now prunes stored values that would densify as the fill. Deciding that is not plain equality, so it is factored into `_differs_from_fill`: `-0.0` compares equal to a `0.0` fill but densifies differently, `isna` is true for a complex with either part NaN, and an object array can hold several NAs at once of which only the fill's own spelling densifies back as the fill.

Unary operators and single-input ufuncs have the same defect and are left alone here — they build results through `_simple_new` rather than `_wrap_result`, and pruning them turns `abs()` on a complex subtype into a `TypeError` for a reason that wants its own fix. The whatsnew is scoped to binary operations accordingly.

GH-45284's underlying cause also survives: `__getitem__` reads a boolean key's `sp_index` rather than its `sp_values`, which `fillna` can still trigger. This PR removes the route that made a comparison produce such a key.
