issues.title: BUG: DataFrame.apply/agg with a callable dropped the extension dtype (GH#61812)

labels.name: Apply
labels.description: Apply, Aggregate, Transform, Map

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

labels.name: Arrow
labels.description: pyarrow functionality

issues.body:
closes #61812

`DataFrame.agg`/`apply` with a callable that reduces each column (or row) to a scalar built the result from the raw Python scalars, so the frame's extension dtype was lost — `df.agg(lambda x: x.mean())` on a `double[pyarrow]` frame returned `float64`, where the string alias `df.agg("mean")` returned `double[pyarrow]`. This routes those results through `ExtensionArray._cast_pointwise_result`, the mechanism `DataFrameGroupBy.agg` already uses for a callable, when the frame has a single extension dtype. Masked and `category` frames lost the dtype the same way and are fixed too.

Sparse frames are excluded: a reduction result has no sparsity to preserve, and `SparseArray`'s cast drops a timezone (GH-61812 does not fix that; it is reachable today through `groupby.agg`).

`DataFrame.nunique` and `DataFrame.corrwith` are implemented via `self.apply`, so each casts its result back to what it returned before — `nunique` to `int64` (matching `count()` and `groupby.nunique`) and `corrwith` to `float64` (a correlation coefficient would otherwise come back as `Int64` for an all-NA result, or as a `category`). Neither method changes behavior.

Not covered here: `df.agg([f])` and `df.agg({"col": f})` assemble results through a different path and still drop the dtype, as they already do on main relative to `df.agg(["mean"])`.

issues.title: BUG: partial string indexing that matches no entries raises KeyError (GH#57596)

labels.name: Datetime
labels.description: Datetime data dtype

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Period
labels.description: Period data type

issues.body:
closes #57596

`DatetimeIndexOpsMixin._partial_date_slice` raised `KeyError` when a partial-string key fell outside the index's range, but returned an empty selection when it fell inside and matched nothing. Callers that need presence semantics — `Index.__contains__`, `.at`, and `.loc`-setitem's missing-key path — read that as a match of length zero, so the assignment in the issue silently set nothing. It now raises `KeyError` whenever the selection is empty, which also makes an in-range miss consistent with the out-of-range case that already raised, and with a `MultiIndex` datetime level, which already raised.

The two `# we are out of range` pre-checks are removed as part of this: they fire only when both bounds lie past the extreme element of a sorted index, which is exactly when the new check raises anyway.

This is a behavior change for getitem — `ser["2024-05"]` where May is absent but in range now raises instead of returning an empty Series — so it has a notable-bug-fix whatsnew entry. Nothing in the test suite asserted the old behavior.

## Summary

Clarifies the `func` parameter description in `DataFrame.aggregate` and `Series.aggregate` to explain how string function names are dispatched. When `func` is a string, it is looked up via `getattr` on the aggregated object first (so `"mean"` resolves to `DataFrame.mean` / `Series.mean`), with a fallback to the `numpy` namespace when the object supports the buffer protocol (`obj.__array__` exists); e.g. `"sum"` resolves to `numpy.sum`. `AttributeError` is raised if no match is found.

Closes #49528.

## Tooling

The patch was drafted by the contributor with assistance from the Hermes Agent CLI running the `minimax-m3` model in the contributor's local Hermes desktop app. The reasoning-effort setting was chosen by the contributor in the Hermes UI and is not visible to the agent, so it is reported here as **unspecified** rather than guessed. All changes were reviewed line-by-line by the contributor before commit, and `pre-commit run --files` was executed locally on the modified files.

## Implementation notes

The dispatch rules described in the new docstring text match the actual behavior in `pandas/core/apply.py`:

- The `Apply` engine class routes `func` strings through `apply_str()` (`pandas/core/apply.py:1031`, also `:330`, `:1347`, `:1690`).

- "numpy MRO fallback" is more accurately phrased as "fallback to the numpy namespace"; Python's `hasattr(np, func)` is a namespace lookup, not an MRO walk.

issues.title: BUG: DateOffset silently truncated non-integer date components

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

issues.body:
Supersedes #69125, which the automation closed because #55909 was not assigned to me yet. The issue is assigned now, and the change is unchanged.

Applying a `DateOffset` multiplies its `relativedelta` by `n`, and dateutil's
`relativedelta.__mul__` casts every component through `int()`, so a fractional
value was discarded without warning:

```python
>>> datetime(2020, 1, 1) + pd.DateOffset(days=1.5)
datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 2, 0, 0)     # a whole day, not a day and a half
>>> datetime(2020, 1, 1) + pd.DateOffset(hours=1.5)
datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1, 1, 30)    # correct
```

The second is correct because a lone sub-daily keyword is handled by `timedelta`,
which represents fractions exactly. Adding any date component switches to the
relativedelta path, so `DateOffset(days=1, hours=1.5)` lost the half hour too.

This raises `ValueError` on the relativedelta path instead, per @jbrockmendel's
comment on the issue. The timedelta path is unchanged, and a float that is a whole
number, such as `days=2.0`, is still accepted.

issues.title: BUG: rolling skew/kurt returned NaN after a window emptied

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

labels.name: Window
labels.description: rolling, ewma, expanding

issues.body:
- [x] closes #69037
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file

`remove_skew` and `remove_kurt` decrement `nobs` and then immediately divide by it:

```cython
nobs[0] -= 1
n = <float64_t>(nobs[0])
delta = val - mean[0]
delta_n = delta / n
```

When the observation being removed is the last one in the window, `n` is `0.0`, so `delta_n` is `inf` or `nan` and the running `mean`, `m2`, `m3` (and `m4` for kurt) are poisoned for every window after it. That is why the reported series return `NaN` even where the final window itself has no missing values.

There is already a recompute path for exactly this kind of damage, but **it cannot fire here**. The guard is

```cython
if (fabs(m3_update) + fabs(m3[0])) * InvCondTol > fabs(new_m3):
    numerically_unstable[0] = True
```

and once `m3_update` is `NaN` that comparison is `NaN > NaN`, which is `False`. So the one case the guard exists to catch is the single case that slips past it silently.

The fix zeroes the moments when `nobs` reaches zero, since an empty window has no moments to carry forward. That addresses the root cause rather than widening the instability check.

This is the same shape as the already-fixed `.Rolling.corr`/`.Rolling.cov` bug in #65739 ("returning NaN for all later windows once a window contained no valid pairs").

Verified by rebuilding both ways. Before the change, both reproducers return `nan`; after, they match a fresh computation over the final window, and independently match scipy:

| | pandas | scipy |
|---|---|---|
| `skew` | `0.0` | `0.0` |
| `kurt` | `-0.41610621014935756` | `-0.41610621014935845` |

Added a parametrised regression test covering both functions. `pandas/tests/window/` is 9003 passed, 45 skipped, 1 xfailed.


This supersedes #69122, which the bot closed because I had commented `take` rather than `/take` on #69037. The issue is now assigned to me. The two CI failures there were an artefact of that closure, not of this change: the log shows `fatal: couldn't find remote ref refs/pull/69122/merge`, because the merge ref disappeared when the PR was closed mid-run.

issues.title: TST: concat with a sparse datetimelike column and a missing column (GH#26288)

labels.name: Testing
labels.description: pandas testing functions or related to the test suite

labels.name: Reshaping
labels.description: Concat, Merge/Join, Stack/Unstack, Explode

labels.name: Sparse
labels.description: Sparse Data Type

issues.body:
closes #26288

`concat` of a frame with a datetime64 `SparseDtype` column and a frame missing that column raised `DTypePromotionError` (through 2.3.x; `NotImplementedError` when the issue was filed). It works on main: GH-68469 fixed it incidentally by replacing the `np.result_type(self.sp_values, type(fill_value))` promotion in `SparseArray._take_with_fill` with `_promote_for_fill`, which is the line the traceback ended at.

Adds the regression test, parametrized over an NA and a non-NA `fill_value` — the latter is the spelling where a bad promotion reads the missing rows back as the fill value rather than raising. Verified it fails on both parameters with that hunk of GH-68469 reverted.

That PR's whatsnew entry now names `concat` and this issue, since 3.1.0 is unreleased and the entry already lists `DTypePromotionError` among the symptoms.

issues.title: BUG: to_clipboard blamed sep for any TypeError in excel mode (GH#44120)

labels.name: IO Data
labels.description: IO issues that don't fit into a more specific label

issues.body:
closes #44120

`to_clipboard(excel=True)` wrapped both `to_csv` and `clipboard_set` in a bare `except TypeError` whose handler warned `"to_clipboard in excel mode requires a single character separator."` and then fell through to the `to_string` path. Any `TypeError` was therefore blamed on `sep` — including `to_csv` rejecting a keyword it does not accept, which is the reported case: `df.to_clipboard(index_names=False)` warns about a separator the user never passed, and the clipboard silently receives the `to_string` representation instead of CSV.

Validating `sep` up front instead means only a genuine separator problem warns and falls back; every other `TypeError` propagates with its own message. Behavior for a non-str, empty, or multi-character `sep` is unchanged.

issues.title: DEPR: deprecate top-level pandas.to_pickle (GH#48402)

labels.name: Deprecate
labels.description: Functionality to remove in pandas

labels.name: IO Pickle
labels.description: read_pickle, to_pickle

issues.body:
closes #48402

`to_pickle` is exported from `pandas/__init__.py` but is not in the API reference, and it is
the only `to_<IO>` writer at the top level — the others are `DataFrame`/`Series` methods, and
only the `read_*` readers are top-level functions. Deprecated per the dev meeting of 2025-09-09.

The name is dropped from `pandas/__init__.py`'s import list and `__all__` and re-exposed through
a module-level `__getattr__` emitting `Pandas4Warning`, following GH-43695 (`Float64Index` et al.)
and GH-68937 (the `pandas.api.typing` `Groupby` spellings). As in GH-68937 the shim sits behind
`if not TYPE_CHECKING:`, since a `__getattr__` visible to type checkers resolves every unknown
`pandas` attribute to `object` and silences `attr-defined` repo-wide.

`pandas.io.pickle.to_pickle` is unchanged and still backs `DataFrame.to_pickle` and
`Series.to_pickle`; it loses `@set_module("pandas")` so that reflective lookups — `pickle.dumps`
of the function object, `inspect.getmodule`, `help` — no longer route back through the deprecated
name. `pandas/_testing/_io.py` and `pandas/tests/io/test_pickle.py` now import it directly. The
`pandas.io.api` re-export is deliberately kept, since this deprecates `pandas.to_pickle` and not
that name.

One thing worth a second opinion: `Index`, `Categorical`, `dict` and friends have no `.to_pickle`
method, so for them the warning names no replacement. Nothing public reproduces what `to_pickle`
did for an arbitrary object on a compressed or remote path — `pickle.dump` infers neither
compression from the suffix nor `storage_options` — and pointing at `pandas.io.pickle.to_pickle`
would advertise a private path. Since the top-level name was never in the reference docs, the
message names the documented replacement and stops, but I'm happy to add wording if we'd rather
say something to those callers.

issues.title: BUG: Series from a pre-2.1 pickle lost its name on copy (GH#61819)

labels.name: IO Pickle
labels.description: read_pickle, to_pickle

issues.body:
closes #61819

`NDFrame.__setstate__` assigned the *pickled* `_metadata` list onto the instance, shadowing the class attribute. pandas 2.1 (GH-51784) renamed the Series entry from `name` to `_name`, so a Series unpickled from an older file carried `_metadata == ["name"]` while the class declared `["_name"]`. `__finalize__` intersects the two lists, got the empty set, and propagated nothing — the name survived the load but vanished on the first `copy`, `reindex`, `astype` or `sort_values`. `__getstate__` then re-emitted the stale list, so re-pickling carried the breakage into the new file.

The restore loop now leaves `_metadata` alone and merges the two lists instead of letting either replace the other. Merging rather than simply dropping the pickled list matters: a stale name and a name a subclass added per instance are indistinguishable from the pickled list alone, and discarding it regressed subclasses that extend `_metadata` in `__init__`. The stale spelling is filtered where it should be — by `__finalize__`'s intersection with the destination's class list.

This is inside the documented support window: `doc/source/user_guide/io.rst` states that pandas 3.x reads pickles back to 2.0.0, and 2.0.x is exactly the affected range. The repo's own `legacy_pickle` fixtures for 1.1.0 through 2.0.3 each contain two named Series that reproduce it.

Tests cover both halves: a synthetic pre-2.1 state (parametrized over name kinds), the shipped 2.0.3 fixture so the emulation cannot silently drift, and a subclass with per-instance `_metadata` guarding against the over-correction.

issues.title: BUG: DataFrame.sparse.from_spmatrix gave the unstored entries a missing value (GH#59212)

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

labels.name: Sparse
labels.description: Sparse Data Type

issues.body:
closes #59212

`scipy.sparse` defines a matrix's unstored entries as zero, and every dtype it supports (bool, int8-64, uint8-64, float32/64, complex64/128) has a representable zero. GH-59063 reported that `from_spmatrix` raised `ValueError` for a bool matrix, because it hardcoded an integer `0` as the fill value, which `SparseDtype` rejects for a bool subtype. GH-59064 fixed that by dropping the fill value entirely, falling back to `SparseDtype`'s NA default — so float and complex matrices came back with `NaN` in the unstored positions and the frame no longer held the same values as `spmatrix.toarray()`. The minimal fix for GH-59063 was a subtype-appropriate zero, which `SparseArray.from_spmatrix` has used all along; this uses the same expression, so the two entry points agree again.

GH-59064 also deleted `to_coo`'s `fill_value != 0` guard and its test, which made `to_coo` silently write zeros in the unstored positions of a column with a non-zero fill value. Restored, made NA-safe (`pd.NA != 0` is `pd.NA`, which cannot be used as a condition), with `pd.NA` added to the test's parametrization.

The two halves have to land together: with the guard restored and `from_spmatrix` left as-is, the `to_coo` example in `doc/source/user_guide/sparse.rst` raises.

issues.title: TST: sparse reindex lost a narrow float subtype (GH#26123)

labels.name: Testing
labels.description: pandas testing functions or related to the test suite

labels.name: Sparse
labels.description: Sparse Data Type

issues.body:
closes #26123

Already fixed by GH-68469, which stopped `SparseArray.take` from promoting the subtype on `type(fill_value)` — `np.result_type(float32, float)` is `float64`, so any fill position widened a narrow float subtype. That PR pinned the behavior at the `SparseArray.take` level only, so this adds the user-level `Series.reindex` regression test the issue reports, and names the issue on the existing whatsnew entry.

The remaining upcasts in the issue's example (`Sparse[int32, 0]` to `float64`, `Sparse[bool, False]` to `object`) are the ordinary upcast on introducing NaN and match dense `reindex` exactly. A differential over every numpy subtype crossed with reindex grow/reorder/subset, `align`, `shift`, `DataFrame.reindex`, and non-default fill values shows no remaining divergence from dense.

issues.title: BUG: Index.difference treating parsable strings as datetimelike members (GH#58971)

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

labels.name: setops
labels.description: union, intersection, difference, symmetric_difference

issues.body:
closes #58971

`Index._difference` resolves membership with `other.get_indexer_for(self)`, and `get_indexer` begins by running the target through `other._maybe_cast_listlike_indexer` — the same label parsing `.loc` and `get_loc` use. For a `DatetimeIndex`/`TimedeltaIndex`/`PeriodIndex` `other`, that turns `"2022-02"` into `Period("2022-02")`, so the string counts as a member. Because the cast is applied to one operand only, the answer depends on which side is `self`: `index2.difference(index1)` came back empty. GH-55108 flipped the lookup direction for perf, which moved which direction shows it rather than introducing it.

Aligning the dtypes before the lookup, as `union` and `intersection` already do, puts that cast out of reach. Membership is then decided by equality, matching `union`, `intersection`, `symmetric_difference` and `isin` — all of which already treat `"2022-02"` and `Period("2022-02")` as distinct, as does `==` on the scalars. `test_float64_index_difference` (GH-35217) pins the same reading, symmetrically, for the float-vs-string version of this case.

Note this makes `index2.difference(index1)` return `["2022-02", "2022-03"]` rather than making `index1.difference(index2)` drop the two periods, so it is the opposite of what the issue asks for and of the stale GH-59148. The dtype comparison is the only added work on the same-dtype path, so GH-55108's speedup is unaffected.

issues.title: BUG: ArrowDtype timestamp setitem silently crossed the tz-aware/naive boundary

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Timezones
labels.description: Timezone data dtype

labels.name: Arrow
labels.description: pyarrow functionality

issues.body:
Setting a tz-aware `Timestamp` into a tz-naive `timestamp[ns][pyarrow]` column stored the value's UTC epoch under a naive target, so it came back shifted by the UTC offset; the reverse direction did the same. Every `datetime64`/`DatetimeTZDtype` equivalent raises `TypeError`.

```python
arr = pd.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="timestamp[ns][pyarrow]")   # tz-naive
arr[0] = pd.Timestamp("2016-01-01 00:00", tz="US/Eastern")
arr[0]   # Timestamp('2016-01-01 05:00:00')   <- the UTC epoch stored as naive
```

`_box_pa_scalar` now raises `TypeError` when the value and the target disagree about being timezone-aware. The guard keys on `datetime`, so the `Timestamp` and plain `datetime.datetime` spellings behave alike, and there is a second guard at the trailing cast, which is where an already-boxed `pa.Scalar` reaches the boundary. Only setitem, `fillna`, `where`/`mask`, `replace` and `reindex`'s fill pass a target `pa_type`, so comparison, arithmetic and `isin` are untouched.

`ArrowDtype._get_common_dtype` stops routing a tz-aware timestamp through `numpy_dtype`, which drops the tz. This is load-bearing rather than a separate fix: without it, `Index.where`/`putmask` answer the new `TypeError` by widening through the common dtype, which collapses the index to tz-naive and silently relabels entries the caller never selected. It independently fixes `concat` and `combine_first`, which were shifting tz-aware values with no setitem involved, and the same path is what `Index.union`/`append`/`join` use — two tz-aware arrow indexes differing only in unit came back relabelled tz-naive and shifted. It also lets an unresolvable pyarrow tz label yield no common dtype rather than raising.

Deliberately out of scope: the array-valued spelling in `_box_pa_array` still crosses the boundary, since the check belongs in `_validate_setitem_value` and that reroute is GH-68419; `merge`'s key casting, `insert`/`shift(fill_value=)` via `_from_sequence`, and the lossy-unit rounding are likewise separate.

issues.title: BUG: Index.insert silently truncating a value into a sparse subtype

labels.name: Dtype Conversions
labels.description: Unexpected or buggy dtype conversions

labels.name: Sparse
labels.description: Sparse Data Type

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

issues.body:
`pd.Index(SparseArray([1, 2, 3])).insert(0, 1.5)` returned `Index([1, 1, 2, 3], dtype='Sparse[int64, 0]')`, where the dense control widens to `float64`. `SparseArray` has no `insert` override, so it falls through to `ExtensionArray.insert`, which relies on `_from_sequence` raising for an item the dtype cannot hold — `SparseArray._from_sequence` coerces instead. Every subtype was affected: `2**63` wrapped to `INT64_MIN`, a `Timestamp` was stored as an integer, and a bool subtype turned `1.5`, `"x"` and a `Timestamp` alike into `True`.

`SparseArray.insert` now validates the item against the subtype and raises, so `Index.insert`'s existing widening arm runs. Two supporting fixes are needed for that arm to return a usable result, and each fixes a user-visible bug of its own:

- `SparseDtype._get_common_dtype` resolves the widened subtype with `find_common_type` rather than `np_find_common_type`. Otherwise `insert(0, True)` raises, because numpy resolves bool + int64 to int64 and `SparseDtype` rejects the bool fill value for it — as it already did for `concat`, `Index.union`, `Index.append` and `DataFrame.combine_first` on that pair.
- `SparseArray._concat_same_type` builds its result with `_simple_new` rather than the constructor, whose `sanitize_array` re-infers an object array of datetimelikes back to `M8`. Otherwise an all-fill-value index (empty `sp_values`) hit the same `ValueError`.

Missing-value inserts are out of scope: a sparse subtype that cannot hold NA still raises or coerces, which needs `ensure_dtype_can_hold_na` to become sparse-aware.

issues.title: BUG: SparseArray.fillna mishandled a datetimelike fill value

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

labels.name: Sparse
labels.description: Sparse Data Type

issues.body:
`SparseArray.fillna` passed the caller's scalar `value` straight to `np.where(isna(self.sp_values), value, self.sp_values)`, leaving numpy to decide what the result held. Only an `np.datetime64`/`np.timedelta64` in the subtype's own unit or a coarser one came through correctly. Every other spelling of a value the subtype can hold left the array wrong under a dtype that still reported the original subtype:

- a boxed `Timestamp`/`Timedelta`, a stdlib `datetime`/`timedelta`, `NaT`, `None`, or `pd.NA` made `sp_values` `object`, holding raw `int64` on a nanosecond unit;
- a lossless numpy scalar in a *finer* unit left `sp_values` in the fill value's unit;
- `np.nan` and date strings raised `DTypePromotionError`.

The dense path is correct for all of them.

The fix unboxes the scalar into the subtype when the subtype can hold it. That needed `_promote_for_fill` split into `_can_hold_for_fill` + `_unbox_for_fill` and recomposed from them: its `maybe_promote` fall-through raises `ValueError: Cannot losslessly convert units` for a `timedelta64` it would have to widen, so it cannot be called speculatively just to ask whether the subtype can hold the value. The split is a pure extraction; the other eight call sites are unchanged.

A value the subtype *cannot* hold still reaches numpy's own promotion untouched, exactly as before. `Series.where`/`DataFrame.where` on a sparse datetimelike column has the same shape but needs a different fix — the result subtype has to come from the fill value rather than from `np.where`'s promotion — so it is left for a follow-up.

issues.title: BUG: replace silently discards a compiled regex on ArrowDtype strings

labels.name: Strings
labels.description: String extension data type and string data

labels.name: Arrow
labels.description: pyarrow functionality

issues.body:
`Series.replace`/`DataFrame.replace` silently discarded a compiled `re.Pattern` on arrow-backed string dtypes:

```python
pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string())).replace(re.compile("^a"), "z")
# ['a', 'b']   <- discarded; object, str, string[python] and string[pyarrow] all substitute
```

`Block._replace_regex` gated compiled patterns on a literal allowlist, `_regex_target_dtype(self.dtype) not in [object, "string"]`. `ArrowDtype(pa.string())` matches neither, so the pattern never reached `replace_regex`. The string spelling of the same pattern was unaffected — `is_re("^a")` is False, so it never hit the guard.

The allowlist is now `is_string_dtype(target) and target.kind != "S"`. The `kind != "S"` half keeps numpy bytes out, since `is_string_dtype` counts them and a regex can never match bytes (without it a `|S2` Series silently upcast to `object` on what is still a no-op). The predicate is still applied to `_regex_target_dtype`, which resolves a `Categorical` to its categories' dtype (GH-68928), so a `Categorical` of arrow strings stops being a silent no-op too.

Widening the gate is not enough on its own: the object-upcast escape hatch on the next lines asks `can_hold_element`, which returns `True` for every `ArrowDtype` (`pandas/core/dtypes/cast.py`, under the comment "This is technically incorrect"), so an unholdable replacement never triggered the upcast. That is already visible on the released string spelling — `replace("^a", 1, regex=True)` raises `ArrowInvalid` and `replace(regex={"^a": 1})` silently stores `"1"`, where every other string dtype upcasts to `object` — and the compiled spelling would join them once the gate admits it. For an arrow string block the decision is now made directly: a `str`, a regex (left to raise on write, as `StringDtype` does), or a scalar NA fits, and anything else upcasts. That branch is gated on the same string predicate, so a non-string arrow column keeps its dtype through a frame-wide sweep like `df.replace(r"^\s*$", 0, regex=True)`.

Not covered here, each a separate defect with its own review surface: dictionary-encoded arrow strings, which `is_string_dtype` rejects, and `pa.string_view()`, where the direct path discards silently just as `string` did while the `regex=` dict path raises `NotImplementedError` from `ArrowDtype.type`, so admitting it to `is_string_dtype` would not be enough.

issues.title: BUG: factorize trusted a pre-encoded pyarrow dictionary

labels.name: Algos
labels.description: Non-arithmetic algos: value_counts, factorize, sorting, isin, clip, shift, diff

labels.name: Arrow
labels.description: pyarrow functionality

issues.body:
`ArrowExtensionArray.factorize` short-circuited when the input was already `pa.dictionary`-typed and returned the stored dictionary as `uniques`. That dictionary is not a factorization of the values the array currently holds: entries can be unreferenced, they can be duplicated, and a null can live in the dictionary rather than in the indices.

So after an ordinary boolean filter, `groupby` invented a group for a value that was no longer in the frame, while `unique`/`value_counts` on the same column disagreed with it:

```python
enc = pa.array(["a", "b", "c", "a"]).dictionary_encode()
df = pd.DataFrame({"k": pd.array(enc, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(enc.type)), "v": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
sub = df[df["v"] > 2]

sub.groupby("k", sort=False)["v"].sum()
# k
# a    4
# b    0   <- "b" appears nowhere in `sub`
# c    3
```

A dictionary holding the same value in two slots additionally split that value across two groups, and a null stored in the dictionary could end up in `uniques`.

The fix re-factorizes in index space — dedupe the stored dictionary, map the indices through it, re-encode, take the uniques back out — so it never materializes the decoded values. Decoding instead silently overflows the 32-bit offsets once the values pass 2 GiB, and the following kernel segfaults. Value types that have no `dictionary_encode` or `take` kernel (nested and view types, `float16`) keep the existing behaviour rather than raising — except under `use_na_sentinel=False` with a null present, where keeping the stored dictionary would leave the null in index space and `factorize` would hand back the `-1` that flag promises not to use; that combination re-raises, as `main` does today.

`uniques` now come out in order of first appearance rather than in the stored dictionary's order, which is what every other dtype does and is visible through `groupby(sort=False)`.

Adjacent defects with the same root cause are left alone deliberately: `_factorize_keys` in `merge`, the `Categorical` constructor, and `unique`/`value_counts`/`mode` all read a stored dictionary the same way, and each needs its own change.

issues.title: BUG: to_parquet (pyarrow) deletes a pre-existing file it cannot open

labels.name: IO Parquet
labels.description: parquet, feather

issues.body:
`DataFrame.to_parquet` (pyarrow engine) raised `PermissionError` and *deleted* the pre-existing file when the local destination was one pandas could not open for writing — a `0o444` file, or one owned by another user in a writable directory.

`pyarrow.parquet.write_table` does `except Exception: os.remove(where)` whenever `where` is path-like, and that fires even when the write never got past *opening* the destination. GH-65811 dropped the pandas-side `get_handle()` open for local paths (completing GH-64590), so pyarrow began opening the path itself; before that, `get_handle` raised first and the file was untouched.

The fix hands pyarrow a `pa.OSFile` that pandas opened, so `where` is not path-like and the cleanup cannot fire. `pa.OSFile` opens in C++ rather than through `builtins.open`, so both properties GH-65811 bought are preserved — no `get_handle`, and a single native open of the destination — and its tests pass unchanged. This also brings `to_parquet` back in line with `to_csv`, `to_feather` and `to_orc`, which all leave the file intact here.

No whatsnew entry: GH-64590 and GH-65811 are both unreleased, so the data loss never shipped.

issues.title: BUG: Value-dependent formatting when casting from datetime to string

labels.name: Datetime
labels.description: Datetime data dtype

labels.name: Dtype Conversions
labels.description: Unexpected or buggy dtype conversions

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

assert pd.__version__ == "3.0.5"
assert np.__version__ == "2.5.1"

np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01 00:00:00.001"],
    pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),
    strict=False
)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01 00:00:01"],  # <- value dependent format
    pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),
    strict=False
)

np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01T00:00:00.001"],
    pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),
    strict=False
)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01T00:00:01.000"],  # <- unit dependent format
    pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),
    strict=False
)
```

### Issue Description

The string formatting of datetimes depends on the values rather than the time unit of the data type. The analogous operation in NumPy only depends on the unit.

I was not able to find a definitive answer on the matter that clarified whether this is intended behavior. I can see that this may have been intended in pandas 1.x where the one and only unit was `ns` which would lead to very long strings in all cases, despite most users probably never working on a ns resolution. 

### Expected Behavior

My understanding is that value-dependent semantics are not desired in pandas these days(?). Given that pandas allows users to define their desired units these days, it seems reasonable to me to make the formatting depend only on the unit rather than the values. 

Alternatively, it may be nice to document the intended formatting semantics (unless I missed them and that is already the case).

issues.title: BUG: read_sas held a SAS7BDAT file open until a cyclic collection

labels.name: IO SAS
labels.description: SAS: read_sas

issues.body:
`SAS7BDATReader` stored a list of its own bound methods on the instance, making every reader a reference cycle: dropping one did not free it, and its file stayed open until the next cyclic collection. So `pd.read_sas(path, chunksize=n)` without a `with` block leaked the file descriptor. `XportReader`, which has no such list, already closed on drop.

The list moves to a class attribute of plain functions, with `collect_page_subheaders` passing the reader explicitly.

This also fixes a flaky CI failure seen mostly on the free-threading build: the suite treats `ResourceWarning` as an error, and a reader leaked by `test_encoding_default_deprecated_header_text_only` (added in GH-66477) was collected at an arbitrary later point, so the failure was charged to whichever unrelated test was running then. That test now closes its reader.

issues.title: BUG: sparse cumsum propagated a stored missing value instead of skipping it (GH#68187)

labels.name: Sparse
labels.description: Sparse Data Type

issues.body:
Follow-up to GH-68187, which added `SparseArray._accumulate` and routed numeric `cumsum` with `skipna=True` to the existing `SparseArray.cumsum`.

`SparseArray.cumsum`'s null-fill-value branch reduced `sp_values` with a bare `ndarray.cumsum()`, so a missing value held *among the stored values* -- rather than left as a gap -- propagated into every later stored value instead of being skipped:

```python
a = pd.Series(pd.arrays.SparseArray([1, np.nan, 2, 0, 5], fill_value=0))
b = pd.Series(pd.arrays.SparseArray([1, 1, np.nan, np.nan, 1], fill_value=np.nan))
(a + b).cumsum()  # [2, nan, nan, nan, nan], where dense gives [2, nan, nan, nan, 8]

pd.DataFrame.sparse.from_spmatrix(csr_matrix([[1.0], [np.nan], [3.0]]))[0].cumsum()
# [1, nan, nan], where dense gives [1, nan, 4]
```

Sparse arithmetic, `DataFrame.sparse.from_spmatrix`, and an explicit `sparse_index` all produce such an array. The fix masks those NAs to the additive identity, accumulates, then restores them -- the shape `nanops.na_accum_func` uses, which cannot be reused directly because it asserts against `datetime64`/`timedelta64`.

The defect predates GH-68187: `git log -L` puts `self.sp_values.cumsum()` with GH-62703/GH-65494. GH-68187 made it reachable from `Series.cumsum`/`DataFrame.cumsum`, which previously raised `NotImplementedError`. Fixing the array method rather than the `_accumulate` routing also repairs a `timedelta64` subtype, where `arr.cumsum()` gave `[1ns, NaT, NaT]` instead of `[1ns, NaT, 4ns]`.

Off-PR I ran a dense-vs-sparse differential over ~11000 cells -- float16/32/64, complex64/128, `m8[ns]`/`[s]`/`[us]`, int64, bool and object subtypes x `IntIndex`/`BlockIndex` x lengths 0-8 x NA placement x `inf`/`-inf`/`-0.0`/imaginary-only NaN x `axis` variants x Series, DataFrame and array entry points -- with no divergence, and confirmed the fix mutates nothing the caller still holds.

issues.title: BUG: to_datetime returned category dtype for categorical input when the cache fired (GH#28629)

labels.name: Datetime
labels.description: Datetime data dtype

labels.name: Categorical
labels.description: Categorical Data Type

issues.body:
closes #28629

`to_datetime`'s internal date cache is applied with `Series.map`, and `map` can hand back the input's own container — `Categorical.map` maps the categories and rebuilds a `Categorical` — or, on its slow path, an object-dtype `Index`. So once the input was long and repetitive enough for `should_cache` to fire, categorical input came back as `category` (or, when every category coerced to `NaT`, `object`) instead of `datetime64`, while the same values just under the threshold came back as a `DatetimeIndex`.

The cache lookup now casts to `cache_array.dtype`, which is by construction the dtype the uncached `convert_listlike` produces, so the cache can no longer be observed in the result.

issues.title: DEPR: Timestamp.timestamp treating tz-naive as UTC (GH#50298)

labels.name: Timezones
labels.description: Timezone data dtype

labels.name: Deprecate
labels.description: Functionality to remove in pandas

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

labels.name: Timestamp
labels.description: pd.Timestamp and associated methods

issues.body:
closes #50298

`Timestamp.timestamp()` interprets a tz-naive `Timestamp`'s wall clock as UTC, while `datetime.datetime.timestamp()` interprets a naive `datetime` as local time. Since `Timestamp.fromtimestamp()` delegates to the stdlib, the two disagree with each other: `Timestamp.fromtimestamp(x).timestamp() != x` in any non-UTC zone.

This deprecates the tz-naive behavior with a `Pandas4Warning`. No returned value changes here; enforcement (naive interpreted as local time, matching the stdlib) would be the 4.0 step, and `ts.tz_localize("UTC").timestamp()` preserves the current behavior. Follow-up to GH-65423, which documented the divergence and was closed in favor of resolving it.

Worth flagging: enforcement would make a naive `.timestamp()` depend on the machine's local timezone, and pandas treats naive datetimes as "no timezone" rather than "local" everywhere else. The counterweight is that `Timestamp` is a `datetime` subclass whose two stdlib-named epoch methods currently contradict each other.

issues.title: BUG: read_csv with engine="pyarrow" ignored skiprows when header is not None (GH#48507)

labels.name: IO CSV
labels.description: read_csv, to_csv

labels.name: Arrow
labels.description: pyarrow functionality

issues.body:
closes #48507
closes #58048

`read_csv(engine="pyarrow")` built pyarrow's `ReadOptions` with `skip_rows = skiprows if header is None else header`, so `skiprows` was dropped for every `header is not None` spelling — including the default `header=0`. The rows meant to be skipped were read as the header and as data, and `usecols`/`index_col` were then resolved against that wrong header row.

`skip_rows` is now `skiprows + header`, which is the composition the other engines already implement and the user guide already documents ("`header` will be relative to the end of `skiprows`"). A negative `skiprows` is clamped to 0 so that it skips nothing as with the `c` and `python` engines, rather than being passed to pyarrow, which rejects it.

GH-58048 is a duplicate report of the same bug, so both are closed here.

`test_skiprows_infield_quote` (GH-14459) passes on the pyarrow engine with the fix and is un-xfailed.

Two tests pin behavior that the fix makes reachable on the default `header` path: a `skiprows` landing on or past the end of the file raises on the pyarrow engine, where the `c` and `python` engines raise `EmptyDataError` or return an empty frame. Both are existing `pyarrow.csv` `skip_rows` limitations that already apply with `header=None`, not something this PR introduces.

issues.title: DEPR: rename Groupby classes to GroupBy (GH#49578)

labels.name: Resample
labels.description: resample method

labels.name: Deprecate
labels.description: Functionality to remove in pandas

labels.name: Window
labels.description: rolling, ewma, expanding

labels.name: API - Consistency
labels.description: Internal Consistency of API/Behavior

issues.body:
closes #49578

`pandas.api.typing` spelled "group by" two ways: `DataFrameGroupBy`/`SeriesGroupBy` with a capital B, and six others without — `RollingGroupby`, `ExpandingGroupby`, `ExponentialMovingWindowGroupby`, `DatetimeIndexResamplerGroupby`, `PeriodIndexResamplerGroupby`, `TimedeltaIndexResamplerGroupby`. Those six are renamed to the `GroupBy` spelling, and the old names still resolve through a module-level `__getattr__` with a `Pandas4Warning`.

Since this module exists for type-hinting, the old spellings are also bound under `if TYPE_CHECKING:` so annotating with one keeps type-checking for the deprecation period. Without that the deprecation has no period at all for its primary use case: `x: pd.api.typing.RollingGroupby` becomes an immediate mypy error, and under `from __future__ import annotations` no runtime warning fires either. `TYPE_CHECKING` itself is deleted at runtime so it does not enter the public namespace.

The private `BaseWindowGroupby` and `GroupbyIndexer` are renamed outright with no shim; neither is re-exported from a public module.

Only `pandas.api.typing` is shimmed. The old names are gone from `pandas.core.window` and `pandas.core.resample`, so `from pandas.core.window.rolling import RollingGroupby` now raises `ImportError` — pandarallel and mapply both do this, and pandarallel subclasses it. That is deliberate, since `pandas.core` is private and the downstream fix is a one-line rename, but flagging it in case reviewers would rather shim those modules too.

One follow-up outside this repo: pandas-stubs re-exports all six old spellings from `pandas.core.window`/`pandas.core.resample`, and stub packages shadow pandas' inline types. Until a companion pandas-stubs PR lands, pandas-stubs users won't see the new names at all, and won't see the deprecation either.

labels.name: IO CSV

issues.body:
closes #51801

``read_csv(StringIO(...), sep="\n", lineterminator="-")`` raised ``ValueError``, but the C engine parses it fine: a custom line terminator clears ``has_carriage``, which leaves ``"\n"`` and ``"\r"`` as ordinary characters that split fields. The guard now fires only when ``lineterminator`` is absent or equal to the separator, and the message says how to get the parse.

A ``bytes``/``bytearray`` ``lineterminator`` is normalized before that comparison. The C engine accepts those spellings, so without it ``lineterminator=b"\n"`` slipped past the narrowed guard into the same silent mis-parse GH-43528 was filed about.

The ``"\r"`` clause of the existing entry is amended rather than duplicated: that raise arrived with GH-66896 and is unreleased, so only the ``"\n"`` case is a user-visible change against 3.0.

issues.title: BUG: Rolling/Expanding skew and kurt wrong on data with a large shared offset

labels.name: Window
labels.description: rolling, ewma, expanding

labels.name: Numeric stability
labels.description: Stability and precision

issues.body:
The sliding moment accumulators behind `Rolling.skew`/`kurt` (and `Expanding.skew`/`kurt`, which
share the kernels) take every deviation against a running mean. On a series carrying a large
offset the mean dwarfs the spread, so the deviations lose most of their significant digits and the
results are silently wrong — on a 4-wide window of values one ulp apart at 1e8, `kurt` returned
213, where the attainable range for 4 points is [-6, 4]. Separately, once a window's observation
count dropped to zero the accumulators divided by it and every later window returned `NaN`.

This anchors the accumulators to each window's first value so an offset shared by the window
cancels exactly, retires that anchor once the window's centre drifts away from it, and replaces
the per-kernel cancellation tests with a shared detector (a NaN arm, an anchor-drift arm, and a
peak-deviation arm). It is the treatment `Rolling.cov`/`corr` already received in GH-66678.

The NaN-forever half is a long-standing bug; the low-variance half surfaced in GH-64366, which
dropped the `m2 <= nobs * 1e-14` guard that had been returning `NaN` there instead of a wrong
number. The underlying precision loss predates both — 2.3.3 pre-centred the values by the rounded
global mean, and GH-62863/GH-63143 dropped that when they introduced the incremental instability
machinery.

Dropping the two per-kernel arms also removes the rescan-every-window fallbacks they triggered, so
this is a speedup as well as an accuracy fix:
`pd.Series(np.tile([-1., 0., 1., 0.], 25_000)).expanding().skew()` goes from 5.3s to 0.7ms (the
old behaviour was quadratic in the length of the series), and
`pd.Series(rng.lognormal(0, 5, 50_000)).rolling(1000).kurt()` from 54ms to 0.6ms.

Accuracy, measured against an exact rational oracle over 83,772 windows per statistic (142 series
× 6 window widths, covering shared offsets, drifting levels, lognormal, mixed-magnitude and
NaN-holed data):

| | p99 rel err | max rel err |
|---|---|---|
| `skew` before | 3.3e+01 | 4.6e+23 |
| `skew` after | 1.0e-11 | 4.9e-08 |
| `kurt` before | 4.8e+02 | 2.9e+32 |
| `kurt` after | 1.8e-10 | 3.5e-07 |

No window in that sweep comes back worse than `main` by more than 1e-6 relative.

Two consequences worth calling out. A window of identical values reached incrementally on offset
data used to come back as a number rather than `NaN`, because the digits the accumulators had lost
left `m2` nonzero; it is `NaN` now, which is what GH-62864 already specifies for a degenerate
window. And the new detector is not free on data that never needed it: in an ABBA-ordered
measurement with untouched `rolling.median`/`var` as controls, `rolling(100).skew()` is 2.6% slower
on uniform data and 12.5% slower on lognormal data, against the wins above.

One known limit, pre-existing and deliberately not widened into here: the same
overflow-in-the-detector shape affects `roll_var` and the `cov`/`corr` diagonal.

issues.title: BUG: DataFrame.agg with a list of funcs rounds uint64 results (GH#65031)

labels.name: Dtype Conversions
labels.description: Unexpected or buggy dtype conversions

labels.name: Apply
labels.description: Apply, Aggregate, Transform, Map

labels.name: Numeric stability
labels.description: Stability and precision

issues.body:
Follow-up to GH-65031, which added the list-of-reductions fast path in
`FrameApply._agg_list_like_frame_reductions`. That path computes DataFrame-level reductions per
dtype group and stacks one 1-row frame per function with `concat`. When the functions return
different dtypes for a column, the stack reconciles them to a common dtype that need not hold
the results:

```python
big = 2**64 - 3
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": pd.Series([big, 1], dtype="uint64")})

df.agg(["max", "count"])
# main:   max -> 1.8446744073709552e+19, dtype float64   (true value 18446744073709551613)
# 3.0.6:  max -> 18446744073709551613,   dtype object
```

`max` returns unsigned and `count` signed, and the dtype that holds both is float64. The
`uint64[pyarrow]` spelling raised `ArrowInvalid` on the same cast instead of rounding.

Now, when the functions disagree on dtype, the stacked frame has to still hold every result
exactly; the columns where it does not are replaced with object, individually, so a column's
output dtype does not depend on its siblings' values. When the cast is refused outright — a
`uint64[pyarrow]` column raises rather than rounding — each column is retried on its own.
Results are compared as object arrays, because a numpy scalar widens the original back to the
stacked dtype and so compares a rounded value against itself; `Series.tolist` is not enough,
since a `Sparse` column's elements stay numpy scalars. `pandas/core/array_algos/quantile.py`
already decides a result dtype with a cast-round-trip check, in the float-to-int direction where
a numpy comparison suffices.

Groups whose functions agree on dtype, and groups whose stacked dtype does hold every result,
are untouched — `df.agg(["sum"])` and ordinary magnitudes keep both their dtype and the speedup
from GH-65031.

The fast path is unreleased, but the check also changes released behavior, so there is an
*Other API changes* entry: `df.agg(["sum", "mean"])` on an int64 column whose sum is not
representable in float64 now returns object where 3.0 returns a rounded float64. Sparing that
case would mean special-casing unsignedness. `Series.agg(["max", "mean"])` and
`df.agg({"a": ["max", "mean"]})` still round, via a different assembly path that this PR does
not touch.

issues.title: BUG: DataFrame.isetitem with an out-of-order loc corrupted the block structure

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

issues.body:
`BlockManager._iset_split_block` passed the caller's `blk_locs` order straight to `Block.delete`, whose docstring says "Assumes `loc` is strictly increasing when list-like". So `df.isetitem([2, 0, 1], value)`, where those positions share a block and only part of it is replaced, left stale and overlapping blocks behind.

The values read back correct, which is what makes this easy to miss. The sum of block placement lengths exceeds the column count, so `_verify_integrity` fails: a later `merge`, `join` or `describe` raises `AssertionError`, and `to_pickle` writes a file that `read_pickle` rejects.

`np.unique` normalizes for the `Block.delete` call only — `blk_locs` is reused two lines down at `locs = blk.mgr_locs.as_array[blk_locs]`, where its order pairs with `value`'s columns. `BlockManager.setitem` already did this (GH-65446); `iset` was the unfixed sibling. The comment there credited `Block.delete`'s precondition, which this change makes obsolete, but the sort is still needed for `_iset_split_block`'s `_blklocs` bookkeeping, so that comment is corrected rather than the code.

Not fixed here:

- A duplicated position (`df.isetitem([0, 0], value)`) still builds a block whose placement repeats that column. This change makes that raise `IndexError` instead of corrupting when the block has a single column; the real fix is to reject a duplicated `loc`, which covers the multi-column case too.
- `_iset_split_block`'s whole-block early return skips the `_blklocs` update, so an unsorted `blk_locs` leaves the cache stale. Not reachable from any public API today, and `BlockManager.setitem`'s `np.unique` is what keeps it that way.
- A reversed-contiguous `BlockPlacement` — which a descending `loc` produces, correctly, both before and after this change — makes default-axis `concat` raise `ValueError: unbounded slice`. Pre-existing and independent: `_iset_split_block` is not called at all for the two-column case that shows it.

issues.title: BUG: DataFrame.clip with an extension-dtype array/Index bound degrades to object

labels.name: Numeric Operations
labels.description: Arithmetic, Comparison, and Logical operations

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

issues.body:
`NDFrame._clip_with_one_bound` converts a non-`Series` list-like bound via `_align_for_op(threshold, axis, flex=None)` and passes the result to `where`. Since GH-61828 that routes an extension-dtype operand through `_maybe_align_series_as_frame`, which now returns an EA-columned `DataFrame` instead of the `Series` it used to return. `DataFrame.where` has an EA-aware column-wise path for a 1-D `other` but none for a 2-D one, so the bound interleaves to an object ndarray.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[10, 20], [30, 40]])

df.clip(lower=pd.array([15, 25], dtype="Int64"), axis=1).dtypes
# object, object   (int64, int64 before GH-61828)

df.clip(lower=pd.array([15, 25], dtype="Int64"), axis=1, inplace=True)
# TypeError: Invalid value '[[15]]' for dtype 'int64'
```

`_align_for_op` now skips that broadcast when `flex is None` — clip is that flag's only caller — so the bound stays a `Series` and takes the working 1-D path; the helper is renamed `_align_series_as_frame` since it no longer has a fallback. `_clip_with_one_bound` then pins `axis=1` when it gets a `Series` back with `axis=None`, since `_align_for_op` had already aligned the bound against `self.columns` and `DataFrame.align(Series, axis=None)` raises.

The object degradation never shipped, so against released 3.0 the only `clip` change is that `df.clip(lower=<extension-dtype array>)` with `axis` omitted no longer raises `ValueError: Must specify axis=0 or 1`.

Routing the bound back through the 1-D path made it reach `np_can_hold_element`'s `dtype.itemsize < tipo.itemsize` comparison, which runs before the `not isinstance(tipo, np.dtype)` guard and so raised `AttributeError` for any non-NumPy `tipo` carrying no `itemsize`. That is a released bug in its own right, not just a `clip` one: on 3.0 it fires for every setitem-shaped path that hands a `SparseArray` into an integer-dtype NumPy column.

```python
ser = pd.Series([10, 20, 30])
sp = pd.arrays.SparseArray([1, 2, 3])

ser.where([True, False, True], sp)                              # AttributeError on 3.0
ser.mask([True, False, True], sp)                               # AttributeError on 3.0
ser[[0, 1]] = sp[:2]                                            # AttributeError on 3.0
pd.Index([10, 20, 30]).putmask(np.array([True, False, True]), sp)  # AttributeError on 3.0
```

The comparison is now skipped when the dtype carries no `itemsize`; such an element falls through to the extension-array branch below, which re-runs the same guards on its densified values, so a `SparseArray` is accepted or rejected exactly as the nullable `Int64` spelling already was.

issues.title: BUG: astype/construction from float to datetime64 is an unchecked narrowing

labels.name: Datetime
labels.description: Datetime data dtype

labels.name: Dtype Conversions
labels.description: Unexpected or buggy dtype conversions

labels.name: Constructors
labels.description: Series/DataFrame/Index/pd.array Constructors

issues.body:
A ``float`` outside the ``int64`` domain cast to ``M8``/``m8`` was silently converted. Positive overflow saturated to ``INT64_MAX`` and read back as a real-looking timestamp; negative overflow landed on ``INT64_MIN``, which *is* the ``NaT`` sentinel, so ``-inf`` became missing data. The only signal was a numpy ``RuntimeWarning``, which pandas does not promote.

```python
pd.Series([np.inf]).astype("M8[ns]")[0]    # Timestamp('2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807')
pd.Series([-np.inf]).astype("M8[ns]")[0]   # NaT
pd.Series([1e30]).astype("m8[s]")[0]       # Timedelta('106751991167300 days 15:30:07')
pd.DatetimeIndex(np.array([np.inf]))[0]    # Timestamp('2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807')
pd.to_datetime(np.array([np.inf]))[0]      # Timestamp('2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807')
```

The timedelta64 family was already guarded by ``cast_from_unit_vectorized``'s ``_raise_if_outside_int64``; datetime64 was the unguarded member, so ``.astype`` disagreed with ``dtype=``, and ``DatetimeIndex`` disagreed with ``TimedeltaIndex`` on the same input. This adds the same check to the two sites that lacked it — ``_astype_nansafe``'s fall-through cast and ``maybe_convert_dtype`` — reusing the message the timedelta peer already emits so the two agree.

``errors="coerce"`` is preserved: ``to_datetime`` blanks just the out-of-range entries rather than letting the raise escape, matching what ``to_timedelta`` already does (GH-66823).

`is_float_dtype` is true for ``Float64``, so ``maybe_convert_dtype`` fired for masked input while ``_astype_nansafe`` — which only sees ndarrays — did not, leaving ``DatetimeIndex(masked)`` raising and ``.astype``/``dtype=`` on the same array silently wrong. `BaseMaskedArray.astype` gets the guard too, so the three spellings agree. The pyarrow-backed and ``Sparse`` float spellings were silently wrong on all three and are covered by the same two sites.

The guard is skipped for a multiplier dtype such as ``M8[10s]``, which pandas rejects outright whatever the values; without that gate an out-of-range float turned a ``ValueError`` about the dtype into an ``OutOfBoundsDatetime`` naming a unit the user never asked for. One known consequence remains: ``Index([inf]).astype("M8[D]")`` now raises ``OutOfBoundsDatetime`` where it raised ``TypeError`` before. Deferring to that ``TypeError`` is not reachable without dropping the guard for ``Series.astype("M8[D]")``, which on main silently turns ``-inf`` into ``NaT``; both arms raise either way, so this narrows the data-dependent-exception problem rather than removing it.

In-range values are untouched, including the deliberate ``float(iNaT)`` → ``NaT`` mapping and ``NaN`` → ``NaT``. Not covered here, and tracked locally instead: ``uint64``, ``complex`` and ``Categorical`` sources, each of which needs a different predicate or a separate API decision.

issues.title: BUG: MultiIndex reports the wrong problem for an over-long key (GH#45762)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Error Reporting
labels.description: Incorrect or improved errors from pandas

issues.body:
closes #45762

A MultiIndex key with more entries than the index has levels was reported as an unsorted index — `df.loc[pd.IndexSlice[2:4, 8:10, 15:19], :]` on a 2-level index asked the user to lexsort an index that was already sorted. Other spellings of the same over-long key leaked a raw `IndexError: list index out of range`.

All three sites that can be handed such a key now raise the `KeyError` that `MultiIndex.get_loc` already uses for an over-long tuple:

- `get_locs`, reached by `.loc` with a nested tuple (the reported repro);
- `_get_loc_level`, reached by `get_loc_level` and `xs`, which leaked the `IndexError` when the key held a slice;
- `_partial_tup_index`, reached by `slice_locs`, `get_slice_bound` and `df.loc[tuple:tuple]`, which gave the same misleading lexsort-depth message even on a fully lexsorted index.

`get_locs`' pre-existing Ellipsis check moves above the new guard so that more specific message is not shadowed.

Trailing entries that consume no level are discounted from the length, because `.loc` passes the column selector down: `df.loc[:, key, :]` reaches `get_locs` and `df.loc["a", :, :]` reaches `_get_loc_level` with more entries than the index has levels. The rule differs per site, which the comments explain — `get_locs` also discounts a trailing bool indexer, since its body resolves one positionally, while `_get_loc_level` resolves a bool indexer against its level and so cannot.

The lexsort-depth message keeps its real job: a key the index genuinely is too unsorted for still reports the depth, covered by a new test alongside the existing ones.

Found while investigating, not fixed here: `df.loc[[("a", 1, 4)]]` silently reads *and writes* row `("a", 1)` rather than raising, because `MultiIndex.get_indexer` truncates an over-long tuple to the index's depth. That is a silent-wrong-data bug in a different mechanism and wants its own issue.

issues.title: BUG: comma read as a decimal separator silently corrupts parsed dates (GH#17265)

labels.name: Error Reporting
labels.description: Incorrect or improved errors from pandas

labels.name: Timestamp
labels.description: pd.Timestamp and associated methods

issues.body:
closes #17265

dateutil's tokenizer folds `<2+ digits>,<digits>` into a single decimal number, and `int()` discards the fraction when that number lands in a year/month/day slot. So `Timestamp("2013,11,04")` returned `2013-04-01` and `Timestamp("Nov 14,2013")` returned year 1 — silently, and through `to_datetime`, `DatetimeIndex`, `Period`, `astype` and `read_csv(parse_dates=)` alike.

`dateutil_parse` now rejects exactly those strings. Everything dateutil handles correctly is preserved: a comma it leaves as punctuation (`"Nov 4,2013"`, `"Nov 14, 2013"`, `"Thu, 14 Nov 2013"`), the ISO 8601 decimal comma for fractional seconds (`"01:02:03,456"`, GH-59256), the same comma on minutes and hours (`"01:02,5"`), and unit-label forms (`"12,5h"`). An explicit `format=`/`date_format=` is unaffected either way.

Three adjacent defects turned up on the way and are deliberately left out, since each needs a different rule rather than a wider version of this one: the `.` spelling of the same bug (`Timestamp("Nov 14.2013")` is year 1 — but `.` is a *supported* date separator, so the guard cannot simply be widened), `_find_subsecond_reso`'s dot-only regex (`Period("2013-11-04 01:02:03,456")` truncates to whole seconds, a gap left by GH-59256), and comma handling in `Timedelta` string parsing (`Timedelta("0 days 00:00:01,500")` is 25 minutes).

issues.body:

`pd.Timestamp("11:00")` is parsed relative to today's date, but `pd.Timestamp("11:0")` comes back as `1-01-01 11:00:00`. `_does_string_look_like_time` requires a two-digit minute, so the one-digit spelling is not recognized as a time-only string and falls through to `dateutil_parse` with `_DEFAULT_DATETIME` (year 1) instead of today.

issues.body:
Changed the return type of write_version_info to str and updated its usage in main. Improved handling of MESON_DIST_ROOT environment variable.

issues.title: BUG/DEPR: low_memory keyword in read_csv

labels.name: IO CSV
labels.description: read_csv, to_csv

labels.name: Deprecate
labels.description: Functionality to remove in pandas

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

issues.body:
`low_memory=True` (the default) can give incorrect results in corner cases, which is the reason why the keyword exists.  Minimal example:

```
N = 65536  # rows in the first internal chunk of an 8-column table
data = (
    "a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h\n"
    + "1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1\n" * N          # chunk 1 -> int64
    + f"{2**64 - 1},1,1,1,1,1,1,1\n"   # chunk 2 -> uint64
    + f"{2**64 - 2},1,1,1,1,1,1,1\n"
)

res = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data))["a"]
exp = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), low_memory=False)["a"]

assert exp.iloc[-1] != exp.iloc[-2]
assert res.iloc[-1] != res.iloc[-2]  #  <- fails because of unwanted casting
```

In the `low_memory=True` case, we do dtype inference in chunks.  In cases where different chunks get different dtypes, the concat does a cast which can be lossy.  `low_memory=False` avoids that by doing the dtype inference on the whole column instead of in chunks.

The alternative I think we should consider is to detect when this casting occurs and then re-parse (with `usecols` restricted to the affected column) in the `low_memory=False` mode.  Then we get the correct result and don't need the user-facing keyword.  The downside is a perf penalty in these corner cases.

Passing `low_memory=False` disables the parallel path, which is what brought this to my attention.

issues.title: API: select_dtypes

labels.name: Needs Discussion
labels.description: Requires discussion from core team before further action

issues.body:
We made a bunch of changes to select_dtypes in July.  I advocate reverting the most niche use cases to simplify the code.  

Summarizing the support that was *added*:

1) Passing an ExtensionDtype class matches every instance of that dtype (instead of raising)
2) Passing a partially-specified IntervalDtype e.g. IntervalDtype(np.int64) (without specifying "closed") matches all IntervalDtypes that match that partial specification.
3) Passing a partially-specified CategoricalDtype e.g. CategoricalDtype(my_categories, ordered=None) matches all CategoricalDtypes with those categories regardless of orderedness.

Summarizing the behavior that *changed* as bugfixes

4) Passing a specific dtype e.g. `np.dtype(np.int64)` matches exactly that dtype, not every integer dtype.
5) Passing a type (that isn't an ExtesnsionDtype subclass) raises instead of matching object dtype.
6) Passing EADtypes like Int64Dtype() would match numpy integer dtypes.

Summarizing deprecations

7) Deprecated accepting "datetimetz" and "datetime64tz" since item 1 now means you can pass pd.DatetimeTZDtype explicitly.

I advocate reverting items 2 and 3 before 3.1 is released, as they contribute a lot of complexity for very niche use cases.  Also we don't have a mechanism to do similar partial-specification matching for DatetimeTZDtype or 3rd party EAs.

labels.name: IO Excel
labels.description: read_excel, to_excel

issues.body:
Hello Team!!!

The ODS writer put a newline character straight into the paragraph text of a cell.
XML collapses that to a space, so a multi-line cell written by pandas shows up as
one line in LibreOffice or Excel. Each line break is now written as a
`<text:line-break/>` element instead.

The reader had the matching gap: it ignored `<text:line-break/>` elements, and
joined the several `<text:p>` paragraphs that other spreadsheet applications use
for a multi-line cell without any separator. Both now yield `"\n"`, so a frame
round-trips through `to_excel`/`read_excel`, and a file written elsewhere reads
back with its line breaks intact.

This picks up #66237, which was closed as stale. The three review points there are
addressed: the qualified names in the reader are plain tuples rather than odf
element instances (that ran once per cell), the paragraph tracking is a boolean
rather than a counter, and the reader test builds its `.ods` file at runtime
instead of adding a binary fixture to the repo.

closes #55728

The reader half also covers what was reported in #53924, which was closed at the time as an upstream issue, so that one is referenced rather than closed here.

issues.title: BUG: read_csv c engine ignored na_values on a converters column (GH#13302)

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

labels.name: IO CSV
labels.description: read_csv, to_csv

issues.body:
closes #13302

When a column has a `converters` entry, the default `c` engine silently ignored `na_values` *and* the default NA strings for that column, where the `python` engine applies them: `_convert_column_data` returned from the converter branch before any NA handling ran. This matches them against the converter's output, as the `python` engine does.

The `converters` docstring for `read_csv`/`read_table` and the matching text in `io.rst` documented the old `c`-engine behavior as the spec ("`na_values` and `keep_default_na` have no effect on a column that has a converter"), so they are updated too. The sharpest user-visible change is that an empty field under `converters={"a": str}` now reads as `NaN` rather than `""` — which is what the `python` engine already returned.

Two deliberate limits, both left for separate PRs:

- A converter that *raises* on the NA token (`converters={"a": float}` with a blank field) still raises here; the `python` engine retries with those rows masked. That is the other half of GH-13302, and the whatsnew and docstring claim only output-matching. `test_converters_raising_on_empty_field` asserts the `c` engine's raise and strict-xfails the `python` engine, so a later fix surfaces as an XPASS.
- GH-13302's discussion favored applying `na_values` to the raw token *before* the converter. That is a semantics change for both engines and would need a deprecation; this PR only reconciles the engines, one of the open items on the GH-12686 tracker.

One consequence worth flagging: under the default `low_memory=True`, a converter column whose leading internal chunk is now entirely NA draws the `Columns (N) have mixed types` warning, because that chunk infers `float64` while a later text chunk infers str. The resulting dtype is correct. This is a pre-existing `_concatenate_chunks` bug — it reproduces with no converter at all, on any column whose first chunk is all-NA — and this PR only routes a new kind of input into it. Fixing it means not counting an all-NA chunk as type evidence, which is general enough to want its own PR.

Note `True == 1`, so a bool returned by a converter matches a numeric `na_values` entry. That is intentional on the `c` side — it agrees with the same read without a converter and with `Series.isin`. The `python` engine computes the same mask but `np.putmask` writes the NaN into a bool array, where it reads as `True`; `test_converters_na_values_bool_output` strict-xfails that engine so a later fix surfaces as an XPASS.

issues.title: BUG: iloc setitem wrote the wrong cells on a Copy-on-Write referenced frame (GH#65446)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

issues.body:
Repairs a regression from GH-65864, which is in 3.0.4 and later.

When another object references a `DataFrame`'s values, `BlockManager.setitem` splits the block so only the targeted columns get copied, then re-expresses the caller's column indexer in the new block's coordinates. GH-65864 collapsed any increasing column selection to `slice(None)` and compensated for reordered ones with an array of positions, plus a reshape of the row indexer to `(n, 1)`. Both substitutions change what numpy does: a slice takes the cross product with the row indexer, an array broadcasts against it. So the referenced path could disagree with the unreferenced one in either direction — writing a cross product where the caller asked for an elementwise pairing, or the other way round.

The column indexer now keeps the kind the caller used: an integer stays an integer, a slice stays a slice (reversed if the selection was), `Ellipsis` normalizes to `slice(None)` since it also selects the axis in full, and anything else stays an array of positions. The row-indexer reshape goes with it — it was independently wrong, turning an intended broadcast into a cross product whenever `np.ix_` had not already run — and so does the `np.squeeze`, which is only correct for `np.ix_` output; a user-supplied 2-D row key still reaches that spot, and not squeezing it is what makes it match the unreferenced path.

Symptoms fixed, all only when another object holds a reference:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(12.0).reshape(4, 3), columns=list("abc"))
ref = df[["a", "b", "c"]]

df.iloc[[2, 0], ::-1] = np.array([100.0, 101.0, 102.0])
# IndexError: shape mismatch: indexing arrays could not be broadcast
#   together with shapes (2,) (3,)

df.iloc[np.array([1, 0]), range(1, -1, -1)] = 99.0
# silently writes 4 cells; without the reference it writes 2

df.loc[np.array([True, False, True, False]), "c":"a":-1] = 99.0
# IndexError: too many indices for array: array is 2-dimensional, but 3 were indexed
```

For the `managers.py` split path the unreferenced path is the oracle: it never enters this code, so referenced-vs-unreferenced is a differential with no shared failure mode. Over 35,728 cases (4 dtypes x 4 frame shapes x 20 row-key spellings x 14 column-key spellings x 7 value shapes, `iloc` and `loc`) `main` diverges in 3,621. The branch's residual divergences are the empty-indexer family, where an early return skips value validation; that predates GH-65864 and is left alone here.

`EABackedBlock.setitem` needed a second change, and it is not covered by that oracle. Keeping the column indexer as an array walks 2-D EA blocks into the `indexer[::-1]` + `value.T` pair, which `slice(None)` had been keeping them out of. Two advanced indices broadcast against each other, and their order does not change the result's orientation, so the `value.T` is spurious there; it is now gated accordingly. Because the unreferenced path always reached that pair through `np.ix_`, the gate also changes **unreferenced** all-`datetime64`/`timedelta64` frames: `df.iloc[[2, 0], [0, 2]] = value` with a 2-D value silently wrote the transposed cells, and a non-square selection raised `OutOfBoundsDatetime`. The datetimelike entry is *not* a GH-65864 regression — `value = value.T` came in with GH-64620 (2026-03-15), and the unreferenced path never enters the block GH-65864 changed — so a backport necessarily carries that older fix too. The entry is in `v3.1.0.rst` as there is no open 3.0.x file (3.0.6 released 2026-09-17).

issues.title: BUG: DataFrame axis=1 reductions accumulated in each block's own dtype (GH#51474)

labels.name: Reduction Operations
labels.description: sum, mean, min, max, etc.

labels.name: Numeric stability
labels.description: Stability and precision

issues.body:
Repairs a silent-wrong-answer defect in the block-wise `axis=1` reduction fast path added by GH-65105 (for GH-51474). That PR is unreleased, so the wrong answers never reached users and there is no *Bug fixes* whatsnew entry.

`DataFrame._reduce_axis1` reduced each block in that block's **own** dtype and combined the per-block partials with a numpy ufunc, where the transpose path it replaced reduced in the common dtype of all blocks. On current `main`:

| frame | `axis=1` | `df.T` (correct) |
|---|---|---|
| int64 + float `sum` | `-9.22e18` | `9.22e18` |
| uint64 + float `sum` | `0.5` | `1.84e19` |
| int64 + uint8 `sum` | `4.6e18` (float64) | `4611686018427387906` (int64) |
| float32 + float `sum` | `inf` | `6.0e38` |
| bool + complex64 `mean` | `1.0` | `1+1j` |

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [2**62], "b": [2**62], "c": [0.5]})
df.sum(axis=1)  # -9.223372036854776e+18
df.T.sum()      #  9.223372036854776e+18
```

Compute one cross-block accumulation dtype with `np.result_type` and `astype` each block to it before reducing. For `mean` the accumulator mirrors `nanmean`: float and complex accumulate in their own dtype and widen only at the division, everything else accumulates in float64. `mean` also stops unconditionally casting the combined result to float64, which is what discarded the imaginary part.

Two places then widen the combined result before writing a missing value into it — the `mean` division and the `min_count` null-out. Both now go through one helper that reproduces what `nanops` produces there (float64 for an integer or bool result, complex128 for complex64), and the `min_count` row count is gated on `skipna` so it matches the mask `_maybe_get_mask` actually builds. Without that gate a `complex64` frame reduced with `min_count` and `skipna=False` came back as `complex128` where `df.T` gives `complex64`.

`find_common_type` cannot serve as the accumulation dtype here: it returns `object` as soon as a bool block is present, which would switch the fix off for exactly the bool+numeric frames that reach this path.

There **is** an *Other API changes* entry, for a behavior change GH-65105 itself introduced and did not document: these reductions on a bool + NumPy-numeric mix no longer reduce through `object`, so an integer `sum` or `prod` can overflow and a float result can lose precision where Python's arbitrary-precision arithmetic was exact, and `min`/`max` on a bool + complex mix return a complex result where they previously raised `TypeError`.

Verified against the transpose oracle, the `axis=0` result on the transposed frame, and the single-block frame `df.astype(np.result_type(*dtypes))`, over roughly 260k dtype × block-layout × method × `skipna` × `min_count` cells, with no value or dtype divergence introduced against `main`. Each of the five families above fails if the fix is reverted, and 18 of the 20 new test cells fail on `main`. The residual divergences are two pre-existing families: `min`/`max` still combine per-block partials and so can land on a different dtype than the transpose, and bool-mixed pairs where the transpose itself gives `object`.

issues.title: BUG: ArrowExtensionArray silently truncated a value an integer dtype cannot hold (GH#68638)

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

labels.name: Arrow
labels.description: pyarrow functionality

issues.body:
`pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").replace(2, 1.5)` returned `[1, 1, 3]` — the replacement landed, truncated toward zero, with no error and no warning. The numpy-backed Series upcasts to float64 and stores 1.5; the masked `Int64` Series raises `TypeError`. Only the arrow-backed one silently corrupted the value.

`ArrowExtensionArray._validate_setitem_value` boxed the value with `pa.scalar(value, type=pa_type)`, which converts unsafely — `pa.scalar(1.5, type=pa.int64())` is `1`. Because that never raised, the block-level machinery above it never engaged and `putmask_inplace` wrote the truncated value. The same boxing pattern appeared a second time in `fillna`.

This rejects a lossy value in `_validate_setitem_value` with `TypeError`, matching `BaseMaskedArray._validate_setitem_value`, and routes `fillna` through that same validation. `Series`/`DataFrame` now raise; `Index.fillna`/`Index.where`/`Index.putmask` upcast, since `Index` has no column-dtype contract to protect — both matching the nullable integer dtypes.

The check is a deny-list rather than masked's allow-list on purpose: an allow-list would also turn `arr[0] = "x"` from `ArrowInvalid` into `TypeError`, which is a separate change with its own test fallout.

It runs over list-likes as well as scalars. `pa.array` applies a safe cast to a numpy array but not to a Python list, so `arr[:2] = [9.5, 8.5]` truncated exactly as `arr[0] = 1.5` did while `arr[:2] = np.array([9.5, 8.5])` raised `ArrowInvalid` — the same operation, spelled three ways, silently corrupting in two of them. A non-finite `Decimal` and a `Fraction` fold into the same `TypeError` for the same reason. The scan short-circuits on a container whose own dtype is integer or boolean; other containers pay a few extra passes (measured at 1e6 elements: float64 ndarray 4.8 -> 6.0 ms, object-of-ints 27.1 -> 32.9 ms, int64 ndarray unchanged).

Routing `fillna` through the validator also tightens the PyArrow-backed `StringDtype`, where `pd.array(["a", None], dtype="str").fillna(b"z")` stored `"z"` and `fillna(np.array([1, 2], dtype=object))` stored `"2"`. `ExtensionArray.fillna` now validates exactly as item assignment does, which in turn accepts a PyArrow *string* scalar; `Series.where` with one stops falling back to `object`.

One behavior change is left unfinished: a 0-d ndarray fill into `Index.where`/`putmask`/`fillna` now raises `ArrowInvalid` after the upcast, where it previously truncated — `_box_pa` cannot box a 0-d ndarray for the widened type. Hoisting the `item_from_zerodim` unwrap out of the integer gate fixes it but regresses `timestamp`/`duration` setitem, so it is left for its own PR.

Adjacent defects found while working on this and deliberately left out: `insert` truncates through `_from_sequence`; `_box_pa_scalar` raises `AttributeError` for a `Timestamp` against a non-matching type; `interpolate`'s linear fast path integer-divides; a dictionary-encoded integer type is not `pa.types.is_integer` and so still truncates.
