issues.title: BUG: ops with an iterator raised TypeError instead of treating it as a scalar (GH#31646)

labels.name: Numeric Operations
labels.description: Arithmetic, Comparison, and Logical operations

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

issues.body:
closes #31646

Comparison and arithmetic between a pandas object and an iterator — a generator, `iter([...])`, `map`, `filter`, `reversed` — raised `TypeError: object of type 'generator' has no len()` (or `len() of unsized object`), because the op sites gated on `is_list_like(other)` or `lib.is_scalar(other)` and then took a length. NumPy arrays and NumPy-dtype Series already treat an iterator as a scalar.

Two helpers in `pandas/core/ops/common.py` replace those gates across the array and frame op sites:

- `is_listlike_for_op(other)` = `is_list_like(other) and not is_iterator(other)`, replacing `is_list_like`.
- `is_scalar_for_op(other)` = `is_scalar(other) or is_iterator(other) or not (is_list_like(other) or hasattr(other, "__len__") or has_castable_attr(other))`, replacing `lib.is_scalar`. Deliberately not the negation of the first: a sized sequence with `__getitem__` but no `__iter__`, and an operand carrying only `__array__` or `__array_interface__`, are not `is_list_like`, yet NumPy coerces them, so they have to stay element-wise.

Only iterators change. A list-like with no length that can be read more than once — an `Iterable` that is not an `Iterator` — stays on GH-62423's deprecation path and keeps its `Pandas4Warning`.

Iterators become scalar-like now rather than after a deprecation cycle, because the current behavior is a crash rather than a result worth preserving — and the merged GH-62423 deprecation already says non-standard list-likes become scalar-like in 4.0. Two of the three user-visible changes replaced a wrong answer rather than a crash: a `Sparse` dtype and an `ExtensionScalarOpsMixin`-based array consumed a length-matching iterator and computed elementwise, and `ArrowDtype` arithmetic looped forever on an endless one (`ser + itertools.count()`).

Two smaller fixes ride along, since they are the same gate being too narrow to serve as a `len()` guard. An object that is neither list-like nor a recognized scalar now operates as a scalar against a `Sparse` dtype, instead of raising `ValueError` about mismatched lengths, and raises `TypeError` from `&`/`|`/`^` instead of a bare `AssertionError`.

`has_castable_attr` gains `__array_interface__` and `__array_struct__`, which `np.asarray` honors and the widened `is_scalar_for_op` would otherwise misclassify as scalars. That also narrows GH-62423 by the same amount: an operand exposing only one of those warned before and no longer does, so it stays element-wise in 4.0 rather than becoming scalar-like.

GH-31646 is labelled *Needs Discussion*, and the objection recorded there is to returning a boolean array when the lengths do not match. Merged GH-62423 settles that direction for every non-standard list-like, so this PR follows it rather than reopening it.

Related, not addressed here: GH-62423 (the deprecation this follows), and `where`/`mask`/`__setitem__`, which have the same shape but want the opposite resolution, since `pd.Series(gen)` materializes.

issues.title: BUG: read_csv silently wrapped out-of-range integers (GH#55232)

labels.name: Dtype Conversions
labels.description: Unexpected or buggy dtype conversions

labels.name: IO CSV
labels.description: read_csv, to_csv

labels.name: NA - MaskedArrays
labels.description: Related to pd.NA and nullable extension arrays

issues.body:
closes #55232

Since 2.0, `read_csv` silently wrapped a value the requested integer `dtype` could not hold — `read_csv(StringIO("x\n-1\n257"), dtype={"x": "UInt8"})` returned `[255, 1]` — where the `Series` and `array` constructors raise.

Three cast sites reached the wraparound:

- `_coerce_to_data_and_mask`'s `isinstance` fastpath raw-astyped instead of calling `_safe_cast`. This is the nullable half, and the actual 2.0 regression; both engines route nullable dtypes through it. Masked slots are filled before the check, since the data behind the mask is meaningless.
- the c engine's int branch in `TextReader._convert_with_dtype`. The check is gated on `user_dtype` rather than skipped for `int64`, so a column that only fits `uint64` now raises for `dtype={"x": "int64"}` instead of coming back as `uint64` with the requested dtype ignored. Inference is unaffected — it passes `user_dtype=0` and keeps the `uint64` fallback result.
- `PythonParser._cast_types`, in both branches an integer cast can reach: the plain ndarray one, and the `ExtensionArray` one that `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` lands in, because `_infer_types` applies the backend before the cast runs.

Nullable dtypes raise `TypeError`, restoring the pre-2.0 message; numpy dtypes raise `ValueError`, reusing the message the parser already produces from the fallback safe-cast block in `_convert_tokens`.

With the fastpath fixed, `BaseMaskedArray._coerce_same_family` (added in GH-66332) is redundant — both call sites fall through to the identical `_coerce_to_array(..., dtype=self.dtype)` — so it is removed. That also drops its one remaining difference, which was a bug: it checked `value._data` at masked positions, so assigning an NA whose stale payload did not fit the target dtype raised.

Deliberately unchanged: `engine="pyarrow"`, which casts the parsed frame in `_finalize_dtype` (the new parser test is `@xfail_pyarrow`); `astype`, which keeps numpy semantics and belongs to GH-45588 — note `Series`/`DataFrame` construction from an existing masked array delegates to `astype`, so only `pd.array` changes there; and float-to-integer *truncation* on the python engine, which `test_read_fwf.py::test_dtype` asserts — floats are compared truncated so only wraparound raises.

Routing the nullable path through `_safe_cast` put `IntegerDtype._safe_cast` on a hot path — it answered "is this cast safe?" by raising and catching a `TypeError`, a fixed ~5µs per call that `read_csv` pays per column per chunk. It now asks `np.can_cast(..., casting="safe")` first, which is behaviour-identical on everything that reaches it and measures 5.30µs → 1.61µs at N=10, unchanged at N=1e6 where the compare dominates.

One divergence this leaves in place, for review: on an *index* column the two engines now report an out-of-range numpy dtype differently — the c engine hits the new check (`ValueError`), while the python engine still raises `OverflowError` from `_agg_index`, which the diff does not touch. The nullable case agrees (`TypeError` on both).

This does not depend on GH-45588, which was raised on the issue as a possible prerequisite.

issues.title: BUG: read_json(orient="table") could not read back non-string labels (GH#19129)

labels.name: IO JSON
labels.description: read_json, to_json, json_normalize

issues.body:
closes #19129

The issue title asks for a `ValueError`, but on current main the symptom is worse than the 2018 report: an ordinary frame with default `RangeIndex` columns round-trips through `orient="table"` to all-NaN with no error at all.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[1.5, 2.5], [3.5, 4.5]])
pd.read_json(StringIO(df.to_json(orient="table")), orient="table")
#     0   1
# 0 NaN NaN
# 1 NaN NaN
```

An int-dtype frame instead raises `IntCastingNaNError` (`Error while type casting for column '0'`), as does a non-string index name; a `MultiIndex` with a non-string level name raises `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'startswith'` on the *write* side.

The schema field `name` is JSON-serialized from the label, so an int label stays the JSON number `5`, while the record keys in `"data"` are `str(label)` (`"5"`). `parse_table_schema` looked the data up by the schema name and matched nothing.

So this makes the labels round-trip rather than rejecting them. Matching is done on the field name's string form, with the original labels restored at the end.

The fast parser perturbs `0.3` into `0.30000000000000004`, which would otherwise make the match fail for a perfectly ordinary frame. A key that parses back to the same double as the perturbed field name spells that label exactly, so `float()` on the key recovers it. The two are not always the same text — `1e16` is written `10000000000000000.0` in the schema and `1e+16` as the key — so the match is on the parsed value, not the spelling. Labels that no key recovers, including every label when `"data"` has no keys at all, fall back to decoding the document a second time at full precision; worth avoiding, since that decode costs a transient roughly 10x the payload size.

A `"data"` payload of arrays rather than objects has no keys at all, so those labels are used as written. Where `"data"` holds objects, two cases raise `ValueError` instead of reading as NaN: two distinct labels that share a string form (`5` and `"5"`), and a label no key matches when some key matches no field — that orphan key is the evidence the label was spelled differently. Without one the column reads as all-missing, which is what a string label already does.

Two write-side fixes come along because the round-trip needs them: `set_default_names` is guarded against a non-string `MultiIndex` level name, and a falsy `Series` name (`0`, `False`, `""`) is no longer replaced by the `"values"` placeholder — only a `None` name is a missing name.

Not addressed here, and left for a follow-up on the write side: `None`, tuple, and duplicate labels still emit a schema `name` that disagrees with the data keys. The full remedy is to derive the schema `name` from the same stringification the C writer uses for object keys, which is a larger change to `build_table_schema` than this needs. GH-25488 proposed switching the data payload to `orient="values"` arrays — correct diagnosis, too invasive.

issues.title: BUG: Index.replace raised instead of widening for a value the dtype cannot hold

labels.name: Dtype Conversions
labels.description: Unexpected or buggy dtype conversions

labels.name: Index
labels.description: Related to the Index class or subclasses

issues.body:
`Index.where`, `Index.putmask` and `Index.insert` all catch a value the current dtype cannot hold, find a common dtype, and retry on it — `where` was aligned with `putmask` deliberately in GH-39412, on the grounds that an Index has no column-dtype contract to protect the way a DataFrame column does.

`Index.replace` was added later (GH-65099, still unreleased) and delegates straight to `Series.replace`, so it never got the retry:

```python
ci = pd.CategoricalIndex(["a", "b", "c"])

ci.where([True, False, True], "z")   # Index(['a', 'z', 'c'], dtype='str')
ci.replace("a", "z")                 # TypeError: Cannot setitem on a Categorical ...
```

The dtypes affected are Categorical, masked and Sparse — the ones whose `Series.replace` raises `TypeError` for a value it cannot hold. Every numpy-backed dtype already widened, because `Series.replace` upcasts there itself.

Four implementation notes:

- Only `TypeError` is caught, not `ValueError` as in `Index.where`: `replace`'s argument validation raises `ValueError`, and no dtype raises it for a value it cannot hold.
- A replacement whose `to_replace` matches nothing is left out of the common dtype, since `Block.replace` skips those pairs rather than widening for them. Matching goes through `mask_missing`, the predicate `Block.replace` itself matches with — a containment check disagrees with it, notably for an ns-resolution `Timestamp` against object.
- An NA `to_replace` is matched against `hasnans`, and needs no re-check after widening.
- Widening can change how `to_replace` compares (a str, or an ns-resolution `Timestamp`, against datetime categories). When it does, the retry re-raises rather than returning data with the replacement silently dropped. On the regex paths there are no matched literals to re-check, so the retry instead re-raises when it replaced nothing — otherwise a `TypeError` raised for some unrelated reason (`mask_missing` crashes comparing datetime categories against a partial datetime string) would come back as an Index whose only change is its dtype.

Not covered: `Sparse` only widens when the value escapes the Sparse family entirely. `replace(1, 5)` still raises, because the widened dtype is Sparse too and `SparseArray.__setitem__` refuses it just the same (GH-21818) — out of scope here. The behaviour is pinned by a test.

Arrow-backed dtypes are out of scope too, pinned by a test alongside the Sparse one: `pyarrow` raises `ArrowInvalid`, a `ValueError` subclass, so the retry never fires for them. Catching it here would not be enough on its own — arrow's `Series.replace` silently no-ops for a value it cannot hold (`pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").replace(1, 1.5)` returns the input unchanged), so that path wants fixing before the Index retry can rely on it.

issues.title: BUG: the logical ufuncs were not rejected against datetimelike data (GH#68524)

labels.name: Numeric Operations
labels.description: Arithmetic, Comparison, and Logical operations

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

issues.body:
`np.logical_and`, `np.logical_or`, `np.logical_xor` and `np.logical_not` returned a result for
datetime-like data, where `&`, `|` and `^` raise `TypeError`:

```python
pi = pd.period_range("2016-01-01", periods=2, freq="D")

np.logical_and(pd.Series([True, False]), pd.Series(pi))
# 0    2016-01-01
# 1         False
# dtype: object          <- a Period in a logical result

pd.Series([True, False]) & pd.Series(pi)
# TypeError: operation 'and_' not supported for dtype 'bool' with dtype 'period[D]'
```

Values NumPy converts to `object` — `PeriodDtype`, timezone-aware `datetime64`, and several
temporal `ArrowDtype`s — came back in the result themselves; the rest were truth-tested on their
integer representation, which made the epoch falsy and `NaT` truthy. `np.logical_or.reduce` and
datetime-like scalar operands leaked the same way.

GH-68452 made the operator spelling raise for every datetime-like operand and added
`disallow_datetimelike_logical_op` with its `_is_datetimelike_array` predicate. The logical
ufuncs were missed by it because they are not in `UFUNC_ALIASES` — they are deliberately not
aliased, since for integer data `np.logical_and` and `&` genuinely differ. This is the ufunc half
of that change: it adds `disallow_datetimelike_logical_ufunc` beside the existing helper, reusing
its dtype predicate, and calls it from the seven `__array_ufunc__` implementations that can reach
datetime-like values — `arraylike.array_ufunc`, `ExtensionArray`, `Index`, `SparseArray`,
`BaseMaskedArray`, `NumpyExtensionArray`, and `ArrowExtensionArray`'s GH-62506 numeric fast path.
Four of those never reach `ExtensionArray.__array_ufunc__` at all and the arrow fast path returns
before it does, so a guard on the base class alone does not cover them.

Note this makes plain `datetime64`/`timedelta64` raise where they previously returned bools.
That is the same trade GH-68452 already made for `&`/`|`/`^` in this release, and it is what
makes timezone-naive and timezone-aware data agree.

Two cases deliberately do *not* match `&`. Arrow boxes any NA-like scalar as a typed null, so
`pd.Series([True, False], dtype="bool[pyarrow]") & pd.NaT` returns `[<NA>, False]` where every
other backend raises; the ufunc rejects it, which is also what fixes the `np.datetime64("NaT")`
spelling of the same null — that one was truth-tested on its int64 and came back `True`. A
datetime-like scalar against an `object`-dtype operand also raises, where `&` truth-tests it; the
ufunc never gave the `&` answer there either, it broadcast the scalar into a `datetime64` result.
The whatsnew names the arrow divergence; the `&` side of it is left for its own change.

The guard steps aside for the whole call whenever any operand is one pandas hands the ufunc off
to. That holds in both directions: a third-party array carrying a real NumPy `M8`/`m8` dtype is
not rejected on its behalf, and a datetime-like *pandas* operand does not take the call back from
such an operand. Deferral is of the whole operation, not of the deferring operand's share of it,
so anything narrower would make the result depend on argument order. An `__array_ufunc__` of its
own is not enough to qualify, though: every `_HANDLED_TYPES` contains `np.ndarray`, so pandas
computes against an `ndarray` subclass rather than deferring to it, and `Index` and the bare
arrays compute against `pd.NA` as well — both stay guarded. The test is `issubclass` on the
operand's type rather than `isinstance`, so that deciding this never reads an attribute off an
operand that answers every attribute, such as a `pd.col` expression.

`_is_datetimelike_dtype` also stops reading `.kind` unconditionally, so an operand whose dtype is
neither a NumPy nor a pandas dtype — a polars `Series`, say — no longer crashes inside pandas,
whether that dtype has no `kind` or one that is not a string. That reached `&`/`|`/`^` as merged
in GH-68452 too, not just the ufuncs added here.

issues.title: BUG: iloc/loc setitem broadcast a 1-D value down rows on an all-datetimelike frame

labels.name: Datetime
labels.description: Datetime data dtype

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

issues.body:
`EABackedBlock.setitem` adapts a 2-D EA block's `(ncols, nrows)` storage layout by swapping the two entries of the indexer tuple rather than transposing `values`, since `EA.T` may not be a view (GH-45419). It reoriented only a 2-D ndarray value to match, so a **1-D value was broadcast down rows instead of across the selected columns**:

```python
arr = np.arange(12).reshape(4, 3).astype("i8")
df = pd.DataFrame(arr.view("M8[s]"), columns=list("abc"))

df.iloc[[2, 0], ::2] = np.array([100, 101], dtype="i8").view("M8[s]")
# each value lands in the wrong column, silently:
#   a=101, c=101 in row 0 and a=100, c=100 in row 2
#   expected (and what a float64 frame does): a=100, c=101 in both rows
```

Where the selection could not absorb the misplaced value it raised instead, as `OutOfBoundsDatetime: Incompatible (high-resolution) value` — the `coerce_to_target_dtype(..., raise_on_upcast=True)` fallback reporting a swallowed shape `ValueError` as a resolution problem, which is not something a user can act on.

The swap is also **not** a reorientation at all when both indexer entries are advanced indexers, since those broadcast against each other, so the unconditional `value.T` was wrong there too — with two list keys this raised, and with two boolean masks it silently wrote the transposed cells.

Both reorientations are now gated on whether the swap actually transposes the selection — it does only when the entries index separate axes, so a scalar entry (which drops one) and two advanced indexers (which broadcast against each other) both opt out, as does a key of two or more dimensions, which makes the selection 3-D.

An indexer tuple short of the column axis, which is what a trailing comma in the key produces, is padded before that gate, since the missing entry is a full slice. `Ellipsis` is normalized to a full slice as well, because `np.ndim(...)` is `0` and it would otherwise read as an axis-dropping scalar when it is the opposite — but only when there is exactly one, so numpy still rejects a duplicate. `np.newaxis` is the mirror case and is carved out: it adds an axis rather than consuming one, so neither the padding nor the gate applies to it. A value that is not an ndarray goes through `_validate_listlike` first, so a `list`, `tuple`, `Index`, `Series`, `Categorical` or other 1D-only EA is reoriented the same way; each of those spellings wrote the wrong cells silently before.

When the value genuinely cannot be broadcast, a 2-D block now names the shapes in frame order rather than the datetime resolution — unless the selection is deeper than 2-D, where no shape would correspond to anything the caller can see, and the original error stands.

Measured against a numpy-backed frame as the oracle: over a 2160-combination sweep (9 row keys × 8 column keys × 9 value shapes × 5 value spellings, `M8[s]` and `m8[s]`), **388 divergences before, 40 after**; over a wider 118,656-cell sweep adding `M8[ns]`, `M8[ns, UTC]` and `period[D]`, **no cell where this writes a value the numpy-backed frame does not**. The divergences that remain are pre-existing families in other layers.

Scope notes, each verified pre-existing and left alone:
- an integer column key means the swap is not a transpose, so `df.iloc[1, 1] = np.array([x])` still raises where a numpy-backed frame broadcasts;
- a 2-D *list* value is rejected upstream of the block, in `_setitem_with_indexer`;
- a 0-d ndarray row key (`df.iloc[np.array(1)] = [...]`) raises `TypeError: len() of unsized object` from `check_setitem_lengths` on a numpy-backed or mixed frame, so the datetimelike path tested here is the one that works, not the odd one out;
- with a 2-D row key the selection is 3-D and the value is passed through unreoriented, so one of the two length-1 2-D value shapes still writes where a numpy-backed frame rejects both. Dropping the unconditional `.T` swaps which one; making that arm raise is a new user-visible rejection and wants its own PR;
- a 1-D block reports a shape failure through the same upcast fallback, as `TypeError: Invalid value ...` or, for `datetime64[s]` with a `datetime64` value, `OutOfBoundsDatetime`. Giving it the new message would change the exception type of `Series` setitem, which wants its own PR.

Two narrowings worth calling out, both of them an all-datetimelike frame giving up a broadcast that no other frame dtype allows:

- an empty value assigned into an empty *row* selection (`df.iloc[[]] = np.array([])`) was a no-op and now raises. The mirror case, an empty *column* selection, went the other way — from `OutOfBoundsDatetime` to the no-op a numpy-backed frame gives.
- a column vector into a single column (`df.iloc[mask, 0] = value.reshape(4, 1)`) used to succeed here, because the unconditional `.T` turned it into a row vector; a numpy-backed frame and numpy itself both reject it, and so does this now. A *row* vector into a single row (`df.iloc[1] = value.reshape(1, 3)`) is the shape numpy does accept, and that one went from `OutOfBoundsDatetime` to writing.

Both are pinned.

`_pd_timedelta` is cached, but `datetime - offset` goes through `__rsub__` and creates a fresh offset on every call, so the cache was always cold. Constructing the `Timedelta` dominated the runtime.

issues.title: API: select_dtypes raises on a partly specified IntervalDtype/CategoricalDtype (GH#40234)

labels.name: Categorical
labels.description: Categorical Data Type

labels.name: Interval
labels.description: Interval data type

labels.name: API - Consistency
labels.description: Internal Consistency of API/Behavior

issues.body:
During 3.1 development `select_dtypes` grew partial-dtype matching: an instance naming only some of its attributes selected the family those attributes describe. This reverts that in favour of one rule — an instance that names an attribute names one exact dtype — while none of it has shipped. Adding the support back later is cheap; removing it after 3.1 would take a deprecation cycle.

Now raising, since no column can have any of these dtypes:

- `pd.IntervalDtype("int64")` / `"interval[int64]"` — no `closed`
- `pd.IntervalDtype(closed="left")` — no subtype
- `pd.IntervalDtype("datetime64", "left")` — subtype has no resolution
- `pd.CategoricalDtype(ordered=True)` — no categories

An instance that names *no* attribute keeps its 3.0 behaviour of selecting the whole family: `pd.IntervalDtype()`, `pd.CategoricalDtype()`, and `pd.CategoricalDtype(ordered=False)`, which is indistinguishable from the bare one since `ordered=False` is the constructor default. The class and the bare string select the family as before — `pd.IntervalDtype`/`"interval"`, `pd.CategoricalDtype`/`"category"` — as do fully specified instances, every other spec form, and the unitless `np.dtype("datetime64")`.

One thing this settles beyond the line count: the helper that existed only to work around `IntervalDtype` hashing as plain `"interval"` once its subtype is `None` goes away, so `select_dtypes` no longer carries its own notion of interval-dtype identity.

Reverts GH-68491, GH-68450, GH-68444, GH-66325 and the partial-matching half of GH-66120, all unreleased. Context in GH-40234.

issues.body:
Follow-up to GH-66956, addressing @jorisvandenbossche's review comment there: that PR warned about the refused numexpr 2.14.1 at `import pandas`, which reaches users who never evaluate anything through numexpr — including the many who have it transitively, since PyTables hard-depends on it.

The warning now fires at most once per process, at the first operation that would actually have been offloaded: arithmetic and comparisons large enough and of the right dtype for numexpr, `where`/`mask`, and `eval`/`query` on the default engine. A small `df + df` stays silent, and so does everything when `compute.use_numexpr` is False. `expressions.py` gains `_evaluate_blocked`/`_where_blocked`, chosen by `set_use_numexpr` only when the option is on and the installed numexpr is blocked; they gate on the same `_can_use_numexpr` predicate the numexpr path uses, so "would have used numexpr" cannot drift from the real decision.

An explicit `engine="numexpr"` still raises `ImportError` rather than warning. Since that path no longer has a warning alongside it, the message now names the refused version instead of telling a user who does have numexpr installed that it "is not installed".

HDF5 `where=` queries remain uncovered, as the whatsnew already states, because PyTables imports numexpr itself. The warning is deliberately not raised there: its text says numexpr "will not be used by pandas", which is false on that path, and making it accurate would need a second message and a second one-shot flag.

issues.title: BUG: DataFrame.isetitem and __setitem__ silently corrupted the frame when the value's column count did not match the target

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: Internals
labels.description: Related to non-user accessible pandas implementation

issues.body:
Found by a post-merge audit of GH-65491, which deleted a FIXME reading "refactor, clearly separate broadcasting & zip-like assignment" on the grounds that it was stale. It was not — it marked this defect. No issue was open for it.

`BlockManager.iset` only validated the value's column count under `if lib.is_integer(loc)` — the GH-46544 guard added in GH-66001. With a sequence or slice `loc` nothing checked that `value` had one column per position, so the zip-like branch's `value[placement.indexer]` stored a block narrower than its placement when the value was too narrow, and silently dropped the extras when it was too wide.

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
df.isetitem([0, 1], np.array([7, 8, 9]))   # no exception
df.shape        # (3, 2)
df._mgr.blocks  # (NumpyBlock: slice(0, 2, 1), 1 x 3, dtype: int64,)
repr(df)        # IndexError: index 1 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 1
df.to_numpy()   # (3, 1) -- column "b" silently gone
```

`DataFrame.__setitem__` reaches the same code whenever the key matches several columns (duplicate or `MultiIndex` columns) and the value is one that `_set_item`'s `np.tile` broadcast skips — a timezone-aware `datetime64` or `period` value, or a 2D array:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2, 3]] * 3, columns=["a", "a", "b"])
df["a"] = pd.Series(pd.date_range("2030", periods=3, tz="UTC"))  # same corruption
```

Both reproduce on released 3.0.5 and on 2.3.3; `iset` there has only the row-shape `AssertionError`.

The fix compares against `blklocs`, which is already computed one line above and normalizes int, slice, boolean-mask and integer-array `loc` into a single length, so one check covers every form. The integer-loc guard stays: `_iset_single` returns before the new check, so it is still load-bearing. An empty `loc` writes nothing, so it is exempt and stays the no-op it is on main.

Two things the guard would otherwise have broken are carried here rather than deferred:

- A scalar `value` sanitizes to one column, so `df.isetitem([0, 1], 5)` — which the method's own docstring documents as `value : scalar or arraylike` — would have hit the new check with a message about "1 columns". It now fills every selected position, as the label spelling does, for each `loc` spelling that selects several (list, slice, boolean mask, and the empty forms).
- `_set_item`'s tiling gate was `not isinstance(value.dtype, ExtensionDtype)` where `iset` uses `is_1d_only_ea_dtype`, so exactly two dtype families — tz-aware `datetime64` and `period` — fell between the two and would have gone from silent corruption to `ValueError` while every neighbouring dtype broadcasts. They now broadcast as well; `np.tile` would degrade the EA to object, so that arm uses `reshape`/`repeat`.

The `isetitem` docstring now states the shape rule the new `ValueError` enforces, which was previously only in the error string.

Not fixed here, and filed locally instead: 1d-only EA values still broadcast for a sequence `loc` (`df.isetitem([0, 1], pd.Categorical([...]))`), so `isetitem` semantics still depend on `value.dtype`; a zero-column 2D value slips past the `len(value) > 1` guards in `_iset_single` and `insert` and corrupts the same way, so repairing only the `iset` arm would leave `df[new] = <0-col>` broken; and the `DataFrame`-value branch of `isetitem` counts `len(loc)`, so a boolean-mask loc is counted by the mask's length.

issues.title: BUG: concat(union_categories=True) conflated True with 1

labels.name: Reshaping
labels.description: Concat, Merge/Join, Stack/Unstack, Explode

labels.name: Categorical
labels.description: Categorical Data Type

issues.body:
`concat(union_categories=True)` silently replaced `True` with `1` when unioning bool-category and integer-category Categoricals:

```python
a = Series(Categorical([1, 2, 3]))
b = Series(Categorical([True, False]))

concat([a, b], ignore_index=True, union_categories=True).tolist()
# [1, 2, 3, 1, False]     <- True became 1
concat([a, b], ignore_index=True).tolist()
# [1, 2, 3, True, False]  <- the default gets it right
```

`union_categories_compat` casts categories with differing dtypes to a common dtype, which for bool and integer categories is object. `union_categoricals` then unions the categories through a hashtable, where `True` and `1` collide, so one replaces the other. The existing `is_unique` guard only caught collapse within a single input, not across inputs.

A Categorical's categories must be unique and uniqueness is decided by hash, so no Categorical can hold both `1` and `True` and there is nothing to return here. `union_categories_compat` now returns `None` when the categories cannot be shown to be all distinct, and the caller casts to object before continuing — returning `None` is not enough on its own, because two object-dtype `CategoricalDtype`s compare equal whenever their categories do, so `dtypes_all_equal` would send the inputs straight back into `union_categoricals`. The result is object dtype with both values intact.

The check is a single pass keyed by the category itself: it refuses a key that turns up under two different types, so `1`/`True` and `1`/`1.0` are refused while duplicate column labels still read back as duplicate columns, and it refuses a pair whose comparison raises rather than letting the error out of `concat` (`Decimal("1")` and `np.int64(1)` hash equal and raise on `==`). Inputs that share one categories object are scanned once, since a categories Index cannot collide with itself. An `inferred_type` shortcut was tried and dropped — an `IntEnum` infers as `"integer"` just as `int` does, so it could not see that case.

Follow-up to GH-65098, which added the `union_categories` keyword in the unreleased 3.1.0 — no whatsnew entry for that reason.

issues.title: PERF: avoid temporary allocations in multi-block DataFrame axis=1 reductions
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


## Reproducible Example

Multi-block `DataFrame` reductions along `axis=1` use the `_reduce_axis1` fast path for operations such as `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`. For eligible NumPy-backed blocks, the current implementation still creates a per-block `middle` vector and then allocates another result while combining it with the accumulated reduction.

These intermediate allocations become significant for DataFrames with many rows and several blocks. For a guarded subset of compatible NumPy blocks, the reduction and combine steps can avoid these temporaries while retaining the existing fallback for other block types and configurations.

```python
from timeit import repeat

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


nrows = 1_000_000
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
df = pd.DataFrame(index=range(nrows))
for i in range(8):
    values = rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1, nrows)
    values[i::1000] = np.nan
    df[f"column-{i}"] = values

assert len(df._mgr.blocks) == 8


def best_ms(func):
    return min(repeat(func, number=5, repeat=7)) / 5 * 1_000


for name in ("sum", "prod", "min", "max"):
    value = best_ms(lambda name=name: getattr(df, name)(axis=1))
    print(f"{name}: {value:.3f} ms")
```

```text

prod: 147.783 ms
min: 181.131 ms
max: 185.854 ms

upstream main (ebcf0ed7):
sum: 39.205 ms
prod: 37.257 ms
min: 18.315 ms
max: 18.293 ms

optimized branch (40817a6d):
sum: 26.450 ms
prod: 26.643 ms
min: 5.681 ms
max: 5.696 ms
```

Compared with upstream main, the optimized implementation reduced runtime by approximately:

* 32.5% for `sum`
* 28.5% for `prod`
* 69.0% for `min`
* 68.9% for `max`

A matched ASV comparison covered 72 cases across:

* `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`
* 2,048, 32,768, and 100,000 rows
* 2 and 8 blocks
* `float64`, mixed `float32`/`float64`, and `int64` blocks

At a significance factor of 1.05, 38 cases improved, 34 were unchanged, and none regressed. Statistically significant improvements ranged from approximately 8% to 60%.

Representative ASV results:

```text

prod, 100,000 rows, 8 int64 blocks: 1.36 ms -> 0.547 ms
min, 100,000 rows, 8 float64 blocks: 1.04 ms -> 0.487 ms

```

Matched ASV peak-memory measurements for 1,000,000 rows and eight `float64` blocks also improved:

```text

min: 174 MB -> 158 MB
```

This is related to #51474 , the broader request to use `_reduce_axis1` for these reductions, and #65105, which implemented the multi-block fast path.

The issue described here is narrower: that fast path is already present, but it still materializes a per-block `middle` vector and an allocating combine result. The proposed optimization avoids those allocations for an explicitly guarded subset of NumPy-backed blocks.

issues.title: PERF: avoid redundant allocations in StringArray duplicated and value_counts

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

## Summary

Python-backed `StringArray` already stores its values in an object ndarray. However, `duplicated` and `value_counts(dropna=True)` currently perform avoidable allocations before hashing for arrays using `pd.NA`.

The two paths incur this overhead differently:

* `duplicated` already passes the existing backing ndarray through `_ensure_data` (`_ensure_data(arr) is arr._ndarray`), so it does not materialize another object ndarray. Its avoidable allocation is the boolean NA mask created by the generic extension-array path.
* `value_counts(dropna=True)` creates a filtered object-array copy through boolean indexing before hashing.

For Python-backed `StringArray` using `pd.NA`, these allocations can be avoided by operating directly on the existing backing ndarray where the missing-value semantics permit it.

## Proposed change

Use the existing backing ndarray directly when:

* The array is Python-backed.
* Its missing-value sentinel is `pd.NA`.
* For `value_counts`, `dropna=True`.

For `duplicated`, avoid constructing the generic NA mask when the backing ndarray can be hashed directly.

Retain the existing generic paths for other missing-value semantics, `dropna=False`, and other string backends.

This does not change public behavior or results.

## Relation to #14860

This is related to #14860, which tracks improving `value_counts` and `duplicated` performance for string data through string-specific hashing.

This change is narrower. It removes avoidable allocations in the Python-backed `StringArray` dispatch path before hashing:

* A boolean NA mask for `duplicated`.
* A filtered object-array copy for `value_counts(dropna=True)`.

It does not change the underlying hashtable implementation or introduce the general string-specific hashing approach discussed in #14860.

## Benchmarks

ASV benchmarks used arrays containing 500,000 elements. Nullable cases replaced every tenth value with `pd.NA`, giving 10% missing values.

Among statistically significant comparisons:

* `duplicated`: 16/18 cases improved, 2 were unchanged, and none regressed. Significant improvements ranged from approximately 9% to 55%.
* `value_counts`: 5/6 cases improved, 1 was unchanged, and none regressed. One no-null, cardinality-50,000 measurement had high variance and is omitted from the representative results.

Representative ASV results:

* `duplicated`, cardinality 256, no nulls, `keep="first"`:
  **19.4 ± 0.03 ms → 8.76 ± 0.1 ms — 54.9% faster.**
* `value_counts(dropna=True)`, cardinality 256, 10% nulls:
  **31.3 ± 0.3 ms → 19.3 ± 0.08 ms — 38.2% faster.**
* `value_counts(dropna=True)`, cardinality 50,000, 10% nulls:
  **59.1 ± 0.3 ms → 45.2 ± 0.4 ms — 23.6% faster.**
* `value_counts(dropna=True)`, cardinality 500,000, no nulls:
  **322 ± 6 ms → 306 ± 3 ms — 4.7% faster.**

## Reproducible timing example

```python
from timeit import repeat

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def make_array(cardinality, has_nulls):
    values = np.resize(
        np.array([f"value-{i}" for i in range(cardinality)], dtype=object),
        500_000,
    )
    if has_nulls:
        values[::10] = pd.NA
    return pd.array(
        values,
        dtype=pd.StringDtype(storage="python", na_value=pd.NA),
    )


def best_ms(func):
    return min(repeat(func, number=5, repeat=7)) / 5 * 1_000


no_nulls = make_array(256, False)
nullable_256 = make_array(256, True)
nullable_50k = make_array(50_000, True)

print("duplicated:", best_ms(lambda: no_nulls.duplicated(keep="first")))
print(
    "value_counts 256:",
    best_ms(lambda: nullable_256.value_counts(dropna=True)),
)
print(
    "value_counts 50k:",
    best_ms(lambda: nullable_50k.value_counts(dropna=True)),
)
```

The script was run sequentially on upstream `main` and this branch. Units are milliseconds.

```text
upstream main baseline (4bcadf56):
duplicated: 19.385
value_counts 256: 31.510
value_counts 50k: 56.471

this branch (4a78335a):
duplicated: 8.960
value_counts 256: 20.346
value_counts 50k: 46.216
```

The relevant upstream files have not changed since baseline commit `4bcadf56`.

## Tests

Coverage has been implemented for:

* All `duplicated(keep=...)` modes.
* Unicode and empty arrays.
* Duplicate missing values.
* Nullable and NumPy-style missing-value semantics.
* Fast-path and fallback dispatch.
* Existing string backends.

issues.title: BUG: ArrowDtype setitem reinterpreted values through their integer storage

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

labels.name: Arrow
labels.description: pyarrow functionality

issues.body:
`ArrowExtensionArray` setitem and `fillna` handed the value straight to `_box_pa`, and pyarrow will convert a temporal array into an integer array without complaint. So a mismatched assignment was silently reinterpreted rather than rejected:

```python
arr = pd.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64[pyarrow]")
arr[:] = pd.date_range("2016-01-01", periods=3)._data
arr   # [1451606400000000, 1451692800000000, 1451779200000000]
```

numpy `int64`, masked `Int64`, `Categorical` and `string` all raise `TypeError` for the same assignment — only the Arrow path accepted it. The reverse direction (an integer array into `timestamp[ns][pyarrow]`/`duration[ns][pyarrow]`) reads back as timestamps, and a scalar `Timestamp` in the same position raised a raw `AttributeError` from inside `_box_pa`.

Adds a three-state predicate — temporal / non-temporal / *unsettled* — consulted by `_validate_setitem_value` before boxing. Unsettled means the value's type does not decide the question (`object` dtype, strings, plain lists); those fall through to the existing behavior, so nothing that worked before starts raising. An all-NA value is likewise exempt, which keeps `where`/`fillna` working against an alignment-produced all-NaN column. That exemption returns typed nulls rather than deferring to `_box_pa`, which has no `double`->`timestamp` cast kernel: an all-NA masked or Arrow-backed float, and any all-NA numeric or boolean value into a `date32`/`date64`/`time64` column, used to raise `ArrowNotImplementedError`.

`fillna` held a verbatim copy of the same `_box_pa` + `except pa.ArrowTypeError` block; it now calls `_validate_setitem_value`, which is what carries the fix to `Series.fillna` and also makes its `limit=None` path agree with `limit=1`.

`_box_pa_scalar`'s unit workaround compounded this: it read `pa_type.unit` for every `Timestamp`/`Timedelta` value regardless of the target. A `string`, `binary` or `date32` target has no `.unit`, hence the `AttributeError`; a target that had one but was the wrong flavor (`Timedelta` into `time64`, `Timestamp` into `duration`) reconciled the units and stored the integer. Gating the workaround on the target hands those to `pa.scalar`, which assigns a `Timestamp` into `date32`/`date64` correctly and rejects the rest as `TypeError`.

Deliberately left for follow-ups: values whose dtype settles nothing (a plain `list` of `Timestamp`s) still reinterpret; reinterpretation *between* temporal types is now rejected for scalars across type families, but not within one — a tz or unit mismatch still goes through integer storage — and not for the array spelling; and `insert`/`shift` bypass the guard via `_from_sequence`.

When a DataFrame exceeds the `max_elements` budget (default 262144), the Styler renderer trims rows and adds a "..." trim row. - In `_translate_latex`, use `d["body_row_indices"]` instead of `concatenated_visible_rows()`
- For trim row (r == -1), skip ctx lookups since no ctx entry exists
- Properly handle concatenated stylers by applying the same ctx offset to their body_row_indices

issues.title: BUG: IntervalIndex set ops and astype with RangeIndex raising TypeError
issues.body:
- [x] closes #68343
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed: `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean on all changed files
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst`

## What this fixes

Set operations between an ``IntervalIndex`` and a ``RangeIndex`` raised a confusing Cython ``TypeError`` when the ``RangeIndex`` was empty:

```python
iv = pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks([0, 2, 4])
iv.union(pd.RangeIndex(0))
# TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)
```

Every other empty array-like (``Index([], dtype="int64")``, ``np.array([])``, empty ``Series``, ``[]``) worked. The mirror (``pd.RangeIndex(0).union(iv)``), ``symmetric_difference``, and the direct constructors (``pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(...))``, ``IntervalArray(...)``, ``RangeIndex.astype("interval")``) hit the same error for empty and non-empty ``RangeIndex`` alike.

## Root cause

``_maybe_convert_platform_interval`` only coerces ``values`` to an ndarray when it lacks a ``dtype`` attribute; ``RangeIndex`` has one, so it reaches the Cython ``intervals_to_interval_bounds`` as a non-ndarray. In set ops, an empty ``RangeIndex`` specifically triggers this because ``_find_common_type_compat`` resolves the common dtype to ``interval[int64, right]`` (an empty ``Index`` resolves to ``object`` instead), so ``other.astype(interval_dtype)`` crashes before the empty-``other`` short-circuit.

## Fix

Convert ``RangeIndex`` to an ndarray in ``_maybe_convert_platform_interval``, the same special-casing place that already handles empty lists (GH19016). After the fix:

- ``iv.union(pd.RangeIndex(0))`` / ``iv.symmetric_difference(pd.RangeIndex(0))`` / ``pd.RangeIndex(0).union(iv)`` return the original interval index
- ``pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(0))`` and ``RangeIndex(0).astype("interval[int64, right]")`` build an empty ``IntervalIndex``
- ``pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(2, 4))`` and ``RangeIndex(2, 4).astype("interval[int64, right]")`` raise the regular ``TypeError: ... is not an interval`` message, consistent with ``pd.IntervalIndex([2, 3])``

## Verification

Run against the ``cb13b0e9a4`` build (main at the time of the report):

- ``pandas/tests/indexes/interval/`` + ``pandas/tests/arrays/interval/``: **1992 passed, 26 skipped, 2 xfailed**
- ``pandas/tests/indexes/ranges/`` + ``pandas/tests/indexes/test_setops.py``: **3739 passed, 28 skipped, 1 xfailed**
- New regression tests: 18 passed (parametrized over ``closed`` and ``sort``)

🤖 Generated with Codebuff
Co-Authored-By: Codebuff <noreply@codebuff.com>

issues.title: BUG: Fix online ewm ignoring decay for single-column frames

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

issues.body:
- [x] closes #66522
- [x] [Tests added and passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#writing-tests) if fixing a bug or adding a new feature
- [ ] All [code checks passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#pre-commit).
- [ ] Added [type annotations](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#type-hints) to new arguments/methods/functions.
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/vX.X.X.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.
- [ ] I have reviewed and followed all the [contribution guidelines](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing.html)

---

Fixes two off-by-a-dimension bugs in `ExponentialMovingWindow.online` that cause it to ignore the decay for single-column DataFrames, returning the unweighted cumulative mean instead of the exponentially weighted mean.

1. In `OnlineExponentialMovingWindow.mean` (`ewm.py`), `update_deltas` was sized from the column count (`shape[-1]`) instead of the number of rows being processed. For a single-column frame this produced a length-0 array. It is now sized from `len(np_array) - 1`, which also correctly handles the `mean(update=...)` path where the input array is `last_value + update`.
2. In `online_ewma` (`online.py`), the deltas array was indexed with the column index `j` (`deltas[j - 1]`) instead of the row index `i` (`deltas[i - 1]`), contradicting the contract in the adjacent comment.

Regression coverage added for single-column DataFrames (both the initial and `update` paths).

issues.title: BUG: DataFrame.replace/Series.replace silently stored a callable value

labels.name: Awaiting Review
labels.description: PR in the maintainers' court; exempt from staleness

issues.body:
`NDFrame.replace` validates `to_replace` up front but never checks `value`. A callable `value` passes straight through, so `s.replace(r"\d", lambda m: "X", regex=True)` stores the function object in the result instead of applying it or raising, and later operations on that object-dtype data fail far from the actual mistake.

```python
s = pd.Series(["a1", "b2"])
s.replace(r"\d", lambda m: "X", regex=True)
# 0    <function <lambda> at 0x...>
# 1    <function <lambda> at 0x...>
```

This adds the same kind of check that already exists for `to_replace`: `replace` now raises `TypeError` when `value` is callable, matching the error already raised for a callable `to_replace` (GH-18634). The check is recursive so it also catches a callable hiding inside a list-like or dict-like `value` (`replace([...], [callable])`, `replace({...: callable})`, `replace(regex={...: callable})`), not just a bare callable passed directly. Covered for `Series` and `DataFrame`, across all of those spellings.

Fixes #68199

issues.title: BUG: factorize ignored use_na_sentinel on dictionary-encoded arrow arrays (#66490)

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

issues.body:
- [x] closes #66490
- [x] tests added / passed
- [ ] passes `pre-commit run --all-files`
- [ ] whatsnew entry

Closes #66490.

`factorize` with default `use_na_sentinel=True` on an `ArrowDtype`-backed `pandas` object whose underlying `pyarrow.dictionary` array stored nulls as a dictionary value (`null_encoding="encode"`) returned the null inside `uniques` instead of using the `-1` sentinel. This made `use_na_sentinel` a no-op whenever the pre-encoded dictionary contained a null entry, e.g.

```python
>>> import pandas as pd, pyarrow as pa
>>> arr = pa.array(["a", "b", "c", None]).dictionary_encode(null_encoding="encode")
>>> pd.Series(arr, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(arr.type)).factorize()
(array([0, 1, 2, 3]), Index(['a', 'b', 'c', <NA>], dtype='...'))
```

With this fix, `factorize` casts such dictionary arrays back to their value type and re-encodes with the requested null encoding so the result matches what a non-dictionary-encoded array of the same values would produce:

```python
>>> pd.Series(arr, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(arr.type)).factorize()
(array([0, 1, 2, -1]), Index(['a', 'b', 'c'], dtype='...'))
```

issues.title: DOC: Document rows skipped by list-valued header for read_csv/read_excel (#66378)

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

issues.body:
Closes https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/66378

Documents what a list-valued `header` does in `read_csv` and `read_excel`.

Verified behavior for list-valued `header`: rows above `min(header)` are skipped, as are any rows between the listed header rows; only the listed rows become the column labels.

The issue also claimed that columns before `min(index_col)` are skipped. That claim is incorrect: `_extract_multi_indexer_columns` only removes the columns listed in `index_col` (they become the row index), while all other columns are retained. The docs now state this accurately in the Excel "Reading a MultiIndex" section.

Changes:
- `doc/source/user_guide/io.rst`: `header` parameter description now states rows above `min(header)` are skipped.
- `doc/source/user_guide/io.rst`: the Excel `MultiIndex` reading section now explains both behaviors (skipped rows and `index_col` columns becoming the row index rather than being skipped).

issues.title: BUG: Correct merge_asof tolerance error message (#66289)
issues.body:
Closes https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/66289

`merge_asof` accepts `tolerance=0` (a meaningful asof semantic meaning exact-match-only), but the `MergeError` raised for negative tolerances said "tolerance must be positive", which is inconsistent. The three guards in `_AsOfMerge._validate_tolerance` reject only strictly-negative values, so the message now reads "tolerance must be non-negative".

- Updated the message in the three guard sites in `pandas/core/reshape/merge.py`.
- Updated tests asserting the old message.
- Added tests verifying `tolerance=0` (and `pd.Timedelta(0)`) are accepted and produce exact-match-only behavior.
- Added whatsnew entry.

issues.title: BUG: clip with missing datetime/timedelta threshold raises TypeError
issues.body:
Closes #44785

`Series.clip` / `DataFrame.clip` with a datetime or timedelta threshold
that contains missing values raises:

```
TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'float'
```

because GH#40420 fills the missing thresholds with `±np.inf` before
comparing, and `±np.inf` cannot be compared against Timestamp or
timedelta values.

This change treats the missing positions explicitly: for datetime-like
thresholds the missing positions are tracked with a mask and the
original values are kept there (matching the documented behavior that
"a missing threshold will not clip the value"), while numeric
thresholds keep the existing `±np.inf` fill path untouched.

- Series threshold (lower/upper bound)
- DataFrame with a Series threshold along `axis=0` (rows) or `axis=1`
  (columns)
- DataFrame with a datetime-like DataFrame threshold

Regression tests added in `test_clip.py` for both Series and
DataFrame, plus a whatsnew entry.

<details>
<summary>Copy-pasteable example from the issue</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.Series([1.0, 1.0], dtype="datetime64[ns]").clip(
    pd.Series([None, 1.0], dtype="datetime64[ns]")
)
```
</details>

cc @ghost (who diagnosed the root cause in #44785)

issues.title: PERF: Skip full array allocation in RangeIndex.isin for small query inputs

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

issues.body:
- [x] closes #66263
- [x] [Tests added and passed](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing_codebase.html#writing-tests) if fixing a bug or adding a new feature

- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.
- [x] I have reviewed and followed all the [contribution guidelines](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing.html)

## Summary

Implements `RangeIndex.isin` directly (GH#66263). When the query `values` are smaller than the index, the new fast path allocates only the boolean result array and checks membership with O(1) `range.__contains__`, computing the target location via `(val - start) // step`. This avoids materializing the full integer array (`self._values`, e.g. an 80MB array for a 10M-entry range) that the generic `algos.isin` path allocates.

- For `len(values) < len(self)`, use the O(1) `range.__contains__` fast path.
- For `len(values) >= len(self)`, delegate to `super().isin` as before.
- Non-sized iterables (e.g. generators) are delegated to the base implementation, preserving `Index.isin` behavior.

## Tests

Added coverage in `pandas/tests/indexes/ranges/test_range.py`:
- Correctness of the fast path across positive/negative steps, negative starts, missing values, and empty queries.
- Agreement with the materialized `Index.isin` for mixed-value queries.
- The fast path does not touch `_values` (via a monkeypatched property that raises).
- Set / non-numeric / generator inputs and the `level` kwarg.
- Fallback to the generic implementation for large queries and TypeError for non-list-like values.

issues.title: BUG: fix read_csv pyarrow engine IndexError for dtype dict missing index_col (#68041)

labels.name: Needs Issue Assignment
labels.description: PR whose author is not assigned to a linked issue

issues.body:
Closes #68041

## Summary
`read_csv` with `engine="pyarrow"` and `dtype_backend="pyarrow"` raised an
`IndexError` when `index_col` was given and a dict `dtype` did not name the
index column:

```python
pd.read_csv(f, dtype={"col2": "int64[pyarrow]"},
            dtype_backend="pyarrow", engine="pyarrow", index_col="col1")
```

In `ArrowParserWrapper._finalize_index`, the dtype-dict branch tried to look up
the index column via `frame.columns[item]`. That label lookup is only valid when
`item` is an integer position; for a string `index_col` missing from the dtype
dict it indexed the Arrow-backed column labels incorrectly and raised
`IndexError: only integers, slices ... are valid indices`.

The nested lookup is now restricted to the integer-`index_col` case (looking the
column name up by position in `frame.columns`). A string `index_col` that is
missing from the dtype dict is left to normal inference, and the remaining
`dtype` keys are applied afterwards in `_finalize_dtype`. A scalar dtype with
`index_col` (Scenario A) was already fixed by #66063 / #45801 and is unaffected.

issues.title: BUG: make Index.get_indexer treat pd.NA as NaN for array/Index targets
issues.body:
- [x] closes #65419
- [x] Tests added and passed
- [x] All code checks passed.
- [x] Added an entry in the latest `doc/source/whatsnew/v3.1.0.rst` file if fixing a bug or adding a new feature.
- [x] I have reviewed and followed all the contribution guidelines.

Check exactly one of the following, per the automated contributions policy:

- [ ] I did **not** use AI to develop this pull request.
- [x] I used AI to develop this pull request. I prompted it to follow `AGENTS.md`, I have reviewed and understood every change, and I have described above how I used it and exactly which tool, model version, and effort setting.

## Summary

`Index.get_indexer` and `Index.drop` treated `pd.NA` inconsistently when matching a NaN label of a string-dtype index:

```python
idx = pd.Index([np.nan, "b"])          # str dtype

idx.get_indexer([pd.NA])                       # [0]  (matched NaN)
idx.get_indexer(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object))  # [-1]  (bug: did not match)
idx.get_indexer(pd.Index([pd.NA]))             # [-1]  (bug: did not match)
idx.drop([pd.NA])                               # worked
idx.drop(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object))       # KeyError (bug)
```

`Index.get_loc(pd.NA)` already matches `np.nan`, so the list-target behavior (and scalar lookup) is the intended semantics; the numpy-array and `Index` targets diverged.

Root cause: `Index._maybe_cast_listlike_indexer` normalizes missing values for a `StringDtype` (na_value `np.nan`) target — `target_index.fillna(np.nan)` — but only when the input was a plain list (`not hasattr(target, "dtype")`). Numpy arrays and `Index` objects already carry a `dtype`, so they skipped the normalization and their `pd.NA` kept a different hash than the stored `np.nan`, missing the lookup.

Fix: drop the `not hasattr(target, "dtype")` gate so array/`Index` targets are normalized too, guarded by `target_index.hasnans` (to avoid a no-op copy on NA-free targets) and excluding `MultiIndex` (whose `hasnans`/`isna` raise `NotImplementedError`).

## Verification

- Reproducer from #65419 now returns `[0]` for list, ndarray, `Index`, and `string`-dtype targets, and `drop` works for all target forms.
- Added `test_get_indexer_pd_na_matches_nan` in `pandas/tests/indexes/base_class/test_indexing.py`.
- `pytest pandas/tests/indexes/` → 18087 passed, 244 skipped, 45 xfailed.
- `pytest pandas/tests/indexes/base_class/` → 136 passed.
- `pytest pandas/tests/extension/test_string.py` → 4528 passed, 796 skipped, 20 xfailed.
- `pytest pandas/tests/reshape/` → 2903 passed, 17 skipped, 6 xfailed.
- `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` on touched files → clean.

## Automated contribution disclosure

- Tool: Pi coding agent (https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-coding-agent)
- Model: deepseek-v4-pro (via company-newapi)
- Reasoning-effort setting: off

The agent reproduced the inconsistency, traced it to the `not hasattr(target, "dtype")` gate in `_maybe_cast_listlike_indexer`, relaxed the gate with a `hasnans` guard and a `MultiIndex` exclusion, and wrote the regression test. I reviewed the change against the indexing code paths, verified the fix with the reproducer and the indexes/string/reshape test suites, and confirmed no regressions.

issues.title: DOC: RFECV per-split ranking and support shapes omit the feature axis

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The [`RFECV` API reference](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_selection.RFECV.html) documents both `cv_results_["split(k)_ranking"]` and `cv_results_["split(k)_support"]` as arrays with shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

Both arrays actually have shape `(n_subsets_of_features, n_features)`, where `n_features` is the number of original input features, `X.shape[1]`. Each row contains a rank or a selection indicator for every original feature. In contrast, `split(k)_test_score` has one scalar per evaluated subset and correctly has shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

### User-facing impact

The documented shape can mislead users interpreting per-fold rankings or selection masks, for example when examining feature-selection stability. Indexing a ranking/support result by subset returns a vector over original features, not a scalar. Code written around the documented one-dimensional structure could therefore use the wrong indexing or aggregation.

This is a documentation mismatch. The reproducer does not show incorrect feature selection, scores, or predictions, and no change to the returned arrays is requested.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFECV
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

X = np.column_stack(
    (np.arange(10.), np.tile([0., 1.], 5), np.ones(10))
)
selector = RFECV(
    Ridge(), cv=2, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
).fit(X, np.arange(10.))

for key in ("split0_ranking", "split0_support", "split0_test_score"):
    print(key, selector.cv_results_[key].shape)

assert selector.cv_results_["split0_ranking"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_support"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_test_score"].shape == (3,)
```

### Observed shapes

```text
split0_ranking (3, 3)
split0_support (3, 3)
split0_test_score (3,)
```

The assertions pass. There are three evaluated subset sizes and three original features.

### Verification scope

Runtime observation: scikit-learn 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2, and Python 3.14.7.

The affected `/1.9/` documentation page was inspected on September 11, 2026 and was labelled 1.9.1. The documentation version and tested runtime version are distinct: the 1.9.1 runtime was not tested for this report.

The [1.9.0 implementation](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py) also explains the feature axis: it collects rankings and supports over folds, evaluated subsets, and original features, then indexes out the fold axis when assigning each per-split result.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Update the two shape annotations in the `RFECV` class docstring in [`sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py):

```diff
-        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)

-        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)
```

Please also clarify the axis meanings in the descriptions:

- Rows correspond to the evaluated subset sizes, ordered consistently with `cv_results_["n_features"]`.
- Columns correspond to the original input features, in their original order. This axis does not shrink as features are eliminated and is not the final selected-feature count, `n_features_`.

For example, `cv_results_["split0_support"][i, j]` indicates whether original feature `j` was selected for the subset represented by row `i` in split 0.

The Notes paragraph also describes the "size" of every `cv_results_` array using the subset-count formula. Consider calling this the **length of the first axis** instead, since the ranking and support arrays are two-dimensional.

This request concerns the docstring and generated API reference only; the existing two-dimensional outputs should remain unchanged.

issues.title: BUG: Explicit validation data does not enable HistGradientBoosting automatic early stopping

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` accept explicit `X_val` and `y_val` but do not enable early stopping with `early_stopping="auto"` on a small training set. This also affects calls that leave `early_stopping` at its default value, `"auto"`.

In the example below, both estimators fit successfully on 30 training samples, but `do_early_stopping_` is `False` and `validation_score_` is empty. Changing only `early_stopping` to `True` enables monitoring of the same validation data and records four validation scores.

The user-facing problem is that the supplied validation data does not participate in the early-stopping checks, despite the documented automatic activation. This is not just missing score history: the validation-based stopping criterion is disabled. In longer runs, this could cause unnecessary boosting iterations and potentially affect generalization. The example establishes disabled monitoring and stopping checks; it does not establish degraded predictions or a production incident.

A workaround is to set `early_stopping=True` explicitly when providing validation arrays.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
)

print(sklearn.__version__)
X = np.arange(40.0).reshape(-1, 1)

for estimator_class in (
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
):
    y = (
        np.sin(X[:, 0])
        if estimator_class is HistGradientBoostingRegressor
        else np.arange(40) % 2
    )
    for mode in ("auto", True):
        estimator = estimator_class(
            early_stopping=mode, max_iter=3, random_state=0
        ).fit(X[:30], y[:30], X_val=X[30:], y_val=y[30:])
        print(
            estimator_class.__name__, mode,
            estimator.do_early_stopping_,
            len(estimator.validation_score_),
        )
```

### Expected Results

With explicit validation arrays, both modes should enable early stopping for both estimators, even with only 30 training samples:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

The version 1.9 documentation specifies automatic activation when either the training sample count exceeds 10,000 or `X_val` and `y_val` are supplied to `fit`:

- [HistGradientBoostingRegressor documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor.html)
- [HistGradientBoostingClassifier documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier.html)

Four scores correspond to the initial model plus three completed boosting iterations. The example tests whether validation monitoring is enabled, not whether fitting must terminate before `max_iter`.

### Actual Results

The reported run on scikit-learn 1.9.0 produced:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

No exception is raised. Automatic mode leaves early stopping disabled and records no validation scores, while explicit `True` monitors the same validation data.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

In [`BaseHistGradientBoosting.fit` at tag 1.9.0](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/gradient_boosting.py), the automatic-mode decision only checks the training sample count:

```python
if self.early_stopping == "auto":
    self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
```

The method has already calculated `validation_data_provided` and checked that both validation arrays are supplied together, but that flag is not included in the automatic-mode decision.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
+ self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000 or validation_data_provided
```

This is a source-based suggestion, not a tested patch.

A regression test should cover both estimator classes with a small training set, explicit validation arrays, and `early_stopping="auto"`, and check:

```python
assert estimator.do_early_stopping_
assert len(estimator.validation_score_) == estimator.n_iter_ + 1
```

Keep `early_stopping=True` as a passing control. Additional coverage should preserve the sample-count rule when validation arrays are absent, including the 10,000-sample boundary, and preserve the existing validation-argument errors.

Related work: [#18748](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/18748) requested custom validation-set support, and [#27124](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/27124) introduced the explicit validation arguments. These references do not establish that no duplicate report exists.

issues.title: BUG: Pipeline.fit_predict skips transform_input for final-step metadata

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With metadata routing enabled and `transform_input=["X_val"]`, `Pipeline.fit_predict` passes transformed training data to the final estimator but leaves `X_val` untransformed. An otherwise identical call to `Pipeline.fit` transforms `X_val` correctly.

In the reproducer, the final estimator receives `X_val = [[15.0]]` through `fit_predict`, although the fitted scaler maps that value to `[[0.0]]`. No exception is raised.

This can put training data and validation metadata in different feature spaces. An estimator that uses the metadata could therefore compute incorrect validation quantities or make different fitting decisions. Preprocessing that changes the feature count could instead cause a shape error. These are potential consequences; the reproducer demonstrates the incorrect metadata, not a production failure or incorrect predictions from a built-in estimator.

The [documented purpose of `transform_input`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.html) is to transform selected metadata before the consuming step receives it, including validation data.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)


class RecordsXVal(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
    def fit(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        self.X_val_seen_ = X_val
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.zeros(len(X))

    def fit_predict(self, X, y, X_val=None):
        return self.fit(X, y, X_val=X_val).predict(X)


X = np.array([[0.0], [10.0], [20.0], [30.0]])
y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
X_val = np.array([[15.0]])

for method in ("fit", "fit_predict"):
    pipe = Pipeline(
        [
            ("scale", StandardScaler()),
            ("model", RecordsXVal().set_fit_request(X_val=True)),
        ],
        transform_input=["X_val"],
    )
    getattr(pipe, method)(X, y, X_val=X_val)
    print(
        sklearn.__version__,
        method,
        "final step received X_val =",
        pipe[-1].X_val_seen_.ravel(),
    )
```

### Expected Results

Both methods should pass the transformed validation value to the final estimator:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [0.]
```

The same is expected on 1.9.0. The scaler is fitted on `[0, 10, 20, 30]`, whose mean is `15`, so transforming `[[15.0]]` gives `[[0.0]]`.

### Actual Results

Running the reproducer separately in the two affected environments produced:

```text
1.9.1 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.1 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
1.9.0 fit final step received X_val = [0.]
1.9.0 fit_predict final step received X_val = [15.]
```

No exception is raised. Only `fit_predict` passes the original validation value to the final estimator.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The likely cause is the final-step parameter handling in [`Pipeline.fit_predict`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.1/sklearn/pipeline.py):

```python
params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
```

Unlike `fit` and `fit_transform`, this does not use `_get_metadata_for_step` for the final estimator. The intermediate-step fix in [#34201](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34201/files) does not change that final-step assignment.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- params_last_step = routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]]
+ params_last_step = self._get_metadata_for_step(
+     step_idx=len(self) - 1,
+     step_params=routed_params[self.steps[-1][0]],
+     all_params=params,
+ )
```

A regression test should assert that the final estimator receives `pipe[:-1].transform(X_val)` after `fit_predict`, with `fit` as a passing control. For example, append this assertion after the reproducer's loop:

```python
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    pipe[-1].X_val_seen_,
    pipe[:-1].transform(X_val),
)
```

This suggestion still needs validation against a patched target-version checkout and the relevant upstream tests.

issues.title: FIX Center X in GLMs and LogisticRegression for features with large offsets
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #35029

Alternative to #34793: includes its centering trick for Ridge cholesky, but guarded by an a priori check (as suggested in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34793#issuecomment-5810816957).

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

- Adds `_dense_mean_variance_axis0`, a Cython single-pass per-feature mean & variance for dense arrays. It is numerically stable for features with large offsets and its cost is close to a single `np.mean` (see `benchmarks/bench_dense_mean_variance.py`).
- GLMs (`PoissonRegressor`, `GammaRegressor`, `TweedieRegressor`) and `LogisticRegression` (all solvers but liblinear, which penalizes the intercept): when `fit_intercept=True` and some feature has `|mean| > 10 * std`, fit on a centered copy of X and correct the intercept afterwards. Otherwise, no copy of X.
- Ridge cholesky: centering trick from #34793 (the Gram matrix is corrected algebraically instead of materializing a centered copy of X), but only when the mean/variance ratio of the features makes it numerically safe. Otherwise, fall back to explicit centering as in main.

Tests check the invariance of `coef_` to feature offsets for all those estimators.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation
- Test/benchmark generation
