issues.title: BUG: LogisticRegression (and other GLMs) can silently return badly wrong coefficients on off-centered data
issues.body:
> [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact scikit-learn's linear models split into two families with very different handling of un-centered features: - `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `Lasso`, `ElasticNet` go through `_preprocess_data`, which centers `X` and `y` (explicitly for dense data, algebraically for sparse) before solving, then reconstructs the intercept afterward. Centering is a pure reparametrization here: for any fixed `coef`, shifting `X` by a constant only shifts the intercept, and the L1/L2 penalty doesn't touch the intercept, so the optimal `coef` is mathematically invariant to any additive shift of the features. Ridge/Lasso exploit this to shield users from poor numerical stability on high mean to variance ratio features. - `LogisticRegression`, `PoissonRegressor`, `GammaRegressor`, `TweedieRegressor` (the `LinearModelLoss` + `NewtonSolver`/lbfgs/newton-cg/newton-cholesky family) do **not** do this. The intercept is just another free parameter solved jointly with the coefficients directly on the raw `X`. There is no `_preprocess_data`-equivalent step. The same invariance holds mathematically for this second family too (same argument: additive shift + unpenalized intercept), but because nothing centers the data first, the solvers can lose that invariance numerically. Concretely: - `newton-cholesky` builds its Hessian from the raw `[X, 1]` design. Eliminating the intercept column during Cholesky factorization implicitly computes `X.T @ X - n * mean(X) * mean(X).T` which can yield catastrophic-cancellation-prone quantity. The scipy solver normally fires a warning or an error in this case, so at least, it's visible for users something is wrong. - `lbfgs` doesn't have a cancellation problem in this sense, but its gradient-norm convergence check can be satisfied prematurely on badly-offset data, silently stopping far from the true optimum, with **no warning at all**. User-facing impact: any real dataset with a feature that's far from zero-mean relative to its variance (a year, a timestamp, an age, a physical measurement with an offset unit) can silently produce badly wrong `coef_`/`intercept_` for these estimators, without any indication something went wrong. I stumbled on this while investigating numerical-stability discussions in #34793 (Ridge's cholesky centering trick). ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Sweep used to generate the plot below:
```python import warnings import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import ( LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, Ridge, TweedieRegressor, PoissonRegressor, ElasticNet, ) def relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio( linear_estimator, dtype="float32", random_seed=0, max_ratio=1e5 ): rng = np.random.RandomState(random_seed) n_samples, n_features = 5000, 5 X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_features)) true_coef = rng.normal(size=n_features) proba = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ true_coef))) y = (rng.uniform(size=n_samples) < proba).astype(int) X, y = X.astype(dtype), y.astype(dtype) linear_estimator.fit(X, y) ref = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() assert np.linalg.norm(ref) > 0.1 # we want coefs that aren't too small ratios = np.logspace(0, np.log10(max_ratio), num=30) errors, has_warnings = [], [] for offset in ratios: with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: linear_estimator.fit((X + offset).astype(dtype), y) shifted = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() errors.append(np.linalg.norm(shifted - ref) / np.linalg.norm(ref)) has_warnings.append(bool(caught)) return ratios, np.array(errors), np.array(has_warnings) models = [ Ridge(solver="cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), Ridge(solver="lbfgs", positive=True, alpha=1 / 5000), ElasticNet(alpha=1 / 5000), LinearRegression(), # GLMs: LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs"), LogisticRegression(solver="newton-cholesky"), TweedieRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), TweedieRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), ] dtypes = ["float32", "float64"] n_cols = 2 n_rows = -(-len(models) // n_cols) # ceil division fig, axes = plt.subplots( n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(5 * n_cols, 3 * n_rows), sharex=True, sharey=True ) axes = axes.ravel() for ax, model in zip(axes, models): results = [relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio(model, dtype=dtype) for dtype in dtypes] for (ratios, errors, has_warnings), dtype in zip(results, dtypes): line, = ax.plot(ratios, errors, label=dtype) ax.scatter( ratios[has_warnings], errors[has_warnings], marker="x", s=10, color=line.get_color(), ) ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02) ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_title(str(model), fontsize=9) ax.tick_params(axis="x", which="both", labelbottom=True) ax.set_xlabel("mean/variance ratio") for ax in axes[len(models):]: ax.axis("off") for ax in axes[::n_cols]: ax.set_ylabel("relative error") axes[0].legend() fig.tight_layout() ```
### Expected Results Fitting on `X + offset` should not change `coef_` (more than floating point noise) or at the very least should not change `coef_` without a warning. ### Actual Results The grid below (generated by the reproducer snippet) sweeps the feature mean/variance ratio (`X + ratio`, unit-variance `X`) from 1 to 1e5, one subplot per estimator, and plots the relative error of `coef_` against the ratio=0 reference, for both `float32` and `float64`, with `×` marking points where a warning was raised: - `Ridge`, `LinearRegression`, `ElasticNet` (top two rows, the `_preprocess_data` family): error stays ~0 across the entire range, in both dtypes. A blip only appears in float32 at the extreme end (ratio ≥1e4), never in float64. - `LogisticRegression`, `TweedieRegressor`, `PoissonRegressor` (bottom three rows, the GLM family), with *either* solver (lbfgs or newton-cholesky): garbage coefficients starting at a ratio as low as ~20-100 in float32 and ~300-5000 in float64. ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.14.6 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:23) [Clang 22.1.3 ] executable: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/bin/python machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.10.dev0 pip: None setuptools: None numpy: 2.5.3 scipy: 1.18.1 Cython: 3.3.0 pandas: 3.0.5 matplotlib: 3.11.1 joblib: 1.6.0 threadpoolctl: 3.6.0 narwhals: 2.26.0 Built with OpenMP: True threadpoolctl info: user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-f48b354e.so version: 0.3.34.106.0 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so version: 0.3.31.dev threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 14 prefix: libgomp filepath: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1.0.0 version: None ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes. I'm about to open a PR with a proposed fixed: detecting high mean/variance ratio and explicitly recentering if needed.

issues.title: FIX Avoid a race in GP kernel hyperparameter discovery [free-threaded]
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #33152.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

`Kernel.hyperparameters` used `dir(self)` to find hyperparameter specifications. During parallel Gaussian process classification, cloning can modify a kernel class dictionary while `dir(self)` examines it, raising `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`.

For kernels using the default `__dir__`, this change copies the instance and class dictionaries before collecting hyperparameter names. It keeps custom `__dir__` discovery for subclasses and falls back to the copied dictionaries if that method raises the reported error.

The parallel GPC test now clones its parameterized kernel. New tests cover the default discovery path, the error fallback, and a subclass that exposes a hyperparameter through a custom `__dir__`.

Local verification passed 284 kernel tests and all four `test_multi_class_n_jobs` cases with a threading backend. Formatting,
lint, and `git diff --check` passed. The available Python interpreter has the GIL enabled, so the free-threaded CI job is still needed to check the original failure.

I'm Luis, and I'm interested in Gaussian processes, Bayesian methods, and the reliability of scientific Python software. I've been looking for focused ways to contribute to scikit-learn, and this issue caught my attention because it connects Gaussian process code with a concrete concurrency failure. issues.title: permutation_importance computes non-zero importance for features the model never uses when max_samples < 1

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm an undergraduate economics student at UC Davis. I use scikit-learn for data analysis and use permutation importance to understand which features matter. This is my first issue filed against scikit-learn.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**What:** When `max_samples` is set below 1, features that the model never uses still get non-zero permutation importances. By definition, shuffling a column the model does not look at cannot change the predictions, so its importance should be exactly 0. With `max_samples=1.0` the importance is indeed 0; the problem only appears when a subsample is used.

**My example:** The model only uses feature 0; features 1 and 2 are pure noise that the model never reads. With `max_samples=0.5`, both features 1 and 2 get an importance of −0.0104. The 5 repetitions (`n_repeats=5`) return exactly the same value, so the standard deviation is 0. The bias changes in magnitude and sign with the subsample size: −0.026 at 0.2 and +0.006 at 0.1. This shows it is sampling noise, not a real feature contribution.

**Cause** (I read `sklearn/inspection/_permutation_importance.py`): The baseline score is computed on all rows, while the shuffled score is computed on the subsampled rows only, and the two are subtracted. The difference therefore mixes in the gap between the full-data score and the subsample score, which has nothing to do with the feature. The docstring says a fresh sample is drawn for each repetition; in practice the subsample is drawn once per feature before the repetitions, and all features share the same random seed — so repeating does not average the bias away (std = 0), and every irrelevant feature gets the same bias.

**Impact on users:** `max_samples` exists to save time on large datasets. With this bug, irrelevant features get spuriously positive or negative importances, which can make them look useful or harmful, and can also corrupt feature ranking.

**AI usage disclosure:** I used an AI assistant to help identify this problem and write the reproduction script. The description above is my own, and the reproduction was run on my own computer.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
print(sklearn.__version__)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
n = 200
X = rng.randn(n, 3)
y = 3 * X[:, 0] + rng.randn(n)          # only feature 0 matters
X[:, 1:] = rng.randn(n, 2)                # features 1, 2: pure noise
model = LinearRegression().fit(X[:, :1], y)  # model uses ONLY feature 0 ...
class OnlyFirst:                              # ... wrapped so it accepts 3 columns
    def fit(self, X, y): return self
    def predict(self, X): return model.predict(X[:, :1])
    def score(self, X, y): return r2_score(y, self.predict(X))
est = OnlyFirst()

r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=0.5, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=0.5):", r.importances_mean)
print("importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):")
print(r.importances[1:])

# Independent expectation: permuting a column the model never reads cannot change
# predictions, so the permuted score equals the score on the SAME rows -> importance 0.
r_full = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=1.0, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=1.0):", r_full.importances_mean)
print("baseline (all rows) r2:", r2_score(y, est.predict(X)))
for ms in (0.2, 0.1):
    r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=ms, random_state=0)
    print(f"max_samples={ms}: importances_mean =", r.importances_mean, " importances_std =", r.importances_std)
```

### Expected Results

For every repetition, the importances of features 1 and 2 should be exactly 0 — identical to the result with `max_samples=1.0`.

### Actual Results

```
1.9.1
importances_mean (max_samples=0.5): [ 1.7655429  -0.01042625 -0.01042625]
importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):
[[-0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625]
 [-0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625 -0.01042625]]
importances_mean (max_samples=1.0): [1.79471992 0.         0.        ]
baseline (all rows) r2: 0.9095261981105188
max_samples=0.2: importances_mean = [ 1.76648851 -0.02631336 -0.02631336]  importances_std = [0.30605997 0.         0.        ]
max_samples=0.1: importances_mean = [1.66914758 0.00620688 0.00620688]  importances_std = [0.73546823 0.         0.        ]
```

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.14.7 (main, Aug  5 2026, 10:29:49) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)]
executable: /Users/luca/Projects/oss-contrib/.venv-skl/bin/python
   machine: macOS-26.6.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.1
          pip: 26.2.1
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.5.3
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: None
       pandas: None
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.7.0
     narwhals: 2.26.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'd be willing to fix this. Idea: draw a fresh subsample for every repetition, and compute both the baseline and the shuffled scores on the same subsampled rows before subtracting. Add a regression test asserting that features the model does not use have exactly 0 importance when `max_samples < 1`.

issues.title: Fix normalized BayesianRidge scores_ (#13852)
issues.body:
Fixes #13852.

### Why

`BayesianRidge.scores_` includes the Gaussian likelihood constant but omits the normalization of its two Gamma priors. This makes the reported values incomplete, particularly when comparing different prior hyperparameters. The final score also needs to use the final fitted coefficients.

### Derivation

With `A = lambda I + alpha X.T X` and `mu = alpha A^{-1} X.T y`, completing the square and integrating out the coefficients gives

```
log p(y | X, alpha, lambda)
= 1/2 [p log(lambda) + n log(alpha) - log|A|
       - alpha ||y - X mu||^2 - lambda ||mu||^2 - n log(2 pi)].
```

The existing precision update equations correspond to Gamma priors with shape `alpha_1 + 1` and `lambda_1 + 1` and rates `alpha_2` and `lambda_2`. Thus each prior term `a log(t) - b t` also requires the constant `(a + 1) log(b) - log Gamma(a + 1)` when `b > 0`. At `b = 0`, the prior is improper, so the undefined constant remains omitted. The user guide gives the completed-square derivation, its equivalent covariance-space form, the derivatives, and the fixed-point updates.

### Changes

- Add the two Gamma normalization constants to `scores_` without changing the fitting updates or predictions.
- Evaluate the final score with the final fitted coefficients.
- Clarify the score API, private method name, and normalization caveats for fitted intercepts and sample weights.
- Compare initial and final scores against independent SciPy Gaussian and Gamma log densities for both `n > p` and `p > n`, including zero-rate priors.

### Verification

The 25 BayesianRidge-relevant tests in `sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_bayes.py` pass with the modified source module loaded against the installed scikit-learn 1.8 runtime. This source checkout lacks compiled extensions, so its native test invocation was unavailable. Ruff format and selected lint checks pass.

#### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm Luis. I really like scikit-learn and wanted to start contributing to it. I looked for smaller issues I could understand and
solve carefully, with the hope of taking on more complex work as I get to know the codebase. This BayesianRidge issue caught my attention because it let me work through the mathematics and make a focused improvement.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a recent CS/AI graduate currently building a personal finance app that uses scikit-learn for some ML-based features (budgeting insights, basic predictive modeling). While setting up a local editable build to start learning the codebase and look for ways to contribute, I was testing edge cases with StandardScaler and noticed it silently returns a scale of 1.0 for zero-variance features (e.g. a single-sample fit) without any warning or documentation of this behavior. I dug into the source (_handle_zeros_in_scale) to confirm it was intentional rather than a bug, and found the public docstring doesn't mention it.

I'd like to help fix this if it's something the maintainers agree is worth addressing — happy to work on either a documentation update or a warning, whichever direction you'd prefer.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

StandardScaler.fit() silently returns a scale of 1.0 (instead of erroring or
warning) when a feature has zero or near-zero variance — e.g. a single-sample
fit, or a constant column. This is implemented via the internal
_handle_zeros_in_scale helper, but the behavior is not mentioned in the
public StandardScaler docstring or the User Guide.

Minimal reproduction:

​```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3]])  # single sample — zero variance
scaler = StandardScaler()
print(scaler.fit_transform(X))
# Output: [[0., 0., 0.]] — no warning, no error raised
​```

This could silently mask real data problems — e.g. an accidental single-row
fit, or a constant column slipping through a preprocessing pipeline —
producing all-zero output with no signal to the user that something
unusual happened.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Adding a note to the StandardScaler docstring (and the corresponding section of the User Guide at doc/modules/preprocessing.rst) explaining that when a feature has zero or near-zero variance, its scale_ is set to 1.0 rather than raising an error or leaving a zero — so the transformed output for that feature will be 0. rather than NaN or inf. This would at least make the existing behavior discoverable without changing any code.

issues.title: CPU oversaturation/oversubscription due to third-party libraries when running containers on Linux

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Background

This is the result of a discussion with @ogrisel and @jeremiedbb, fleshed out and with some additional ideas. I make my suggestion at the end, but will require feedback before I do any of the work.

### The problem

When using a container on Linux (Docker, Kubernetes, anything using cgroups), you can set a CPU quota, something like "this process gets 2 cores worth of compute."

Unfortunately, not all third-party C libraries know this. At minimum OpenBLAS does not seem to know about this limit (). So if you have 64 core machine, and run a Kubernetes pod with 8 cores, and OpenBLAS will think it has 64 cores, and it will be much much slower. Similarly libgomp and libomp. MKL builds on OpenMP so maybe no point in filing there until libgomp/libomp are fixed.

* https://github.com/OpenMathLib/OpenBLAS/issues/6059
* libgomp need to file once I have bugzilla access.
* https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/225493

This is a performance problem for scikit-lean users.

### Demonstration

My CPU has 12 cores. I set up a cgroup with equivalent of 2 cores, but OpenBLAS still reports 12 cores:

```
$ systemd-run --user --scope --property CPUQuota="200%" -- python -c "import threadpoolctl; import numpy; print(threadpoolctl.ThreadpoolController().lib_controllers[0].get_num_threads())"
12
```

### Potential fixes

I am going to be fixing one case as a side-effect of https://github.com/joblib/joblib/issues/1846: when using `joblib.Parallel`, the number of cores will be constrained using `threadpoolctl`, including in sequential cases. However, this is a strange fix where if you don't use `joblib`, you still have the same performance problem.

So what else can be done until OpenBLAS any other relevant libraries fix this issue?

#### Option 1: joblib or scikit-learn set the limit correctly, on import

Instead of doing this in `Parallel` in the sequential case, do it on import of `joblib` or maybe `sklearn`: `threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))`.  (Technically this won't fix the above example because of https://github.com/joblib/loky/issues/634 but it will work in Docker or Kubernetes, and everywhere once that issue is fixed).

Pros:

* Fixes the limit for all use cases.

Cons:

* Importing a library changing global configuration. This is not very nice.

#### Option 2: sklearn sets the limit whenever calling into OpenMP or OpenBLAS

Pros:

* If you do `with threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1))` it undoes the limits when done, so it's not a _permanent_ global config change, it's just DTRT.

Cons:

* This adds performance overhead of all these calls.
* Lots of code changes.

#### Option 3: Documentation of the problem and how to solve it

Pros:

* No impacts on global behavior.

Cons:

* Most people won't notice the documentation.
* If the situation improves or changes, most people won't re-read the updated docs.

#### Option 4: Warn on import

If `os.process_cpu_count() > joblib.effective_cpu_count(-1)` then that means cgroups is restricting CPU count further, so warn the user and tell them what to do. In practice should probably also docs to explain in more detail.

Pros:

* More likely to be noticed than docs.

Cons:

* Users will still have to do work.

### My suggestion

After further thought, I think setting the limit on import (option 1) is actually reasonable. The hope is that this is a stop-gap and can eventually be removed once the relevant libraries DTRT, and in practice for the vast majority of people this is the right thing to do.

If that's not acceptable, docs + warning is what I would suggest doing.

I can proceed with either, once there is some consensus.

issues.title: DOC: clarify that recursion method computes conditional partial dependence
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #27441 (documentation aspect).

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Issue #27441 reports that `partial_dependence()` gives different results for `method='recursion'` vs `method='brute'` on tree-based estimators when features are correlated, and asks for the documentation to clarify the distinction rather than leaving it implicit.

The existing `pdp_method_differences` note says the methods "might differ" but does not explain the semantic root cause. This PR makes the distinction explicit:

1. **`doc/modules/partial_dependence.rst`** — extends the note to state that `'brute'` computes the **interventional** PDP `E[f(x_S, X_C) | do(X_S = x_S)]` (the quantity typically intended), while `'recursion'` (tree-based only) computes the **conditional** PDP `E[f(x_S, X_C) | X_S = x_S]`, which reflects the training data's correlation structure. Explicitly states the two are not equivalent for tree-based estimators when features are correlated.

2. **`sklearn/inspection/_partial_dependence.py`** — adds a one-line pointer in the `'brute'` bullet of the `method` parameter docstring so the distinction is visible at the API surface, not only in the narrative docs.

No code behavior is changed. This is a pure documentation clarification that directly addresses what the issue asks for ("it should be communicated clearly in the documentation that (i) the two methods are not equivalent for tree based algorithms, and (ii) that method = 'recursion' actually computes the conditional ... instead of the ... interventional ...").

#### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm Mayank (@qtjg). I use scikit-learn for ML work and ran into this exact confusion when interpreting PDPs for a model with correlated features. The issue has been open since 2020 and the fix is purely documentary — happy to adjust wording if maintainers prefer a different framing.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Research and understanding (reading the issue, the existing note, and the relevant docstring)
- Documentation (drafting the RST addition and the docstring pointer)

I reviewed the diff, verified the RST parses cleanly with docutils, confirmed the Python file is still valid AST, and checked that the mathematical notation matches the existing style in the file. Per the Automated Contributions Policy, this pull request includes code written with the assistance of AI. The code has **not yet been reviewed** by a human.

issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #7050

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This PR implements **Variable Importance in Projection (VIP)** scores for :class:`~sklearn.cross_decomposition.PLSRegression`.

- Adds `vip_` attribute of shape `(n_features,)` exposed on fitted `PLSRegression` models, computed via `_variable_importance_in_projection`.

issues.title: GaussianRandomProjection and SparseRandomProjection with n_components="auto" break get_feature_names_out and pandas output

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug

`BaseRandomProjection.fit` ends with `self._n_features_out = self.n_components`. With the default `n_components="auto"` this stores the string `"auto"` instead of the inferred `n_components_`. As a result `get_feature_names_out` raises `TypeError` and `set_output(transform="pandas")` fails inside `fit_transform` for both `GaussianRandomProjection` and `SparseRandomProjection`.

The common estimator checks do not catch this because they force `n_components=2` on both classes, and `test_random_projection_feature_names_out` also uses `n_components=2`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.random_projection import GaussianRandomProjection

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(10, 1000)
rp = GaussianRandomProjection(eps=0.5).fit(X)
print(rp.n_components_, repr(rp._n_features_out))
rp.get_feature_names_out()
```

The same happens with `SparseRandomProjection`, and with `rp.set_output(transform="pandas").fit_transform(X)`.

### Expected Results

110 feature names `gaussianrandomprojection0` to `gaussianrandomprojection109`, and a DataFrame with 110 columns when pandas output is requested.

### Actual Results

```
110 'auto'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File ".../sklearn/base.py", line 1064, in get_feature_names_out
    return _generate_get_feature_names_out(
  File ".../sklearn/utils/validation.py", line 2471, in _generate_get_feature_names_out
    [f"{estimator_name}{i}" for i in range(n_features_out)], dtype=object
TypeError: 'str' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
```

### Versions

scikit-learn 1.9.1, numpy 2.5.3, scipy 1.18.1, Python 3.12.14, Linux. The assignment is unchanged on current `main`.

The fix is to store `self.n_components_` instead. I have it ready with tests and will open a PR.

I used an AI coding assistant to help find this and draft the report. I ran the reproduction myself and checked the output above.

issues.title: Incorrect random_state description in RANSACRegressor documentation
issues.body: ### Introduce yourself Hi! I am new to the scikit-learn community. I am a data scientist and often use `scikit-learn` for my experiments. I recently used `RANSACRegressor` and noticed a possible documentation issue. ### Describe the issue linked to the documentation The `random_state` parameter is currently documented as: `The generator used to initialize the centers`. This description appears unrelated to `RANSACRegressor` and actually related to a clustering algorithm . In the implementation, `random_state` is used with `sample_without_replacement` to randomly select data subsets during RANSAC iterations. These subsets are then used to fit candidate models. The issue also stays in the final `sklearn` documentation linked here : [ransac](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.RANSACRegressor.html. ### Suggest a potential alternative/fix Suggested correction : `random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None Controls the randomness of the data subsets selected during RANSAC iterations. Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls. See :term:`Glossary `.` I have tested the change locally, and the RANSAC test suite passes: 27 passed in 0.47s I would be happy to submit a pull request for this documentation fix if the issue is valid.

issues.title: FIX validate X before estimating the bandwidth in KernelDensity
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #29443. See also #31436, an earlier attempt by joeyspagnoli that was closed before merging.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
With `bandwidth="scott"` or `bandwidth="silverman"`, `KernelDensity.fit` read `X.shape` to estimate the bandwidth before `validate_data` ran. A 1d array therefore raised `IndexError: tuple index out of range` and a list of lists raised `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'shape'` instead of the usual input validation error.

This PR moves the `validate_data` call above the bandwidth estimation. Nothing else changes. The estimated bandwidth is the same for any valid 2d input because `validate_data` does not change the shape.

A new test in `sklearn/neighbors/tests/test_kde.py` covers both string bandwidths. It checks that a 1d array raises the standard `Expected 2D array, got 1D array` error and that a list of lists gives the same `bandwidth_` as the equivalent array. The test fails on `main` with the two errors above.

#### Introduce yourself
I am 区梓灏, a student from China. I have been sending small tested bug fixes to open source machine learning libraries and picked this issue because the root cause is clear and the fix is two lines.

#### AI usage disclosure
I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (e.g., when writing an implementation or fixing a bug)
- Test/benchmark generation
- Documentation (including examples)
- Research and understanding

I reviewed the change and the test myself and can explain them on request.

#### Any other comments?
I checked the change on a GitHub Actions runner by copying the two changed files over an installed scikit-learn wheel. The new test fails on the unpatched package and passes with the patch, and the rest of `test_kde.py` still passes.
- Unpatched wheel, new test only: https://github.com/Nicholas022400701/oss-ci/actions/runs/35361829631 shows `IndexError: tuple index out of range` for both parametrizations.
- Patched wheel, whole `test_kde.py`: https://github.com/Nicholas022400701/oss-ci/actions/runs/35361829629 and https://github.com/Nicholas022400701/oss-ci/actions/runs/35361829889 both report 59 passed. issues.title: Clarify parameter/hyperparameter terminology in the cross-validation workflow diagram
issues.body:
### Introduce yourself

I teach machine learning engineering to people who are new to machine learning.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

I use `GridSearchCV` to help learners understand grid search, model selection, and good practice. I think it is a fantastic teaching tool, and the user guide is excellent.

I've taught this section several times and have repeatedly needed to explain why the diagram says "parameters" when we are discussing hyperparameters. This is a recurring point of confusion in my teaching, which prompted this issue.

The overall workflow diagram in the cross-validation user guide uses the labels **"Parameters"** and **"Best parameters"**.

User guide:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html

Direct link to the diagram:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/_images/grid_search_workflow.png

My learners are meeting the terms "parameter" and "hyperparameter" for the first time. They are still learning the difference between settings we specify or search over, such as a decision tree's maximum depth, and values the model learns during fitting.

When I explain grid search, I describe it as comparing hyperparameter settings. The diagram calls these "Parameters" and "Best parameters". I then have to explain why the same settings are being called by two different names, while learners are still trying to understand what those names mean.

I understand that scikit-learn uses "parameters" for estimator constructor settings. The glossary explains this convention:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

The cross-validation guide also uses the word "hyperparameters". A short explanation at the diagram would help beginners connect the two terms.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Could a short note be added beside or below the diagram to explain how "parameters" relates to "hyperparameters"? For example:

> Here, "parameters" means configurable estimator settings. These can include machine-learning hyperparameters, such as a decision tree's `max_depth`, as well as other configuration choices, such as which estimator or pipeline step to use. They are different from values learned by the model during fitting.

The note could link to the glossary:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

The diagram could keep its existing labels. The note would help beginners understand why settings such as `max_depth` may be called "hyperparameters" in machine-learning terminology while scikit-learn uses the broader term "parameters".

issues.title: DOC Clarify n_jobs in BaggingClassifier and BaggingRegressor
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Refs #14228. The new wording is modeled on the RandomForest `n_jobs` docstring from #14628.


#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

This PR only changes the `n_jobs` description in `BaggingClassifier` and `BaggingRegressor`.

The current text says jobs run in parallel "for both fit and predict". That doesn't tell the reader what gets split across the jobs, and for the classifier it misses `predict_proba`, `predict_log_proba` and `decision_function`, which also run in parallel.

The new text names every parallel method and says the work is parallelized by splitting the base estimators across jobs. RandomForest says "over the trees", but Bagging hands each job a group of estimators, so I went with "splitting the base estimators across jobs". `_partition_estimators` makes `min(n_jobs, n_estimators)` groups, which means an `n_jobs` larger than `n_estimators` gives no extra speed-up. The sentences about `None`, `-1` and the Glossary are unchanged.

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_base.py#L171-L181

Where each method runs in parallel:

- `fit`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L541
- `predict_proba` (classifier `predict` calls it): https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1025
- `predict_log_proba`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1099
- `decision_function`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1176
- regressor `predict`: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/4358542a1bd39af2e7e1cbace8b9fed067473c5b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py#L1433

I also timed each method at `n_jobs` 1, 2, 4 and 6 on my own machine (Windows 11, 6 physical cores, scikit-learn 1.10.dev0 built from `4358542`). Every run used `n_estimators=100` with the default trees, and each number is the median of 5 runs after a warm-up. Trees don't have a `decision_function`, so that row uses `SVC` as the base estimator. The last row is a control. With a KNN base estimator and `oob_score=True`, most of `fit` is OOB scoring, and its time doesn't drop as `n_jobs` goes up. Times are in seconds.

| Method | n_jobs=1 | n_jobs=2 | n_jobs=4 | n_jobs=6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `BaggingClassifier.fit` | 3.65 | 2.04 | 1.08 | 0.72 |
| `BaggingClassifier.predict` | 1.48 | 0.90 | 0.61 | 0.57 |
| `BaggingClassifier.predict_proba` | 1.32 | 0.83 | 0.60 | 0.57 |
| `BaggingClassifier.predict_log_proba` | 1.79 | 1.23 | 0.75 | 0.64 |
| `BaggingClassifier(SVC()).decision_function` | 4.28 | 2.48 | 1.60 | 1.19 |
| `BaggingRegressor.fit` | 3.73 | 2.08 | 1.23 | 0.86 |
| `BaggingRegressor.predict` | 1.89 | 1.26 | 0.87 | 0.78 |
| Control: `BaggingClassifier(KNeighborsClassifier(), oob_score=True).fit` | 3.19 | 3.49 | 3.43 | 3.40 |

<details>
<summary>Timing script</summary>

```python
r"""Local evidence for the n_jobs docstrings of BaggingClassifier and BaggingRegressor.

Times each public method at several n_jobs values through the public API only,
plus two controls that n_jobs should not speed up. Kept outside the scikit-learn
clone.

Usage (--calibrate times each step once at n_jobs=1, to pick data sizes):

    python bagging_n_jobs_timing.py --calibrate
    python bagging_n_jobs_timing.py --clf-samples 2500 --reg-samples 3000 \
        --predict-samples 60000 --svc-test 1000 --knn-samples 7500
"""

import argparse
import contextlib
import io
import os
import statistics
import time
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import joblib

import sklearn
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification, make_regression
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier, BaggingRegressor
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier, KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.svm import SVC

N_JOBS = [1, 2, 4, 6]  # 6 = physical core count of the test machine
N_REPEATS = 5
N_ESTIMATORS = 100
N_FEATURES = 20
RANDOM_STATE = 0
RESULTS_FILE = Path(__file__).with_name("bagging_n_jobs_results.md")

# Thresholds for the pass/FAIL checks
CLEARLY_FASTER = 0.8  # at 2 jobs, a method must take under 80% of its 1-job time
NOISE = 1.1  # a higher n_jobs may be at most 10% slower than the previous one
OOB_FLAT = 0.7  # KNN fit (mostly OOB scoring) must stay above 70% of its 1-job time
CAP_FLAT = 0.9  # with 2 estimators, 4 and 6 jobs must stay above 90% of 2 jobs


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--calibrate", action="store_true",
                        help="time each step once at n_jobs=1 to size the data")
    parser.add_argument("--clf-samples", type=int, default=8_000,
                        help="training samples for BaggingClassifier")
    parser.add_argument("--reg-samples", type=int, default=8_000,
                        help="training samples for BaggingRegressor")
    parser.add_argument("--predict-samples", type=int, default=50_000,
                        help="samples passed to the prediction methods")
    parser.add_argument("--svc-train", type=int, default=2_000,
                        help="training samples for the SVC decision_function run")
    parser.add_argument("--svc-test", type=int, default=5_000,
                        help="samples passed to decision_function")
    parser.add_argument("--knn-samples", type=int, default=6_000,
                        help="training samples for the KNN OOB control")
    return parser.parse_args()


def make_data(args):
    """Synthetic data, split into a training part and a prediction part."""
    Xc, yc = make_classification(
        n_samples=args.clf_samples + args.predict_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES,
        n_informative=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xr, yr = make_regression(
        n_samples=args.reg_samples + args.predict_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES,
        n_informative=10, noise=10.0, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xs, ys = make_classification(
        n_samples=args.svc_train + args.svc_test, n_features=N_FEATURES,
        n_informative=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xkc, ykc = make_classification(
        n_samples=args.knn_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES, n_informative=10,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    Xkr, ykr = make_regression(
        n_samples=args.knn_samples, n_features=N_FEATURES, n_informative=10,
        noise=10.0, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    )
    n, m, s = args.clf_samples, args.reg_samples, args.svc_train
    return {
        "clf": (Xc[:n], yc[:n], Xc[n:]),
        "reg": (Xr[:m], yr[:m], Xr[m:]),
        "svc": (Xs[:s], ys[:s], Xs[s:]),
        "knn_clf": (Xkc, ykc),
        "knn_reg": (Xkr, ykr),
    }


def run_once(func):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    func()
    return time.perf_counter() - start


def median_time(func):
    """Median wall-clock time of func() over N_REPEATS runs, after one warm-up."""
    func()  # warm-up: starts the worker processes; not recorded
    return statistics.median(run_once(func) for _ in range(N_REPEATS))


def time_fit(label, estimator_class, X, y, **params):
    """Time fit on a fresh estimator for each n_jobs value."""
    print(f"timing {label} ...", flush=True)
    times = {}
    for n in N_JOBS:
        estimator = estimator_class(n_jobs=n, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, **params)
        times[n] = median_time(lambda: estimator.fit(X, y))
    return times


def time_method(label, fitted, method, X):
    """Time one prediction method of a fitted estimator for each n_jobs value."""
    print(f"timing {label} ...", flush=True)
    times = {}
    for n in N_JOBS:
        fitted.set_params(n_jobs=n)
        times[n] = median_time(lambda: getattr(fitted, method)(X))
    return times


def fit_for_prediction(estimator):
    """Fit once with all jobs; prediction timings then change n_jobs only."""
    return estimator.set_params(n_jobs=max(N_JOBS))


# --- go/no-go checks --------------------------------------------------------


def is_parallel(times):
    """Clearly faster at 2 jobs than at 1, and never slower as n_jobs rises."""
    t = [times[n] for n in N_JOBS]
    return t[1] < CLEARLY_FASTER * t[0] and all(
        later <= NOISE * earlier for earlier, later in zip(t, t[1:])
    )


def stays_flat(times):
    """A fit that is mostly OOB scoring does not get faster as n_jobs rises."""
    base = times[N_JOBS[0]]
    return base > 0 and all(times[n] >= OOB_FLAT * base for n in N_JOBS)


def capped_at_two(times):
    """With 2 estimators, more than 2 jobs gives no further speed-up."""
    return all(times[n] >= CAP_FLAT * times[2] for n in N_JOBS if n > 2)


# --- modes ------------------------------------------------------------------


def calibrate(data):
    """Single runs at n_jobs=1, to pick data sizes before the full run."""
    X, y, X_pred = data["clf"]
    clf = BaggingClassifier(n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, n_jobs=1,
                            random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    print(f"BaggingClassifier.fit            {run_once(lambda: clf.fit(X, y)):6.2f} s"
          "  (target 3-5 s)")
    print(f"BaggingClassifier.predict_proba  "
          f"{run_once(lambda: clf.predict_proba(X_pred)):6.2f} s  (target >= 1 s)")

    X, y, X_pred = data["reg"]
    reg = BaggingRegressor(n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, n_jobs=1,
                           random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    print(f"BaggingRegressor.fit             {run_once(lambda: reg.fit(X, y)):6.2f} s"
          "  (target 3-5 s)")
    print(f"BaggingRegressor.predict         "
          f"{run_once(lambda: reg.predict(X_pred)):6.2f} s  (target >= 1 s)")

    X, y, X_pred = data["svc"]
    svc = fit_for_prediction(BaggingClassifier(
        SVC(), n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(X, y)
    svc.set_params(n_jobs=1)
    print(f"BaggingClassifier(SVC()).decision_function "
          f"{run_once(lambda: svc.decision_function(X_pred)):6.2f} s  (target >= 1 s)")

    for name, estimator_class, knn, (X, y) in [
        ("BaggingClassifier", BaggingClassifier, KNeighborsClassifier(), data["knn_clf"]),
        ("BaggingRegressor", BaggingRegressor, KNeighborsRegressor(), data["knn_reg"]),
    ]:
        est = estimator_class(knn, n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, oob_score=True,
                              n_jobs=1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
        print(f"{name}(KNN).fit, oob_score=True "
              f"{run_once(lambda: est.fit(X, y)):6.2f} s  (target 3-5 s)")


def full_run(data):
    """Time every documented method and both controls; return table rows."""
    rows = []  # (label, times, check or None)

    X, y, X_pred = data["clf"]
    rows.append(("BaggingClassifier.fit",
                 time_fit("BaggingClassifier.fit", BaggingClassifier, X, y,
                          n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS),
                 is_parallel))
    clf = fit_for_prediction(BaggingClassifier(
        n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(X, y)
    for method in ["predict", "predict_proba", "predict_log_proba"]:
        label = f"BaggingClassifier.{method}"
        rows.append((label, time_method(label, clf, method, X_pred), is_parallel))

    X_svc, y_svc, X_svc_pred = data["svc"]
    svc = fit_for_prediction(BaggingClassifier(
        SVC(), n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(X_svc, y_svc)
    label = "BaggingClassifier(SVC()).decision_function"
    rows.append((label, time_method(label, svc, "decision_function", X_svc_pred),
                 is_parallel))

    Xr, yr, Xr_pred = data["reg"]
    rows.append(("BaggingRegressor.fit",
                 time_fit("BaggingRegressor.fit", BaggingRegressor, Xr, yr,
                          n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS),
                 is_parallel))
    reg = fit_for_prediction(BaggingRegressor(
        n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)).fit(Xr, yr)
    label = "BaggingRegressor.predict"
    rows.append((label, time_method(label, reg, "predict", Xr_pred), is_parallel))

    # Control 1: OOB scoring runs sequentially at the end of fit. KNN fits almost
    # instantly but is slow to predict, so this fit is mostly OOB scoring.
    for name, estimator_class, knn, (Xk, yk) in [
        ("BaggingClassifier", BaggingClassifier, KNeighborsClassifier(), data["knn_clf"]),
        ("BaggingRegressor", BaggingRegressor, KNeighborsRegressor(), data["knn_reg"]),
    ]:
        label = f"Control: {name}(KNN).fit, oob_score=True"
        rows.append((label,
                     time_fit(label, estimator_class, Xk, yk, estimator=knn,
                              n_estimators=N_ESTIMATORS, oob_score=True),
                     stays_flat))

    # Control 2: estimators are split into at most n_estimators groups
    label = "Control: BaggingClassifier.fit, n_estimators=2"
    rows.append((label, time_fit(label, BaggingClassifier, X, y, n_estimators=2),
                 capped_at_two))
    return rows


# --- report -----------------------------------------------------------------


def format_table(rows):
    first, last = N_JOBS[0], N_JOBS[-1]
    lines = [
        "| Timing (s) | " + " | ".join(f"n_jobs={n}" for n in N_JOBS)
        + f" | Speed-up {first} to {last} | Check |",
        "|---" * (len(N_JOBS) + 3) + "|",
    ]
    for label, times, check in rows:
        cells = " | ".join(f"{times[n]:.3f}" for n in N_JOBS)
        speedup = f"{times[first] / times[last]:.2f}x" if times[last] > 0 else "n/a"
        result = "" if check is None else ("pass" if check(times) else "FAIL")
        lines.append(f"| {label} | {cells} | {speedup} | {result} |")
    return "\n".join(lines)


def environment_report():
    buffer = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buffer):
        sklearn.show_versions()
    return (f"Physical cores (joblib): {joblib.cpu_count(only_physical_cores=True)}\n"
            f"Logical cores (os): {os.cpu_count()}\n{buffer.getvalue()}")


def main():
    args = parse_args()
    data = make_data(args)
    if args.calibrate:
        calibrate(data)
        return

    rows = full_run(data)
    all_pass = all(check(times) for _, times, check in rows if check is not None)
    report = "\n\n".join([
        f"# Bagging n_jobs timing, {datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}",
        f"Settings: {vars(args)}, n_estimators={N_ESTIMATORS}, "
        f"n_features={N_FEATURES}, median of {N_REPEATS} runs after 1 warm-up, "
        "default joblib backend.",
        format_table(rows),
        f"Automatic checks: {'all pass (go)' if all_pass else 'some FAIL (review)'}",
        f"## Environment\n\n```\n{environment_report()}```",
    ])
    RESULTS_FILE.write_text(report + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print("\n" + format_table(rows))
    print(f"\nAutomatic checks: {'all pass' if all_pass else 'some FAIL'}")
    print(f"Saved to {RESULTS_FILE}")


if __name__ == "__main__":  # required on Windows: joblib starts new processes
    main()
```

Run with: `python bagging_n_jobs_timing.py --clf-samples 2500 --reg-samples 3000 --predict-samples 60000 --svc-test 1000 --knn-samples 7500`

</details>

I wasn't sure whether the docstring should mention OOB scoring. With `oob_score=True`, the OOB step at the end of `fit` is a plain `for` loop over the estimators, so `n_jobs` doesn't speed it up. issues.title: BUG fetch_file(url, folder=...) crashes with confusing FileNotFoundError instead of creating the directory

labels.name: Low Priority
labels.description: Low priority issues and pull requests

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

`sklearn.datasets.fetch_file(url, folder=...)` raises a confusing, low-level `FileNotFoundError` instead of creating the target directory when the caller passes an explicit `folder` that doesn't exist yet.

The docstring for `folder` doesn't state that the directory must already exist:

> `folder` : str or Path, default=None
> Directory to save the file to. If None, the file is downloaded in a folder with a name derived from the URL host name and path under scikit-learn data home folder.

But directory creation only happens for the *default* case:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/datasets/_base.py#L1639-L1642

```python
if folder is None:
    folder = Path(get_data_home()) / folder_from_url
    makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)
```

`makedirs(..., exist_ok=True)` is nested inside `if folder is None:`, so it only runs when `fetch_file` derives the folder itself. When the caller explicitly passes `folder=`, no directory creation happens at all. Downstream, `_fetch_remote` (same file, around line 1502) does:

```python
temp_file = NamedTemporaryFile(
    prefix=remote.filename + ".part_", dir=folder_path, delete=False
)
```

which raises `FileNotFoundError` if `folder_path` doesn't exist — an opaque, low-level crash referencing an internal `.part_...` temp-file name that the user never specified, rather than a clear message about the missing directory.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_file

# Using a local file:// URL as the "remote" source, no network required.
src_file = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "source.csv"
src_file.write_text("a,b,c\n1,2,3\n")
url = "file://localhost" + str(src_file)

target_dir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "does_not_exist_yet"
print("target_dir exists before:", target_dir.exists())

fetch_file(url, folder=target_dir)
```

### Expected Results

Either the directory gets created (matching what already happens for the default `folder=None` case — verified working), or a clear, actionable error naming the missing directory.

For comparison, the default-folder path already creates the directory transparently and succeeds:
```python
result = fetch_file(url)  # folder=None (default)
print(result, result.exists())  # succeeds, directory auto-created
```

### Actual Results

```
target_dir exists before: False
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/.../does_not_exist_yet/source.csv.part_1flw14k2'
```

### Versions

Reproduced on current `main`, no network access required (repro uses a local `file://` URL). This appears to have existed since `fetch_file` was introduced (#29354) — no prior discussion of this specific asymmetry found.

---

I dug into this while looking for an unrelated fix and haven't opened a PR — the obvious fix is to move (or duplicate) the `makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)` call so it also runs for a caller-supplied `folder`, mirroring the default-path behavior. Happy to put a PR together if that direction looks right to a maintainer.

issues.title: Support infinite values in DecisionTree/RandomForest/ExtraTrees (now that NaN is supported)

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Hello,

I am facing a problem where the proper handling of infinite values would be helpful. Since the introduction of the support for missing values (#23595/#26391/#27966), I was wondering to what extent it would be possible to handle those.

Currently:

```
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [np.inf], [10.0]])
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]
DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X, y)
# ValueError: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float32').
```

This is because infinite value is explicitly rejected regardless, in `BaseDecisionTree._compute_missing_values_in_feature_mask` (`sklearn/tree/_classes.py`):
A second guard in `_validate_X_predict` (same file) does the same at predict time.

```
if not np.isfinite(overall_sum):
    # Raise a ValueError in case of the presence of an infinite element.
    _assert_all_finite_element_wise(X, xp=np, allow_nan=True, **common_kwargs)
```

Both guards live on `BaseDecisionTree`, shared by all four tree classes; `RandomForest*`/`ExtraTrees*` call the same method rather than duplicating it. 

`GradientBoostingClassifier`/`Regressor` don't set `allow_nan` and aren't affected either way. Small number of call sites.

### Describe your proposed solution

The splitter already tolerates infinite values without modification. Unlike NaN, +inf/-inf are ordinary totally-ordered floats (-inf < finite < +inf), so <= comparisons already place them correctly, with no new split-evaluation logic needed like NaN required. Verified by monkeypatching out just the two guards: DecisionTreeClassifier fits and predicts correctly on +inf/-inf data, including placing a real split threshold at -inf. Checked sklearn/tree/_splitter.pyx too: thresholds are computed as feature_values[p_prev]/2.0 + feature_values[p]/2.0 (sum-of-halves, to avoid overflow on large finite values), with a fallback to feature_values[p_prev] if the result lands exactly on +INFINITY/-INFINITY. With real -inf in the data this fallback is a no-op (-inf sorts first, so the fallback value is -inf too).

check_estimators_nan_inf (the common test for this) is already skipped entirely for these estimators (gated by one allow_nan tag covering both NaN and inf), so relaxing the guard doesn't remove existing coverage, though new tests would need to be added for inf specifically. Proposal: relax the two guards (behind allow_nan or a new dedicated tag), and add that dedicated inf/NaN test coverage.

issues.title: Add Information Value (IV) / Weight-of-Evidence binning as metric and feature-selection

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.


### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Rank a feature's predictive strength against a binary target by binning it (equal-frequency or optimized) and computing Information Value: `sum((pct_event - pct_nonevent) * log(pct_event / pct_nonevent))` over bins.

This is a standard univariate feature-screening step in binary classification, conceptually adjacent to things sklearn already ships in `sklearn.feature_selection` (`mutual_info_classif`, `f_classif`, chi2) as a way to rank/filter features before modeling. Notably this metric does not depends on imbalance. 

### Describe your proposed solution

'sklearn.metric.IV(X,y, bins=10) would be useful for establishing Information value. Then 'sklearn.feature_selection.information_value(X, y, bins=10)' returning per-feature IV, using equal-frequency quantile binning by default (fast, matches the common textbook definition).


### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Checked scikit-learn's issue tracker for "Information Value" and "Weight of Evidence" - found nothing (no open request, no closed-as-declined). The realistic existing option is `optbinning`, a purpose-built, actively maintained package that solves actual bin optimization (via a CP/MIP solver) rather than plain quantile cuts.

IV/WOE binning is old and widely used, but specifically within credit-scoring-style binary classification rather than general ML - similar concern to the adjacent PSI request I'm also filing. Raising it mainly to get a maintainer judgment on record, since I couldn't find this discussed anywhere in scikit-learn's history.



### Additional context

`mutual_info_classif` already covers "how predictive is this feature" in a distribution-agnostic way; IV specifically gives interpretable, additive-across-bins output that credit-risk practitioners rely on for regulatory model documentation, which is the main reason it persists as a distinct metric rather than being subsumed by mutual information in that field.

issues.title: PRF Mitigation heuristics for HGB scalability
issues.body:
Finally, I have something that has a uniformly positive impact on the 8 scenarios I'm testing:
- Big machine with default OMP settings
- Big machine with `OMP_PROC_BIND=close` (avoids penalizing runs that use fewer threads than what's available on the machine)
- Laptop with active wait disabled (the default behavior of conda-forge packages)
- Laptop with active wait enabled

(× libgomp & libomp for each of those)

And it can be very/hugely beneficial in some scenarios (2-10x speed-ups):
- small to medium datasets on a big machine
- small to medium-big datasets on laptops with active wait disabled

#### Reference Issues/PRs

Implements item 4 (partially), item 5 and item 6 of https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34764#issuecomment-5343004000

I'd also say it closes #14306, though that issue does have some ideas that aren't implemented here, in particular parallelizing over blocks of samples × features when building histograms. Benchmarks show HGB does keep scaling up to 16-32 threads for many medium/big datasets, as long as active wait is enabled, which I'd personally consider good enough for now.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

- Detect whether the OpenMP runtime uses active wait, i.e. whether idle threads spin instead of sleeping while waiting for work (`_openmp_uses_active_wait` in `sklearn/utils/_openmp_helpers.pyx`). This is done by parsing the environment dump the runtime prints under `OMP_DISPLAY_ENV=VERBOSE`, in a short-lived subprocess. Active wait makes rejoining a parallel region much cheaper, so all the heuristics below branch on it.
- Cap the number of threads used to grow each tree, based on the number of features and samples (`BaseHistGradientBoosting._get_heurirstic_optimal_n_threads`), instead of always using every available thread.
- Same idea for binning: `_BinMapper`'s `n_threads` parameter is renamed to `max_n_threads` since it's now only an upper bound, the actual thread count used being derived from the amount of data to bin.
- In `Splitter.split_indices`, fall back to a single-threaded partitioning pass when there isn't enough work per thread to justify the chunking/offset bookkeeping of the multi-threaded version.
- In `Splitter.find_node_split`, when active wait is disabled, skip parallelizing over features when there are too few of them relative to `n_threads`.

#### AI usage disclosure

Mostly not, except for the active wait detection: Claude helped find a way to make the subprocess-based `_openmp_uses_active_wait` fast enough not to matter (result cached after the first call, subprocess kept minimal to avoid a full `import sklearn`).

#### Benchmarks

https://pr-81.sklbench-dashboard-preview.pages.dev/

I still have to run some tests on windows.

issues.title: CI Turn sphinx warnings into errors on pushes to main
issues.body:
Current state sphinx warning are turned into errors in PRs and only for files that PRs touch.

The issue is that, in a given PR, some changes to the doc may break references, or similar, in other parts of the doc that are not touched by the PR and so go unnoticed into main.

We recently had 2 examples during the release of 1.9.1 because the CI failed there (it's more likely to fail because the release PR contains many modified files from all the picked commits). see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34915 and https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34916. It's annoying to have to deal with that during the release, but more importantly it's bad that we don't detect it earlier.

This PR proposes to turn all sphinx warnings into errors when we run a full doc build on pushes to main and maintenance branches. Even if we merge a PR that breaks the doc build on main, it won't fire in all PRs because they still only check warnings in the files they modify.

issues.title: PolynomialCountSketch.bitHash_ docstring says dtype=float32 but is actually int64

labels.name: Needs Triage
labels.description: Issue requires triage

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for general ML work. I found this while cross-checking
the `PolynomialCountSketch` docs against its implementation for an unrelated
performance PR (#34919) and noticed the `bitHash_` attribute's documented
dtype doesn't match what the code actually produces.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`PolynomialCountSketch`'s `bitHash_` attribute is documented as:

```
bitHash_ : ndarray of shape (degree, n_features), dtype=float32
    Array with random entries in {+1, -1}, used to represent
    the 2-wise independent hash functions for Count Sketch computation.
```

but it is actually set with:

```python
self.bitHash_ = random_state.choice(a=[-1, 1], size=(self.degree, n_features))
```

`numpy.random.RandomState.choice` with an integer array `a=[-1, 1]` and no
explicit `dtype` produces an integer array, not `float32`. This has been the
case since the class was introduced (scikit-learn/scikit-learn#13003, 2019),
so it is not a regression, just a docstring that was never accurate.

User-facing impact is limited (the attribute is internal-ish and the class
still works correctly), but anyone relying on the documented dtype — for
example writing code that assumes `bitHash_.astype(np.float32, copy=False)`
is a no-op, or reasoning about memory usage from the docstring — would be
misled.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.kernel_approximation import PolynomialCountSketch

X = np.random.RandomState(0).random_sample((50, 20))
ps = PolynomialCountSketch(degree=2, n_components=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print(ps.bitHash_.dtype)
```

### Expected Results

```
float32
```
(matching the docstring)

### Actual Results

```
int64
```

### Versions

```
System:
    python: 3.14.6 (v3.14.6:c63aec69bd5, Jun 10 2026, 08:07:54) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)]
executable: /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.14/bin/python3
   machine: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0
          pip: 26.1.2
   setuptools: 83.0.0
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: 3.3.0
       pandas: None
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.6.0
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.25.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

I'd be happy to open a PR to fix the docstring to say the actual dtype
(`int64`, or more precisely whatever `numpy.random.RandomState.choice`
returns for an integer input array) once this is triaged.

issues.title: TST Add common tests for callback support
issues.body:
This PR is a first batch of common tests for callback support in estimators. So these are common tests for estimators. Common tests for callbacks will come in a different PR.

Here are the first checks that I thought about. We can of course add more check in subsequent PRs when they come to mind.
- add checks in estimator_checks
    - check that an estimator has a single root context
    - check that setup and teardown are called exactly once each
    - check that for each context, on_fit_task_begin and on_fit_task_end are called exactly once and in that order
    - check that the estimator passed to the callback is the one being fitted (particularly useful for meta-estimators)

Since we're using testing helpers outside of the callback module I was not satisfy to import stuff from `sklearn.callback.tests.xxx`, so I moved `callback.tests._common` into `callback._testing` so that we don't import stuff across test files. This is the reason why the diff impacts that many files, but the real stuff happens in `estimator_checks` and `test_common`.

As we usually do for common tests about things that are not part of the scikit-learn compatibility contract, i.e. third-party don't have to use it, I did not include the new checks into `yield_all_checks` but run them in a dedicated common test instead.

I added a list of all the estimator that don't support callbacks yet to skip the test. We'll remove them from the list one at a time when we start adding callback support in more estimators (i.e. after we have merged the metadata routing PR).

closes https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/33324

> [!WARNING]

If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

_ACA Where do we want to use `sample_weight` by default?_

With #31413 ~~soon to be~~ merged, we have defined the mechanism for the auto-routing strategy in scikit-learn (and for use in third party libraries). It will be easily possible to define per estimator which methods of the estimator will request which metadata if users set `set_config(enable_metadata_requests=True)`. (Context: At one point in the future this setting will become the default, but for now it is opt-in.)

The way to do this is to call `add_auto_request` inside an estimator's `get_metadata_routing` method:

```py
class XYZEstimator(BaseEstimator):

    def get_metadata_routing(self):
        ...
        requests.fit.add_auto_request("sample_weight") # <--- one-liner to add auto-requests
        ...
```

The effect of adding an auto-request is that then `XYZEstimator.fit()` automatically requests and uses `sample_weight` if the user has passed it into the top-level meta-estimator or cross validation.

This issue is to define the scope of the auto-requests. 

We have discussed this in our bi-weekly meeting on pushing the subject of auto-requests and here we want to give everybody who is interested the opportunity to share their ideas on the following questions:

- Which metadata should get auto-requested ("sample_weigh", "X_val", "sample_weight_val", custom metadata, other?)
- Should we add auto-requests to `fit` and `score` everywhere or are there estimators where that doesn't make any sense?
- Which type of tests do we need?

My personal take would be to work these questions out in separate POC PRs.

CC @scikit-learn/core-devs for gathering opinions. I'm especially interested in the opinions of the statistically more inclined core devs (since we can figure out the engineering part pretty easily). Happy to discuss this in calls also.

issues.title: DOC Correct the description of `tol` in the k-means estimators
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Addresses the documentation half of #22519. Does not close it: that issue also
carries a proposal to *change* the convergence criterion, which is left open.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
`tol` is documented across the k-means estimators as:

> Relative tolerance with regards to Frobenius norm of the difference in the
> cluster centers of two consecutive iterations to declare convergence.

That sentence appears in five places and is inaccurate in all of them, in three
different ways. It also reads as if the normalisation were relative to the
centers themselves, which is what the reporter of #22519 originally expected.

**1. `KMeans` and `k_means` — scaled by the feature variance.**
`fit` sets `self._tol = _tolerance(X, self.tol)`, i.e. `mean(var(X, axis=0)) * tol`,
so convergence is declared when

```
(center_shift ** 2).sum() <= tol * mean(var(X, axis=0))
```

```
mean(var(X))        : 0.0839
_tolerance(X, 1e-4) : 8.39e-06     # actual threshold
mean(var(10*X))     : 8.388
_tolerance(10X,1e-4): 8.39e-04     # 100x larger
```

`MiniBatchKMeans` already documents this correctly ("a smoothed,
variance-normalized ... mean center squared position changes"), so `KMeans` was
inconsistent with its own sibling.

**2. `_kmeans_single_lloyd` / `_kmeans_single_elkan` — absolute.**
These are called with `tol=self._tol`, a value that has *already* been scaled,
so for them the threshold is absolute. Calling it "relative" is wrong in the
opposite direction.

**3. `BisectingKMeans` — absolute, unlike `KMeans`.**
It passes the raw `self.tol` to the inner k-means; `self._tol` is computed by
the inherited `_check_params_vs_input` but never used on that path:

```
user tol              : 0.0001
_tol (variance-scaled): 0.0820
tol passed to inner k-means: 0.0001      # raw value
```

So a `tol` that works for `KMeans` does not mean the same thing for
`BisectingKMeans`. This one surprised me, and it is the reason the wording is
not shared between the two classes.

This PR describes each of the three cases explicitly. Documentation only;
there is no behaviour change, and no changelog fragment since no behaviour
changed.

I deliberately scoped this to documentation. #22519 also contains a 2022
suggestion by @jeremiedbb to make the criterion a genuinely relative center
shift, with a deprecation cycle; that is a behaviour change and I did not want
to assume a four-year-old plan is still current, so I left it for a separate
discussion. Happy to adjust the wording, or to fold in the user guide if you
think `modules/clustering.rst` should say something too.

#### Introduce yourself
I use scikit-learn for general ML work. I came across #22519 while reading
around the k-means implementation and noticed the `tol` docstring didn't
match what the code actually does in any of the three cases described above.

#### AI usage disclosure
I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (e.g., when writing an implementation or fixing a bug)
- Research and understanding

- `pytest --doctest-modules sklearn/cluster/_kmeans.py sklearn/cluster/_bisect_k_means.py` → 5 passed

issues.title: FIX Reference-count BLAS thread limit in pairwise distance reductions
issues.body:
<!--
Thanks for contributing a pull request! Please ensure you have taken a look at
the contribution guidelines: https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/index.html
-->

#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #31884

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
When calling `ArgKmin64.compute()` or `RadiusNeighbors64.compute()` concurrently across threads (e.g. using `joblib.Parallel(backend="threading")`), numerical corruption occurs in environments running OpenBLAS compiled with the OpenMP threading layer.

The root cause is overlapping `threadpoolctl` context manager lifecycles: `threadpoolctl` changes process-global C state (`openblas_set_num_threads`). When Thread A exits its `compute()` block, it prematurely restores the thread limit back to default (e.g. 12) while concurrent threads are still running `_gemm` operations, corrupting OpenBLAS's non-reentrant static packing buffers.

This PR introduces `_RefcountedBLASLimit` in `sklearn.utils.parallel`. It reference-counts concurrent entries across threads so the BLAS thread limit stays pinned to 1 as long as any reduction is active, and only restores the original thread count once the last concurrent thread exits.

#### Any other comments?
- Added unit tests for `_RefcountedBLASLimit` in `test_parallel.py`.
- Added a multithreaded regression test in `test_pairwise_distances_reduction.py`.
- Included a towncrier news entry.
