issues.title: FIX count_nonzero skipping CSR format check for negative axes
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

None (bug found by inspection; no existing open issue or PR covers it).

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

`count_nonzero` only supports CSR input (it indexes `X.indptr` / `X.indices` assuming CSR layout). The guard that enforces this lived in the same `if/elif` chain as the negative-axis aliasing:

```python
if axis == -1:
    axis = 1
elif axis == -2:
    axis = 0
elif X.format != "csr":
    raise TypeError(...)
```

Because `axis == -1` / `axis == -2` match first, the `elif` format check never executes. A non-CSR matrix (e.g. CSC) passed with `axis=-1` or `axis=-2` returns **incorrect counts** instead of raising.

Repro (before this PR):
```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import csc_matrix
from sklearn.utils.sparsefuncs import count_nonzero

X = np.array([[0,3,0,0,1,0],[2,-1,0,7,0,3],[0,0,4,0,0,0],[9,8,7,1,6,2]], float)
Xcsc = csc_matrix(X)
count_nonzero(Xcsc, axis=0)   # correctly raises TypeError
count_nonzero(Xcsc, axis=-2)  # BUG: returns [2 4 1 6 0 0] instead of raising
```

**Fix:** change `elif X.format != "csr"` to a standalone `if` so the format check runs regardless of axis value.

#### Introduce yourself

Hi! I'm Viraj, a CS senior at Penn State (Schreyer Honors College). I use scikit-learn in my ML research -- currently working on a retrieval-augmented classification paper. Found this bug while reading the sparse utils source code.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (identifying the fix and writing the regression test)
- Research and understanding

#### Any other comments?

- Added a regression test in `test_count_nonzero` asserting `axis=-1`/`-2` on a CSC matrix raise `TypeError`, matching the existing `axis=0`/`1` behavior.
- Added a changelog fragment (`34875.fix.rst`).

issues.title: FIX Avoid densifying sparse columns in QuantileTransformer/RobustScaler quantile computation
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #34298. Fixes #34857.

Supersedes #34451, which proposes the same `_sparse_column_percentile`-style fix for #34298 but without the part fixing #34857. Credited @Stag51 as co-author on the commit implementing it and in the changelog.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

Two related bugs in how `QuantileTransformer` (and `RobustScaler`) compute quantiles from sparse columns:

- #34298: with `ignore_implicit_zeros=False`, computing the quantiles densified the column into an `n_samples`-sized array, which can be very slow or OOM for extremely sparse matrices.
- #34857: when a column hit the subsampling path, only `subsample * len(column_nnz_data) // n_samples` non-zero values were kept, this can round down to a handful of points, so large chunks of the output distribution collapse to a single value.

To fix #34298, I added `_sparse_column_quantile`, which computes `nanquantile`-equivalent results directly from the non-zero data plus an implicit-zero count, without ever densifying the column.

I also ported the same fix to `RobustScaler`, which had the identical densify-then-`nanpercentile` pattern.

For #34857, the subsampling path now draws up to `self.subsample` non-zero values directly and subsamples the implicit-zero count proportionally instead => The amount of real signal retained no longer depends on how sparse the column is relative to `n_samples`. But the calculation volume is limited to O(`self.subsample`) which is the purpose of this parameter.

I used AI assistance for:
- Writing this PR description
- Helping with tests & changelog

issues.body:
Fixes #34661

#### Reference Issue
Fixes #34661

#### What does this implement/fix?
`dump_svmlight_file(X, y, multilabel=True)` with a one-dimensional dense `y` passed the 1d array straight to the Cython writer `_dump_svmlight_file`, which indexes it as a 2d buffer (`y.shape[1]`, `y[i, j]`) and crashes the interpreter with a segmentation fault. issues.title: PRF Ridge - centering trick for cholesky solver
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

None, I started investigated for a speed gain while comparing speed/profiles with the scikit-learn-intelex (oneDAL) implementation.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

- It uses an algebra trick to avoid the need for re-centering in Cholesky
- It refactors a bit the validation so to avoid a double pass of `check_array` (and to avoid a copy in the algebraic centering Cholesky path).

Those relatively simple changes provide a speedups ranging from ~1.2x to 2x.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (many iterations)
- Comments
- Research and understanding

#### Benchmarks

Benchmarks are run through the  PR: https://github.com/probabl-ai/scikit-learn-benchmarks/pull/31 (see bot comments with links to dashboards)

The benchmark cases are the same than the ones used to compare with [scikit-learn-intelex](https://uxlfoundation.github.io/scikit-learn-intelex), they are a mix of synthetic and real-world datasets.

issues.title: PRF: Over-subscription in pairwise_distances with `backend="threading"` + BLAS-pthreads

labels.name: Parallelism and scalability
labels.description: All things related to efficient handling of cores via thread-based or process-based parallelism.

issues.body:
> 🚨 This is a complex issue that already has experts working on it. Please don't start work on this without first coordinating with them.

`sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances` accepts a `n_jobs` parameters and uses `joblib.Parallel(backend="threading", n_jobs=n_jobs)` under-the-hood. But this parallelization happens on top on openBLAS parallelism, and can lead to what looks like over-subscription.

(but maybe it's not over-subscription, and something else, like cost of repeated small parallelized blas calls, etc. I haven't investigated) 

Results from a small benchmark script shows that limiting blas to 1 thread helps scaling as `n_jobs` grows (and usually achieves best performance compared to n_jobs=1 with blas parallelism enabled):

``` 
--- n_samples=2000  n_features=200 ---
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=0:      33ms
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=1:      52ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=0:      66ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=1:      53ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=0:      76ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=1:      35ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=0:     102ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=1:      25ms

--- n_samples=4000  n_features=200 ---
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=0:     150ms
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=1:     226ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=0:     107ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=1:     102ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=0:     141ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=1:      75ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=0:     163ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=1:      70ms

--- n_samples=8000  n_features=200 ---
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=0:     547ms
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=1:     864ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=0:     375ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=1:     296ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=0:     356ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=1:     217ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=0:     362ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=1:     204ms
```

Results with 10 or 1000 features are similar, but for n_samples=2000, the n_jobs=1 pin-blas=0 variant wins.

The script:

<details>

```python
import argparse
from itertools import product
import time
from statistics import median

import numpy as np
import threadpoolctl

from sklearn.metrics import pairwise_distances


def bench_once(X, n_jobs, pin_blas):
    if pin_blas:
        with threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(1, user_api="blas"):
            return pairwise_distances(X, X, n_jobs=n_jobs)
    return pairwise_distances(X, X, n_jobs=n_jobs)


def bench(X, n_jobs, pin_blas, reps):
    bench_once(X, n_jobs, pin_blas)  # warmup / compilation
    times = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        bench_once(X, n_jobs, pin_blas)
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return median(times)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--n-samples", type=str, default="2000,4000,8000")
    parser.add_argument("--n-features", type=str, default="200")
    parser.add_argument("--n-jobs", type=str, default="1,4,8,14")
    parser.add_argument("--reps", type=int, default=30)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    n_samples_list = [int(v) for v in args.n_samples.split(",")]
    n_features_list = [int(v) for v in args.n_features.split(",")]
    n_jobs_list = [int(v) for v in args.n_jobs.split(",")]

    rng = np.random.RandomState(4872)

    for n_samples, n_features in product(n_samples_list, n_features_list):
        X = rng.rand(n_samples, n_features)
        print(f"\n--- n_samples={n_samples}  n_features={n_features} ---")

        for n_jobs in n_jobs_list:
            for pin_blas in [False, True]:
                t = bench(X, n_jobs, pin_blas, args.reps)
                print(f"  n_jobs={n_jobs:>3} | pin-blas={pin_blas:>1}: {t * 1000:7.0f}ms")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

</details>

Note: the default metric is euclidean, but I think I observed similar behavior with cosine too. l1 doesn't call blas so it doesn't have the same issue.

issues.title: FIX RadiusNeighborsRegressor silently returns a sentinel for empty neighborhoods with integer targets
issues.body:
Reference Issues/PRs
--------------------
Fixes #12960.

What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
---------------------------------------------------

`RadiusNeighborsRegressor` builds the placeholder for samples with no neighbors
inside `radius` with:

```python
empty_obs = np.full_like(_y[0], np.nan)
```

`np.full_like` inherits the target dtype, and casting NaN into an integer target
is undefined. The result is a sentinel that is indistinguishable from a real
prediction:

```python
X = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0]])
est = RadiusNeighborsRegressor(radius=0.5).fit(X, np.array([0, 1, 2]))
est.predict([[100.0]])
# main: array([0])          <- 0 is a plausible prediction here
# this PR: array([nan]) + UserWarning
```

The reported value was `-9223372036854775808` in the original issue and is `0`
on numpy 2.x; either way it is platform-dependent garbage.

There is a second, worse consequence. The "no neighbors" warning is guarded by:

```python
if np.any(np.isnan(y_pred)):
```

`np.isnan` on an integer array is always `False`, so once the NaN had been cast
away the warning could never fire. Integer targets therefore failed silently in
both directions: wrong value *and* no warning. Float targets were unaffected,
which is why this went unnoticed.

Mixed batches were also affected, and this is the case most likely to reach a
user unnoticed:

```python
est = RadiusNeighborsRegressor(radius=0.6).fit(X, np.array([0, 1, 2]))
est.predict([[1.0], [100.0]])
# main:    array([1., 0.])    <- second entry is not a prediction
# this PR: array([ 1., nan]) + UserWarning
```

The fix promotes the placeholder to a float dtype so NaN is representable:

```python
empty_obs = np.full_like(
    _y[0], np.nan, dtype=np.promote_types(_y.dtype, np.float16)
)
```

`np.promote_types(dtype, np.float16)` reproduces the dtype `np.mean` already
returns for the non-empty rows (`int32/int64 -> float64`, `float32 -> float32`,
`float64 -> float64`), so predictions are unchanged wherever neighbors exist and
`float32` targets keep their precision rather than being widened.

Any other comments?
-------------------

**Tests.** Two non-regression tests, ten parametrised cases: empty
neighborhoods across `int32/int64/float32/float64` and both weightings, and a
partially-empty batch. Each asserts NaN, a floating result dtype, and that the
`UserWarning` actually fires. Against `main` five of the ten fail (every integer
case); all ten pass with this change.

**Validation caveat, stated plainly.** I could not build scikit-learn from source
on this machine; the C++ toolchain fails on the macOS SDK headers, unrelated to
this change. I validated by applying the patched `_regression.py` over an
installed 1.8.0 and running `sklearn.neighbors.tests.test_neighbors`:

```
pristine 1.8.0, its own tests                     585 passed, 436 skipped
patched _regression.py, its own tests             585 passed, 436 skipped
```

identical, so no regression in the released test suite. Running `main`'s test
file against installed 1.8.0 produces 10 pre-existing failures purely from the
version skew (confirmed with none of my changes applied), and the same 10 with
this change plus my 10 new tests passing. CI here is authoritative over my local
numbers.

One incidental effect: the fix removes roughly 185 spurious
`RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in cast` warnings from that test run.

**One design question for the reviewer.** I kept the existing contract of
NaN-plus-`UserWarning` rather than raising, since that is what float targets have
always done and changing it would be a behaviour break for them. Integer targets
now simply behave like float ones. If the preference is to raise on empty
neighborhoods, that is a different and larger change and I am happy to take it
instead.


#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (fixing the bug)
- Test/benchmark generation
- Drafting this PR description

Per the Automated Contributions Policy, the change was reviewed, run and verified before
submission rather than submitted unread.

issues.title: FIX handle non-subscriptable sparse input in ColumnTransformer
issues.body:
## Summary

`ColumnTransformer` now converts non-subscriptable sparse inputs to CSR before
column selection. This allows supported sparse data such as DIA-format arrays
to pass through the same column-selection path as CSR and other subscriptable
formats.

## Root cause

`ColumnTransformer._check_X` accepted every SciPy sparse format unchanged, but
column selection relies on `X[:, columns]`. Sparse formats that do not implement
`__getitem__` therefore failed with `TypeError: '<format>_array' object is not
subscriptable`, even when the selected transformers supported sparse input.

## Validation

- Reproduced the original DIA-array failure against the released scikit-learn
  wheel.
- Applied the proposed conversion in a controlled check and confirmed the same
  `ColumnTransformer` pipeline completes with the expected shape and values.
- Ran a source-level regression check for `_check_X` covering DIA and CSR.
- Ran `git diff --check` and Python syntax compilation for the modified files.
- The full native pytest target could not run because this Windows checkout has
  no C/C++ compiler to build scikit-learn's extensions.

Closes #30275


## AI assistance disclosure

I identified and reproduced the issue, then used OpenAI Codex to assist with the implementation and regression-test work. I personally reviewed the resulting diff and ran the validation commands listed above to verify the fix. Any full-suite or local-environment limitations are documented in the validation section.

issues.title: ENH Newton-CD part 8: add multinomial NewtonCDSolver

labels.name: Waiting for Second Reviewer
labels.description: First reviewer is done, need a second one!

issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Part 8 of #33160, follow-up of #34561.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
#34561 introduced the `solver="newton-cd"` which uses coordinate descent without gram matrix (=Hessian), i.e. like `ElasticNet(precompute=False).` It only uses the full hessian implicitly. This works by **taking the square root** of the Hessian (X'WX) and formulating the update step (one Newton iteration) as a least squares problem with penalty.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This does not work out of the box for the multinomial/multiclass setting because the pointwise hessian (W) is not diagonal.
> Several attempts of approximations that e.g. glmnet uses don't converge on simple problems.

This PR extends #34561 by introducing a dedicated coordinate descent solver for the multinomial. It uses an analytic LDL decomposition of the pointwise hessian (aka covariance of the multinomial) in order to take the square root of X'WX.

This is a very good solver for `n_features > n_samples`, thus closing this gap in solver options (currently only saga, but it often has concergence issues).

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In PCA, if an input matrix has linear dependencies, some singular values will be zeros, which also makes the components in that case be zeros.

These have no effect on the results and should be omitted, since they effectively aren't components, just padding, but scikit-learn doesn't discard them.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)

n = 10
S = rng.standard_normal((n+1, n))
S = S.T@S
mu = rng.standard_normal(size=n)
X = rng.multivariate_normal(mu, S, size=100)
X[:, 2:5] = X[:, [0]]

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
pca = PCA().fit(X)

import polars as pl
pl.DataFrame(pca.components_)
```

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Ledoit Wolf is a method for shrinking the empirical covariace matrix for data, and is already available in this library. The process essentially does three steps:
1) make the empirical covariance matrix
2) calculates some parameters (beta / delta) that are then used to calculate the shrinkage coefficient
3) use the results from steps (1) and (2) to make the desired output.

Given random p-vector X,  step (1) is just doing E[ X X^T ) - E[ X ] E[X^T ] the way you expect. Step (2) is calculating variables beta and delta that invariably involve calculating E[ X_i X_j ] and E[ X^2_i X^2_j ], just with a typical mean calculation. What I am proposing is extending these calculations, where weights can be leveraged to do the expected value calculations. This will allow the user to, for example, do the calculation on the exponentially weighted covariance matrix, but really use any weighting they choose. By setting weights = np.ones( X.shape[0] ) by default, we can maintain the current standard output. If desired, this procedure might possibly be extended to OAS (another shrinkage matrix).

### Describe your proposed solution

I am proposing adding the named variable "weights" to the "fit" function inputs for the LedoitWolf class (and any other necessary changes under the hood).

issues.title: PERF Use threads for LogisticRegressionCV parallelism on free threaded Python
issues.body:
On free-threaded Python, parallelism with threads is often faster due to reduced overhead. So it's useful to use threads when there is no GIL.

In this case, I added a benchmark, ran it with `main`'s algorithm (threads only for `sag` and `saga`) and with the PR (everything is threads), and combined the tables. As one would expect, `sag` and `saga` don't change much (and any change is just noise), but the other solvers run faster when switched to threads. Lower is better:

| 4      | lbfgs           | 2.118               | 0.889              |
| 8      | lbfgs           | 2.136               | 0.723              |

| 8      | newton-cd-gram  | 2.351               | 0.875              |
| 1      | newton-cg       | 3.188               | 3.141              |
| 4      | newton-cg       | 2.749               | 1.047              |
| 8      | newton-cg       | 2.477               | 0.809              |
| 1      | newton-cholesky | 2.955               | 2.98               |
| 4      | newton-cholesky | 2.501               | 0.995              |
| 8      | newton-cholesky | 2.235               | 0.826              |
| 1      | sag             | 6.665               | 6.604              |

| 1      | saga            | 7.104               | 6.955              |

| 8      | saga            | 1.504               | 1.505              |

---

Benchmark script:

```python
"""
Test performance of LogisticRegressionCV fitting with different solvers and
parallelism levels.
"""

from time import time

import numpy as np

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegressionCV
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=100_000, n_features=20, n_informative=2, n_redundant=2, random_state=42
)

train_samples = 10_000  # Samples used for training the models
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    shuffle=False,
    test_size=100_000 - train_samples,
)

print("| n_jobs | solver          | elapsed |")
print("|--------|-----------------|---------|")

for solver in [
    "lbfgs",
    "liblinear",
    "newton-cd-gram",
    "newton-cg",
    "newton-cholesky",
    "sag",
    "saga",
]:
    for n_jobs in [1, 4, 8]:
        lr = LogisticRegressionCV(
            Cs=np.logspace(-6, 6, 101),
            cv=10,
            l1_ratios=(0,),
            scoring="neg_log_loss",
            max_iter=1_000,
            use_legacy_attributes=False,
            n_jobs=n_jobs,
            solver=solver,
        )
        start = time()
        lr.fit(X_train, y_train)
        print(f"|{n_jobs:8}| {solver:16}|{round(time() - start, 3):9}|")
```

issues.title: ENH Add huber loss to HistGradientBoostingRegressor
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #31542.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

This PR adds the Huber loss as a new `loss="huber"` option for `HistGradientBoostingRegressor`, following Friedman (2001), algo 4. The Huber loss combines the squared error for small residuals with the absolute error for large residuals, making the estimator robust to outliers in `y` — the same loss that has long been available in the exact `GradientBoostingRegressor` but was missing for the histogram-based implementation.

Implementation details:

- The existing `HuberLoss` class from `sklearn._loss.loss` is registered under the name `"huber"` in the HGBT loss registry.
- The breakpoint `delta` is recomputed at each iteration as the `quantile` of the absolute residuals via `set_huber_delta`, which is shared with the classic `GradientBoostingRegressor` and now also supports `sample_weight=None`. For the baseline prediction, `delta` is initialized from the residuals w.r.t. the (weighted) median of `y`.
- The existing `quantile` parameter of `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` is reused for `loss="huber"`, defaulting to 0.9 (mirroring the `alpha=0.9` default of `GradientBoostingRegressor`).
- Since the Huber loss is piecewise quadratic/linear, its exact hessian is 1 inside the quadratic region and 0 outside of it. The Newton boosting split finding of HGBT requires positive hessians, so the approximate hessian is the constant 1 everywhere (an upper bound of the exact hessian), consistent with the `absolute_error` and `quantile` losses. This also gives `constant_hessian=True` when no sample weights are passed, enabling the faster gradient-only path.
- Leaf values are updated with the Friedman line search (`fit_intercept_only`) as for the other non-differentiable losses.

Tests added in `sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/tests/test_gradient_boosting.py`:

- fit/score coverage, allowed `quantile` values, invalid `quantile` validation, default quantile (0.9), `sample_weight` support
- `test_huber_delta_updated_each_iteration`: checks that `delta` is set once for the baseline prediction and then recomputed at each iteration, and that it decreases as the residuals shrink
- `test_huber_outlier_robustness`: checks that `loss="huber"` achieves a lower median absolute error than `loss="squared_error"` on outlier-contaminated targets

I also verified that the full test files of `sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/tests/test_gradient_boosting.py`, `sklearn/ensemble/tests/test_gradient_boosting.py`, `sklearn/_loss/tests/test_loss.py`, the warm start / monotonic constraints tests and the SGD huber tests still pass.

#### First time contributor introduction

This is my first contribution to scikit-learn. I was looking for a meaningful way to contribute to the project and found #31542 labeled "help wanted", which seemed like a well-scoped but interesting feature to work on.

#### AI usage disclosure

- Code generation (e.g., when writing an implementation or fixing a bug)

issues.title: RFC Always store fitted attributes as Numpy
issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

This is an issue related to #34152 but is also a standalone issue.

While thinking about #34152 and working on #34324 I thought that it might be a good idea if the fitted attributes of an estimator were always Numpy arrays. The current plan is to store fitted attributes in the namespace/device of `X`.

Reasons to do this:
1. users most often use fitted attributes for inspection/debugging/plotting. Having them in a consistent array namespace makes this easy to do. If the namespace is input dependent then you have to change your debugging/plotting code. Say you run the same script on a machine with a CUDA GPU and on your laptop with no GPU. While it is not difficult to use write code that uses `move_to()` to conditionally bring the attributes to Numpy for plotting, it is tedious.
2. Today attributes are Numpy, by keeping them Numpy we remove one source of bugs/differences. Enabling array API by default would not change this
3. Part of #34324 that is not great/tricky is dealing with estimators that sometimes support array API. For example for some hyper-parameter values array API is supported and for some not. The tricky question: What should the type of the fitted attributes be?
4. You can `fit` with one array namespace/device and `predict` with a different one without any conversion
5. An estimator fitted with pytorch/CUDA can be unpickled on a machine without CUDA and even without pytorch

Something to check is how much overhead/performance loss we get in `predict` and other inference methods if we have to convert the fitted attributes relevant for predicting from Numpy to the array namespace of the input each time. Though I suspect that conversion is fast. It might add appreciable overhead if you are predicting on very few samples, but the absolute time will be short in those cases (and you could just use the CPU?). We would need to introduce a way to make it easy to convert fitted attributes to Numpy in each estimator to avoid lots of boilerplate. What are other reasons to not do this?

What do others think?

issues.title: Pandas output path fails to reject infinite values during transform
issues.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When using `set_output(transform="pandas")`, `SelectKBest.transform` does not reject infinite values in a pandas `DataFrame`. This is a regression introduced by [PR #25102](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/25102).

The pandas-output path passes `cast_to_ndarray=False` to `_validate_data`, which causes `check_array` to skip its `force_all_finite` validation. This allows invalid numeric inputs through `transform` instead of raising the expected validation error.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif

X_train = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "a": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
        "b": [1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0],
    }
)
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]

selector = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=1).set_output(transform="pandas")
selector.fit(X_train, y)

X_bad = X_train.copy()
X_bad.loc[0, "a"] = np.inf

print("Input containing infinity:")
print(X_bad)
print()

try:
    result = selector.transform(X_bad)
    print("Transform succeeded (no error raised):")
    print(result)
except Exception as exc:
    print("Error:", exc)
```

### Expected Results

The input containing infinity should be rejected during `transform`:

```
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Error: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float64').
```

(This is the behavior when `set_output` is not used.)

### Actual Results

No validation error is raised; transform silently succeeds:

```
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Transform succeeded (no error raised):
     b
0  1.0
1  2.0
2  1.0
3  2.0
```

### Versions

```
scikit-learn 1.9.0
Python 3.11.13
Linux
NumPy 2.4.6
SciPy 1.17.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The pandas-output path should preserve DataFrame containers without changing the estimator's validation behavior. Infinite values should continue to be rejected consistently during `transform` regardless of the output format setting.

issues.title: FIX SequentialFeatureSelector backward auto-selection always removes one feature (#26369)

labels.name: Waiting for Second Reviewer
labels.description: First reviewer is done, need a second one!

issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Closes #26369.

This revives the fix from the stale #26480 (no maintainer review since Jan 2024), but keeps the change minimal: it does **not** add the extra `tol`-sign validation that PR proposed, since the `tol` docstring already documents that `tol` may be negative for backward selection.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

For `SequentialFeatureSelector` with `direction="backward"` and `n_features_to_select="auto"`, `old_score` was initialized to `-np.inf`, exactly as for forward selection. The auto-selection stopping criterion is:

```python
if is_auto_select and ((new_score - old_score) < self.tol):
    break
```

On the first backward iteration this is `(new_score - (-inf)) < tol` → `inf < tol` → always `False`, so the loop never stops on the first step and **at least one feature is always removed**, even when removing any feature decreases the score. (As noted by `@betatim` in the issue, this was the root cause.)

The fix initializes `old_score`, for backward auto-selection only, to the cross-validation score obtained with **all** features — the correct reference point for deciding whether the first removal is worthwhile. Forward selection keeps the `-np.inf` initialization (its reference is "no features yet"). The extra `cross_val_score` call is only performed in the backward auto-select case, so other code paths are unaffected.

Reproducer from the issue (all features informative, so removing any hurts):

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.feature_selection import SequentialFeatureSelector
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=100, n_features=3, n_informative=3, noise=0, random_state=0)
sfs = SequentialFeatureSelector(
    LinearRegression(), n_features_to_select="auto", tol=0, direction="backward", cv=2
).fit(X, y)
print(sfs.get_support())   # before: one feature dropped; after: [ True  True  True ]
```

#### Any other comments?

- Added a non-regression test (`test_backward_auto_keeps_all_features_when_removal_hurts`).
- Updated `test_n_features_to_select_auto`: the backward case previously relied on the buggy behavior (positive `tol` + all-informative data forced a removal). It now uses a negative `tol` for backward (as the docstring sanctions) and data with uninformative features, so backward selection correctly drops only the uninformative ones.
- Full `test_sequential.py` suite passes locally (75 passed).

issues.title: `CalibratedClassifierCV(method="sigmoid")` should always take the raw logits as inputs instead of the predicted probabilities
issues.body: This is a defect [I first observed while reviewing the temperature scaling PR](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31068#discussion_r2012459507): if the uncalibrated classifier only exposes a `decision_function` and no `predict_proba` (which is the case for SVMs for instance) our implementation of sigmoid calibration (aka Platt-scaling) is fine because the output values of `decision_function` are morally logits between -inf and +inf with 0 as the default decision threshold. But if the uncalibrated classifier already exposes a `predict_proba` method (e.g. `GaussianNB`), our current implementation takes the predicted probabilities as input of the parametrized sigmoid function. This is incorrect: we should the log of the probabilistic predictions (incremented by a small epsilon) to feed logits as inputs to the sigmoid function. I had started an unfinished WIP branch now turned into a draft PR (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34313) to attempt to fix this problem and started to do empirical evaluation to assess the impact of this change in examples. Early results were very promising. However, it would now need work to be sync with main again after the merge of the temperature scaling PR and I got distracted and this was burried in my personal TODO list of WIP stuff to revive. Meanwhile, the following paper by @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller et al. was published, and it confirms that it is empirically much better to take the logits, in which case it is a very competitive calibration method (better than most other calibration methods on average on a large set of data & model pairs). CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30188 Side note: I suspect that OvR Platt-logits followed by post-hoc class-wise renormalization would also work very well in the multiclass setting, but this does not seem to have been explored in the above paper from a cursory glance. Do you confirm @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller?

issues.title: Fix HDBSCAN with non-zero cluster_selection_epsilon on NumPy 2.x
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

  Fixes #33219.
  (#33355 was closed as a duplicate of the same NumPy 2.x issue.)

  #### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

  Fitting `HDBSCAN` with a non-zero `cluster_selection_epsilon` raised on NumPy 2.x:

      TypeError: only 0-dimensional arrays can be converted to Python scalars
  
  In `sklearn/cluster/_hdbscan/_tree.pyx`, `traverse_upwards` assigned the result
  of a boolean-mask lookup (`cluster_tree[...]['parent']` and `['value']`) directly
  to a typed scalar. Those lookups return a **size-1 array**, and NumPy 2.x no longer
  permits the implicit size-1-array-to-scalar conversion that earlier versions
  silently allowed, so the assignment raised.

  This only affects the epsilon code path (`epsilon_search` → `traverse_upwards`),
  which is why it surfaces solely with a non-zero `cluster_selection_epsilon`, for
  both `eom` and `leaf` selection methods.

  The fix indexes the size-1 arrays explicitly with `[0]` to extract the scalar.
  This restores the documented epsilon-merging behavior and matches the output of
  the standalone `hdbscan` package referenced in the issue.

  A non-regression test (`test_hdbscan_epsilon_merges_micro_clusters`, parametrized
  over `eom`/`leaf`) reproduces the crash on hierarchical data (tight micro-clusters
  nested inside far-apart super-clusters) and asserts that a large enough epsilon
  merges them back into the expected super-clusters. It fails with the original
  `TypeError` before the fix and passes after.

  #### First time contributor introduction

  Hi! I use scikit-learn's `HDBSCAN` to cluster text-embedding vectors (for a
  misinformation / fact-checking project), reducing with UMAP first. I hit this
  crash when enabling `cluster_selection_epsilon` to merge nearby micro-clusters,
  traced it to the size-1-array conversion removed in NumPy 2.x, and figured a
  one-line fix plus a regression test was a good first contribution.

  #### AI usage disclosure

  I used AI assistance for:
  - Code generation (e.g., when writing an implementation or fixing a bug)
  - Test/benchmark generation
  - Documentation (including examples)
  - Research and understanding
  
  #### Any other comments?

  The change is minimal and `traverse_upwards` is exercised only on the epsilon
  path. Full `sklearn/cluster/tests/test_hdbscan.py` passes (150 tests), and
  `ruff`/`cython-lint` are clean.

issues.body:
## Summary

Closes #33712

This PR adds a new `replaced_undefined_by` parameter to all classification metric functions that previously used `zero_division` to handle undefined metric cases (e.g. division by zero when no predictions are made for a class). The old `zero_division` parameter is deprecated with a `FutureWarning`.

## Changes

- Added `_check_replaced_undefined_by()` helper function alongside the existing `_check_zero_division()`
- Updated `_prf_divide()` to accept `replaced_undefined_by` kwarg; legacy `zero_division` path preserved
- Updated `_warn_prf()` to show the actual replacement value and reference `replaced_undefined_by` in advice
- Updated all 7 affected public functions:
  - `precision_recall_fscore_support`
  - `precision_score`
  - `recall_score`
  - `f1_score`
  - `fbeta_score`
  - `jaccard_score`
  - `classification_report`
- Updated `@validate_params` constraints for each function
- Default changed from `0` to `np.nan`
- Expanded test suite with 11+ smoke tests covering default behavior, explicit values, multiclass, and deprecation warnings

## Behavior Change

**Before:**
```python
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score
f1_score([1,1,1], [0,0,0])  # => 0.0 + UndefinedMetricWarning
```

**After:**
```python
f1_score([1,1,1], [0,0,0])                              # => nan (new default)
f1_score([1,1,1], [0,0,0], replaced_undefined_by=0.0)  # => 0.0
f1_score([1,1,1], [0,0,0], zero_division=0)             # => 0.0 + FutureWarning (deprecated)
```

issues.title: FIX Nystroem with precomputed kernel and n_components < n_samples
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs

Fixes #29353

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

When kernel="precomputed", Nystroem.fit only subsampled the rows of the
kernel matrix. That left a non-square basis kernel of shape
(n_components, n_samples), so pairwise_kernels raised a ValueError and you
could never set n_components smaller than n_samples with a precomputed
kernel.

The fix takes the square submatrix indexed by basis_inds on both axes for the
basis kernel, and slices the basis columns in transform. A sparse CSR
precomputed kernel is densified with .toarray() before the svd and the
normalization matmul, because np.asarray does not densify scipy sparse
matrices.

I also kept the validation that used to come for free through
pairwise_kernels: gamma, coef0 and degree are still rejected for a
precomputed kernel, and the precomputed fit kernel must be square. A
non-square precomputed kernel now raises a clear error message.

Two new non-regression tests cover this. One checks that fit_transform with a
precomputed RBF kernel and n_components < n_samples matches passing the data
directly with kernel="rbf", for both dense and CSR input. The other checks
the clear error on a non-square precomputed kernel.

#### AI usage disclosure

I used AI assistance for:
- Code generation (e.g., when writing an implementation or fixing a bug)
- Test/benchmark generation
- Research and understanding

I reviewed, built, and tested all of these changes myself, I understand them,
and I can explain them on request.

#### Any other comments?

In the precomputed case components_ is not meaningful and transform expects an
X of the same shape as in fit. jeremiedbb raised both points in the issue. I
left that behavior as is to keep this PR focused on the bug, but happy to
document it or follow up in a separate change if you prefer.

issues.title: BUG: Silent float32 upcasting to float64 in Pipeline/StandardScaler causes 2x memory bloat

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When processing massive financial tick data (e.g., shape `(10_000_000, 50)`), quant systems typically cast down to `np.float32` to keep the data within RAM limits. 

However, passing a `float32` NumPy array through a `Pipeline` containing a `StandardScaler` silently upcasts the transformed output back to `float64`. This creates a silent memory copy that doubles the RAM requirement, frequently triggering Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kills on high-frequency streaming applications.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

# Generate a mock financial tick dataset in float32
X_financial_ticks = np.random.randn(1_000_000, 10).astype(np.float32)

print(f"Input dtype: {X_financial_ticks.dtype}")
print(f"Input memory: {X_financial_ticks.nbytes / 1e6} MB")

# Pass through a standard pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler())
])

X_transformed = pipeline.fit_transform(X_financial_ticks)

print(f"Output dtype: {X_transformed.dtype}")
print(f"Output memory: {X_transformed.nbytes / 1e6} MB")
```

### Expected Results

**Expected Results:**

```
Input dtype: float32
Input memory: 40.0 MB
Output dtype: float32
Output memory: 40.0 MB
```

### Actual Results

**Actual Results:**
```
Input dtype: float32
Input memory: 40.0 MB
Output dtype: float64
Output memory: 80.0 MB  <-- 100% memory bloat
```


### Versions

I would like to investigate the `check_array` / `dtype` handling inside `StandardScaler.transform` to ensure it respects the input dtype without silently upcasting, provided the user explicitly inputs float32.

issues.title: FIX SimpleImputer with missing_values=None
issues.body:
#### Reference Issues/PRs
Fixes #19071.
This also takes over the stalled direction from #19079 with a smaller scoped patch.

#### What does this implement/fix? 
`SimpleImputer` documents `missing_values=None` as supported, but numeric strategies such as `mean` and `median` failed for object arrays containing `None`. Validation converted the data before the imputer could build a mask for `None`, so users got a NaN validation error instead of imputation.

This PR keeps object ndarray inputs as object long enough to compute the missing-value mask, then converts the masked numeric data to `float64` for the existing mean/median computation. It also keeps `None` and `np.nan` distinct for object arrays, while ppreserving the existing list-input behavior where `None` is treated as `np.nan` when `missing_values=np.nan`.

Tests added for:
- `missing_values=None` with `mean` and `median`
- object arrays containing both `None` and `np.nan`
- the existing list input behavior with `missing_values=np.nan`

- `pytest sklearn/impute/tests/test_impute.py -q`

issues.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

Because of the ongoing Mini Shai Hulud attack against CI & OSS supply chain (see [Postmortem: TanStack npm supply-chain compromise](https://tanstack.com/blog/npm-supply-chain-compromise-postmortem) for details), I think we should review and possibly straighten our CI before releasing 1.9.

In particular, we use the unsafe `pull_request_target` in several workflows which is a documented attack vector of the Mini Shai-Hulud worm that currently still spreads by corrupting an increasing number of npm and pypi packages.

## Short term:

- Regularly check that the dates of https://pypi.org/project/scikit-learn/#files match our manually triggered release dates (this seems to be the case as of today 2026-05-13)
- Review our `publish_pypi.yml` and `wheels.yml` workflows to make sure it is not subject by cache poisoning attacks (from a cursory glance it does not think we use any build cache, but we should double-check).
- Review findings reported by `zizmor .github/workflows/publish_pypi.yml` and `zizmor .github/workflows/wheels.yml`.
- Assess if workflows that use `pull_request_target` can have a side effect on our release process.
  - Note: I asked the following to Claude: https://claude.ai/share/c6aea06a-a9dc-4e55-b5f4-830254166994 (TL;DNR it isn't too worried, but we should probably spend more time reading this analysis in more details).
- Unzip and review the contents of the generated wheel files in the release branch prior to uploading to look for unexpected payload.
  - EDIT: I asked Claude (same conversation as the one linked above) to do that on the latest nightly wheel and it did not find anything fishy.

## Medium/Long term

- Hash-pin all github actions used in the `publish_pypi.yml` and `wheels.yml` workflows.
- Use relative dependency cooldown for GitHub Actions updates via dependabot:
  - https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/supply-chain-security/dependabot-options-reference?versionId=free-pro-team%40latest&productId=code-security&restPage=tutorials%2Csecure-your-dependencies%2Cautomating-dependabot-with-github-actions#cooldown-
- Find ways to avoid the use of `pull_request_target` in our regular dev CI.
- Address any remaining "findings" reported by running `zizmor .` in our repo (currently `191 findings (73 suppressed, 32 fixable): 4 informational, 26 low, 1 medium, 87 high`, many of which are related to `pull_request_target` and unpinned action references).
- Use relative dependency cooldowns when generating lock files as soon as implemented in mamba and conda-lock:
  - https://github.com/conda/conda-lock/issues/908
  - https://github.com/mamba-org/mamba/pull/4228
- Isolate the release process in a dedicated repo with a easy to audit, limited number of config files/action logs/user permissions, see:
  - https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/29178
  - https://github.com/numpy/numpy-release
  - https://github.com/scipy/scipy-release


I labeled this PR as block as I think we should at least do the short terms items prior to releasing.

We can probably create sub-issues for things we agree are good ideas.

issues.title: ENH TimeSeriesSplit: add walk_forward rolling-origin mode
issues.body:
## Summary

This PR adds an **opt-in walk-forward / rolling-origin mode** to
`sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit` via:

- `n_splits="walk_forward"` (sentinel mode)
- `min_train_size` to specify the initial training window size for expanding walk-forward evaluation
- `step` to control the stride between successive test starts

The goal is to support walk-forward evaluation workflows commonly used in time
series forecasting, while preserving existing `TimeSeriesSplit` behavior for
integer `n_splits`.

## Motivation

`TimeSeriesSplit` is currently primarily **`n_splits`-driven** ("choose number of
folds, then infer fold boundaries"). A common alternative workflow is
**window-size-driven** ("choose initial train length, test horizon, stride, and
derive how many splits exist from the data length").

This PR provides that window-size-driven workflow as an explicit opt-in mode via
`n_splits="walk_forward"`.

## API

### Expanding (cumulative) walk-forward

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

cv = TimeSeriesSplit(
    n_splits="walk_forward",
    min_train_size=1260,
    test_size=1,
    step=21,
    gap=0,
)
```

### Rolling (fixed-size) train window walk-forward

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

cv = TimeSeriesSplit(
    n_splits="walk_forward",
    max_train_size=1260,
    test_size=1,
    step=21,
    gap=0,
)
```

## Walk-forward mode semantics

In `n_splits="walk_forward"` mode:

- `test_size` defines the width of each test window.
- `gap` keeps its existing meaning: number of samples excluded between the end
  of train and start of test.
- `step` defines the stride between successive test starts (defaults to 1 if not
  provided).
- The training window is:
  - **expanding** when `max_train_size=None` (uses `min_train_size` to define the
    first train window), or
  - **rolling** when `max_train_size` is provided (fixed-size training window).

Note: depending on `step` and `test_size`, successive test windows may overlap.

## Validation / parameter rules (walk_forward)

- `test_size` must be specified.
- `step` must be a positive integer (defaults to 1 if not provided).
- `gap` must be a non-negative integer.
- Exactly one of `min_train_size` or `max_train_size` must be provided:
  - expanding mode: `min_train_size` is required and `max_train_size=None`
  - rolling mode: `max_train_size` is required and `min_train_size=None`

In `n_splits="walk_forward"` mode, the number of splits depends on `n_samples`,
so `get_n_splits(X)` uses `X` to infer the number of feasible splits.

## Backward compatibility

- Existing behavior for integer `n_splits` remains unchanged.
- Walk-forward semantics are opt-in via `n_splits="walk_forward"`.
- `step` and `min_train_size` are only valid in walk-forward mode.

This uses a sentinel `n_splits="walk_forward"` opt-in to avoid ambiguity and
preserve the existing integer `n_splits` semantics, consistent with prior
discussion in #23780.

## Example usage

Expanding walk-forward example:

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

X = np.arange(20)

splitter = TimeSeriesSplit(
    n_splits="walk_forward",
    min_train_size=5,
    test_size=2,
    gap=1,
    step=3,
)

print("Number of splits:", splitter.get_n_splits(X))

for i, (train_idx, test_idx) in enumerate(splitter.split(X)):
    print(
        f"Split {i}: "
        f"train [{train_idx[0]}:{train_idx[-1]+1}], "
        f"test [{test_idx[0]}:{test_idx[-1]+1}]"
    )
    if i >= 3:
        print("...")
        break
```

Expected output:

```text
Number of splits: 5
Split 0: train [0:5], test [6:8]
Split 1: train [0:8], test [9:11]
Split 2: train [0:11], test [12:14]
Split 3: train [0:14], test [15:17]
...
```

## Related issues / prior discussion

- Addresses #22523 (rolling/sliding / walk-forward time series splitting):
  https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/22523

issues.title: Add "auto" option as default solver to GLMs
issues.body:
Currently, our GLMS like `LogisticRegression`, `PoissonRegressor` and others have default `solver="lbfgs"`. Unfortunately, this solver cannot solve L1-penalized objectives. Therefore, `LogisticRegression(l1_ratio=1)` errors.

I propose to change the default solver to `"auto"` with the meaning:
1. The solver chosen may change from version to version. (But this should happen rarely.)
2. The solver chosen is fit for the purpose no matter which panalty is chosen.
3. Start with
   - No penalty and L2 penalties: `"lbfgs"`
   - L1 and enet: `"saga"`, or, if #33160 gets merged first, one of the new `"newton-cd"` methods

Linked to / duplication of #5736

issues.title: FIX Prevent segfault in TSNE with PCA init on constant data
issues.body:
#### Reference Issue
Fixes #28368 (ref: #32788 which is a duplicate issue)

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This PR fixes a bug where `TSNE` with `init='pca'` produces `NaN` values (leading to potential segmentation faults in the C++ extension) when the input data has zero variance (constant values).

**The Issue:**
In `_t_sne.py`, the PCA initialization step attempts to normalize the first principal component by dividing by its standard deviation: `X_embedded / np.std(...)`. When the input data is constant, the standard deviation is `0.0`, resulting in `NaN` propagation.

**The Fix:**
I added a safe-guard check for the standard deviation.
- If `std < 1e-12` (effectively zero), the division is skipped, and the embedding is only scaled by the default factor (`1e-4`).
- Otherwise, the standard normalization logic is applied.

**Verification:**
Added a regression test `test_tsne_pca_init_constant_data` in `sklearn/manifold/tests/test_t_sne.py` which asserts that fitting on a constant matrix (`np.ones`) produces finite values and does not crash.

#### Other comments
The fix uses a tolerance check (`< 1e-12`) rather than strict equality (`== 0`) to handle floating-point nuances, ensuring robustness for near-constant data.

issues.title: Add class_weight support to Naive Bayes models (GaussianNB, MultinomialNB, BernoulliNB)
issues.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Naive Bayes classifiers (GaussianNB, MultinomialNB, BernoulliNB, ComplementNB, CategoricalNB) currently do not support the class_weight parameter, while almost all other scikit-learn classifiers do. This creates API inconsistency and requires users to manually compute and pass sample_weight for imbalanced datasets.

# Current Workaround

```py
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.utils.class_weight import compute_sample_weight
sample_weight = compute_sample_weight('balanced', y)
gnb = GaussianNB()
gnb.fit(X, y, sample_weight=sample_weight)
```

# Proposed Enhancement

```py
gnb = GaussianNB(class_weight='balanced')
gnb.fit(X, y)
```


### Describe your proposed solution

Add a class_weight parameter to all Naive Bayes classifiers that internally converts class weights to sample weights before calling the existing fit() logic. This leverages the fact that all NB classifiers already support sample_weight in their fitting methods.

```py
class GaussianNB(_BaseNB):
    _parameter_constraints: dict = {
        "priors": ["array-like", None],
        "var_smoothing": [Interval(Real, 0, None, closed="left")],
        "class_weight": ["dict", "balanced", None],  # NEW
    }

    def __init__(self, *, priors=None, var_smoothing=1e-9, class_weight=None):
        self.priors = priors
        self.var_smoothing = var_smoothing
-->  self.class_weight = class_weight 
```


### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

This is a improvement for API consistency. While the workaround exists, having uniform behavior across classifiers reduces confusion and improves discoverability, especially for beginners.

issues.title: DEP deprecate LogisticRegression parameters C, introduce new regularization parameter alpha

labels.name: High Priority
labels.description: High priority issues and pull requests

milestone.description: Planning for the 1.10 release: - November 2, 2026: Release candidate 1.10.0.dev0 - November, 16 2026: Release 1.10.0

issues.body:
### Reference Issues/PRs
Closes #28711.
Related to #11865.

**Update June 2026** (scikit-learn sprint)

### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This PR
- for class `LogisticRegression`
  - deprecates parameter `C` in 1.10
    - will raise warning in 1.12
    - will remove `C` in 1.14
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alpha`
  - sets default `alpha="1/n_samples" such that it is the same as `C=1`
- for class `LogisticRegressionCV`
  - deprecates the parameter `Cs` 
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alphas`
  - deprecates attributes `C_` and `Cs_` in 1.10, removal in 1.14 
  - introduces new attributes `alpha_` and `alphas_`

<details>

**NOTE**: This "details" contains the outdate/old content.

**Update March 2026** after merge of #32659.

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
This PR
- for class `LogisticRegression`
  - deprecates parameter `C` 
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alpha`
  - ~~deprecates the parameter `penalty`~~
  - ~~changes the default of `l1_ratio` from `None` to `0`~~
- for class `LogisticRegressionCV`
  - deprecates the parameter `Cs` 
  - introduces the new penalty parameter `alphas`
  - deprecates attributes `C_` and `Cs_`
  - introduces new attributes `alpha_` and `alphas_`
  - ~~deprecates parameter `penalty`~~
  - ~~changes the default of `l1_ratios` from `None` to `(0,)`~~
- for class `StackingClassifier`
  - Additional informative warning for default `final_estimator=None` which uses `LogisticRegression()`
 
</details>

**Note:** Together with #32659, the way to specify penalties is then 100% aligned with 
- `SGDClassifier(alpha=.., loss="log_loss")` (this is even the identical model!)
- `ElasticNet(alpha=.., l1_ratio=..)`
- `Lasso(alpha=)`
- `PoissonRegressor(alpha=)`
- other GLMs

All use `1/(2n) * sum(deviance loss) + alpha/2 * ||w||_2`. See #15657 for further reasons of this choice.

For historians, the parameter `scale_C` which devided `C` by `n_samples` was once deprecated in #821.

<details>

**NOTE:** This is outdated content.

#### Open questions
1. Default `alpha`
   While the future default is currently `alpha=1`, a much smaller value might be better in practice, e.g. alpha=1e-4. Tiny regularization is also the main effect of `C=1` as it scales the penalty by 1/n_samples.

   For optimal prediction $p=P(Y|X)$, the expected log loss is the Shannon entropy (up to a factor) $E[log loss] = H(p) = -p \log(p) - (1-p)\log(1-p)$. The maximum is achieved at p=0.5 with H=0.69, some more values: H(1e-3) = 0.007, H(1e-6) = 1.5e-5. This shows, that `alpha=1` is a pretty strong penalty (for features of scale 1 or smaller).

2. Depending on the default of `alpha`, a good default for `StackingClassifier(final_estimator=..)` is basically no or tiny regularization.

</details>

### Any other comments?
This will be a highly controversial issue, therefore a lot of fun ahead 🎉 

<details>

**Outdated content**
**The main reason for this change is that the current API is objectively bad design.** ~~Currently, I need to specify 3 parameters (`penalty`, `C`, `l1_ratio`) for just 2 effective parameters (the L1 and L2 penalization). On top, it warns a lot when mixing those, e.g. `penalty="l2"` and `l1_ratio=0`, but why on earth...~~

</details>

#### More arguments for `alpha` instead of `C`
1. API consistency: LogisticRegression is the only linear model using an anti-penalty `C`, all the others use penalty `alpha`, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/28711#issuecomment-2030156413.
4. Literature:
  - The invention of using a Ridge penalty with logistic regression, https://www.jstor.org/stable/2347628 (Cessie et al 1992), uses a penalty (like `alpha`) and not an anti-penalty (like `C`). The papers for Lasso & Elastic-Net in combination with logreg do the same (use penalty like `alpha`).
  - I have a hard time (=I did not succeed) to find any (famous) ML book like ESL using the anti-penalty.
5. Other reference packages: The most famous R package glmnet (and others) uses a penalty (like `alpha`, they call it `lambda`, but that does not work in Python) and not an anti-penalty (like `C`).
6. Point of view of optimization: the penalty (like `alpha`) version can be seen as regularization to prevent singular behaviour (analogous to Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm), see Nocedal.
7. Original decision and discussion: I cannot find any discussion about the original introduction of `C` vs. `alpha` in LogisticRegression in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/commit/2993becc3dde6c15b11e0f79a05dc8bc022fd9cb. My guess is that liblinear's parameter names were just inherited.
8. Practicality: One never needs `C=0` (`alpha=np.inf`), but `C=np.inf` (`alpha=0`) is used very often. Zero is a much better defined value than infinity.
9. `C` interferes with class weights. Higher class weights means less regularization.
10. The main reason for `C` (and IFAIC its origin) is the analogy with support vector machines. SVM were once very powerful, but have become less and less important in practice. My prediction: this trend will continue.

#### Study of possible default values for the penalty
See https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32042#issuecomment-4366344257 and the linked notebook https://github.com/lorentzenchr/notebooks/blob/master/logistic_regression_optimal_penalty.ipynb.

issues.title: pairwise_distances_argmin_min / ArgKMin64 is not thread-safe
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

Problem found while test investigating failures found in #30041. I crafted a minimal reproducer below. It might be caused by a race condition (corruption) of shared intermediate buffers used in OpenMP threads.

Some remarks:

- the problem happens with either strategy ("parallel_on_X" vs "parallel_on_Y");
- running the reproducer with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` hides the problem;
- running the reproducer with a lower than default value for `OMP_NUM_THREADS` makes the problem less likely to happen;
- using `threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=1, user_api="openmp")` does not hide the problem for some reason...

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.metrics._pairwise_distances_reduction._argkmin import ArgKmin64
import numpy as np
from joblib import delayed, Parallel
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_info
from pprint import pprint

pprint(threadpool_info())
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = rng.randn(97, 149)
Y = rng.randn(111, 149)


# Note: strategy does not matter.

    k=1, metric="euclidean", strategy="parallel_on_X", return_distance=True
)
```

issues.title: Add Accumulated local effects (ALE) to inspection

labels.name: Moderate
labels.description: Anything that requires some knowledge of conventions and best practices

issues.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'd love to push the inspection module further by adding Accumulated local effects (ALE) from Apley 2020. A great description can be found in Christoph's online book https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/ale.html

ALE fix the problem of partial dependence that they force the model to be evaluated on impossible or rare feature combinations. ALE are defined for numeric features that can be binned. From both bin edges, the slope of the partial dependence is calculated locally, i.e., only using observations in the bin. The slopes from all bins are cumsummed and vertically centered to the average response or prediction.

### Reference

Apley, Daniel W., and Jingyu Zhu. 2020. Visualizing the Effects of Predictor Variables in Black Box Supervised Learning Models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology, 82 (4): 1059–1086. doi:10.1111/rssb.12377.

### Describe your proposed solution

Pseudo code to calculate ALE for one feature:

``` py
pd_slopes = np.zeros_like(bins)

for i, bin in enumerate(bins):
  X_bin = pick n_per_bin = 200 rows from data in bin
  if X_bin is empty:
    next
  pd = partial_dependence_brute(model, X_bin, grid = [lower bin edge, upper bin edge], sample_weights)
  pd_slopes[i] = pd[1] - pd[0]

return np.cumsum(pd_slopes)
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

issues.title: Try running examples in parallel during doc build
issues.body:
We are already using sphinx-gallery 0.17 which has added the feature to run examples in parallel see https://github.com/sphinx-gallery/sphinx-gallery/pull/877. See [sphinx-gallery doc](https://sphinx-gallery.github.io/stable/configuration.html#parallel) for how to configure it.

matplotlib is currently trying it and it seems to show interesting improvements in their CI see https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/28617#issuecomment-2252108112.

I expect that for scikit-learn the speed-up may be a little bit less than for matplotlib since some examples are already using multiple cores (e.g. with `n_jobs=2`). I had a quick look during the sphinx-gallery PR and it was making the doc a bit quicker locally: https://github.com/sphinx-gallery/sphinx-gallery/pull/877#issuecomment-2184534205.

General directions:
- configure sphinx-gallery to use 2 cores in `doc/conf.py`
```py
sphinx_gallery_conf = {
    ...
    'parallel': 2,
}
```
- open a PR with `[doc build]` commit to do a full build
- also generate the doc locally e.g. with `spin docs clean` + `spin docs html` and see how much sphinx-gallery parallel settings make a difference

labels.name: autoclose

issues.body:
<!--
Thanks for contributing a pull request! Please ensure you have taken a look at
the contribution guidelines: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
-->

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.

In the GP regression `sample_y` method, `rng.multivariate_normal` is called with its default `method` argument, i.e. "svd". This is fine when `sample_y` is called on a small number of points, but I found that for a large set of evaluation points, this could get quite costly. 

Using the example in the docs,

```python 
X = np.linspace(start=0, stop=10, num=1_000).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.squeeze(X * np.sin(X))

gpr = GaussianProcessRegressor(Matern(nu=2.5))

_ = gpr.fit(X,y)

x_sample = np.random.uniform(0,10,1000)
_ = gpr.sample_y(x_sample)
# takes 0.6 seconds, of which 0.4 is in multivariate_normal 

x_sample = np.random.uniform(0,10,5000)
_ = gpr.sample_y(x_sample)
# takes 38 seconds, of which 36 is in multivariate_normal 
```
Repeating the same exercise with `method = "cholesky"` in `rng.multivariate_normal` reduces the runtime to a much more reasonable 2.5 seconds. 


#### Any other comments?

I kept the default to "svd" so users shouldnt see any change unless they opt in.

issues.title: FEAT Polynomial Chaos Expansions
issues.body:
*Note: I've labeled this PR as [MRG], following [this section](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/contributing.html#pull-request-checklist) from the Developer's Guide, but please let me know if this is inappropriate at this stage.*

## What is it?

The [Polynomial Chaos expansion (PCE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial_chaos) is a supervised learning technique that is used to represent and propagate uncertainties in complex models. It is a well-known tool for sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification, that has been used in a variety of applications, see, for example, [[Ghanem1991](https://books.google.com/books/about/Stochastic_Finite_Elements.html?id=WzgKyTQQcAwC)] and [[Najm2009](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/abs/10.1146/annurev.fluid.010908.165248)].

The basic idea is to represent the parameters (input features) of the model as random variables with an associated probability density function. The model output, which is also a random variable, is then expressed as a polynomial function of the input random variables.

The Polynomial Chaos methodology has found widespread use in engineering and applied sciences in the last decades, because it presents a systematic and efficient framework for dealing with parameteric uncertainty in mathematical models.

This is a proposal for an implementation that adds Polynomial Chaos expansions to `scikit-learn`.

## How does it work?

Given a set of input features $X$, sampled from an assumed distribution, the Polynomial Chaos approximation for the model output $y = f(X)$ is

$$ y = \sum_{j} c_j \Psi_j(X),$$

where $\Psi_j$ is a multivariate orthogonal polynomial basis function, and $c_j$ is a coefficient in the expansion. The type of orthogonal polynomial depends on the assumed distribution for the input features. For example, the [uniform distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_uniform_distribution) is associated with the [Legendre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_polynomials) polynomials, the [normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution) is associated with the [Hermite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite_polynomials) polynomials, and other distributions can be matched to similar orthogonal polynomials from the [Askey scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Askey_scheme), see [[Xiu2002](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/pdf/10.1137/S1064827501387826)].

![polynomials](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/assets/15999604/a1cf5cb4-8a24-4f2d-9b6c-8f1952a8442f)

*(Note that I'm deliberately ignoring some mathematical details in this description - I do take care of these in the actual implementation.)*

## Implementation details

In `scikit-learn` language, the PCE can be interpreted as a pipeline with a nonlinear [tranformer](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/data_transforms.html) that transforms the input features into orthogonal polynomial features, followed by a [linear regression](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression.html) step:

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrthogonalPolynomialFeatures # new

pce = Pipeline([
    ('transformer', OrthogonalPolynomialFeatures()),
    ('linear_model', LinearRegression())
])
```

Thus, this PR introduces two new classes: `OrthogonalPolynomialFeatures` and `PolynomialChaosRegressor`. The former is a transformer class that is an extension of the existing [PolynomialFeatures](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.PolynomialFeatures.html) class, but uses orthogonal polynomials instead of simple monomials. The latter is a [`BaseEstimator`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.base.BaseEstimator.html) that implements the pipeline described above.

After fitting, the PCE can be used as a surrogate model to replace further evaluations of the model problem (using the [`predict`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/tutorial/statistical_inference/supervised_learning.html) method from the `BaseEstimator` class).

## Why add Polynomial Chaos expansions to `scikit-learn`?

Existing tools for constructing PCEs are either not written in Python ([uqlab](https://www.uqlab.com/), [dakota](https://dakota.sandia.gov/about-dakota/)), have poor performance in high dimensions ([chaospy](https://github.com/jonathf/chaospy)) or have complex API designs ([pygpc](https://github.com/pygpc-polynomial-chaos/pygpc)). Recognizing these limitations, I believe there is a clear opportunity for a well-designed PCE tool that overcomes these issues.

The construction scheme (a pipeline with a nonlinear `transformer` followed by a `linear_model`) outlined in the previous section, aligns seamlessly with `scikit-learn`s modular API. In addition, we can use the many [`linear_model`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/classes.html#module-sklearn.linear_model)s in `scikit-learn` to help avoid overfitting, a common problem when constructing PCEs with noisy and/or limited data. It's worth mentioning that `chaospy` and `pygpc` already rely on `scikit-learn` estimators for similar purposes.

To illustrate the efficiency statement above, we compare the performance of `chaospy`, `pygpc` and the [scikit-learn implementation](https://github.com/PieterjanRobbe/scikit-learn/tree/polynomial_chaos) by constructing a PCE for the Sobol function in 4 dimensions (i.e., 4 input features). The [Sobol function](https://www.sfu.ca/~ssurjano/gfunc.html) is a well-known test function in sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification.

![timing-dim4](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/assets/15999604/47588ae3-bd65-4615-9020-e98d8cb15e9b)

The figure on the left shows the time needed to construct the PCE as a function of the maximum degree of the polynomials in the expansion. The figure on the right shows the same, but now with a logarithmic vertical axis. The `scikit-learn` implementation is significantly faster than the established tools, depite the reasonably moderate dimension. When considering dimensions other than 4, we observe a similar or even better speedup, see [this notebook](https://github.com/PieterjanRobbe/scikit-learn-polynomial-chaos-benchmarks/blob/main/comparison.ipynb).

## Global Sensitivity Analysis

A common postprocessing step after the Polynomial Chaos expansion has been fitted is to perform a [Global Sensitivity Analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensitivity_analysis) by computing the so-called [Sobol sensitivity indices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance-based_sensitivity_analysis). These indices rank the input features by importance, by computing what fraction of the variance of the output they explain. When a PCE surrogate model has been fitted, these indices can be computed analytically, see for example [[Sudret2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0951832007001329)].

In the proposed implementation, the sensitivity indices can be computed by calling the `main_sens()` and `total_sens()` methods against an instance of the `PolynomialChaosRegressor` class.

As a side note, I found [this PR](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/22453) that also discusses Global Sensitivity Analysis. However, the method proposed in the latter PR is a pure sampling-based method, and sensitivities extracted from Polynomial Chaos expansions can be a lot more reliable (see the Ishigami example in the documentation for a comparison between the two).

## Motiviation

This porposal has mainly been written because of my disappointment with the existing tools. I regularly use Polynomial Chaos expansions for research purposes, and not having a reliable, scalable and user-friendly implementation available has hurt me on more than one occasion. Hence the motivation to supply my own implementation.

I sincerely welcome feedback and collaborations to make this porposal a valuable addition to the `scikit-learn` ecosystem. Thanks!

## References

The [**number**] after each reference indicates the number of citations (following Google scholar).

[[Ghanem1991](https://books.google.com/books/about/Stochastic_Finite_Elements.html?id=WzgKyTQQcAwC)] Ghanem, R. G., and Spanos, P. D. "Stochastic finite elements: a spectral approach", Springer New York, 1991. [**8500+**]

[[Xiu2002](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/pdf/10.1137/S1064827501387826)] Xiu, D., and Karniadakis, G. M. "The Wiener-Askey polynomial chaos for stochastic differential equations." *SIAM Journal on scientific computing* 24(2), 2002. [**5500+**]

[[Sudret2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0951832007001329)] Sudret, B. "Global sensitivity analysis using polynomial chaos expansions." *Reliability engineering & system safety* 93(7), 2008. [**2500+**]

[[Najm2009](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/abs/10.1146/annurev.fluid.010908.165248)] Najm, H. N. "Uncertainty quantification and polynomial chaos techniques in computational fluid dynamics." *Annual review of fluid mechanics* 41, 2009. [**1000+**]

issues.title: [MRG] partial_fit for BayesianGaussianMixture

labels.name: autoclose
labels.description: PR automatically closed 14 days after setting the label

issues.body:
#### Reference Issue
Implements #8714 Online Inference for BayesianGaussianMixture

#### What does this implement/fix? Explain your changes.
Implements a partial_fit() method for BayesianGaussianMixture models, which allows for online or minibatch inference.  It simply sets the posterior from the previous fit as the new prior,  a method known as [Streaming Variational Inference](http://proceedings.mlr.press/v45/Huynh15.pdf).  Under very mild conditions, the expectation of the posterior on each batch forms an unbiased estimate of the posterior on the whole data, so after going through all batches the models will be very similar.  Due to the stochastic nature of the fitting process, it often reaches a lower Evidence Lower Bound than fitting the model to the whole dataset, because it is less likely to get stuck in local minima during optimization.

I included an example identical to the one comparing Bayesian and non-Bayesian mixture models, but with many more samples to take advantage of the speed increase.

#### Any other comments?
Was not sure what tests were required/useful, since it just sets a few parameters and then makes use of the existing fit() function which has its own tests.  I also wanted add the image from the example to the mixture docs but couldn't figure out how auto_examples worked.
