issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Follow-up to #142171, addressing https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142171#pullrequestreview-5293434424.

`minConstraint` and `maxConstraint` each read both sides of a resource: min also rejects an unchanged limit below the minimum, and max also rejects an unchanged request above the maximum. #142171 skipped both checks together only when the request AND the limit both matched the stored container. A resize that changes only one side re-ran the check on the side that didn't move, rejecting a value already accepted before the LimitRange tightened — the exact case in the linked review comment, a request-only resize getting rejected on a limit that never changed.

`minConstraint` and `maxConstraint` now take a `skipRequest` and a `skipLimit` flag, guarding only the half of the check that reads that side. The limit-to-request ratio still requires both unchanged, since it reads both to compute one value; changing either side can change the ratio itself. Applied at both the container and the pod level, the same two places #142171 wired the ratchet through.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166. Follow-up to #142171.

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Three new cases in `TestLimitRangerValidatePodResize`: a container's over-max limit staying unchanged while only its request resizes (the reviewed scenario), the symmetric case for an under-min request while only the limit resizes, and the same at the pod level. Checked against a pre-fix checkout that all three fail there and pass here.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
LimitRanger's resize ratchet from #142171 now skips the request-side and the limit-side check of a resource independently: a resize that only changes one side no longer re-validates the other, unchanged side against a min or max it no longer satisfies.
```


YES. Used to check the diagnosis and fix against the source (a second pass after my own), and to help draft and format this description.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Fixes #142357: `usesIndivisibleHugePagesValues` scans the whole old pod spec and sets a single `AllowIndivisibleHugePagesValues` flag if any container, the pod-level resources, or the overhead held one indivisible hugepages value anywhere. `validateResourceQuantityHugePageValue` skips the divisibility check for every hugepages entry in the new spec whenever that flag is true — so a brand-new indivisible value in an unrelated container, or a different indivisible value under the same resource name, ratchets off a stored value it was never equal to.

`GetValidationOptionsFromPodSpecAndMeta` already builds `StoredResourceQuantities` from the old spec for the #141166 burndown, and `validateResourceQuantityHugePageValue` already checks it at the same location as the general resource-quantity ratchet — this is the same fix #142323 applied to RuntimeClass's `overhead`, which had the identical whole-object blanket-flag pattern. This PR drops the blanket flag and its now-unused helpers for pods too, and relies on the per-value match alone: an unchanged stored value still passes, a new or different one is validated in full, same as on create.

This PR is stacked on #142323 — it depends on the `StoredResourceQuantities` plumbing that PR adds, and the diff here is only the last commit (`048b6071494`); everything before it is #142323's own commits. Can't land before that one merges.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142357
Related to #141166

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Only the last commit is new; the rest is #142323 for context since this branches off it.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed a pod/pod-template validation gap where a stored hugepages value that was indivisible by the hugepages size let any other, unrelated hugepages value in the same pod skip that same check, even a brand-new one that was never itself accepted.
```

#### What happened?

`GetValidationOptionsFromPodSpecAndMeta` sets `PodValidationOptions.AllowIndivisibleHugePagesValues` from `usesIndivisibleHugePagesValues(oldPodSpec)`, a single bool for the whole pod: true if *any* container, the pod-level resources, or the overhead in the old spec held a hugepages value that isn't a positive integer multiple of the hugepages size. `validateResourceQuantityHugePageValue` skips the divisibility check entirely for every hugepages entry in the *new* spec whenever that flag is true.

That means once one container's stored hugepages value happens to be indivisible (the known case is an old `2^64`-scale value that overflowed the divisibility check before it existed), a completely unrelated, brand-new indivisible hugepages value anywhere else in the same pod — a different container, a different hugepages size, a value that was never stored anywhere before — also passes validation. The flag is supposed to grandfather in a specific stored value; instead it opens the check for the whole object.

#### What did you expect to happen?

Only the exact stored `(container, resource name, quantity)` that was already accepted should be exempt from the divisibility check on update. A hugepages value that's new, or under a different resource name, or under a different container, should be validated in full — same as it would be on create.

#### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Given a Pod (or a Deployment/ReplicaSet/etc. pod template, which goes through the same options builder) with two containers:

```yaml
containers:
- name: a
  resources:
    limits: {hugepages-2Mi: 18446744073709551616}   # already indivisible, already stored
    ...
- name: b
  resources:
    limits: {}   # no hugepages at all
    ...
```

Update it, leaving container `a` untouched, and adding a brand-new, itself-indivisible value to container `b`:

```yaml
containers:
- name: a
  resources:
    limits: {hugepages-2Mi: 18446744073709551616}   # unchanged
    ...
- name: b
  resources:
    limits: {hugepages-1Gi: 3Mi}   # new, not a multiple of 1Gi
    ...
```

This update is accepted. It should be rejected the same way a fresh pod with `hugepages-1Gi: 3Mi` and no prior indivisible values anywhere is rejected (`3Mi is not positive integer multiple of hugepages-1Gi`).

#### Anything else we need to know?

RuntimeClass's `overhead` field had the identical pattern (a whole-object blanket flag) until kubernetes/kubernetes#142323, which narrowed it there to an exact stored-value match using `PodValidationOptions.StoredResourceQuantities` (already computed for the #141166 burndown). `GetValidationOptionsFromPodSpecAndMeta` already builds that same `StoredResourceQuantities` set for pods, and `validateResourceQuantityHugePageValue` already checks it there — the only missing piece for pods is that `usesIndivisibleHugePagesValues` still sets the wider flag on top of it, which shadows the precise check. A fix (drops the blanket flag and its now-dead helpers, relies on the existing per-value match alone, adds a regression test) is ready and PR'd; it's stacked on #142323 since it depends on that PR's `StoredResourceQuantities` plumbing, and can't land before it.

#### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
```
master (unreleased)
</details>

#### Cloud provider

<details>
N/A — validation-only, does not depend on a specific provider.
</details>

/sig api-machinery

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

With `DRAFractionalCapacityRange` on, `validateRequestPolicyValidValues` decides whether two options are the same by comparing `AsDec().String()`. That string tracks the Dec scale, not the value, so `1` and `1.0` come out as `"1"` and `"1.0"` and both are accepted. `1.0Ki` and `1.00Ki` happen to match today only because `ParseQuantity` pads every Dec value to nano scale. #141306 stops padding anything already at nano scale or coarser, and with it applied the two keys come out as `"1024.0"` and `"1024.00"`, so that pair is accepted as well.

The list is already required to be sorted, which puts equal values next to each other. Under the gate I now compare each adjacent pair with `Cmp` in the pass that checks the order, and report the second one as the duplicate. The key is gone entirely, which also takes care of `1e100000` producing a key a hundred thousand characters long. Integer mode is untouched and still keys on `Value()`. The existing test has `9.9` next to `10` count as one option there, and it still does.

A list past the size limit is still reported by that limit and not entry by entry, as before, together with any order error. An unsorted list that repeats a value is reported for the order alone, since the duplicate is only looked for between neighbours. Two of the #141166 markers in `validation_device_capacity_test.go` go away, and there are new rows for `1.0Ki` against `1.00Ki`, an out-of-order repeat, an oversized list of one value, a pair built with `NewScaledQuantity` at two different scales so the case does not depend on how the parser pads, and values with an exponent of 100000. On the update side, a stored pair of spellings is left alone by a label change and checked again when its capacity changes; a list of ten identical values, the size limit, reports nine duplicates.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This is stricter under the gate, inside the ratchet that is already there. `validateDevice` skips capacity validation when a device's capacity map is unchanged, so a stored pair of spellings is left alone by a metadata-only update and rechecked when that map changes. #141644 moves that boundary up to `spec.devices`, and I'll rebase onto it once it merges.

The duplicate error reports `1Ki` where it used to report `1024.000000000`, and a value with a huge exponent reports its short form where it used to echo the hundred-thousand-digit key.

I left the integer-mode saturation markers alone. Dropping `Value()` there changes which fractional values count as one option, and that wants its own discussion.

#141306 should merge after this one.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
With DRAFractionalCapacityRange enabled, a ResourceSlice whose requestPolicy.validValues lists the same quantity more than once is now rejected, whichever way the quantity is spelled. An update that leaves a device's capacity unchanged is not affected.
```


#### What this PR does / why we need it:

In `the_real_fifo.go`, `RealFIFO.whileProcessing_locked` holds the FIFO lock during batch processing whenever the queue exceeds `2 * batchSize` (2000 items) to prevent unbounded growth. While that lock is held, the reflector cannot push new watch events into the queue.

To get back below the 2000-item threshold and release the lock quickly, `RealFIFO.PopBatch` needs to drain up to `batchSize` (1000) items at once and apply them under a single store write lock in `threadSafeMap.Transaction` (`thread_safe_store.go`). However, `PopBatch` currently breaks the batch as soon as it sees a duplicate key. When a small set of objects updates repeatedly, batch sizes collapse from 1000 down to single or double digits. The queue stays stuck above 2000 items, the FIFO lock stays held across many tiny batches, the store's `RWMutex` write lock is acquired dozens of times instead of once, and the reflector is starved.

This change removes the duplicate-key break in `RealFIFO.PopBatch` (`the_real_fifo.go`) and tracks per-key state across the batch in `processDeltasInBatch` (`controller.go`) so `OnAdd`/`OnUpdate` handlers still receive the proper `old` object before the batch transaction commits to the store.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`GenerateSelfSignedCertKeyWithOptions` hardcoded `rsa.GenerateKey(cryptorand.Reader, 2048)` for both the CA and the serving certificate, so the apiserver's `--cert-dir` certificates (`server/options/serving.go`) and the loopback client certificate (`serving_with_loopback.go`) could not use a post-quantum key even once the rest of the stack could.

This adds a `KeyGenerator` option to `SelfSignedCertKeyOptions`. It defaults to the existing 2048-bit RSA key, so output is unchanged for every current caller.

Two behaviors follow from the key type rather than from configuration:

* `keyEncipherment` is asserted only for RSA keys. ML-DSA and ECDSA sign only, and asserting the usage for them produces a certificate no library will honor. This implements the note left in `GenerateSelfSignedCertKeyWithOptions` by #142273.
* A non-RSA key is encoded as PKCS#8; RSA keeps its PKCS#1 encoding so the default output is byte-for-byte what it was.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141838

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Tests cover RSA, ECDSA P-256, and ML-DSA-65. Each generates, parses back through `keyutil.ParsePrivateKeyPEM`, carries the expected key usages, and the serving certificate verifies against the generated CA, so the ML-DSA path is exercised end-to-end.

Rebased on #142273, which has merged. The note it left in GenerateSelfSignedCertKeyWithOptions about key encipherment is removed here, since the key type is now configurable and the usage follows the key.

/assign @everettraven
/sig api-machinery
/sig auth

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
`SelfSignedCertKeyOptions` in `k8s.io/client-go/util/cert` accepts a `KeyGenerator`, allowing self-signed certificates to be generated with a key algorithm other than RSA. The default remains a 2048-bit RSA key.
```

YES. Claude Code was used to navigate the existing key algorithm handling, draft this change and its tests, and run the verification described above. I reviewed every line and am responsible for the result.

issues.title: Make `conversion-gen` automatically pick up autogenerated conversion functions of types across packages

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

issues.body:
### What happened?

Right now, if you have a cross-package type reference, e.g. the `authorization.k8s.io` type `AuthorizationConditionsRequest` refers to `AdmissionRequest` in `admission.k8s.io`, `conversion-gen` fails with

```go
	if in.AdmissionRequest != nil {
		in, out := &in.AdmissionRequest, &out.AdmissionRequest
		*out = new(admission.AdmissionRequest)
		// FIXME: Provide conversion function to convert admissionv1.AdmissionRequest to admission.AdmissionRequest
		compileErrorOnMissingConversion()
	} else {
		out.AdmissionRequest = nil
	}
```

in the generated code on the `authorization.k8s.io` side. This is because `conversion-gen` doesn't "see" any ready-made conversion for `AdmissionRequest` between its internal and external versions. However, `conversion-gen` is in fact responsible for generating that conversion too, hence it doesn't exist up front.

This can be worked around by adding the following to `pkg/apis/admission/v1/conversion.go`:

```go
// Convert_v1_AdmissionRequest_To_admission_AdmissionRequest just calls the covering autogenerated function, but is defined and thus
// "exported" in conversion.go, such that it is usable by other API groups that embed AdmissionRequest.
func Convert_v1_AdmissionRequest_To_admission_AdmissionRequest(in *admissionv1.AdmissionRequest, out *admission.AdmissionRequest, s conversion.Scope) error {
	return autoConvert_v1_AdmissionRequest_To_admission_AdmissionRequest(in, out, s)
}

// Convert_admission_AdmissionRequest_To_v1_AdmissionRequest just calls the covering autogenerated function, but is defined and thus
// "exported" in conversion.go, such that it is usable by other API groups that embed AdmissionRequest.
func Convert_admission_AdmissionRequest_To_v1_AdmissionRequest(in *admission.AdmissionRequest, out *admissionv1.AdmissionRequest, s conversion.Scope) error {
	return autoConvert_admission_AdmissionRequest_To_v1_AdmissionRequest(in, out, s)
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I want `conversion-gen` to understand what `Convert_X_Z_To_Y_Z` functions it will generate, and call those automatically when creating the conversions.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Consider the type structure e.g. in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137633
Make a cross-API-package type reference in core Kubernetes, and try to generate a conversion.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The true device consumption of a claim is only determined inside the allocator's backtracking search. Every enforcement point that exists today — admission, `PreFilter`, `Filter`, `Reserve` — runs strictly before or after that search, so a policy can veto the result but cannot participate in producing it. For `AllocationMode: All`, `FirstAvailable` and fractional capacity there is no correct place to check a limit outside the search, which is why DRA device consumption per tenant cannot be capped correctly today.

The allocator already has an internal `constraint` abstraction with exactly the required semantics, used to implement `DeviceConstraint`. This PR exposes it to callers:

- `structured.AllocationConstraint` — an interface whose `Add` is consulted when a device is about to be included in a result and whose `Remove` is called during backtracking, so rejection steers the search to the next candidate instead of failing the node.
- `structured.DeviceAllocation` — the final values for one candidate device: `Claim`, `Request`, `DeviceClassName`, `Device`, `ConsumedCapacity` (rounded per the device's requestPolicy) and `AdminAccess`.
- `structured.NewAllocationConstraintFunc` — called once per `Allocate`, so a provider can build per-node state.
- `structured.WithAllocationConstraints` — an option on `NewAllocator`. With no provider supplied the code path is identical to today.
- `dynamicresources.SetAllocationConstraintProvider` — a package-level setter for out-of-tree scheduler binaries, the same pattern as `structured.EnableAllocators`.

The hook runs in `allocateDevice` after capacity computation, so a constraint sees the same rounded `ConsumedCapacity` numbers that end up in the allocation result, and before the result is recorded, so rejection rolls back cleanly through the existing `deviceRollbackState` path.

With a constraint that rejects the first entry of a `FirstAvailable` list, the allocator continues with the next entry rather than failing the node — graceful degradation when a budget runs out. With `AllocationMode: All`, a constraint that counts devices sees the actual count for the chosen node, not a fixed 32.

No policy ships in-tree. The option is inert unless an out-of-tree binary supplies a provider. The stable and experimental allocators do not implement the hook yet and the option fails loudly rather than being silently ignored.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Related to #141510

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- This is a source-only change; no KEP is needed per the discussion in the issue.
- The hook lands in the incubating allocator only. Stable and experimental will absorb it when they next absorb incubating code; requesting constraints while those allocators are selected returns an explicit error.
- The `dynamicresources` setter is a package-level variable set once at binary startup, before framework construction. Construction is single-threaded. A `KubeSchedulerConfiguration` field is the natural beta follow-up, justified by a real consumer that alpha produces.
- cluster-autoscaler consumes this allocator through `structured/schedulerapi` and is a plausible second consumer for scale-up simulation with policy-limited capacity, but is not wired in this change.
- Per the issue, the `structured` subtree under `k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation` is scheduler-consumed but falls back to the SIG Node owner; moving it to SIG Scheduling in OWNERS is a separable cleanup.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Added `structured.WithAllocationConstraints` on `NewAllocator` and `dynamicresources.SetAllocationConstraintProvider`, letting an out-of-tree scheduler supply DRA allocation constraints that participate in the allocator's backtracking search. No in-tree behaviour changes.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

```docs
NONE
```

YES. An AI coding agent implemented the option plumbing, the allocator hook, the adapter and the unit tests. All changes were reviewed and verified by the author.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`kubectl create quota --hard` and `kubectl set resources --limits/--requests`
accepted entries with an empty resource name, producing a resource list keyed
by `""`:

```
$ kubectl create quota demo --hard==1 --dry-run=client -o yaml
spec:
  hard:
    "": "1"
```

`populateResourceListV1` (create_quota.go) and `parseResourceList`
(set_resources.go) split each entry on `=` and only verified that there were
exactly two parts, so `parts[0] == ""` passed through. The API server rejects
such an object, but the client-side dry-run output looks valid, so the error
surfaces later at apply time rather than at the point of the typo.

Both helpers now reject an empty resource name. This is consistent with
`parseScopes` in the same file, which already rejects an empty quota scope,
and with `ParseLiteralSource`, which rejects a leading `=` for configmap and
secret literals.

The change is scoped to empty names only. Full qualified-name validation was
considered and deliberately left out: `.spec.hard` legitimately accepts
extended resources (`nvidia.com/gpu`), prefixed forms (`requests.cpu`,
`limits.memory`) and `count/<resource>.<group>` entries, and a client that is
stricter than the server would be its own bug.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142295

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Unit coverage added for both helpers, covering `=1` and an empty name in the
middle of a list (`cpu=1,=1`), alongside the existing valid cases.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
kubectl: `create quota --hard` and `set resources --limits/--requests` now
reject entries with an empty resource name instead of producing a resource
list keyed by an empty string.
```

### What happened?

`kubectl create ingress` accepts a `--default-backend` value whose service name or port is empty, and an `--annotation` whose key is empty.

`--rule` already requires a non-empty service name and port (`[\w\-]+`). `--default-backend` only checks that the value splits into two `:` fields, so both of these succeed:

```console
kubectl create ingress bad --default-backend=:8080 --dry-run=client -o yaml
kubectl create ingress bad --default-backend=svc: --dry-run=client -o yaml
```

The generated Ingress uses an empty backend service name or an empty port.

`--annotation` has the same gap. Validation only checks that `key=value` splits into two parts, so this is accepted:

```console
kubectl create ingress bad --default-backend=svc:80 --annotation==oops --dry-run=client -o yaml
```

That stores an annotation whose key is `""`. The error text already says the format is `key=[value]`, which requires a key.

### What did you expect to happen?

`--default-backend` should be rejected unless both the service name and the port are non-empty, matching `--rule`.

`--annotation` should be rejected when the key is empty.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```console
kubectl create ingress bad --default-backend=:8080 --dry-run=client -o yaml
kubectl create ingress bad --default-backend=svc: --dry-run=client -o yaml
kubectl create ingress bad --default-backend=svc:80 --annotation==oops --dry-run=client -o yaml
```

At the unit level, `CreateIngressOptions.Validate` in `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go` returns nil for `DefaultBackend` values `:8080` and `svc:`, and for annotation `=oops`.

### Anything else we need to know?

`Validate` rejects a missing `:` and a value with no port (`xpto`), but `len(strings.Split(o.DefaultBackend, ":")) != 2` still allows an empty side. Annotation validation uses `len(strings.SplitN(annotation, "=", 2)) != 2` and does not reject an empty key. A client-side check can reject those cases and add coverage next to the existing cases in `TestCreateIngressValidation`.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Rebases #137310 onto current master. GitHub does not allow reopening a closed PR after its branch has been force-pushed, so this PR replaces it.

`InterPodAffinity` and `PodTopologySpread` are among the most CPU-intensive scheduler plugins: for each node they iterate over existing pods and re-evaluate affinity term matching, namespace label lookups and topology key resolution. This PR adds a caching layer that memoizes those results per (namespace, pod name, node), with incremental invalidation on pod add, update and delete, so that same-signature pods and repeated scheduling cycles reuse the pre-calculated score maps instead of recomputing them.

The rebase adapts the cache to master's `InterPodAffinityHostnameFastPath` restructuring:

- `preFilterState` keeps master's cluster-wide field names and term-scope classification; the cache operates on those fields rather than the pre-fast-path names.
- `getExistingAntiAffinityCounts` returns a third value, the per-pod contribution map, alongside master's `(counts, hasHostScopedAntiAffinity)`. Master's callers ignore it; the cache path consumes it.
- `getIncomingAffinityAntiAffinityCounts` keeps master's term-list signature and returns per-pod contributions as a third value.
- In `PreFilter`, the cache read/write path is confined to the non-fast-path branch, where the semantics match the original design. The fast-path branch is left uncached for now, because hostname-scoped and cluster-wide terms have different invalidation granularity and the cache needs a follow-up design for that case.
- `topologyToMatchedTermCountList.recordMatch` now returns the entries it appended, so the caller can attribute them to the contributing pod without a second pass.

Two pre-existing defects in the tests are fixed: `TestIncomingPodCacheProxyPodEvents` set the pod-template-hash as a label while the production code reads it from annotations, and its custom comparers dereferenced nil on a cache miss.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Related to #137654

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- The original #137310 was closed by the lifecycle robot as rotten, not by review. Nothing in that closure reflects a technical decision.
- The cache is gated behind `EnableInterPodAffinityCache=true`. When the variable is unset, the code path is identical to master. The env-var toggle is a development aid; converting it to a proper feature gate is a follow-up before this can merge.
- This is a rebase of a WIP PR onto 5,474 commits of master drift, not a finished implementation. The `InterPodAffinityHostnameFastPath` fast-path branch does not use the cache yet, and the scoring-side cache for `PodTopologySpread` retains the original design unadapted to any master changes on that side.
- Verified: `go build ./pkg/scheduler/...`, `go vet` on the three touched packages, and `go test` on `interpodaffinity`, `podtopologyspread` and `cacheplugin` all pass.
- The autoscaler-side prototypes mentioned in #137654 (kubernetes/autoscaler#9461, kubernetes/autoscaler#9523) were both closed unmerged and are not kube-scheduler code; the scheduler-side need remains open.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
NONE
```

YES. An AI coding agent performed the rebase, resolved the conflicts against master's InterPodAffinityHostnameFastPath restructuring, and fixed the two pre-existing test defects. The author reviewed all changes.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`CalculateTimeoutForVolume` scales a recycler pod's timeout with the PV capacity (`(pvSize / 1Gi) * timeoutIncrement`), and both the `hostpath` and `nfs` plugins assign the returned `int64` straight to the recycler pod's `activeDeadlineSeconds`. The API server rejects that field above `math.MaxInt32` (2147483647), so the arithmetic has two separate ways to produce a pod that cannot be created.

**The result exceeds the ceiling.** At a capacity of 71,582,789 Gi (~68 PiB, a Pi being 1048576 Gi) the timeout reaches 2,147,483,670, which is 23 seconds over the limit, and recycling fails. Past `math.MaxInt64` the capacity saturates and the timeout stays far above the ceiling rather than degrading.

**The product wraps before the ceiling can apply.** `Value()` saturates at large capacities, so a 100E volume leaves a Gi count of 8,589,934,591. Any increment above 1,073,741,824 overflows the multiplication: at `math.MaxInt32` the product lands on -10,737,418,239, falls below `minimumTimeout` and returns 50. The increment comes from `--pv-recycler-increment-timeout-nfs`, an `int32` with no validation bound, so the largest volumes end up with the shortest deadlines.

This PR clamps the result at `math.MaxInt32`, and checks the multiplication against the remaining headroom before performing it so the clamp is reachable.

Tests: the three cases in `pkg/volume/util/util_test.go` previously marked `TODO(#141166)` now assert the cap, and two cases cover the wrap — 100E with an increment of `math.MaxInt32`, and 2Gi with the same increment, where the product fits `int64` but not `int32`. Reverting either guard fails them.

Part of #141166

/assign @thc1006

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The headroom check arrived in the second commit, after review; happy to squash before merge.

```release-note
NONE
```

#### What type of PR is this?
/kind cleanup

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR graduates the declarative validation markers in `certificates/v1` and `certificates/v1beta1` from beta to GA by removing the `+k8s:beta(since: "1.37")` prefixes across all CSR condition rules.

Specifically:
- Dropped `+k8s:beta(since: "1.37")` from all 6 declarative validation tags in `v1` and `v1beta1` (`listType`, `listMapKey`, `customUnique`, `optional`, `zeroOrOneOfMember`).
- Removed the now-redundant handwritten `Approved`/`Denied` mutual-exclusion check in `validateConditions` (along with dead local variables `hasApproved`/`hasDenied`, `allowBothApprovedAndDenied` option field, and helper functions).
- **Ratcheting Safety**: Deleting the handwritten check is safe because `unionValidate` ratchets on union membership (`union.go:211-225`). For legacy CSRs that already carry both conditions, union membership is unchanged on update, returning `nil`—preserving the exact same backwards-compatibility tolerance previously provided by `allowBothApprovedAndDenied`.
- Updated unit tests in `validation_test.go` and `declarative_validation_test.go` to drop obsolete test cases and `.MarkBeta()` expectations.
- Regenerated validation code (`zz_generated.validations.go`) and protobuf definitions.

### What happened?
In `pv_controller` (`isVolumeReleased` in `pkg/controller/volume/persistentvolume/pv_controller.go:1382`), the controller inspects the local informer claim cache (`ctrl.claims.Get(claimName)`) to verify if a claim bound to a PV is released before marking the volume released or performing volume cleanup.

**Race Window:**
If a claim state changes or is updated in the API server, but the local informer cache experiences watch delay, `pv_controller` reads stale claim state from its cache and can proceed to release or delete a persistent volume prematurely.

### What did you expect to happen?
Before executing irreversible volume deletion or release actions, `pv_controller` should re-verify the live PVC object against the API server.

### Related Pull Requests
- #141891 (`pv_controller`: revalidate claim live before deleting released volume)

`master` / `v1.32+`

issues.body:
### What happened?
Controllers handling `node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service` taints (`podgc` and `attachdetach`) rely on local informer caches (`nodeLister`) to inspect Node objects before executing non-reversible force operations (e.g., force-deleting terminating pods or force-detaching volumes):
- `podgc`: `pkg/controller/podgc/gc_controller.go:127`
- `attachdetach`: `pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler.go:148` (`hasOutOfServiceTaint` → `rc.nodeLister.Get`)

**Race Window:**
Taint is removed in the API server (or node becomes Ready again) → watch event is delayed / not yet delivered to local informer store → controller reads stale node from cache → force-deletes pod or force-detaches volume.

This violates the safety guarantee of `out-of-service` taints and can produce split-brain scenarios (two running instances of the same pod on different nodes).

### What did you expect to happen?
Before executing force deletion or force detachment authorized by out-of-service taints, the controller should re-verify the live Node object against the API server to ensure the `out-of-service` taint is still active.

### Related Pull Requests
- #141887 (`podgc`: revalidate node out-of-service taint live before force deleting)
- #141888 (`attachdetach`: revalidate out-of-service taint live before force detaching)

### Kubernetes Version
`master` / `v1.32+`

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as relevant to workload-aware scheduling WG.

issues.body:
### What happened?

The Indexed Job using `spec.scheduling.schedulingPolicy.gang` never finishes if any index's pod terminates after at least one other index has completed. The replacement pod is created but never scheduled.

The scheduler's pod informer excludes Succeeded/Failed pods, so completed members leave the PodGroup state (cache.removePod → removePodGroupMember). The gang plugin's PreEnqueue gate then rejects the replacement with waiting for minCount pods from a gang to appear in scheduling queue because `AllPodsCount() < minCount`, and nothing re-admits it.

The only requeue hints are a new group pod or a minCount change. The Job controller never lowers minCount as indexes complete (`syncGangMinCount` derives it from `spec.parallelism` only).

**Impact**
Any gang Job whose indexes finish at different times and then loses a pod (crash, eviction, node loss). Only exits are activeDeadlineSeconds or a manual minCount patch. This will eventually block kubernetes-sigs/kueue#13715 defaulting gang on managed Jobs.

### What did you expect to happen?

The replacement schedules and the Job completes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Scheduler side: I added a new table entry in `TestPodGroupScheduling` to admit a gang of 3 (minCount: 3), UpdatePodStatus two members to Succeeded and one to Failed, and then create a replacement in the same PodGroup, WaitForPodsScheduled on it. The test times out after 30s with no scheduling attempt. (planning to add this test to the KEP update PR for beta https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/6345).
- Job controller side: Verified by tracing the code. One PodGroup per Job, recreated indexes reference it, minCount unchanged.

### Anything else we need to know?

#### Fix (Job controller, this issue)

In `syncGangMinCount`, when `minCount` was defaulted rather than user-set, use `max(1, parallelism - status.Succeeded)`. After the first completion the threshold tracks remaining work. This is controller-only and is not blocked on #136334.

Open point for review: a user-set `minCount` is left alone. A user who sets it on an Indexed Job will still hit this after the first completion. Weather documenting that vs clamping user-set values too, is the sig-apps call.

Note: Add the scheduler-side test case from the reproduction of this issue to kubernetes/enhancements#6345. This is in additon to Job-controller integration test asserting `minCount` drops as indexes succeed.

#### Scheduler-side recovery threshold (not this issue)

Originally listed here as the long-term fix via #136334. Per the WG Workload-Aware Scheduling meeting on 2026-09-24, that work is split:

- `PodGroupSatisfied` condition (`NeverSatisfied` / `Healthy` / `Degraded`) proceeds under #136334.
- The `minAvailable` threshold is deferred. The WG position is that a floor the group must not drop below is a disruption-policy concept, not a `GangSchedulingPolicy` field, and needs its own KEP after the disruption-mode design settles.

Neither piece changes the fix above. Revised design note: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wnV7XGWjt0pwDH_d67qvYxCtse5R_ZZylPxMHIJuOys/edit?tab=t.0

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Scheduler filtering and kubelet admission share the same InferForScheduling call. When a kubelet restarts with a feature gate disabled, it re-admits its running pods and rejects those that still require the feature; the pod ends up Failed with PodFeatureUnsupported. That is the intended default: in most cases a pod that depends on a feature the node no longer provides should not keep running.

Some features are only needed at pod setup, or provide optional functionality a running pod can lose. For them, killing the pod on re-admission is worse than letting it continue without the feature, yet the framework gives such a feature no way to tell first admission from re-admission.

The allocation manager already keeps a checkpoint with an entry for every pod it has admitted. Use it as the source of truth: canAdmitPod looks the pod up in the checkpoint and passes the result to admit handlers in a new PodAdmitAttributes.PreviouslyAllocated field, and the declared features handler copies it into PodInfo.PreviouslyAdmitted for the feature to read. The checkpoint is restored before the sync loop starts and canAdmitPod runs before the new allocation is stored, so the flag is false on first admission and true on re-admission after a restart. It is always false during scheduling. Features that do not read it keep the current fail-closed behavior.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142328

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The mechanism is planned to be used in KEP-6122 and KEP-6369

issues.title: Node Declared Features: allow a feature to opt out of re-admission enforcement after kubelet restart

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

An extension to the Node Declared Features (NDF, KEP-5328) framework so that an individual feature can distinguish *first admission* of a pod from *re-admission* of a pod that was already admitted on this node before a kubelet restart, and choose not to require the feature in the latter case.

Today `Feature.InferForScheduling(podInfo *types.PodInfo)` receives only `Spec` and `Status`, and the same call is used in three places:

- scheduler `PreFilter` / `SignPod` (`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodedeclaredfeatures/nodedeclaredfeatures.go`), with `PodInfo{Spec}` only,
- kubelet first admission (`pkg/kubelet/lifecycle/handlers.go`, `declaredFeaturesAdmitHandler.Admit`),
- kubelet re-admission after restart, which goes through exactly the same `HandlePodAdditions -> allocationManager.AddPod -> canAdmitPod -> Admit` path.

There is no signal available to the feature that would let it tell the last two apart.

Proposed change (prototyped, all additive, no behavior change for existing features):

1. `types.PodInfo` gets a new field `PreviouslyAdmitted bool` ("the kubelet holds a persisted allocation for this pod from an earlier admission; always false during scheduling").
2. `lifecycle.PodAdmitAttributes` gets `PreviouslyAllocated bool`.
3. `allocation.manager.canAdmitPod` populates it from `m.HasPodAllocatedResources(pod.UID)`. The allocation manager restores its `allocated_pods_state` checkpoint synchronously in `NewManager`, before the sync loop starts, and `canAdmitPod` runs before `SetAllocatedResources`, so on first admission the value is `false` and on re-admission after restart it is `true`. Since `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` is GA and locked to `true` in 1.35, this checkpoint is always present; it stores an entry for every admitted pod (including BestEffort), keyed by pod UID.
4. `declaredFeaturesAdmitHandler.Admit` copies the flag into `PodInfo`.

A feature that wants "soft" re-admission then implements:

```go
func (f *myFeature) InferForScheduling(podInfo *types.PodInfo) bool {
    if podInfo.PreviouslyAdmitted {
        return false
    }
    return podUsesFeature(podInfo.Spec)
}
```

### Why is this needed?

KEP-5328 currently documents a single, fail-closed policy for kubelet restarts:

> Node declared features are checked by the scheduler during scheduling and then validated again by the Kubelet's admission handlers before a pod's containers can start. This validation is critical for handling cases where a node's declared features change after a pod has been scheduled.
>
>If a Kubelet restarts with a different configuration (e.g., a feature gate is disabled), its declared features may change. Upon restart, the Kubelet re-evaluates all existing pods for admission and if a running pod requires a declared feature that the node no longer provides, the Kubelet's admission check will fail. Consequently, the pod will not be started and will be transitioned to a `Failed` phase. This ensures that a pod does not run on a node that cannot support its feature requirements. This behavior is consistent with the best practice of draining a node before making significant configuration changes, such as toggling feature gates.
>
> — keps/sig-node/5328-node-declared-features/README.md:440-442

This is the correct default for most NDF features: if the node can no longer provide something the pod fundamentally depends on, the pod should be evicted.

However, there is a class of features where this is unnecessarily disruptive:

- the feature only affects pod setup and is irrelevant once the pod is running, or
- the feature provides optional, additive functionality that a running pod can simply lose without breaking.

An example is KEP-6122 (Configurable Scaling Delay, targeting Alpha in v1.38). It uses NDF in its intended role: a kubelet with `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUsScaleDownDelay` enabled declares the feature in `node.status.declaredFeatures`, and the scheduler only places pods that set `scaleDownGracePeriodSeconds` on nodes that declare it, so a pod never lands on a node that would silently ignore its grace period. The same KEP explicitly departs from the KEP-5328 default for one case ("Grace Period Not Honored" section): when the gate is turned off on a node that already runs such a pod and the kubelet restarts, the pod is not rejected, because killing a running latency-sensitive workload is worse than resizing it without the preparation window. The kubelet is instead expected to apply the next scale-down without the delay and report it via the `PodResizeInProgress` condition message and a `ScaleDownGracePeriodNotHonored` event. Its PRR rollback answer is built on this: existing pods keep running, only the delay is lost.

With today's NDF framework that behaviour cannot be implemented. The scheduler's node filter and the kubelet's admission check are driven by the same `Feature.InferForScheduling` method, so a feature that returns `true` to obtain scheduler filtering also gets fatal kubelet re-admission after a restart with the gate disabled: the pod fails with `PodFeatureUnsupported` and is killed.

That is bumped in 1.35 recently [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/9bfa496a57ae26804f0f5bc23959ef332143576f). Are there any plans to make a patch release for 1.35 this month or next month? Based on [previous releases for 1.35](https://kubernetes.io/releases/1.35/) it looks like the release cadence is about once a month.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Several of the integer/overflow checks on `resource.Quantity` tightened during the #141166 burndown now reject a resource quantity that was already stored and accepted before the check tightened, once any other part of the same object changes on an update. An update that does not touch that specific field should not start failing because of it.

This adds a `StoredResourceQuantitySet` carried on `PodValidationOptions` and `PersistentVolumeClaimSpecValidationOptions`: on update, a `(resource name, quantity)` pair the stored object already held under that exact field is not re-validated, while a changed value is still validated in full, same as on create.

The set is keyed by *location* (container kind and name plus limits/requests for pods, capacity/allocatable for Node), not by resource name alone. Keying by name alone would let a value one container (or list) already holds unchanged wave through a different, newly-changed occurrence of the same value showing up somewhere else in the object, or a same-named container that moved between the containers/initContainers/ephemeralContainers lists on a template update — this PR's tests cover both cases explicitly.

Equality is `Quantity.Cmp`, not `String()`, so two spellings of the same value (`500m` vs `5e-1`) match — the same rule the existing ResourceQuota ratchet already uses.

Covers:
- `ValidatePodUpdate`, `ValidatePodTemplateUpdate`, `ValidatePodEphemeralContainersUpdate`, `ValidatePodResize` — via `PodValidationOptions`, wired through `GetValidationOptionsFromPodSpecAndMeta` so every pod update strategy (plain update, ephemeral-containers subresource, resize subresource, and the podtemplate strategy) gets it without a separate change per strategy. `spec.overhead` is included.
- Node `status.capacity` / `status.allocatable` on update.
- `PersistentVolumeClaim` `status.capacity` and `status.allocatedResources` on update.
- RuntimeClass `overhead` on update, including the pre-existing `AllowIndivisibleHugePagesValues` hugepages-divisibility allowance, narrowed here to an exact stored-value match so a changed or newly-added hugepages entry can't ratchet off an unrelated stored one.

`ValidateNode` also gained a `stored` parameter: `nodeStrategy.ValidateUpdate` calls both `ValidateNode` (the create-path checks) and `ValidateNodeUpdate` and appends both error lists, so `ValidateNode` needed the same stored set or its own nil-stored call would re-reject an unchanged value regardless of what `ValidateNodeUpdate` decided. Covered by a new `TestValidateUpdate` case in `pkg/registry/core/node` that goes through the real strategy, not just the isolated validation-package unit test.

RuntimeClass overhead validation shares `ValidateContainerResourceRequirements` with the container path and picks up the same options-based ratchet; `runtimeclass.strategy.ValidateUpdate` builds a `StoredResourceQuantitySet` from the old overhead directly, since RuntimeClass already has the old object on hand and doesn't need the pod path's options plumbing.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Addresses the TODO items assigned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141166#issuecomment-5780114790 (pod update, ephemeral-container, resize, PodTemplate, Node and PVC status paths), plus the RuntimeClass overhead group from the same bullet. Builds on the options-based ratchet approach from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141166#issuecomment-5739915444, reviewed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141166#issuecomment-5779016410.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed a set of update validation regressions where a `resource.Quantity` value already accepted and stored before recent integer-overflow checks tightened would cause any update to the containing Pod, Node, PersistentVolumeClaim status, or RuntimeClass to fail, even when that value was not itself being changed.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

```docs

```

#### AI usage disclosure:

YES. Used to check the diagnosis and fix against the source (a second pass after my own), and to help draft and format this description.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`exceedsAllowed` returned false whenever the product of the request and the ratio had a scale below `inf.Scale`. The premise was that no limit could exceed such a product, but a limit has its own mantissa and scale. A request of `1e2147483647` with a limit of `10000e2147483647` cleared a `1k` ratio, and core validation accepts that pair. In that branch the comparison works from the digit counts and the scales, since that scale has no decimal. The check now compares magnitudes. An operand below zero is taken by its size. A scale that fits `inf.Scale` still forms the product and hands it to `Cmp`.

The ratio in the message came from dividing two float64 projections, which printed `+Inf` or `NaN` once an operand passed that range. It now divides the quantities directly and keeps the six decimals it has always shown. Scales too far apart for that give an exponent and a mantissa rounded to the six decimals. The coefficient quotient is normalized before rounding, or a request of `10000000` against a limit of `1e50` reports zero.

Every case `admission_overflow_test.go` pins for #141166 is cleared. New cases cover a negative operand on either side, two spellings of one request, scales far apart, and both sides of the rounding boundary. The helpers have tables of their own.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#141348 removed a local comparator on review. `cmpScaled` is not that comparator returning for speed. A scale past `inf.Scale` has no Quantity for `Cmp` to take.

The negative pair follows the first option its pinned case offers, no error for a ratio under the maximum, since the magnitudes give the ratio the LimitRange means. Rejecting negatives outright would be a small change instead.

The check is stricter than before. A pair that was accepted and stored can now be rejected on an update. That takes a request and ratio whose scales sum below `inf.Scale`, or an operand below zero. An ordinary non-negative pair is answered as before. `SupportsAttributes` lets the `resize` subresource through, and since #142171 the pods branch of `ValidateLimit` skips a pair the resize leaves unchanged, so a stored pair only meets the stricter check once one of its sides changes.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
LimitRanger now enforces maxLimitRequestRatio for requests and limits at the largest exponents, and its error message reports the ratio to six decimals instead of +Inf or NaN when an operand exceeds float64.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

```docs
NONE
```

YES. An AI coding assistant drafted the change, the tests and this description. I reviewed and edited them and ran the tests and linters locally.

As per discussion/suggestion:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141965#discussion_r4028002133

Right now, in TAS, tests at scale equal to or below 100 nodes run with a single topology domain rack-0 always.
We will end up with a single candidate placement, which means we are not testing topology aware scheduling properly.

In this PR, we are introducing changes for these tests, to be able to end up with multiple placements, and evaluate the best candidate for each subsequent podgroup scheduling, to exercise and test TAS effectively.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When a pod group fails to schedule, the `PodGroupInitiallyScheduled` condition carries only the group-level message:

```
pod group is unschedulable, minCount (80) cannot be satisfied: 30 scheduled, 0 remaining
```

That states how many pods are missing but not why no node could host them. Debugging a gang then means reading the `FailedScheduling` events of individual pods and reconstructing the node picture by hand, and for a large gang most of those events are lost to deduplication by message. The seven objects involved in one cycle (the PodGroup, its pods, the nodes, the conditions and the events) each carry a different fragment, which is what makes the investigation slow.

This PR aggregates the per-pod `FitError` diagnosis of one failed pod group cycle along the node dimension and attaches the result to the PodGroup condition:

```
pod group is unschedulable, minCount (2) is not yet satisfied: 1 scheduled, 1 remaining
1/2 pods placed in this cycle, 3 nodes in placement.

Saturated nodes (1) - accepted some gang pods, rejected others:
  node-a: accepted 1, rejected 1 (Insufficient cpu)

Excluded nodes (2) - rejected every pod:
  1 node: node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity]
  1 node: untolerated taint
```

Two classes cover the whole placement. A node either accepted at least one gang pod, in which case its capacity ran out part-way and it is reported as saturated with its accepted and rejected counts, or it accepted none, in which case a constraint ruled it out from the start and it is reported as excluded. Excluded nodes are clustered by their dominant rejection reason rather than listed individually, so the reader sees how many nodes failed for each cause. Pods that never reached the scheduling algorithm because the group became infeasible first are counted separately on a `Not evaluated:` line, so they are not mistaken for pods that were evaluated and rejected.

Design points worth reviewing:

- **Excluded nodes are a remainder, not a per-pod product.** `FitError.Error()` multiplies `absentNodesStatus` by `NumAllNodes - NodeToStatus.Len()`, which is correct for the single pod it describes. Accumulating that product across pods would count (node, pod) pairs: a gang of 70 pods failing in `PreFilter` against 5000 nodes, where `NodeToStatus` is empty and `Len()` is 0, would report `Excluded nodes (350000)`. This PR instead takes `NumAllNodes - len(accepted)`, which counts each node once.
- **No snapshot re-read.** Nodes that no failed pod recorded explicitly cannot be enumerated by name without reading the node list, which a later cycle may already be mutating. They are counted as a remainder and attributed the dominant absent reason. Cost stays proportional to the entries the filter phase already wrote.
- **`rejected` counts failed pods only.** `SchedulePod` discards the diagnosis of a pod it placed, so the rejections that pod observed are not recoverable. The count is stated for what it is rather than padded.
- **Nothing is written back into `podGroupResult.status`.** That status is cloned into every pod's `PodScheduled` condition and `FailedScheduling` event by `handleSchedulingFailure`, so a multi-kilobyte node table would be duplicated once per pod and would weaken event deduplication. The diagnosis reaches the PodGroup condition only. `TestPodGroupDiagnosisDoesNotFanOutToPods` drives the real `handleSchedulingFailure` and asserts the table appears in the PodGroup condition and in neither the pod conditions nor the events.
- **Suppressed while waiting for preemption.** `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` writes the same `PodGroupInitiallyScheduled=False / Unschedulable` condition whether the group is waiting for preemption or is genuinely unschedulable, and the preemption path appends the `PodGroupPostFilter` result to the group status. Rendering a node table there would state a terminal verdict while preemption may still succeed, and would displace the message describing what is being preempted. The guard returns no diagnosis and the existing message is kept.
- **Suppressed when a filter extender is configured.** `numNodesToFind` is reduced to 1 only when there is neither an extender filter nor scoring. With a filter extender the node scan can therefore stop early once enough framework-feasible nodes are found, only for `findNodesThatPassExtenders` to discard all of them, and the pod still ends with a `FitError`. The nodes left unscanned fall through to the default `absentNodesStatus`, which carries no reason, and would render as an empty-reason row blaming nodes that never saw the pod. Until that case can be distinguished, the diagnosis declines to render rather than attribute a rejection it cannot prove.
- **Bounded size.** 10 saturated node lines, 5 excluded reason buckets, and 16384 characters per layer, with truncation stated in the text so a truncated message never reads as a complete one. The per-layer budget stays well below the 32768 character limit on `metav1.Condition.Message` so that an ancestor composite pod group can prepend its own propagation prefix.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Related to #141025

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This is a deliberately narrow first stage. It adds no API field, reads nothing that the scheduling cycle did not already produce, and changes no per-pod message. Node resource figures (free and allocatable per node) are out of scope: the scheduler samples nodes instead of evaluating all of them, so a resource number quoted for a node that was never evaluated would be wrong, and a wrong number is worse than no number.

Two follow-ups would remove the remaining approximations and are not attempted here: partitioning the gang by `PodSignature` so that a heterogeneous gang no longer has to collapse differing per-node reasons into one dominant reason, and moving the aggregation off the scheduling critical path by accumulating it incrementally as each pod fails and attaching it when the last pod is patched.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
When a pod group fails to schedule, the `PodGroupInitiallyScheduled` condition now summarizes the placement along the node dimension: it reports how many pods were placed, and lists saturated nodes with their accepted and rejected pod counts alongside excluded nodes clustered by rejection reason.
```

```docs
NONE
```

YES. An AI coding agent assisted with the implementation, the unit tests and the wording of this description. Every change was read and verified by the author, who takes responsibility for it.

#### What type of PR is this?
/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Quick and dirty POC for the WAP triggering logic adjustments needed to extend the idea from https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/6194 to CPG hierarchies.

The TL;DR decision tree when to trigger WAP, based on the type of the root group and its scheduling policy:
- **Flat `PodGroup`**:
  - Initial scheduling attempt (`initiallyScheduledPods < minCount`, assuming `minCount = 1` for `Basic` below):
    - Prioritize binding over preemption, regardless of policy (`Basic` or `Gang`).
  - Subsequent scheduling attempt (`initiallyScheduledPods >= minCount`):
    - `Basic` policy:
      - Prioritize binding over preemption (bind if $\ge 1$ new Pod was scheduled in memory).
    - `Gang` policy:
      - Prioritize preemption over binding (return `PartialSuccess` if $\ge 1$ unscheduled Pod failed in-memory scheduling; attempt preemption first, and fall back to binding if preemption fails).

- **`CompositePodGroup`**:
  - Initial scheduling attempt (`initiallyScheduledGroups < minGroupCount`, assuming `minGroupCount = 1` for `Basic` below):
    - Prioritize binding over preemption, regardless of policy (`Basic` or `Gang`).
  - Subsequent scheduling attempt (`initiallyScheduledGroups >= minGroupCount`):
    - `Gang` policy: Every group in the hierarchy is a gang. Prioritize preemption over binding (return `PartialSuccess` if any child group returned `PartialSuccess` or `Unschedulable`).
    - `Basic` policy: Prioritize binding over preemption (if at least one child with new pods returned `Success`, return `Success` and bind; else if children with new pods only achieved `PartialSuccess`, return `PartialSuccess` and run preemption).

/hold

#### What type of PR is this?

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds the alpha `informer_initialization_duration_seconds` histogram for named shared informers. It measures from `RunWithContext` until the first cache sync, covering LIST, WatchList, retries, fallback, queue draining, and indexer population; it excludes asynchronous handler delivery.

#### What type of PR is this?

<!--
Add one of the following kinds:
/kind bug
/kind dependency
/kind cleanup
/kind documentation
/kind feature

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change
/kind deprecation
/kind failing-test
/kind flake
/kind regression
-->
/kind cleanup

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Authorizing a node's `get` request for a Secret that is reachable only through the PV chain (`node <- pod <- pvc <- pv <- secret`) falls back to a DFS over the authorizer graph, because Secret and PV vertices have no authoritative destination edge index. When many PVs share the same Secret, the DFS becomes pathologically slow while holding the graph read lock. In our case, a single Secret referenced by CSI `nodeStageSecretRef` is shared by 400,000 PVs.

Two causes, fixed separately:

**The visited set made traversal quadratic.**

`VisitingDepthFirst` used `intsets.Sparse` to track visited vertices. Its 256-bit blocks form a linked list, which `Has` and `Insert` search from the head. Vertex IDs are spread across the graph, and neighbors arrive in arbitrary map order, so membership checks often traversed about half the list. As a result, visiting n vertices cost O(n²). In a CPU profile with 100,000 PVs, about 60% of samples were in `intsets.(*Sparse).block/Insert/next`. The set was replaced with **a short linear list that switches to a map when it fills up**. 


**The traversal always started from the expensive end.**
`hasPathFrom` walked forward from the resource, so a secret shared by 400k PVs enumerated all 400k PVs before descending toward any node. The **reverse walk** from the node is bounded by what that node's own pods reference,
independent of how shared the secret is, and needs no destination-edge filter, since every edge into a node comes from an object that node already refers to. **The traversal now starts from whichever end has the lower degree**. Forward remains the default, so a secret referenced by a single pod does not pay for the node's whole subgraph.

Benchmark over 400k PVs on 1000 nodes (400 pods/node), each PV bound through a PVC to a pod, all sharing one secret:
| case | before | after |

| shared secret, allowed | 7.31 s | 32.6 µs |
| shared secret, unrelated node | 18.11 s | 360 ns |
| shared secret at 100k PVs, allowed | 115 ms | 6.0 µs |
| shared secret at 100k PVs, unrelated node | 272 ms | 344 ns |

issues.body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

`printProjectedVolumeSource` is an `if / else if` chain over the four projected source kinds it knows about (`secret`, `downwardAPI`, `configMap`, `serviceAccountToken`). It has no arm for `ClusterTrustBundle` or `PodCertificate` and no fallback, so those sources are silently dropped and the volume block ends after the `Type:` line:

```
Volumes:
  creds:
    Type:  Projected (a volume that contains injected data from multiple sources)
```

Both source kinds are GA and enabled by default since v1.37 (`ClusterTrustBundleProjection` and `PodCertificateRequest`, both marked `LockToDefault in 1.38`), so this is not gated-off output. `describeVolumes` itself already handles every `VolumeSource` kind and has a `default: <unknown>` arm; only the per-projection chain was incomplete.

`podCertificate` is the more user-visible of the two: a pod does not start until certificates have been issued for every `podCertificate` source in its spec, and `kubectl describe pod` is the first place an operator looks when a pod is stuck.

This PR prints both in the style of the existing sources:

```
Volumes:
  creds:
    Type:                      Projected (a volume that contains injected data from multiple sources)
    ClusterTrustBundleName:    my-bundle
    Path:                      trust-bundle.pem
    Optional:                  false
    PodCertificateSignerName:  example.com/signer
    KeyType:                   ED25519
    CredentialBundlePath:      credentials.pem
```

Two details worth calling out:

- A cluster trust bundle is selected either by `name` or by `signerName` plus a `labelSelector`; the printer reports whichever form is set, rendering the selector with `metav1.FormatLabelSelector`.
- Kubelet writes either a single credential bundle or a separate key and certificate chain, so only the paths that are actually populated are reported, and `maxExpirationSeconds` is printed only when set.

No existing output changes: the added lines appear only for projected sources that produced no output at all before.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:

Fixes #142309

**Special notes for your reviewer**:

`TestDescribeProjectedVolumeSources` covers both bundle selection forms and both pod-certificate path layouts. All four cases fail on master and pass with the fix.

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**

```release-note
kubectl describe pod now shows `clusterTrustBundle` and `podCertificate` projected volume sources, which were previously omitted from the Volumes section.
```

issues.body:
### What happened?

`kubectl describe pod` prints nothing for a projected volume source of type `clusterTrustBundle` or `podCertificate`. The volume is listed, but the block ends after the `Type:` line, so there is no indication of what is actually projected into the pod:

```
Volumes:
  creds:
    Type:  Projected (a volume that contains injected data from multiple sources)
```

Projected sources of type `secret`, `configMap`, `downwardAPI` and `serviceAccountToken` are printed as usual.

Both of the affected sources are GA and on by default since v1.37 (`ClusterTrustBundleProjection` and `PodCertificateRequest` in `pkg/features/kube_features.go`, both marked `LockToDefault in 1.38`), so this is not gated-off output.

Cause: `printProjectedVolumeSource` is an `if / else if` chain over the four source kinds it knows about, with no branch for `ClusterTrustBundle` or `PodCertificate` and no fallback, so those entries are silently skipped:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/58cd835870c09a025a9ee4974ec5d8e9e2415e25/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/describe/describe.go#L1076-L1097

`describeVolumes` itself already handles every `VolumeSource` kind and has a `default: <unknown>` arm; only the per-projection switch is incomplete.

### What did you expect to happen?

The projected sources to be listed in the same style as the other kinds, for example:

```
Volumes:
  creds:
    Type:                          Projected (a volume that contains injected data from multiple sources)
    ClusterTrustBundleName:        my-bundle
    Path:                          trust-bundle.pem
    Optional:                      false
    PodCertificateSignerName:      example.com/signer
    KeyType:                       ED25519
    CredentialBundlePath:          credentials.pem
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

No cluster feature configuration is needed on v1.37+. Create a pod with a projected volume:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: projected-creds
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: creds
      mountPath: /var/run/creds
  volumes:
  - name: creds
    projected:
      sources:
      - clusterTrustBundle:
          name: my-bundle
          path: trust-bundle.pem
      - podCertificate:
          signerName: example.com/signer
          keyType: ED25519
          credentialBundlePath: credentials.pem
```

```console
$ kubectl describe pod projected-creds | grep -A5 Volumes:
```

The `creds:` block stops after the `Type:` line.

At the unit level, describing a pod whose only volume is a projected volume with a `clusterTrustBundle` source produces output containing neither the bundle name nor the path.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is the same class of gap as #142208 (`fileKeyRef` missing from the container env output): a source kind added to the API without a matching arm in the describer.

`podCertificate` is the more user-visible of the two, since a pod does not start until certificates have been issued for every `podCertificate` source in its spec, and `kubectl describe pod` is the first place an operator looks when a pod is stuck.

I have a fix with unit tests and will open a PR shortly.

/kind bug
/sig cli
/area kubectl

issues.title: Pod inside its startup period becomes Ready after a kubelet restart

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: needs-sig
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `sig/foo` label and requires one.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

issues.body:
### What happened?

A container still in its startup period is NotReady, as expected. Restart the kubelet on that node and the pod goes Ready within a few seconds, without the startup probe ever succeeding, and it stays Ready.

`isContainerStarted` looks up the probe workers to tell whether a container has a startup probe. `SyncPod` builds the pod status before it calls `AddPod`, so right after a kubelet restart there is no worker yet and the container is marked started. That value is kept across syncs and `worker.doProbe` stops probing once it is set, so nothing puts it back.

With a readiness probe the pod stays NotReady, but the startup gate opens and the liveness probe starts running against a container that is still warming up.

Opened #142303 with a fix.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod stays NotReady until the startup probe succeeds. Restarting the kubelet should not change whether a container counts as started.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod with a startup probe that keeps failing and no readiness probe:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: slow-start
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
    startupProbe:
      exec:
        command: ["false"]
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 180
```

Once it is running:

```
$ kubectl get pod slow-start -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}'
false
```

Restart the kubelet on that node, wait a few seconds, then check again:

```
$ kubectl get pod slow-start -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}'
true

$ kubectl get pod slow-start
NAME         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
slow-start   1/1     Running   0          5m
```

The startup probe is not run again after this.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

With `ChangeContainerStatusOnKubeletRestart` disabled (the default since 1.35), a container still inside its startup period is reported as started on the first sync after a kubelet restart.

`isContainerStarted` looks up the startup probe worker, but SyncPod generates the pod status before `AddPod` registers it. `Started` is then preserved across syncs and the startup worker stops probing, so the pod becomes ready without passing its startup probe, and the liveness probe can kill a container that is still warming up.

This PR checks the pod spec for a startup probe inside the gate-disabled branch, after the preserved `Started=true` check. The gate-enabled path is unchanged.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Rejects empty resource names in `kubectl create quota --hard` and `kubectl set resources --limits/--requests`.

issues.body:
### What happened?

`kubectl create quota --hard` and `kubectl set resources --limits/--requests` accept resource list entries with an empty resource name. For example:

```console
kubectl create quota demo --hard==1 --dry-run=client -o yaml
```

The command succeeds and produces a ResourceQuota whose `.spec.hard` map contains an empty-string key:

```yaml
spec:
  hard:
    "": "1"
```

The same parser path is used by `kubectl set resources` (`parseResourceList`), so `--limits==1` / `--requests==1` are accepted the same way.

This is inconsistent with nearby validation: `parseScopes` already rejects an empty quota scope (`""`), and `ParseLiteralSource` rejects a leading `=` for configmap/secret literals.

### What did you expect to happen?

The command should reject `<resource>=<value>` entries when the resource name is empty, instead of creating a ResourceList keyed by `""`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run:

```console
kubectl create quota demo --hard==1 --dry-run=client -o yaml
```

The command currently succeeds with an empty hard resource name.

At the unit level, `populateResourceListV1("=1")` in `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_quota.go` returns a non-nil ResourceList and no error. The twin helper `parseResourceList` in `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/set/set_resources.go` has the same gap.

### Anything else we need to know?

`populateResourceListV1` / `parseResourceList` split on `=` and only check that there are exactly two parts. They do not reject `parts[0] == ""`. A client-side fix can reject empty resource names and add regression coverage in the existing quota / set-resources tests.
