issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig scheduling

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When the preemptor's pods leave the preempting set, their PreEnqueue gate opens, but they still need an event to get back into the active queue. `prepareCandidateAsync` activates the preemptor only when the async preemption fails or when the last victim is preempted in memory. A last victim that was already deleted produces neither: the status patch or the delete call returns `IsNotFound`, which is treated as success, and the victim's deletion event was consumed earlier. The preemptor therefore stays in the unschedulable pod pool until the queue is flushed, as described in #141694.

The completions that skip a deletion event are not enumerable from the executor: an in-memory preemption, a victim already deleted via the API, and a victim that is assumed and then forgotten when another component rejects it. This PR activates the preemptor whenever the goroutine completes. `Activate` is a no-op for a pod that is already in the active queue, so the normal event path is unaffected.

The change follows the direction Huang-Wei suggested in #141694: remove `preemptedLastVictimInMemory` and activate unconditionally when the goroutine completes, preferring accuracy over the small cost of an extra activation (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141694#issuecomment-5579516542).

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #141694

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- The new regression test `TestPrepareCandidateAsyncActivatesPreemptorOnCompletion/last_victim_already_deleted_via_API` fails against the unpatched executor (it times out after 30s waiting for activation) and passes with this change.
- Existing tests are updated to the completion-time activation contract: `TestPrepareCandidate` subtests now assert `expectedActivatedPods`, `TestAsyncPreemptionFailure` verifies the preemptor is always activated, and the `gated preemptor is eventually scheduled even if victim deletion doesn't raise queue hints` scenario no longer relies on flushing the unschedulable queue. It now expects the preemptor to be scheduled directly; without the patch, the scenario never gets the preemptor into the active queue.
- Tests that build the framework now pass `WithPodActivator`, because the activation call is no longer conditional.
- `go test ./pkg/scheduler/...` is green.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

Yes. Bug fix:

```release-note
Fixed a bug that could leave a preemptor pod stuck in the unschedulable pod pool until the scheduling queue was flushed, when an asynchronous preemption completed without a deletion event for the last victim (for example, when the victim was already deleted).
```

This PR was written in part with the assistance of generative AI.

issues.title: Kubelet emits spurious Pod status updates due to nondeterministic allocated resource health ordering

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

issues.body:
### What happened?

With `ResourceHealthStatus` enabled, kubelet can change the order of entries in `status.containerStatuses[*].allocatedResourcesStatus` even when device and claim health have not changed.

There are two nondeterministic paths in kubelet v1.36.3:

1. The device manager constructs each `ResourceStatus.Resources` slice by iterating a map of device IDs. The same resource IDs can therefore be emitted in a different order on later syncs.
2. The DRA manager rebuilds `AllocatedResourcesStatus` by iterating `resourceStatusMap`. This can reorder device-plugin and claim statuses, for example:

```text
[nvidia.com/gpu, claim:channel]
[claim:channel, nvidia.com/gpu]
```

The resulting Pod status is semantically unchanged but serialized differently. Kubelet treats it as a status change and sends a Pod status update. The API server then stores a new resource version and broadcasts a full `MODIFIED` watch event. This can create continuous status and watch churn for otherwise unchanged Pods.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should produce a stable `AllocatedResourcesStatus` representation when resource health is unchanged. Both the outer `[]ResourceStatus` and each inner `[]ResourceHealth` should have deterministic ordering, so repeated syncs do not cause unnecessary Pod status updates.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run kubelet v1.36.3 with `ResourceHealthStatus` enabled.
2. Start a Pod whose container has at least two device-plugin devices and a DRA resource claim with health reporting. Generic test device-plugin and DRA drivers are sufficient.
3. Keep all reported health values unchanged.
4. Trigger or wait for repeated Pod status syncs and watch:

```console
kubectl get pod <pod> -w -o json
```

5. Observe that either:
   - entries in a `ResourceStatus.Resources` slice change order, or
   - entries in `AllocatedResourcesStatus` change order.

The Pod `resourceVersion` advances and a `MODIFIED` watch event is emitted despite no health change.

This can also be reproduced in unit tests by calling the two `UpdateAllocatedResourcesStatus` implementations repeatedly with multiple map entries and asserting that their output is canonical.

### Anything else we need to know?

The relevant v1.36.3 code paths are:

- Device ID map iteration while constructing `ResourceStatus.Resources`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49c14f82ca9748897f0189be31cbf9c2f4085fc1/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L1162-L1177
- DRA map iteration while rebuilding `AllocatedResourcesStatus`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49c14f82ca9748897f0189be31cbf9c2f4085fc1/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go#L936-L943
- The device-manager-then-DRA call order: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/49c14f82ca9748897f0189be31cbf9c2f4085fc1/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L1135-L1145

A minimal fix is to canonicalize the final status by `ResourceStatus.Name` and each resource list by `ResourceHealth.ResourceID`, with regression tests covering stable output across repeated calls.

/sig node

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig node
/sig storage

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

In `v1.PodVolumeHealth`, the `healthConditions` list is defined as:
```go
// +listType=map
// +listMapKey=status
// +listMapKey=reason
// +k8s:maxItems=16
```
Declarative validation in `pkg/apis/core/v1/zz_generated.validations.go` requires each condition to have a unique `(status, reason)` pair and caps the total items at 16.

When a CSI driver reports volume health statuses containing duplicate `(status, reason)` entries or more than 16 conditions:
1. `mapVolumeHealthConditions` in `pkg/volume/csi/csi_client.go` did not deduplicate or cap the entries.
2. `SetPodVolumeHealth` in `pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go` accepted the conditions without deduplication into `m.podStatuses[pod.UID]`.
3. When `syncPod` attempts to patch the pod status on the API server, the patch fails with validation error `422 Unprocessable Entity` (`duplicate value: {"status": ..., "reason": ...}`).
4. Because the status patch fails with an error, `syncPod` aborts before evaluating `m.canBeDeleted(pod, status)`, causing the pod to be stuck in terminating/deleting state and Kubelet to enter an infinite patch retry loop.

This PR fixes this issue by:
1. Deduplicating conditions by composite key `(Status, Reason)` (preserving the first occurrence) and capping at `MaxVolumeHealthConditions = 16` in `pkg/volume/util/util.go:DeduplicateVolumeHealthConditions`.
2. Applying deduplication and capping in CSI client mapping (`mapVolumeHealthConditions`).
3. Deduplicating conditions in Kubelet `status_manager`: both in `SetPodVolumeHealth` before updating cached status and in `normalizeStatus` before patching to the API server.
4. Adding comprehensive unit tests covering deduplication, capping, and status normalization in `pkg/volume/util`, `pkg/volume/csi`, and `pkg/kubelet/status`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142280

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed a bug where duplicate (status, reason) volume health conditions reported by a CSI driver caused Kubelet pod status patching to fail with a 422 validation error, blocking pod deletion.
```

issues.body:
Reflector calls watch cache twice on every event, first time with event and second time to update RV via `UpdateResourceVersion`. This behavior is expected and documented in reflector so this PR proposes to handle second call `UpdateResourceVersion` in more efficient manner.

Call to `UpdateResourceVersion` after an event means that RV is not expected to change. If we detect RV didn't change we can just exit early and avoid taking a write lock and broadcasting RV change that really happen.

In this PR we propose to check watch cache RV under a defensive `RLock`, while not needed it has no significant performance impact. Technically if we assume that `UpdateResourceVersion` is called from reflector loop that is the only loop updating RV the lock is not needed, but as all accesses to RV happen under lock let's be future proof. `RLock` performance is negligable as it doesn't block readers which is the main issue here.

/kind feature

NONE
```
/assign @wojtek-t 
/cc @mborsz

#### What type of PR is this?

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

PR #140664 removed the fallback in `VerifyContainerCPULimit` and `VerifyContainerMemoryLimit` where container limits defaulted to pod-level limits when empty. It updated `verifyContainersCgroupLimits` in `test/e2e/common/node/pod_level_resources.go`, but `VerifyPodContainersCgroupValues` in `test/e2e/common/node/framework/podresize/resize.go` was not updated.

As a result, when pods with pod-level resources and containers without limits are created or resized in `pod_level_resources_resize.go`, Kubelet applies the pod-level limits to the container cgroups on Linux nodes (`getCPULimit` / `getMemoryLimit` in `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_linux.go` and `pkg/kubelet/util/util.go:GetLimits`). However, `VerifyPodContainersCgroupValues` expected `"max"`, causing 14 PLR tests in `pod_level_resources_resize.go` to fail on CI with:
```
value of cgroup "/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max" for container "c1" was "99614720"; expected one of ["max"]
```

This PR introduces `ApplyPodLevelLimitsToContainer` in `test/e2e/common/node/framework/podresize/resize.go` to apply pod-level CPU and memory limits when container-level limits are not explicitly set, matching Kubelet runtime behavior, and adds unit tests in `resize_test.go`.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

A `DeviceTaintRule.spec.deviceSelector` that is present but has no `driver`, `pool`, or `device`
set matches every device from every driver in the cluster. This is easy to trigger by mistake.

The feature #141831 added a non-blocking `Warning` on creating such device taint rule with an empty selector.

As a part of follow-up discussion on the above between @liggitt and @pohly, a following 3 phase approach was suggested:

* Phase 1 - Adding a warning when a user creates a `DeviceTaintRule` with empty selector. This was implemented with #141831
* Phase 2 - Add a boolean field "all" to the `DeviceTaintRule.spec.deviceSelector`. The user can set `all: true` indicating the clear intent of selecting every devices from every driver in the cluster. So, if `all: true` is set, warning is not required. At the same time, continue to accept empty selector with warning as above. This PR implements this Phase 2 recommendation.
* Phase 3 - In a future release, drop the support for empty selector and continue to use `all: true` as the only way to select all devices.


As mentioned above, this PR implements the support for a boolean field `all` in the `DeviceTaintRule.spec.deviceSelector`.
Live-verified on a real `v1.37.0` cluster, swapping a patched `kube-apiserver` binary onto a running control plane and back (before/after, same cluster):

The functionality of the field is captured in the following table.

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `deviceSelector: {all: true}` | Didn't exist | Created, no warning, matches all devices in the cluster |
| `deviceSelector: {all: false}` | Didn't exist | Rejected as invalid request |
| `deviceSelector: {all: true, driver: ...}` | Didn't exist | Rejected as invalid request (can't specify driver/pool/device if `all: true`) |
| `deviceSelector: {}` (empty) : No Change | Created, **with warning** (post Phase 1) | Created, **with warning** |
| `deviceSelector: {driver: ...}` : No Change | Created, no warning | Created, no warning |


Please find here some of the examples from live setup:

###### CASE all: true

```
#Running pods before device taint  rule

$kubectl  -n ysb-dra-ns1 get pods
NAME                                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
dra-example-driver-kubeletplugin-tmrq8   1/1     Running   0          13m
gpu-workload2-758967d5b-54wvk            1/1     Running   0          12m

$  cat dtr_all_true.yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceTaintRule
metadata: {name: taint-empty-selector}
spec:
  deviceSelector:
    all: true
  taint: {key: example.com/incident-response, value: "true", effect: NoExecute}

# No Warning Generated Since the Intent is Clear
$  kubectl  -n ysb-dra-ns1 apply -f dtr_all_true.yaml
devicetaintrule.resource.k8s.io/taint-empty-selector created

# Evicts similar to empty selector

$  kubectl  -n ysb-dra-ns1 get pods
NAME                                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
dra-example-driver-kubeletplugin-tmrq8   1/1     Running   0          14m
gpu-workload2-758967d5b-wcbjv            0/1     Pending   0          8s
$ 

```

###### CASE all: false

```
$  cat dtr_all_false.yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceTaintRule
metadata: {name: taint-empty-selector}
spec:
  deviceSelector:
    all: false
  taint: {key: example.com/incident-response, value: "true", effect: NoExecute}

# Request is rejected. all: false doesn't make sense.
$  kubectl  -n ysb-dra-ns1 apply -f dtr_all_false.yaml
The DeviceTaintRule "taint-empty-selector" is invalid: spec.deviceSelector.all: Invalid value: false: must be either unset or set to true
$ 

```

###### CASE all: true with driver specified

```
$  cat dtr_all_true_with_driver.yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceTaintRule
metadata: {name: taint-empty-selector}
spec:
  deviceSelector:
    all: true
    driver: gpu.example.com
  taint: {key: example.com/incident-response, value: "true", effect: NoExecute}

$  kubectl  -n ysb-dra-ns1 apply -f dtr_all_true_with_driver.yaml
The DeviceTaintRule "taint-empty-selector" is invalid: spec.deviceSelector.all: Invalid value: true: must not be combined with `driver`, `pool`, or `device`

```


#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Related to #141422
Next phase of #141831 as recommended by the reviewers


#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This is implementation of phase 2 of the proposed plan to handle #141422.
Reference: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141831#discussion_r4016905668


#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
`DeviceTaintRule` now has a new boolean field `all` for `DeviceTaintRule.spec.deviceSelector`.
The field `all` can be set to `true` to indicate a clear intent to match every device from every driver in the cluster. 
The `all` field can't be set to `false`.
If `all: true` is set, other `deviceSelector` fields like driver, pool or device, can't be set, since all devices are selected.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:
```docs

```

YES. Used to help scope the fix locations, draft the implementation and unit test. All changes
reviewed, tested (unit tests + live kind-cluster verification), and understood by the author before
submitting.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind flake
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`OpenWebSocketForURL` in the e2e framework rewrote the scheme of the `*url.URL` it was given in place: `https` became `wss`, anything else became `ws`. On a second call with the same URL the scheme was already `wss`, which is not `https`, so it was turned into plain `ws` and the dial sent plaintext HTTP to the TLS port. Go's HTTP server answers that with `400 Bad Request` before the request reaches any handler, and the websocket client reports it as `bad status`.

The "Pods should support retrieving logs from the container over websockets" conformance test builds the URL once and retries the websocket read with `gomega.Eventually`. Whenever the first attempt succeeded but the container had not flushed `container is alive` yet, every retry failed with `bad status` until the 2 minute timeout. That is exactly the signature in #142284:

- the apiserver log shows one `CONNECT .../log?container=main` with `hijacked=true` and nothing afterwards, and the kubelet served that one `/containerLogs` request with 200;
- Gomega's message ends with "At one point, however, the function did return successfully" and an empty string.

The helper now works on a copy of the URL and treats `wss` like `https`, so repeated calls behave like the first. The other callers (`exec` over websockets in the same file and `kubectl port-forward` websocket test) call the helper once and are unaffected.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142284

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The new unit test starts an `httptest` TLS server with a websocket handler and dials it three times with the same URL. Before the fix, the second attempt fails with `websocket.Dial ws://127.0.0.1:...: bad status` and the server logs `client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server`, the same pair of messages as in the failing CI runs.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
NONE
```

```docs

```

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind flake

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The failing test preloads ResourceSlices whose names collide with the deterministic names assigned by the fake client's GenerateName reactor. During reconciliation, the old slice is deleted and the replacement is created with the same name. Depending on informer timing, a delayed delete event can temporarily hide the replacement in the mutation cache, causing the re-sync to issue a second create.

This changes only the fixture names for the pre-existing slices so they cannot collide with names generated during the test. The generation reconciliation behavior under test remains unchanged, while the fake-client-only delete/create name collision is removed.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

#142274

### Which jobs are failing?

`ci-kubernetes-e2e-kops-aws-500-node-dra-with-workload-amazonvpc-using-cl2`

### Which tests are failing?

- `kubetest2.Up`
- Job-level `Overall`

ClusterLoader2 and the DRA workload never started because cluster creation did not complete.

### Failure example

- Prow: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kops-aws-500-node-dra-with-workload-amazonvpc-using-cl2/2101869215270047744
- Build log: https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kops-aws-500-node-dra-with-workload-amazonvpc-using-cl2/2101869215270047744/build-log.txt
- Instance groups: https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kops-aws-500-node-dra-with-workload-amazonvpc-using-cl2/2101869215270047744/artifacts/instancegroups.yaml
- AWS resource dump: https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kops-aws-500-node-dra-with-workload-amazonvpc-using-cl2/2101869215270047744/artifacts/toolbox-dump.yaml

### What happened?

The cluster was configured with:

- 500 worker nodes
- One `c8a.12xlarge` control-plane instance
- A public AWS Network Load Balancer for the Kubernetes API

The diagnostic resource dump contains exactly 500 running worker instances, all `t3a.medium`, but no control-plane instance.

Because there was no control-plane backend:

1. `kops validate cluster` could not connect to the API load balancer on port 443.
2. Every validation attempt failed with an `i/o timeout`.
3. Worker `nodeup` processes could not reach `kops-controller` on port 3988.
4. Validation timed out after 75 minutes.
5. ClusterLoader2 and the DRA workload were never executed.

Representative validation failure:

```text
unexpected error during validation: error listing nodes:
Get "https://api-...elb.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/api/v1/nodes":
dial tcp ...:443: i/o timeout
```

Representative worker bootstrap failure:

```text
no kops-controller server responded
Post "https://10.0.155.161:3988/bootstrap":
context deadline exceeded
```

The initial S3 `HeadBucket` 404 in the log is expected and is not the cause; the job subsequently creates the state bucket successfully.

issues.title: scheduler: allow a caller-supplied SharedDRAManager

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

issues.body:
**What would you like to be added?**

A `WithSharedDRAManager` option on `scheduler.New`, so a caller can supply its own `fwk.SharedDRAManager`. With none supplied, nothing changes. Same shape as `WithNodeInfoSnapshot` (#139926).

**Why is this needed?**

`frameworkruntime.WithSharedDRAManager` already accepts a manager, and the interface is documented as the way to simulate DRA state. `scheduler.New` is the only place that hard-codes what gets passed to it.

Kueue admits Workloads before their Pods exist, so it builds ResourceClaims from a PodSet template and needs the DRA plugin to judge those, not the cluster's. It can't today, so it calls `structured.Allocator` directly and the two can drift.

Same gap downstream in kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-library#34, fixed in kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-library#35.

/sig scheduling

{\"status\":\"Degraded\",\"reason\":\"missing_controller\",\"message\":\"missing controller for k8s\"}" pod="default/test-sc-poly-csi-nvme-554fccf545-s5jls"
```

It seems like volume health check started, then volume got deleted, and then health check failed.
Kubelet got `NodeGetVolumeHealthResponse` with 2 messages containing the same `reason`, and then it just got stuck.
I lost the CSI driver logs of this call, but the pod has been stuck for several hours, and for the last few hours CSI driver does not report any NodeGetVolumeHealth calls for this volume, so it seems like kubelet got an invalid value once, and it's indefinitely trying to write it to storage, blocking pod deletion.

The easiest way to resolve this was to restart the kubelet.

### What did you expect to happen?

1. When kubelet gets invalid volume health status, it should repeat NodeGetVolumeHealth before retrying to write it to apiserver.
2. Kubelet should not run NodeGetVolumeHealth and NodeUnstageVolume for the same volume simultaneously. As I see in the CSI spec, concurrent calls for the same volume should only happen if CO loses state ([spec](https://github.com/container-storage-interface/spec/blob/master/spec.md?#concurrency)). I don't have a proof that I got parallel calls for this volume, but I don't know how else I could get error messages like "all connection to storage backend is lost" right at the moment of pod deletion.
3. If kubelet somehow gets volume health status after starting pod shutdown, it should discard it.
4. In general, I don't see why one invalid state update blocks other updates. I would expect that if there are 2 different actions going on (updating `.status` and pod deletion) and one of the actions is failing, then kubelet would add the failed action to backlog and proceed, instead of blocking other actions.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I don't have a ready-to-use reproducer because I got this error seemingly as a consequence of a race condition between NodeGetVolumeHealth and NodeUnstageVolume CSI calls, using an internally developed CSI plugin.
I think it should be reproducible with any volume health report with 2 messages with the same `reason`.
For example:
```json
[{"message":"missing controller for storage","reason":"missing_controller","status":"Degraded"},{"message":"missing controller for k8s","reason":"missing_controller","status":"Degraded"}]
```

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature
/kind failing-test
/kind flake

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Most of the time, String for a resource.Quantity as returned by ParseQuantity is safe to use concurrently, but not always: when the input string isn't already in the canonical form, then the instance has no cached string and String mutates it when first called, leading to data races. This also happens when encoding as protobuf because Size (another conceptually read-only method) mutates the instance when calling String. Encoding as JSON or CBOR don't do this.

Because it is not predictable for callers when String or encoding are safe when done concurrently, it is better to make both read-only, which matches the normal expectation.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141404

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

To mitigate potential performance regressions during decode + encode, ParseQuantity now always caches a string on all return paths. OTOH, this itself can cause a performance regression when the generated cached string isn't used. The expectation is that non-canonical input is the exception, so hopefully this won't matter.

/assign @jpbetz 

Loosely related to making Quantity safer to use (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141166).

Brought up before in https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EG7JC6T/p1784208713996489, with no responses. As discussed there and in the issue, data races caused by this have been observed in the kubelet and kube-apiserver.

Mutation was added originally in:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1ef19062096c4fcf8ddeaf3a46731d9f262a0c04/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go#L560-L563

Then converted to string in:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/26033

This is from 2016. In both cases it is unclear which specific use cases benefit from this optimization, so it's a bit hard to tell how relevant this is nowadays. Maybe caching of object serialization (added in 2019, see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/81914) makes it less important?

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
resource.Quantity: calling String or encoding a quantity is now guaranteed to not mutate the instance. Previously it did in some cases. If you know that an instance will need the string representation multiple times, use CacheString to pre-populate the value at a time when the caller owns the instance and can safely mutate it. This is not necessary for instances coming from ParseQuantity, only for instances created differently or modified through math operations.
```

issues.body:
/sig scheduling
/area scheduler
/kind feature
### Description
In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140670, status condition updates for `PodGroup` and `CompositePodGroup` were integrated into the scheduler pipeline.
Currently, in `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` (`pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go`), status updates for every group within a hierarchy are performed sequentially and synchronously on the main scheduling goroutine:
```go
for _, podGroupResult := range podGroupResults {
    pgi := podGroupResult.podGroupInfo
    if pgi.CompositePodGroup != nil {
        sched.submitCompositePodGroupResult(ctx, podGroupResult)
        continue
    }
    queuedPodInfos := rootPodGroupInfo.QueuedPodInfos[pgi.GetKey()]
    sched.submitPodGroupResult(ctx, schedFwk, podGroupState, queuedPodInfos, podGroupResult)
}
```
Each call to `submitCompositePodGroupResult` / `submitPodGroupResult` issues an individual, synchronous status patch request to the API server (`util.PatchPodGroupStatus` / `util.PatchCompositePodGroupStatus`).
### Why this is a problem
For larger or deeper hierarchies containing multiple intermediate composite groups and leaf pod groups, issuing sequential synchronous HTTP patch calls directly on the scheduling thread:
- Multiplies scheduling cycle latency linearly by the number of groups in the subtree.
- Contributes to head-of-line (HoL) blocking in the active scheduling queue, as the scheduler cannot pick up the next queued workload until all status updates complete.
### Potential Mitigations to Discuss
- **Asynchronous dispatch**: Offload status patching to background goroutines (similar to `sched.runBindingCycle`) or a dedicated worker queue so the main scheduling goroutine can immediately proceed to the next cycle.
- **Concurrent patching**: If status updates must be bounded or completed within the cycle, patch group statuses concurrently (e.g., using an `errgroup` or bounded worker pool) rather than strictly sequentially.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind cleanup
/sig api-machinery

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Extends `TestAggregatedAPIServerRejectRedirectResponse` to cover redirect
rejection by the aggregator availability controller.

The existing test covers redirects for proxied user requests, but its
discovery endpoint returns HTTP 200, so it does not exercise the
availability controller's redirect handling.

This change registers a separate APIService whose discovery endpoint
returns HTTP 301. The test requires `Available=False` with reason
`FailedDiscoveryCheck` and a discovery failure identifying that status.
The existing redirect-target guard also detects any attempt to follow the
redirect.

Using a separate APIService preserves the existing proxied-request
coverage. Only the integration test changes; no production code, API
behavior, or dependencies are modified.

Fixes #112776

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig node

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Picks up the `kubelet QoS CPU/memory sums and reserve-percentage arithmetic` TODO from the #141166 burndown.

The QoS container manager accumulates per-pod requests into int64 totals and then takes a percentage of them:

```go
qosMemoryRequests[qosClass] += podMemoryRequest
burstableLimit := allocatable - (qosMemoryRequests[Guaranteed] * percentReserve / 100)
```

Neither step is bounded:

- The quantity accessors feeding the sums saturate at the int64 rail rather than wrapping, so an oversized request arrives as `MaxInt64` and the running total wraps negative on the next addition.
- `value*percent` overflows once value exceeds `MaxInt64/percent`, and the wrapped product bears no relation to the input. At `MaxInt64` and 50% the expression evaluates to **0**, so the reservation disappears entirely and the cgroup limit derived from it is wrong.

Both totals now go through a saturating add, and the percentage splits the value into hundreds and remainder so neither product can overflow. That form is exactly equal to the direct expression wherever the direct expression does not overflow, so behaviour is unchanged for realistic inputs — `TestPercentOfMatchesDirectExpression` pins that across 909 value/percent pairs.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Reaching these overflows needs absurd inputs, so this is hardening rather than a bug anyone is hitting. I took it because it is on the burndown list; say the word if you would rather it stay as a TODO.

**Testing caveat worth your attention:** this package is linux-only and I develop on darwin. `GOOS=linux go vet` and `go test -c` both pass, so it compiles, but I could not execute the test binary locally. The two helpers are pure functions with no linux dependency, so I ran the same assertions standalone and all pass, including the equivalence sweep. I would appreciate a reviewer confirming under CI rather than taking my word for it.

While writing the test I initially asserted `percentOf(MaxInt64, 50) == MaxInt64/100*50`, which is wrong — the exact floor is `MaxInt64/2`. The standalone run caught it. Mentioning it because it is the kind of off-by-a-rounding-step that is easy to wave through in review.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed the kubelet QoS container manager computing incorrect cgroup memory limits when summed pod requests or the reserve percentage calculation overflowed int64.
```

#### AI usage disclosure:

Written with the assistance of Claude (Claude Code). The overflow behaviour and the equivalence of the replacement arithmetic were verified by execution; the code, tests and this description were reviewed by hand.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Picks up the `ceil(MilliValue/MilliValue)` TODO from the #141166 burndown.

The downward API converts a container resource into the caller's divisor units by dividing through `float64`:

```go
int64(math.Ceil(float64(cpu.MilliValue()) / float64(divisor.MilliValue())))
```

That loses information twice:

- `float64` carries a 53 bit mantissa, so any value above 2^53 is rounded before the ceiling is taken. A memory request of `9007199254740993` bytes is reported as `9007199254740992`.
- `MilliValue`/`Value` saturate at the int64 rail, so a quantity that does not fit is reported as a plausible byte count rather than as an error.

This reads both operands through the checked accessors added in #141305 and divides in integer arithmetic. The ceiling rounds up from the truncated quotient rather than computing `v+d-1`, which would overflow near the rails.

The four conversions (cpu, memory, hugepages, ephemeral-storage) are duplicated across three packages, so each copy collapses onto a shared helper in its own package rather than repeating the arithmetic sixteen times. kubectl cannot import `pkg/api`, so the duplication between the trees stays as it is:

- `pkg/api/v1/resource/helpers.go`
- `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/util/resource/resource.go`
- `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/set/env/env_resolve.go`

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Part of #141166

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Callers already substitute `1` for an unset divisor, so a zero divisor is unreachable today. The helper guards it anyway, because unlike the float division it replaces, integer division by zero panics — I did not want the refactor to turn an existing garbage result into a crash.

Two cases were added to `TestExtractResourceValue`: a memory request of 2^53+1, which returned 2^53 before this change, and `100E`, which does not fit in an int64 and previously reported a saturated byte count instead of an error. I confirmed the first case actually fails against the old expression rather than passing vacuously.

I have not claimed any other item on the burndown; happy to take more of the unowned TODOs there if this shape looks right.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed the downward API reporting an incorrect value for container resource quantities above 2^53, and silently reporting a saturated value for quantities that do not fit in an int64.
```

#### AI usage disclosure:

Written with the assistance of Claude (Claude Code). The float64 precision loss and the saturation behaviour were verified empirically before the change; the code, tests and this description were reviewed by hand.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

- WaitForNRestartablePods has no references beyond its declaration and comment.
- FilterNonRestartablePods is called only by that unused helper.

- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101281830744363008 (2026-09-19 12:07 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-beta/2101658314709405696 (1.37, 2026-09-20 13:03 UTC)

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-master

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The job runs out of its kubetest budget, not out of tests. It passes `--timeout=120m` to kubetest, which covers cluster up, the tests and teardown. Up and teardown are steady at about 15 minutes together, which leaves roughly 105 minutes for the suite. In 14 of the 15 timed-out master runs the suite finished with `91 Passed | 0 Failed` after 105 to 112 minutes and the budget ran out in the teardown steps; in the other run ginkgo was interrupted at 113 minutes with one spec still running (`90 Passed | 1 Failed`).

The suite's runtime is not fixed. The same 91 specs took 76 minutes in a passing run on 2026-09-19 at 14:08 UTC (https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101312282582585344) and 106 minutes in the timed-out run two hours earlier (https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101281830744363008), on the same Kubernetes commit (`v1.38.0-alpha.0.948+96b5e4e3ae3f8d`) and the same COS image. So a code or image change alone does not explain the timeouts; whether something makes the resize path slower under some conditions is open. Across the 59 runs since 2026-09-16 the test phase ranged from 76 to 113 minutes; the 45 passing runs took 76 to 103 minutes with a median of 87, and passing and timed-out runs occur on the same commits.

Almost all of that variance sits in one feature. `[Feature:InPlacePodVerticalScaling]` is 63 of the 91 specs and took 57 minutes in the fast run and 86 in the slow one; the other 28 specs took 19 minutes in both. 62 of the 63 resize specs are slower in the slow run, by 20 seconds at the median and up to 83 seconds, with no single spec standing out, so the extra time is inside the resize specs themselves. What inside them is slower I have not established; the kubelet logs of both runs show no deferred or infeasible resizes.

This is the same shape as #141186 on `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-alpha-features`, which runs almost the same focus. That was resolved by kubernetes/test-infra#37724: kubetest to `--timeout=180m`, the prow timeout to 3h20m, and the job moved to release-informing, on the basis that alpha-feature lanes do not fit the two-hour release-blocking budget. The note on that issue that the 1.37 blocking board shows the same thing (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141186#issuecomment-5316283473) was not followed up for the sig-release jobs, which still have `--timeout=120m` and a 2h20m prow timeout in `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-release/gce-cos-e2e-master.yaml` and `release-branch-jobs/1.37.yaml`.

### Anything else we need to know?

Update after upodroid's comment (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142262#issuecomment-5759352510): the next step is on the test side. SIG Node is asked to look at reducing the resize specs' execution time or their run-to-run variance while keeping the coverage. Skipping the resize tests is not on the table, and a timeout increase or dashboard change is not agreed; it would come after that attempt, if at all. A test-side owner is not confirmed yet.

Background for whoever picks it up: InPlacePodVerticalScaling is Stable since 1.35, and this lane is the only blocking coverage the 63 resize specs have. The sig-node node-e2e lanes skip `[Feature:InPlacePodVerticalScaling]` explicitly or do not focus on it; the node alpha-features lane (`ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features`) ran 3 memory-backed-volume resize specs in its latest build, none of the 63. The job runs ginkgo with `--nodes=1`, and the presubmit alpha-features job sets `--ginkgo-parallel=1` explicitly, so I have not assumed parallelism is safe for these specs. The sibling job's uncensored timing distribution is in the comments.

SIG Node's call on whether this blocks v1.38.0-alpha.1 on 2026-09-23 is still needed, with the reason and any conditions; I will relay it to the Release Signal lead and the release-cut representative. FLAKY on the CI Signal board is a tracking category and says nothing about the cut.

This is not #142205. That one is a single spec (the allocated pods endpoint test) failing on the kind alpha-beta lane. Here the specs pass, apart from the one interrupted run, and the job runs out of its time budget.

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig testing
/sig node
/sig release

/kind flake
/priority critical-urgent
/cc @kubernetes/release-team-release-signal

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`Validate` matches each `--rule` against `ruleRegex`, whose path group
is `(?P<path>/.*)` and so accepts a comma. `buildIngressRules` and
`buildTLSRules` then discard that match and re-split the raw rule on
`,` and `=`, always reading the first comma as the start of the TLS
clause. A comma is a legal URL path character, so the two parsers
disagree about the same rule.

The loud case is a panic:

```console
$ kubectl create ingress ing --rule="foo.com/a,b=svc:8080" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml
panic: runtime error: index out of range [1] with length 1
```

The quiet case is worse. A path carrying its own `=` and `:` is
accepted and builds a different object than the one asked for:

```console
$ kubectl create ingress ing --rule="foo.com/a=b:c,d=svc:8080" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml
```

gives backend `b:c` on path `/a` instead of `svc:8080` on `/a=b:c,d`,
plus a `tls` block with `secretName: svc:8080` that was never
requested. No error, no warning.

This matches each rule once through the compiled `ruleRegex` and
builds the spec from its named groups, so the parse that validates a
rule is the parse that builds it. `buildHTTPIngressPath` and
`buildIngressBackendSvc` now take the already-parsed parts instead of
re-splitting strings.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142260

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Behaviour on every rule that is valid today is unchanged: the existing
`TestCreateIngress` and `TestCreateIngressValidation` cases pass
untouched.

Three regression cases are added to `TestCreateIngress`. All three
panic or misparse against master at 400031d6953 and pass with this
change:

- `foo.com/a,b=svc:8080` - comma in the path, no TLS
- `foo.com/a,b=svc:8080,tls=secret1` - comma in the path, with TLS
- `foo.com/a=b:c,d=svc:8080` - path carrying `=` and `:`

A narrower fix would be to reject commas in paths instead. I did not
take that route because `ruleRegex` accepts them today and they are
valid URL path characters (sub-delims, RFC 3986), so rejecting them
would turn a crash into a new restriction on valid input. Happy to
change direction if sig-cli prefers it.

The `regexp.Compile` in `Validate` became a package-level
`regexp.MustCompile`, which drops the unreachable "failed to compile
the regex" branch.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
kubectl create ingress: fixed a panic when a `--rule` path contains a comma. A comma inside a rule path is no longer parsed as the start of the `,tls` clause, so the path and backend are built as written.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

```docs

```

#### AI usage disclosure:

AI tools were used to assist with drafting this issue and to support
the development and verification of the proposed fix. I am
responsible for the submitted changes.

issues.body:
### What happened?

`kubectl create ingress` panics when a `--rule` path contains a comma.
No cluster is needed; `--dry-run=client` is enough:

```console
$ kubectl create ingress ing --rule="foo.com/a,b=svc:8080" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml
panic: runtime error: index out of range [1] with length 1

goroutine 1 [running]:
k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create.buildHTTPIngressPath(...)
	k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go:396 +0x168
k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create.(*CreateIngressOptions).buildIngressRules(...)
	k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go:368 +0xd0
k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create.(*CreateIngressOptions).buildIngressSpec(...)
	k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go:312 +0xcc
```

A comma is a legal URL path character (a sub-delim in RFC 3986), and
`ruleRegex` accepts it: the path group is `(?P<path>/.*)`. So the rule
passes `Validate`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/400031d6953/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L223

The builders then discard that match and re-split the raw rule string,
treating the first comma as the start of the TLS clause.
`buildIngressRules` cuts the rule at `strings.Split(rule, ",")[0]`,
leaving `foo.com/a`, so `buildHTTPIngressPath` finds no `=` and indexes
past the end of the slice:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/400031d6953/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L365
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/400031d6953/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L396

`buildTLSRules` does the same split and reads the remainder as a TLS
clause:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/400031d6953/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L324

So validation and construction parse the same rule differently.

The panic is the loud case. A path that also carries `=` and `:` is
accepted and silently builds a different object than the one asked for:

```console
$ kubectl create ingress ing --rule="foo.com/a=b:c,d=svc:8080" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: ing
spec:
  rules:
  - host: foo.com
    http:
      paths:
      - backend:
          service:
            name: b
            port:
              name: c
        path: /a
        pathType: Exact
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - foo.com
    secretName: svc:8080
status:
  loadBalancer: {}
```

The backend is `b:c` on path `/a` instead of `svc:8080` on
`/a=b:c,d`, and there is a TLS block with `secretName: svc:8080` that
was never requested. No error, no warning.

### What did you expect to happen?

The rule parsed the way `ruleRegex` reads it: the TLS clause is the
optional trailing `,tls[=secret]`, not the first comma anywhere in the
rule. For `foo.com/a,b=svc:8080`:

```yaml
spec:
  rules:
  - host: foo.com
    http:
      paths:
      - backend:
          service:
            name: svc
            port:
              number: 8080
        path: /a,b
        pathType: Exact
```

and no `tls` block, since `,tls` is absent.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

No cluster required. Each of these panics:

```console
$ kubectl create ingress ing --rule="foo.com/a,b=svc:8080" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml
$ kubectl create ingress ing --rule="/path,x=svc:8080" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml
$ kubectl create ingress ing --rule="foo.com/a,b=svc:8080,tls=s1" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml
```

For the silent misparse:

```console
$ kubectl create ingress ing --rule="foo.com/a=b:c,d=svc:8080" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml
```

At the unit level, adding a `TestCreateIngress` case with the rule
`foo.com/a,b=svc:8080` panics against master.

### Anything else we need to know?

Long-standing: the double parse dates from the original
`create ingress` implementation, and the code is unchanged on master
at 400031d6953.

A PR follows that matches each rule once with the compiled `ruleRegex`
and builds the spec from its named groups, so the parse that validates
a rule is the parse that builds it. It carries regression tests for
both the panic and the misparse.

Found through AI-assisted code review. The transcripts above are real
output from kubectl v1.36.0 and from a `./cmd/kubectl` build of master
at 400031d6953.

/sig cli

issues.body:
## kubelet: don't pre-commit 200 for container logs

#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When a container is gone from the runtime but its Pod still exists, the kubelet log endpoint can return HTTP 200 with the error in the response body. This makes kubectl logs exit successfully even though the logs could not be retrieved. The issue happens because the response is written to before the runtime checks whether the container exists, which commits the status as 200. This change moves that write until after the container lookup succeeds and only does it for Follow requests, where the early flush is needed. Missing containers now return a proper HTTP error while the normal case stays unchanged.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142258

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The main change is limited to the kubelet log-serving path: the response is no longer committed before we know the container exists. The early write is still kept for Follow requests, so their behavior is unchanged. I verified the fix locally by removing a container from a kind cluster and confirming the log request changes from HTTP 200 to a non-2xx response. There are no API, wire, or flag changes; this only fixes the error status returned for missing containers. I also kept the related comment and test changes small and focused on the behavior being fixed.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

- Yes, kubelet now returns a proper HTTP error when logs cannot be retrieved because the container no longer exists in the runtime, instead of HTTP 200 with the error message as the log body. kubectl logs will now exit non-zero in this case instead of silently succeeding.

```

### What happened?

When a container has been removed from the runtime but its Pod still exists, the kubelet /containerLogs endpoint can return HTTP 200 with the error message in the response body. kubectl logs then prints the error as if it were log output and exits 0, so clients cannot tell that the log fetch failed.

The root cause is an unconditional zero-byte Write() in GetKubeletContainerLogs, which is used to flush headers early for streaming logs. net/http commits the response as 200 on the first write, so an error found later by ContainerStatus() cannot change the status. The affected path is getContainerLogs() → GetKubeletContainerLogs() → GetContainerLogs(), with the container lookup happening after the response has already been committed.

### What did you expect to happen?

When the container no longer exists in the runtime, the kubelet should return a non-200 HTTP error before anything is written to the response. This allows kubectl logs and other clients to correctly detect that fetching the logs failed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a pod with a long-running container:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: repro
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo hi; sleep 3600"]
```
2. Wait for the pod to become Running, then remove the container directly from the runtime without deleting the Pod:

>  Ive used kind here, hence the docker specific commands

```
docker exec <node> crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock ps -a
docker exec <node> crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock stop <container-id>
docker exec <node> crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock rm <container-id>
```
3. Fetch the logs:
```
kubectl logs repro -c c
kubectl get --raw '/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/repro/log?container=c' -v=8
```
Observed:

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The dynamic and metadata shared informer factories have no way to stop one informer. `StartWithContext` runs every informer under the factory's context and marks it started for good, and `SharedInformer` has no stop of its own, so an informer for a resource the server no longer serves (a deleted CRD or APIService) keeps listing and watching it until the factory shuts down. Its reflector fails every LIST with 404 and retries at the backoff cap, one `Failed to watch` line per [30, 60)s per informer, forever, since the backoff reset never fires while the error persists (`reflector.go:62-67`).

That is #79610, open since 2019. The garbage collector and the resource quota controller obtain a metadata informer per monitored resource from the factory kube-controller-manager shares between them, drop the monitor when the resource disappears, and leave the informer running. #142072 has a soak measurement of the result: about 250,000 such lines per day, 93.9% of the controller manager log at 48 hours, growing within a leader's tenure and resetting only on a leadership change.

This adds `Release(gvr) bool` to both factories:

- `ForResource` counts its callers.
- `StartWithContext` runs each informer under its own child context and keeps the cancel function.
- `Release` decrements the count; when the last caller has released the resource it cancels that informer, drops it from the factory, and reports that it did. A later `ForResource` builds a fresh informer, and the next `Start` runs it.

The count is what makes this safe on a factory shared by several controllers: the garbage collector releasing a resource does not stop an informer the quota controller still holds. Every `ForResource` must be paired with exactly one `Release`, which the interface documents. Callers that never call `Release` see no change: their informers live until `Shutdown`, as today.

Adding a method to `DynamicSharedInformerFactory` and `metadatainformer.SharedInformerFactory` follows #114434 (`Shutdown`) and the later `StartWithContext`; there are no in-tree implementations besides the real ones, and the client-go CHANGELOG notes that mocks need the new method, as it did for `TypedInformer`.

Wiring the garbage collector and the quota controller to call `Release` when they drop a monitor is a separate change on top of #142039 and #142073, so that this one stays a small additive API.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Related to #79610, #142072, #138800

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Two tests per package, run under `-race`: the shared-holder contract (two callers, first `Release` leaves the informer running, last one stops it, `ForResource` then returns a fresh informer that syncs, releasing an unheld or unknown resource is a no-op) and a concurrent `ForResource`/`Start`/`Release` loop that must not race and after which `Shutdown` must return once the context is cancelled. `Shutdown` also returns after a `Release` with the parent context still live, since the informer goroutine's `wg.Done` runs on the child cancel.

Verified end to end through the real `GarbageCollector` wired as kube-controller-manager wires it (create a CRD, let the GC sync an informer for it, delete the CRD, let the GC sync again): on `main` the informer keeps running and logs `Failed to watch ... the server could not find the requested resource` five times in 30s; with this change plus the GC calling `Release` on monitor removal it is stopped within seconds and the line does not appear, 3/3 runs. That integration test comes with the GC wiring PR.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
client-go: the dynamic and metadata shared informer factories gained `Release(gvr)`, which stops and drops the informer for a resource once every `ForResource` caller has released it, so informers for resources the server no longer serves can be stopped without shutting down the factory.
```

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When every container sample for a Running pod is filtered out by cAdvisor stats collection, `ListPodStats` omits the pod before collecting its volume stats. A pod in restart backoff can therefore lose its Summary API volume stats and the PVC metrics derived from them even though its volumes remain mounted.

Build pod references in a single pass over the unfiltered cAdvisor data, while collecting container stats only for samples that pass the existing terminated-container filter. Use the existing pod-status lookup to retain pods without live samples only when their cached phase is Running, and preserve the existing start-time requirement.

The regression covers restart backoff, a restarted container, terminal and pending pods, missing pod status, removed cgroups, and missing start time.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #141350

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Validation on Linux with Go 1.27.1:
- The new crashloop regression fails on unmodified master at `81b21d46dd9`: the pod list is empty instead of containing the Running pod and its volume stats.
- All eight regression cases pass with the fix.
- `go test -p=2 ./pkg/kubelet/stats ./pkg/kubelet/metrics/collectors -count=1` passed.
- `gofmt` and `git diff --check` passed.

Reproduction is at the unit-test level; the reporter's live CSI-backed cluster scenario has not been rerun locally. The CRI stats provider is unchanged.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Kubelet's cAdvisor stats provider now retains volume statistics for Running pods when all their container samples are filtered out during restart backoff.

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The Job controller tracks pending Pod creations and deletions by namespace/name. If a Job is deleted while a Pod creation is in flight and another Job is immediately created with the same name, the replacement can inherit the old Job's unsatisfied expectation. `syncJob` then skips `manageJob`, leaving the replacement unreconciled until another event or the expectations timeout.

This change clears Pod expectations from the Job delete-event handler, matching the existing behavior of the ReplicaSet and DaemonSet controllers.

It also adds a deterministic integration test. The test blocks the old Job's Pod POST after the creation expectation has been raised, deletes and recreates the Job under the same name with a new UID, waits for the informer to observe the replacement, and then releases the old request. It verifies that the replacement Job is reconciled and receives its suspended condition.

Without the fix, the test reproduces the stale-UID status error from the issue and times out waiting for the replacement Job:

```
Precondition failed: UID in precondition: <old UID>, UID in object meta: <new UID>
```

With the fix, the integration test passes.

I was assigned to #142142 on September 16 and started investigating the reproduction and integration coverage before #142236 was opened. #142236 implements the same expectation cleanup with unit coverage; this PR includes the integration reproduction requested in the issue discussion.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142142

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Local verification:

- The new integration test fails on unmodified `master` with the stale-UID error and an unreconciled replacement Job.
- The new integration test passes three consecutive runs with this change.
- `go test ./pkg/controller/job/...` passes.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed an issue where a Job recreated with the same name as a recently deleted Job could remain unreconciled because it inherited pending Pod expectations from the previous Job.
```

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature
/sig network
/sig api-machinery

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Migrates the maximum length validation for `IngressClassSpec.Controller` to declarative validation.

The existing 250-character limit is now expressed using:

```go
// +k8s:alpha(since: "1.38")=+k8s:maxLength=250
Controller string `json:"controller,omitempty" protobuf:"bytes,1,opt,name=controller"`

issues.body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

`GetDiskFormat` shells out to `blkid -p -s TYPE -s PTTYPE -o export` and maps **exit code 2** to `("", nil)` ("disk is unformatted"). However, blkid also exits with code 2 when the device node exists but its data cannot be read (e.g. an I/O error on the storage data path). As a result, `GetDiskFormat` returns the identical result for two very different situations:

1. A genuinely blank disk → `("", nil)` (expected)
2. An existing device with data whose data path is currently unreadable → `("", nil)` (misleading)

Any caller that uses an empty format to decide whether to format a device cannot distinguish the two cases, which can lead to data loss.

Real-world impact: in Longhorn (a CSI storage system consuming mount-utils), NodeStageVolume attempted `mkfs.xfs` on existing volumes containing user data because blkid probed them as unformatted while the engine data path was temporarily broken. The formatting only failed because mkfs itself hit read errors, so data loss was avoided by luck, not by design
(longhorn/longhorn#14042).

**How this PR fixes it**:

When blkid reports no filesystem (exit code 2), probe the device with a direct 4 KiB read before reporting it as unformatted:

- The first block can be read (including a short read ending in `io.EOF`) → keep returning `("", nil)`
- The first block cannot be read at all (zero bytes returned, or a read error other than `io.EOF` such as `EIO`/`ENODATA`) → return an error

Design notes:

- Per the `io.ReaderAt` contract, a short read may return both a positive byte count and a non-nil error. A partial read ending in `io.EOF` (device smaller than the probe size) is accepted; any other read error or a read of zero bytes is treated as unreadable.
- A **missing device node** (`fs.ErrNotExist`) keeps the historical `("", nil)` behavior, since existing callers and unit tests probe paths that may not exist on the host (e.g. `/dev/fake-disk` with FakeExec).
- The change is confined to the exit-code-2 branch; all other blkid outcomes (success, other exit codes) are unchanged.

**Scope and limitations** (deliberate tradeoff, see review discussion):

This is intentionally a **narrow guard**, not a complete blank-device proof. It only rejects devices whose first block cannot be read at all. In particular:

- It does not detect partial failures where the first block is readable while other regions that blkid inspects are failing (util-linux low-level probing can fail at offsets other than the first block and still return the same NOTFOUND status).
- It does not verify that the readable content is actually blank.
- The helper uses a normal `os.Open`, while blkid opens its device with `O_NONBLOCK`, so the probe path does not have identical I/O semantics.

The rationale for this tradeoff: it covers the demonstrated failure mode (a fully unavailable data path, as in longhorn/longhorn#14042) with low compatibility risk, and keeps the safety decision centralized in `GetDiskFormat`. A stronger invariant — requiring positive evidence of a genuinely usable blank device — likely touches more than this exit-2 branch and deserves its own discussion.

**Testing**:

- New `TestCheckDeviceReadable` covering: readable device (4 KiB / 8 KiB), device smaller than one block (partial read + EOF, still readable), empty file (unreadable), and nonexistent path (historical behavior).
- New `TestGetDiskFormatUnreadableDevice` covering the end-to-end paths with FakeExec simulating blkid exit code 2: blank-but-readable device returns `("", nil)`, unreadable device returns an error, nonexistent path returns `("", nil)`.
- Full `go test ./...` in `staging/src/k8s.io/mount-utils` passes with no regression (verified that the `ErrNotExist` passthrough keeps all existing fake-path tests green).

Fixes #142243

**Release note**:
```release-note
`mount-utils` GetDiskFormat now returns an error instead of an empty format when the device exists but its first block cannot be read, preventing callers from accidentally formatting a device that may contain data.
```

issues.title: [BUG] GetDiskFormat in k8s.io/mount-utils returns ("", nil) for unreadable devices, leading callers to destructive mkfs

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

issues.body:
### What happened?

`GetDiskFormat` in the staging repo `k8s.io/mount-utils` (staging/src/k8s.io/mount-utils/mount_linux.go) shells out to
`blkid -p -s TYPE -s PTTYPE -o export <disk>` and maps **exit code 2** to `("", nil)` ("disk is unformatted").

However, blkid also exits with code 2 when the device node **exists but its data cannot be read** (e.g. the storage backend is temporarily unavailable). As a result, `GetDiskFormat` returns the exact same result for two very
different situations:

1. A genuinely blank disk → `("", nil)` (expected)
2. An existing device with data whose data path is currently unreadable → `("", nil)` (misleading)

Any caller that uses an empty format to decide whether to initialize/format a device cannot distinguish the two cases.

Real-world impact: in Longhorn (a CNCF storage system using mount-utils via the CSI stack), this caused NodeStageVolume to attempt `mkfs.xfs` on existing volumes containing user data, because blkid probed them as unformatted while the engine data path was temporarily broken. The formatting only failed because mkfs itself hit read errors, so data loss was avoided by luck, not by design.
See longhorn/longhorn#14042 for the full incident log.

Relevant code:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/mount-utils/mount_linux.go#L667-L686

```go
if err != nil {
    if exit, ok := err.(utilexec.ExitError); ok {
        if exit.ExitStatus() == 2 {
            // Disk device is unformatted.
            return "", nil
        }
    }
    ...
}
```
Impact: Potential Data Loss
This bug creates a data-loss window. If the underlying data path recovers between filesystem detection and the formatting operation, mkfs.xfs -f may succeed and overwrite existing filesystem metadata, resulting in permanent data loss.


### What did you expect to happen?

`GetDiskFormat` should distinguish a blank disk from an unreadable device, for example:

- Perform a small read (e.g. first 4 KiB) on the device when blkid reports  no filesystem, and return an error if the read fails, or
- Inspect blkid's stderr/exit-code semantics more precisely so that  read failures are not reported as "unformatted".

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Using the scsi_debug module to create a device whose reads fail:

```bash
# 1. Create a scsi debug device that fails READ commands (error=3: medium error)
modprobe scsi_debug dev_size_mb=16 every_nth=1 opts=2

DEV=$(ls -d /sys/bus/pseudo/drivers/scsi_debug/adapter*/host*/target*/*/block/* | xargs -n1 basename)
echo "Device: /dev/$DEV"

# 2. blkid behaves identically to a blank disk
blkid -p -s TYPE -s PTTYPE -o export /dev/$DEV
# → no output, exit code 2 (same as a zeroed blank disk)

# 3. While a direct read fails
dd if=/dev/$DEV of=/dev/null bs=4k count=1
# → input error / I/O error
```

A consumer calling `GetDiskFormat("/dev/$DEV")` receives `("", nil)`, so it will take the "unformatted disk" path although the device is not readable.
A zeroed blank disk returns the identical value.

(Any other way of producing an unreadable block device, e.g.
device-mapper `error` target, reproduces the same behavior.)

### Anything else we need to know?

- The same `("", nil)` result is also produced for **non-block files**
  (e.g. an empty regular file), which is how the behavior was verified
  without kernel modules.
- Longhorn has worked around this at the CSI layer by re-verifying device
  readability before entering the formatting path
  (longhorn/longhorn#14042), but other in-tree and out-of-tree consumers
  of mount-utils remain exposed.
- Happy to submit a PR once the maintainers agree on the desired semantics.

  systems)
```

issues.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Before: `controller.ComputeHash` hashes the PodTemplateSpec with FNV-32a, turns the sum into a decimal string with `fmt.Sprint`, and passes that to `rand.SafeEncodeString`, which returns one character per input character. A sum below 1000000000 has nine digits, so the hash is nine characters instead of ten, and smaller sums are shorter still. Roughly a quarter of the 32 bit range lands in that band, so short hashes are common rather than a corner case. The suffix on a ReplicaSet or ControllerRevision name, and the value of the `pod-template-hash` label, vary in length with the template.

After: the sum is formatted to a fixed width of ten digits before it is encoded, so `ComputeHash` always returns ten characters.

How: one call changes from `fmt.Sprint` to `fmt.Sprintf("%010d", ...)` in `pkg/controller/controller_utils.go`. `Sum32` returns a `uint32`, whose largest value is ten digits, so the padded form is always exactly ten.

This does not roll existing workloads, which is the first thing worth checking. Both controllers that use the hash find their current object by content, not by hash. The Deployment controller uses `FindNewReplicaSet`, which compares templates through `EqualIgnoreHash` after deleting the `pod-template-hash` label. The DaemonSet controller uses `Match`, which compares the serialized patch stored in the ControllerRevision. An existing ReplicaSet or ControllerRevision is still matched after an upgrade and keeps the hash it was created with. Only objects created from then on carry the padded hash.

The new test builds 500 templates that differ by one label value and asserts every hash is ten characters. On master it fails on the first template that hashes short, reporting hashes of eight and nine characters.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #134975

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The hash value itself changes for templates whose sum has fewer than ten digits, because padding adds a leading `0` that `SafeEncodeString` then encodes. Templates whose sum already has ten digits keep the hash they had.

`rand.SafeEncodeString` is shared with other callers, so the padding belongs in `ComputeHash` rather than in the encoder.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
The pod template hash used in ReplicaSet and ControllerRevision names, and in the `pod-template-hash` label, is now always 10 characters. It was previously shorter for about a quarter of pod templates. Existing ReplicaSets and ControllerRevisions keep their current names and labels; only newly created ones use the padded hash.
```

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`DefaultPodLevelResources` documents that ephemeral containers are excluded from pod-level resource defaulting, since they cannot specify resources and don't contribute to QoS. It builds the `v1Pod` it aggregates from accordingly (`Containers` and `InitContainers` only).

However, `aggregateContainerLimits`'s candidate-filtering step calls `VisitContainers(spec, AllContainers, ...)`, and `AllContainers` includes `EphemeralContainers`. Since an ephemeral container can never carry a resource limit, visiting one deletes every candidate resource from the set, so pod-level limit defaulting silently becomes a no-op for any pod that has an ephemeral container.

Ephemeral containers can't be present on pod create, so this only surfaces on the `/resize` subresource path: after `kubectl debug` attaches an ephemeral container, a resize that sets a pod-level request no longer gets the pod-level limit defaulted, even though the identical resize on the same pod before debugging does.

This PR restricts the visit in `aggregateContainerLimits` to `InitContainers|Containers`, matching the `v1Pod` that is actually passed to `resourcehelper.AggregateContainerLimits` and the documented behavior.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142212

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Added a regression test case (`single container limit defaulting unaffected by ephemeral container`) to `TestApplyPodLevelResourceDefaults` in `pkg/registry/core/pod/strategy_test.go`, mirroring the existing "single container limit defaulting" case but with an ephemeral container added to the pod spec. Verified it fails without the fix (`expected non-nil limits`) and passes with it.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed a bug where pod-level resource limit defaulting (with `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourcesFixDefaulting` enabled) was silently skipped for pods that have an ephemeral container (e.g. attached via `kubectl debug`), because ephemeral containers were incorrectly included when checking whether all containers specify a limit for a given resource.
```

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When a Job is deleted and a new Job is created with the same name (a common pattern for
Helm-installed one-shot Jobs, cron-like external recreation, GitOps reconciliation, etc.), the
new Job can end up with 0 active pods and never make progress, because it inherits an
unsatisfied pod create/delete expectation left over from the deleted Job.

`deleteJob`, the Job controller's informer delete-event handler, already clears the
consistency store and the finished-job expectations for the deleted Job, but never calls
`jm.expectations.DeleteExpectations`, the tracker that `manageJob` checks
(`satisfiedExpectations`) before it will create or delete any pods. If the deleted Job had an
outstanding expectation (for example a pod create that was in flight, or that raced with the
delete and never got observed), that expectation stays keyed by the Job's namespace/name and
blocks the newly created Job under that same name until the unrelated 5 minute
`ControllerExpectationsTimeout` expires on its own.

The ReplicaSet controller's `deleteReplicaSet` already does this correctly (calls
`rsc.expectations.DeleteExpectations(logger, key)` on delete, with the comment "so if we
create a new one with the same name it starts clean"). This brings `deleteJob` in line with
that existing, already-relied-on pattern rather than introducing a new one.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142142

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This only clears the pod create/delete expectations tracker (`jm.expectations`), the one that
actually gates `manageJob`. It does not change `consistencyStore.Clear` or
`finishedJobExpectations.Delete`, which `deleteJob` already handles correctly.

What was tested: new test `TestDeleteJobClearsPodExpectations` in
`pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go` sets a fake pending creation expectation for a
Job's key (simulating an in-flight create that was never observed), calls `deleteJob`
directly, and asserts the expectations are satisfied afterward, so a Job recreated under the
same name is immediately eligible for `manageJob` again instead of waiting out the timeout.
Confirmed it fails against unmodified code and passes after the fix. `go test
./pkg/controller/job/...`: all existing tests plus the new one pass. `go vet
./pkg/controller/job/...` and `gofmt -l` on both touched files: clean. Not tested: an actual
end-to-end delete+recreate race against a real apiserver (the exact timing window that
triggers the underlying `UID in precondition` conflict is hard to reproduce deterministically
in an integration test); the fix and its test target the narrower, deterministic root cause
(the missing expectations clear on delete) rather than the timing-dependent trigger.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed a bug where a Job recreated with the same name as a just-deleted Job could be stuck
with 0 active pods for up to 5 minutes, because it inherited an unsatisfied pod
create/delete expectation from the deleted Job.
```

/kind bug
/sig node

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

On large-memory nodes the linear Burstable `oom_score_adj` formula collapses small/medium containers to 999, so a memory-guaranteed orchestrator and a bursty executor are indistinguishable, and Burstable sits only 1 point below BestEffort.

When `KubeletLogarithmicOOMScoreAdj` is enabled, Burstable scoring uses:

`800 - 400*(R/L) - 350*(log2(1+R)/log2(1+C))`

- logarithmic request scaling so 50Mi vs 500Mi vs 64Gi stay distinct on 1TiB–4TiB nodes
- per-container `request/limit` so memory-guaranteed containers rank safer than overcommit/burst containers
- baseline 800 so mild bursts do not invert kill order vs BestEffort (1000)

Guaranteed (`-997`), BestEffort (`1000`), node-critical, and sidecar clamping from #128029 are unchanged. Gate off (default) keeps the 2015 linear formula.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142230

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- Alpha, default `false`, kubelet-only. No API/CRI/QoS class change.
- A few issue-table cells differ by 1 from `math.Round` of the published formula; tests lock the formula, not the hand-computed table.
- `bits.Len64` was considered for integer-only log2; it does not match the issue numbers, and this path is not hot. Happy to switch if you prefer integer-only.
- Follows the same no-KEP path as #128029, with a feature gate for rollback as the issue requested.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Added kubelet feature gate KubeletLogarithmicOOMScoreAdj (alpha, default off). When enabled, Burstable container oom_score_adj uses logarithmic memory-request scaling and the per-container memory guarantee (request/limit) so small containers on large-memory nodes no longer collapse to 999.

#### What type of PR is this?

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The `convertResource*ToString` helpers in `pkg/api/v1/resource`, `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/util/resource`, and `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/set/env` relied on `float64` division (e.g. `float64(cpu.MilliValue()) / float64(divisor.MilliValue())`), which led to two problems:
